CodeMender updates (v0.14.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Better pull request scans: cm find --diff now catches removed security controls and gives large files more time (configurable with --diff-job-timeout).
  • Unified sessions: --deep and --diff scans now appear as a single session in cm session list, cm report, and cm stats.
  • Moved code in cm verify: cm verify now finds code that moved since cm find and updates the finding's location.
  • Guided activation: cm now opens the activation page and waits for activation instead of exiting.
  • New cm find flags: --deep-max-turns limits exploratory steps per file in --deep scans, and --enable-bash allows shell commands during scans.
  • Improved detection: More distinct findings per file and more precise CWE classification for weak hashing and randomness.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed scans of repositories reached through nested symbolic links.
    • Fixed findings for nonexistent files and over-merged findings.
    • Shell scripts created by cm verify are now executable.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.35.600-gke.140:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Improved containerd resilience against state corruption if a node reboots while unpacking container images.
  • Fixed an issue where the periodic configuration drift health check failed with a version not supported error while a cluster upgrade or rollback was in progress.
  • Fixed an issue where audit-proxy retried audit log exports indefinitely on permanent errors, generating excessive audit logging traffic.
  • Fixed an issue where the Kubernetes preflight health check scanned all namespaces in the admin cluster instead of the target cluster's namespace, causing cluster upgrades to fail if an unrelated cluster had stale reconciling resources.
  • Fixed an issue where upgrading or recreating a node during maintenance mode could proceed before storage volumes finished detaching, resulting in orphaned CSI VolumeAttachment resources or I/O errors. After the fix, node drain verifies that kubelet unmounts all host volumes and that CSI VolumeAttachment resources detach before completing the drain.
  • Fixed an issue where Certificate Authority (CA) rotation failed for self-managing clusters (admin, hybrid, and standalone). The failure occurs during the final phase of the rotation when attempting to move management resources back from the temporary bootstrap cluster to the self-managing cluster, which can leave the cluster in an unmanageable state. You must upgrade your clusters to version 1.35.600-gke.140 before you rotate your CAs.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Monitor response and playbook health with the Response Health Hub

Google SecOps now includes the Response Health Hub curated dashboard, a central location for monitoring playbook performance, execution latency, automation effectiveness, and integration health across environments.

Key capabilities include:

  • Volume and adoption tracking: Monitor total playbook execution volume, daily trends, completion success rates, and queued playbook backlogs.
  • Attachment and rerun insights: Track average and maximum playbooks attached per case or alert, and identify playbooks with high rerun counts.
  • Execution latency diagnostics: Compare end-to-end playbook execution time against active action execution time, and drill down into the 30 slowest playbook and action runs.
  • Playbook and integration health monitoring: Investigate the latest failed playbook runs, highest failure-rate and terminated playbooks, and integration action error reasons.
  • Automation effectiveness metrics: Compare automated versus manual case closure rates and Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR).

For more information, see Monitor response and playbook health.

title: TIL: Check Ports Before Deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a)
description:
A port conflict can turn a straightforward database installation into hours of troubleshooting. One of the simplest ways to avoid this is to scan every node before deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a).

During a deployment for a large government analytics platform, a pre-installation check revealed that two machines still had an old instance occupying port 5258. Replacing the machines before installation helped the team avoid troubleshooting the conflict during deployment.

The lesson: port verification should be part of your GBase Database deployment checklist, not an afterthought.

1. Understand the ports before deployment

GBase Database(GBase 8a) uses three main component types:

  • GCware: Provides cluster consistency services and metadata management.
  • GCluster: Handles SQL parsing, optimization, and distributed execution planning.
  • GNode: Handles data storage and computation.

The deployment plan should document the required ports for each component. The following ports are used in the environment described here; verify them against the documentation for your specific GBase Database release and configuration.

Component or service Port
GCluster 5258
GNode 5050
GCware 5918, 5919
syncServer 5288
GCRecover 6268
Remote management 16066–16166

Do not treat this table as a substitute for version-specific configuration documentation. Record each port's component, purpose, communication direction, and firewall requirements.

2. Scan for port conflicts on every node

An old database instance or another service may already be listening on a required port. Discovering this before installation is much easier than diagnosing a service that fails to start afterward.

On Linux systems with ss, run:

for p in 5258 5050 5918 5919 5288 6268; do
  if ss -H -lntp 2>/dev/null |
     awk -v port="$p" '
       {
         addr = $4
         sub(/^.*:/, "", addr)
         if (addr == port) found = 1
       }
       END { exit !found }
     '; then
    echo "LISTENING: port $p"
  else
    echo "No TCP listener found: port $p"
  fi
done

This checks for TCP listeners on the specified ports. It does not prove that a port is available for every protocol or configuration, and insufficient permissions may hide process details.

For further investigation, use:

sudo ss -lntp
sudo lsof -nP -iTCP:5258 -sTCP:LISTEN

Replace 5258 with the port you need to investigate.

Important: A port scan identifies current listeners, not every possible future conflict. Check the intended service configuration and repeat the scan after reinstalling or cloning a machine.

3. Check system resources at the same time

Port availability is only one part of GBase Database deployment readiness. A quick resource check can reveal other potential issues before installation.

free -h
nproc
df -h /data

These commands report memory, available CPU cores, and filesystem capacity for /data. Adjust the filesystem path to match your planned data directory.

Compare the results across nodes. Inconsistent resources or insufficient disk space can undermine an otherwise successful installation.

4. Include firewall rules and remote management ports

A deployment may succeed while remote access fails later because the firewall rules are incomplete.

The remote management range deserves particular attention. Confirm which ports the selected release actually requires, which hosts need access, and which firewall rules must be applied. Avoid opening an entire port range indiscriminately; follow the product's requirements and your organization's security policy.

Document the rules before deployment and coordinate with the network team so that connectivity can be verified systematically.

5. Make port checks part of automated provisioning

For a small deployment, checking ports manually may seem sufficient. For a cluster with many Data nodes, repeatable checks are more reliable than memory.

A practical GBase Database deployment checklist should include:

  • [ ] Verify required ports on every node.
  • [ ] Investigate unexpected listeners and identify their owning processes.
  • [ ] Confirm firewall rules and communication paths.
  • [ ] Compare CPU, memory, and disk capacity across nodes.
  • [ ] Repeat the checks after machine replacement, reinstallation, or cloning.
  • [ ] Save the results with the deployment records.

Automating these checks in a provisioning pipeline makes the results reproducible and easier to audit.

Final takeaway

A few minutes of pre-installation verification can prevent avoidable deployment delays. The larger the GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster, the more valuable it becomes to standardize checks across every node.

Check the ports before you install—not after a service refuses to start.

How does your team handle port validation during database deployment: manual checks, automated scripts, or a dedicated infrastructure checklist?

title: Railway vs Render vs Northflank in 2026
description:
Railway, Render, and Northflank are the three app platforms we see developers put side by side most often in 2026. All three will take a container or a git repo and give you a running URL, so the demo looks the same on every one. The differences that matter show up a month later: on the invoice, in how the bill is calculated, and in what happens when the project you shipped as a side project turns into something you actually depend on.

This post is a buyer's comparison. We'll cover what each platform is good at, how each one prices, and the buyer each one is really built for. Then we'll be straight about where Ownkube fits and where it doesn't. If you're coming from Heroku specifically, our Heroku alternatives guide covers that migration in more detail.

The short version

  • Railway has the best raw developer experience of the three, and it bills purely on metered usage by the second. The catch is that the metered model is postpaid, so a service you forget about keeps spending, and the old free plan has shrunk to about a dollar of credit a month.
  • Render is the most predictable and the most Heroku-like. You pick a fixed instance size and pay a flat rate for it. The catch is that you pay for that instance whether it's busy or idle, and Render is drifting upmarket (a new $499-a-month Scale plan, SSO, SCIM, HIPAA).
  • Northflank is the most powerful and the only one of the three that can run in your own cloud account. It's also the cheapest on raw CPU. The catch is that it still puts Kubernetes in front of you (its own tagline is "making Kubernetes boring"), and it's built for platform teams more than for one developer with a side project.
  • Ownkube is for personal software and small teams: a prepaid wallet so nothing surprises you, a choice of metered or flat pricing per app, and managed Postgres from $4 a month. It's the least suited of the group if you want a single throwaway server or GPU training runs.

The rest of this post is the detail behind that call.

How they price: the structure behind the number

The prices below move, so treat them as the shape of each model rather than a quote. The structural differences are the part that stays true.

Ownkube Railway Render Northflank
Pricing structure Metered or a flat-price box, your choice per app Metered usage, per second Fixed instance sizes + a workspace plan Metered usage per vCPU-hour (fixed plans optional)
Billing method Prepaid wallet the plan loads and usage drains Plan credit, then postpaid to your card Postpaid to your card Postpaid pay-as-you-go
Entry plan Pay as you go (top up from $5), Personal $5/mo, Team $20/mo $5 plan (includes $5 usage) Free workspace, small instance from about $7/mo Free tier, then pay-as-you-go
Free tier None; Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up that never expires About $1 of credit a month Real, but web services spin down and a free Postgres expires in 30 days A couple of always-on services
Own cloud AWS today, same app with no rewrite No No Yes, multi-cloud
Egress $0.02/GB (Germany) to $0.13/GB (Mumbai), outbound only About $0.05/GB About $0.15/GB over the included amount About $0.06/GB

Three different philosophies sit in that table. Railway meters everything and bills you after. Render sells you a fixed box and bills you a flat rate for it. Northflank meters like Railway but will also run inside your own cloud account. The thing all three share is that the spend is postpaid: the meter runs, or the box exists, and the invoice arrives at the end.

The four things that actually differ

1. Prepaid wallet vs the surprise invoice

This is the difference most people feel first, because it's the one that shows up as a bad morning. Railway and Northflank are postpaid metered, which is the model behind every "I left a service running and got a four-figure bill" story. Render hides the same problem in a different shape: you pay for the instance while it sleeps, so the waste is quiet instead of loud.

Ownkube runs on a prepaid wallet. Your plan loads credit each month (Personal loads $5, Team loads $20), and usage draws it down per minute. When the balance reaches zero, your apps pause and your data stays put until you top up or the next monthly load arrives. Nothing runs up a card you weren't watching. For personal software and small teams, spending being bounded by a number you chose on purpose is worth more than shaving a cent off the per-hour rate.

2. Metered or flat, and you pick per app

Railway only meters. That's great for an app that idles most of the day and painful for a busy one, because the number keeps moving. Render only does fixed sizes. That's predictable and it means you pay for idle. Both models are fine; the problem is that each platform forces one on you for everything you run.

Ownkube lets you choose per deployment. Run a bursty web app metered so an idle hour costs almost nothing, and put a steady worker on a flat Spark or Core box so its price never moves, in the same project, and flip either one later. Metered CPU and memory both bill on what the app actually uses, and an idle web app can sleep, metering nothing until the next request wakes it. Databases and caches are always a flat box (a database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, a Valkey cache box from $2), because those hold memory and run continuously either way.

3. Where your app is allowed to run

Railway and Render run your app on their infrastructure. For a weekend project that's fine. When a customer's security team asks for the app inside their own cloud account, neither has an answer.

Northflank can run inside your own cloud, and it's a genuine strength: if multi-cloud is your main requirement, give it a serious look. Its own-cloud story is built for platform teams standing up infrastructure. Ownkube starts you on managed compute with nothing to set up, and when an app has to run in your own or a customer's AWS account, the same app ships there with no rewrite, with its logs, metrics and health checks. GCP and Azure are coming soon.

4. Who the platform is actually built for

This one is easy to miss because it hides in the roadmap rather than the pricing page. Railway shrank its free plan and is pushing toward Pro and Enterprise. Render just added a $499-a-month Scale plan with SSO, SCIM, and HIPAA eligibility. Both are healthy moves for those companies, and both point the same direction: upmarket, toward platform and compliance buyers. Northflank was aimed at platform teams from the start.

The developer shipping a real side project, or the team of three that wants to look like a bigger company without hiring for it, is being quietly left behind by two of the three. That's the buyer Ownkube is built for. "A cloud for personal software" is the whole thesis.

An honest note on raw price

If your only question is the lowest possible dollar-per-vCPU, Ownkube is not always the answer, and we'd rather say so than pretend. Northflank's metered CPU works out cheaper than ours per vCPU. Railway's per-second CPU lands close to ours. Where Ownkube wins on the number is memory: our rate per GiB is well under Railway's, and personal software tends to be memory-heavy and CPU-idle, so the app sits on the memory line most of the day. A typical always-on app of that shape comes in under the equivalent Railway bill once you add both lines together.

But raw rate is the wrong thing to optimize for at this size. The money you actually lose on a small platform is the forgotten service that metered all month, the fixed instance that sat idle, or the migration you have to pay for when your app has to move. Structure beats rate at this scale, which is why we lead with the wallet and the full-stack total instead of a price war.

Now price the whole app

The per-vCPU argument misses the point because nobody ships a bare web process. A real app is a web service plus a managed Postgres plus a cache, and that is where the comparison actually lands. Railway, Render, and Northflank all bill the database and the cache as separate line items with a markup over the raw compute. Ownkube meters the app per minute and runs Postgres and the cache on near-cost boxes (a database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, a Valkey cache box from $2), so the parts that run all day are the parts where we are cheapest.

Price one representative stack: a small always-on web app (1 vCPU, 1 GiB), a managed Postgres (1 GiB RAM, 10 GB), and a small Redis-compatible cache.

Monthly cost, full stack Ownkube Railway Render Northflank
Web app (1 vCPU / 1 GiB, always on) ~$12 ~$18 to $30 ~$25 ~$18
Managed Postgres (1 GiB / 10 GB) ~$11 ~$18 ~$22 ~$14
Cache (small Redis-compatible) ~$5 ~$5 to $8 ~$10 ~$5
Total ~$27 ~$44 to $56 ~$57 ~$37

Treat the numbers as illustrative: competitor plans are mapped to the nearest real tier from their published pricing as of October 2026, and the metered platforms (Railway and Ownkube) move with how busy the app is, so an idle app costs Ownkube less than the figure above and a CPU-hot one costs more. Northflank stays the closest of the three, which is fair: its metered compute is genuinely cheap. The gap comes from the database and the cache. You can run the same comparison with your own sizes on the homepage calculator.

Where Ownkube fits

Pick Ownkube if the following sound like you:

  • You want to ship an app or a database in seconds with no cloud account to set up, and you want the bill to be a balance you loaded.
  • You want to choose predictable flat pricing or pay-for-what-runs metering per app, instead of having one model forced on everything.
  • You may one day need the same app inside your own or a customer's AWS account, with its logs and metrics, and you want that to be a move rather than a rewrite.
  • You're one developer or a small team, and you'd rather the platform handle TLS, managed Postgres, a Valkey cache, autoscaling, logs, metrics, and zero-downtime rollbacks than hire someone to.

Pick something else if you want a single $5 server for a throwaway project (a self-hosted option is simpler, see our self-hosted PaaS comparison), if you need GPU training runs today (Northflank), or if raw dollar-per-vCPU is the only axis you care about (Northflank again).

Reference: For the side-by-side breakdown, see Ownkube vs Render in the docs.

Closing

Railway, Render, and Northflank are all good platforms, and each earns its place: Railway for developer experience, Render for predictability, Northflank for power and multi-cloud. The gap they share for personal software is the invoice model. Two of them can surprise you, and one makes you pay for idle.

Ownkube is the other shape. Ship in seconds on Ownkube Compute with nothing to set up, load a wallet instead of exposing a card, keep the credit you do not spend, and price the whole app instead of the vCPU. Deploy my first app.

title: Create an Uber Clone in 1 Minute
description:
A lot has changed since 2018, both in programming and in Codename One. Back then I wrote Create an Uber Clone in 7 Days: Build a real world full stack mobile app in Java. Today you can start with the application those seven days were meant to teach you to build, then spend your time making it yours.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

Meet Wayline, a full-stack, white-label ride-hailing application written in Java. Rider and driver apps, an administration console, payments, live tracking and push notifications are already connected to a Java backend. You get the application and its source, ready to adapt to your business. Open the Initializr, choose Wayline, give it your own name and package, and generate the project. That's the one-minute task. Downloads and a first build depend on your machine; launching a real transport service still takes real work.

The source is 100% free, under MIT No Attribution, also called MIT-0. No royalties, no revenue share, no required subscription to use Wayline. You can modify it, sell your application and keep your changes private. Hosting and external services carry their own costs and terms. Your application belongs to you.

Coming This Week

Today is the full application tour, including the code and the parts you would adapt for your own business. The next six posts look at the tools that help you build and ship that work:

  • Saturday, October 17: Spring Data-Style Repositories Compiled to Native Code. Generated ORM repositories, isolation and completion callbacks.
  • Sunday, October 18: Thymeleaf, Spring MVC and htmx for Native Java Backends. Thymeleaf-style templates, Spring MVC-style controllers and htmx.
  • Monday, October 19: Build Your App Theme Without a Display Server. A fully headless compiler and the visual details worth checking after the change.
  • Tuesday, October 20: Give Your Desktop App a Useful Title Bar and Real Tools. Integrated title content on all three desktop OSs, the Process API and streaming ZIP support.
  • Wednesday, October 21: Let Users Install Your Java Web App Again. PWA support returns to the ParparVM JavaScript port.
  • Thursday, October 22: A Java IDE in Your Browser, With Your Files in Your Browser. An early preview of what I'm calling Not a Cloud IDE.

Choose a destination.
Accept a ride as a driver.
Manage the service.

A full-stack Java application you can make your own

Wayline includes both sides of the service. The frontend implements the rider, driver and administrator workflows across mobile, desktop and browser builds. The backend owns authentication, ride matching, pricing, payments and the database. This is a white-label application you can brand and extend, with the operational details already expressed in code.

The project has three modules: common for the frontend, backend for the server and shared for the typed contract between them. Both sides use Java. You can follow a button press through an API call, a service and a repository without switching languages or maintaining a second set of request models.

Here is the booking method in the shared RiderApi interface:

@POST("/api/rides")
void request(@Body RideRequestDto request,
        OnComplete<Response<RideDto>> callback);

The interface carries @RestClient. The build generates its client implementation and the RiderApiServer contract. Wayline's RiderEndpoint implements that contract, injects the Rides service and delegates the request:

@Override
public RideDto request(RideRequestDto request) throws Exception {
    return rides.request(Caller.name(), request);
}

The rider identity comes from the authenticated caller. The client supplies the trip it wants, and the server decides whether the signed-in user can request it. Spring-style dependency injection and authorization keep that decision in the backend; generated DTO serialization and API bindings keep the frontend and backend in agreement.

You can run the server on the JVM while developing, then package it as a native executable with ParparVM. The frontend shares its screens and behavior across targets. The user's guide tours the application, while the implementor's guide follows each feature into its classes. All the Wayline screenshots below come from those guides and open at full size when clicked.

Start with the whole trip

The application opens in the mode that fits the signed-in user. Riders get the booking screen, drivers get their shift, and administrators get the console. An account can have several roles and switch between them. These are distinct workflows within one shared application, so you don't maintain three unrelated clients.

A new user registers, verifies a phone number and chooses whether to share usage statistics. The development profile displays verification codes instead of sending an SMS, so you can try the flow before connecting a provider.

Sign in, create an account or choose the server.
Register to ride or apply to drive.
Verify a phone number; development shows the code.
Choose whether this device shares usage statistics.

The rider searches for a destination, sees the route and compares three vehicle categories with a fare for each. Home and Work shortcuts save repeated typing. Ride preferences cover quiet trips, accessibility and pets, and can restrict matching to women drivers based on the driver's profile.

After requesting, the rider follows the approaching driver, sees the car and plate, and can call or message them. At the end, the flow moves to a rating, optional tip and itemized receipt.

Compare vehicle categories and quoted fares.
Follow the driver to pickup.
Rate the completed ride and choose a tip.

The screen follows the server's state. A button asks for a change; the server decides whether that change is valid. The repositories use conditional updates so competing actions can be settled by the database. That matters when a cancellation and an acceptance arrive together.

The request flow is visible in Rides:

public RideDto request(String rider, RideRequestDto request) throws IOException {
    validate(request);
    String id = attempt(() -> open(rider, request));
    live.rideChanged(id, RideState.REQUESTED, rider, "", "");
    search(id);
    return read(id, rider);
}

open is transactional. It serializes competing requests from the same rider before creating the ride; attempt handles the retry path. Once that work returns, the service publishes the change and starts matching. The details that prevent two active rides belong here, where every client gets the same rules.

The normal journey is shown here. The application also handles declined offers, expiry, cancellation and payment failures.

Give the driver an application too

A ride-hailing demo that stops at the passenger screen leaves most of the service for you to build. Wayline includes driver signup, document submission and review, then the actual working day.

Submit the documents needed to apply.
See where an application stands.
Go online when ready to take rides.

An offer shows the pickup, destination, fare and a countdown. During a trip the driver sees the route and the next action, including the amount to collect for a cash ride. The earnings view shows daily totals and the balance recorded by the service.

Follow the trip and complete it.
Inspect earnings and the recorded payout balance.

When the driver switches to a navigation app or locks the phone, the mobile background-location service keeps reporting during the shift. Reports are spaced by time and distance instead of forwarding every location change. iOS uses background location; Android uses a location foreground service. The browser and desktop preview don't reproduce that mobile background behavior.

Shift.begin() starts tracking and, on Android, creates the foreground service with a method reference for its background task:

service = ForegroundService.start(CHANNEL, "You're online",
        "Wayline shares your location with riders while you drive.", null,
        Shift::keepAlive);

Shift.end() removes the location watcher and stops that service when the driver goes offline. The same class throttles reports by distance and elapsed time, including a heartbeat for a parked car.

There are ride widgets outside the main screen too. The rider's active trip appears as an iPhone Live Activity, an ongoing Android notification, or a small desktop/simulator window. A browser has no equivalent surface in Wayline. The lock-screen section explains the distinction: the iPhone implementation updates when the app receives messages, and doesn't use ActivityKit's direct server push token. A suspended app can therefore leave the activity showing its last received state.

The widget's layout is Java too. This excerpt from RideCard.descriptor() supplies the compact iPhone presentation:

return new LiveActivityDescriptor(RideActivityKeys.KIND)
        .setContent(content())
        .setCompactLeading(new SurfaceText("${driver}").setFontSize(13)
                .setMaxLines(1))
        .setCompactTrailing(new SurfaceText("${eta}").setFontSize(13)
                .setColor(SurfaceColor.ACCENT));

The complete descriptor also supplies expanded and minimal layouts. LiveActivity.start(descriptor(), now) starts it, and current.update(now) sends new state. Wayline registers the resulting activity ID with the backend so later push messages can address it.

Live updates over WebSockets

An open app needs to hear when the ride changes or the driver moves. LiveChannel opens a WebSocket and hands its callbacks back to the UI event thread:

socket = WebSocket.build(url)
        .onConnect(ws -> CN.callSerially(() -> opened(mine)))
        .onTextMessage((ws, text) -> CN.callSerially(() -> frame(text, mine)))
        .onClose((ws, code, reason) -> CN.callSerially(() -> lost(mine)))
        .onError((ws, err) -> CN.callSerially(() -> lost(mine)))
        .connect(10000);

This is the connection portion of LiveChannel.open(). Its helpers handle reconnects, heartbeats and stale callbacks from previous connections. The app obtains a short-lived, single-use ticket through its authenticated API before connecting to /ws/live.

The backend endpoint implements WebSocket and is registered with @WebSocketMapping("/ws/live"). It redeems the ticket, checks the account and adds the connection to LiveHub. When a ride changes, the hub constructs the message:

Map<String, Object> frame = new LinkedHashMap<String, Object>();
frame.put("type", "ride");
frame.put("id", id);
frame.put("state", state.name());
String text = Json.write(frame);

It sends that frame through WebSocketSession.sendText to the rider, the driver and connected administrators. Driver positions have their own message type. Removing an admin role also closes that account's old connections, so a previously authorized socket cannot keep receiving fleet locations. The live channel guide traces both sides.

Push v3 callbacks and backend delivery

The live WebSocket channel serves an app that is open. Push covers the rider with a phone in a pocket and the driver who has just been offered a job.

The frontend uses the Push v3 PushClient API. This is the registration code inside Notifications.start():

client = PushClient.builder(AppConfig.PUSH_APP_KEY)
        .listener(new Listener())
        .build();
client.register();

Its PushListener receives the token through onRegistration and ride notifications through onMessage:

@Override
public void onRegistration(PushSubscription registered) {
    subscription = registered;
    signedIn();
}

The message callback reads the payload and opens the relevant ride screen:

@Override
public void onMessage(PushMessage message) {
    Object ride = message.getData().get("rideId");
    Object role = message.getData().get("role");
    String title = message.getTitle();
    if (ride != null && title != null && title.length() > 0
            && Session.user() != null) {
        Nav.showRide(role == null ? Nav.RIDER : String.valueOf(role));
    }
}

The screen fetches the current ride state rather than trusting an old notification. Silent messages can update the Live Activity without opening a screen. These callbacks run on the UI event thread.

The app registers a device token for the signed-in account and removes that association on sign-out. A notification carries the ride ID and role so tapping it opens the right screen, which then reads the current ride from the server. Expiring driver offers use a short lifetime so a delayed notification doesn't look like a fresh job.

On the backend, RidePushes builds the message with ordinary Java calls:

return PushNotification.builder()
        .title(title)
        .body(body)
        .collapseKey("ride-" + id + "-" + role)
        .data("rideId", id)
        .data("state", state.name())
        .data("role", role);

CloudPushSender sends the built notification and device targets through CloudPush:

PushResult result = push.send(message, to);
accepted = result.isAccepted();

The call runs on a background task so the ride request doesn't wait for the push service. Acceptance here means the service accepted the notification; it isn't proof that someone read it. Wayline also checks the latest ride state before composing a notification, preventing a delayed acceptance event from announcing a ride that has since been canceled.

The server publishes ride changes after they commit. A push delivery failure doesn't undo an accepted ride. Those are small decisions that make a much bigger difference than adding another animation to the booking screen.

Wayline includes the integration, while development logs notifications to the console. Real mobile push requires the app and server keys and platform credentials described in the push setup. Android push starts disabled so a generated project can build before you have a Firebase or Huawei configuration.

The admin console is part of the product

Someone has to approve drivers, answer a payment question and find out why a rider was blocked. Those jobs shouldn't require opening a database console.

On a phone, administration is one screen at a time. The dashboard starts with work needing attention, then shows current activity and trends. An application review includes documents, and moderation records both the reason and the administrator responsible.

Inspect daily rides and fares.
Review a driver application.
See an account and its moderation history.

On a wide screen, the same app becomes a console with navigation and room for a list beside the selected item. This is a layout you can work in all day:

The wide dashboard puts activity and trends together.
Review applications without losing the list.

Flagging and blocking aren't the same operation. A flag calls attention to an account; a block signs it out and prevents access until it is lifted. The people view includes role changes, ride history and financial totals. The rides view lets an administrator inspect or cancel work and request a card refund where applicable.

The backend guards the awkward cases too. Inside Accounts.suspend(), an administrator cannot strand someone halfway through a ride by disabling the account:

if (suspended && signIn.isEnabled() && cleanup.inRideUnderWay(username)) {
    throw new ResponseStatusException(409,
            "That account is on a ride. Block it when the ride has ended");
}

The operation runs in a transaction and records who changed the account and why. The administrator must end the ride first. That rule protects both participants even if moderation is invoked through a different client.

Search accounts, change roles and inspect history.
Filter and inspect rides across the service.

Pricing is editable: base fare, distance, time, minimum fare, fees, commission, and multipliers. The payments list distinguishes a completed refund from one still pending. The live map shows online cars, and the guide screenshot below captures its empty state rather than inventing a busy fleet.

Inspect charges and their payment state.
Set the service prices in the console.
The live map, here with no drivers online.

Billing includes the awkward cases

The wallet stores payment methods, and receipts break down the fare. Development uses simulated cards with test behavior for success, decline and uncertain results. Real payment providers sit behind a PaymentProvider interface.

Keep a default card or choose cash.
Read the fare breakdown and payment result.

A completed ride and a settled payment are separate facts. Wayline commits the trip, calls the payment provider without holding that database transaction open, then records the result. Charges carry a key derived from the ride so retrying an uncertain request can reuse the same payment identity. This call from Payments.settle() makes that key explicit:

reference = charge("ride-" + ride.getId(), ride.getRider(), ride.getMethodId(), amount,
        ride.getCurrency(), "Wayline ride");

The helper resolves the stored provider references and delegates to PaymentProvider.charge. A definite decline becomes FAILED; an I/O failure leaves the result PENDING so recovery can ask again using the same key.

If the server stops between those steps, a recovery pass revisits pending payments. A definite decline is treated differently from a lost response. Refunds can be pending too; the admin screen doesn't call the money returned just because a provider accepted the request.

The included Stripe adapter uses hosted card setup so card details don't pass through the app's server. It has tests against stand-in provider responses, but hasn't been validated against a Stripe account. Before taking real payments, exercise its full flow with your provider and complete the missing production work described in the billing section: webhooks, required cardholder authentication, driver transfers and your tax/invoice rules.

In particular, Cash out currently records a payout in the ledger; it doesn't transfer money to a driver's bank. That is a concrete extension point, not a hidden promise behind a finished-looking button.

Maps change the starting economics

In 2018, native maps were central to this kind of app. We still support native maps, including the platform integration described in the guide. Wayline focuses on hosted map data rendered by Codename One's MapView, which gives a small operator more control over the provider and the cost model.

The default setup draws OpenStreetMap vector tiles from OpenFreeMap without an API key. Routes use the OSRM demo service, and place search goes through your backend to Photon. These are separate choices, not one inseparable maps account. The map factory selects the tile source and style directly:

MapView map = new MapView(tiles == null ? MvtTileSource.openFreeMap() : tiles,
        Look.dark() ? MapStyle.dark() : MapStyle.light());
map.setWheelZoom(true);
map.moveCamera(center, zoom);

This excerpt comes from Maps.create(). Maps.useTiles(TileSource source) supplies a replacement source, which also lets the screenshot tests use bundled tiles instead of depending on a network service.

You can point the app at your own tile and routing services, or choose hosted providers. A small business can begin without a map SDK billing account and later choose whether it wants a provider bill or the work of hosting its own data services. Self-hosting still costs money and operational time; public routing and search servers aren't a production service guarantee. The default routes don't include live traffic.

That changes the question from “which map vendor must this application use?” to “which service fits this region and volume?” The maps chapter of the implementor's guide shows the replacement points and the decisions to make before launch.

The vector map follows the dark theme.
The rider experience in a wide desktop window.

Readable Java, even when an agent makes the change

You can hand an agent the job of changing a fare rule, adding a service area or branding the screens. Java's strict types and straightforward structure help keep that work readable. A request has a declared type, a service has explicit dependencies, and a repository states what it reads. A changed method signature must agree with its callers.

Wayline gives the agent the same things I want as a developer: named responsibilities, conventional code, tests and a development MCP endpoint. You can review the resulting diff and follow the behavior through the application. The code remains yours to understand and maintain.

Spring Security users should recognize the authorization rules. This excerpt is part of SecurityConfig's API chain:

.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers(AntPathRequestMatcher.antMatcher("POST",
                "/api/account/register")).permitAll()
        .requestMatchers("/api/driver/**").hasRole(Roles.DRIVER)
        .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole(Roles.ADMIN)
        .anyRequest().authenticated())

The complete chain configures JWT authentication and other protections. The server reads the caller from its security context, rather than accepting a rider identity supplied by the client. The APIs use Codename One packages and supported Spring-style conventions; this isn't a Spring runtime hidden in the project.

The data layer is similarly recognizable. Wayline's RideRepository begins:

@Repository(entity = Ride.class, key = String.class)
public interface RideRepository extends CrudRepository<Ride, String> {
    Ride findFirstByRiderAndStateIn(String rider, RideState[] states);
    Ride findFirstByDriverAndStateIn(String driver, RideState[] states);
}

The build writes the query implementation. Services decide what changes belong in one transaction. If you prefer a direct data access object, the backend also generates DAOs. This separate example from the database guide shows that lower-level style using its Reminder entity:

Dao<Reminder> reminders = em.dao(Reminder.class);
Reminder reminder = new Reminder();
reminder.title = "renew the certificate";
reminder.due = new Date();
reminders.insert(reminder);

Reminder stored = reminders.findById(Long.valueOf(reminder.id));
stored.done = true;
reminders.update(stored);

On the frontend, a helper creates an ordinary component, gives it a test name and attaches an action. This is Wayline's button helper:

private static Button button(String text, String name, String uiid,
        ActionListener<ActionEvent> onClick) {
    Button button = new Button(text, uiid);
    button.setName(name);
    if (onClick != null) {
        button.addActionListener(onClick);
    }
    return button;
}

The UIID connects it to CSS. The primary style uses shared variables for branding and shape:

WlPrimary {
    color: var(--brand-contrast);
    background-color: var(--brand);
    border-radius: var(--radius);
    font-family: "native:MainBold";
    font-size: 2.9mm;
    text-align: center;
    padding: 2.75mm 4mm 2.75mm 4mm;
    margin: 1.6mm 0 0.8mm 0;
}

The variables and their dark variants live near the top of theme.css. An agent changing your brand color has a clear place to edit, and a human reviewing the change can see whether it touched anything else.

You can inspect these excerpts in the Wayline source. The implementor's guide links each feature to its implementation and explains how to adapt it.

Settings are part of making the app yours

Wayline includes light and dark themes, distance units and translations into English, Spanish, French, German, and Hebrew. The Hebrew layout runs right to left. Wide settings screens stay in a readable column instead of stretching every field across the monitor.

Account, ride and appearance preferences.
The same settings in dark mode.
Hebrew text and right-to-left layout.
Usage statistics remain a device-level choice.

Settings adapt to a desktop window.

Some settings are hooks for your product policy. The promotions switch is stored, but Wayline sends no promotions. The emergency contact and automatic trip-sharing preference are stored without sending messages; the ride's Share action is separate. The guide calls these out so you can decide what they should mean for your service.

Run it, then change one thing

Generate the Wayline template from the Initializr. It renames the Java package, artifacts and application configuration for your project. With JDK 17 or newer and Maven installed, start the development backend from the generated project's root:

CN1_PROFILE=dev backend/server.sh run

In another terminal, start the simulator:

mvn verify -Psimulator -DskipTests -Dcodename1.platform=javase

The development profile uses an in-memory database, demo accounts and simulated external services. The launch instructions list the accounts and show how to run the rider and driver together. Keep that profile for development.

For a browser version hosted by the same backend:

backend/server.sh web
CN1_PROFILE=dev backend/server.sh run

Then open http://localhost:8080/. The first command builds the browser application; rerun it after changing the client. Server packaging can also produce a native binary.

Before handing a change to an agent, give it a useful check. The backend test command is:

mvn -pl shared,backend -Dcodename1.platform=backend test

The suite covers roles, the ride lifecycle and payment outcomes, among other service behavior. Native compiled test execution is available as a local-only option in the testing guide. The development profile's /mcp endpoint gives an agent another way to inspect the backend; it isn't an endpoint to expose publicly without the production authentication configuration.

Build a service your market needs

I see this as an opening for startups whose idea begins with ride hailing. Airport transfers, a specialist fleet or transport for a particular community can start here, then build the part that makes the service useful to those people. Make something better.

A taxi company can run its own branded, hosted app with central management. The taxi-station adaptation discusses a fixed fleet, manual dispatch and phone bookings as changes to make. Those additions aren't all finished screens in Wayline, but the guide shows where they belong.

I can see a cottage industry around that work: developers who adapt and operate these applications for local businesses. A small operator gets more freedom over its brand and service rules, and the developer can spend time on the local requirements instead of recreating the wallet and sign-in flow. Whether that becomes a business depends on finding operators whose problems you can solve. The starting code is now available to try.

More This Week

Spring Data-style repositories, statically compiled

A finder such as findFirstByDriverAndStateIn puts a query next to the rest of the entity's data access. The new repository generator supplies its implementation, including support for declared queries and CASE expressions.

@Repository(entity = Ride.class, key = String.class)
public interface RideRepository extends CrudRepository<Ride, String> {
    Ride findFirstByDriverAndStateIn(String driver, RideState[] states);
}

You get Spring Data-style finder methods and familiar Hibernate persistence conventions with generated Java implementations. Native builds compile those implementations ahead of time. There is no repository classpath scan or runtime proxy generation, and the resulting calls are available to the compiler for optimization.

Transaction isolation and callbacks deal with the next question: when can another part of the system act on that result? A completion callback runs after the database acknowledges the commit. If the callback fails, the database change is still committed, so retrying the entire operation is the wrong default.

Saturday's repository and transaction article covers both the convenience and the boundaries, including bulk updates, supported isolation levels and durable event delivery.

Thymeleaf, Spring MVC and htmx in a native backend

Thymeleaf-style templates, Spring MVC-style controllers and htmx make a useful combination for a fast server-rendered admin site. Our implementation compiles the supported template syntax into Java renderers, then into the native backend. The controller can return a page or a fragment for htmx:

return Htmx.isRequest(request) ? "products :: catalog" : "products";

Typed model access becomes direct Java access. Production requests execute compiled rendering code, without parsing templates or interpreting property expressions. That is the performance advantage of doing the template work during the build.

Sunday's Thymeleaf and Spring MVC article follows a working catalog through controllers, form errors and partial updates. It also explains what this subset leaves out.

A stylesheet shouldn't need a monitor

The CSS compiler is fully headless. The same mvn cn1:css goal can run on a worker without a display server or framebuffer setup. Removing that machinery removes startup work and display-dependent assumptions from theme compilation.

This is also a substantial change to an old compiler with fragile corners. Fonts, image borders and physical-unit conversions deserve visual checks even when a build succeeds. Monday's headless CSS article shows the workflow and what to compare.

Use the desktop title area

The title area of our native macOS editor prototype. Document actions share the top row with the OS controls, leaving the ribbon and document below.

Putting Save, Search or document controls in the window title area is a niche feature. If you're building an editor, it can save a whole row. Codename One supports it in the native macOS, Windows and Linux ports while keeping real OS window controls.

editor.getToolbar().setTitleComponent(title);

With custom title mode selected, the framework reserves room for the native controls and separates interactive components from draggable background. Tuesday's desktop tools article explains the differences between the three operating systems.

Run an external tool from Java

The new shared com.codename1.io.ProcessBuilder started with backend needs, then extended naturally to desktop apps. You can launch an installed command, stream its input and output, wait with a timeout and inspect its exit status.

boolean available = com.codename1.io.ProcessBuilder.isSupported();

Mobile and browser targets return no process-launch capability. Tuesday's article covers that boundary and the output-draining pattern that keeps a full pipe from hanging the worker.

Export a ZIP without inventing an archive format

The ParparVM runtime now provides streaming java.util.zip APIs, including ZIP, GZIP, and checksums. An app can export data through the familiar stream interfaces; a backend can write an archive straight to its response.

zip.putNextEntry(new java.util.zip.ZipEntry("report.txt"));
zip.write("Completed rides\n".getBytes("UTF-8"));
zip.closeEntry();

This excerpt assumes an open ZipOutputStream. The desktop tools article also shows the helper for preserving an executable launcher's Unix permissions, and the limits of the streaming subset.

Install the web app again

PWA support disappeared during the move from TeaVM to ParparVM. JavaScript builds now generate the manifest, icons and service worker again, giving supporting browsers an installable application and cached offline launch.

Wednesday's PWA article covers deployment, cache updates and the difference between an offline UI and a ride request that still needs a server.

Not a Cloud IDE

The experimental browser IDE opens a Java project with an editor and a running preview. Compilation and execution happen in the page, and files stay in this browser's storage. The cloud build server does its usual job when you explicitly request a platform build.

This is a very early preview. It won't replace IntelliJ or reproduce all of Java inside JavaScript. It can let someone try an app before installing a development environment, then download the project when they're ready to continue locally. Thursday's IDE tour shows that path and explains browser-local storage.

Where is this going?

Everywhere. Wayline is the first step in a wider collection of full-stack application templates in Initializr. We plan to do this for many more applications, including delivery: choose a template, generate your own project, then build the service your market needs. Raising the starting point is good for the whole market. Your moat can grow in the part competitors can't get from a template: the service you provide, the relationships you build and the problems you understand better. Starting with an application as substantial as Wayline gives you more time to build that advantage. I want to see what you make of it.

title: October 05, 2026
description:
Agent Platform Workbench

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Change

The BigQuery JupyterLab plugin is now enabled independently of the Dataproc plugin: it is enabled by default and can be turned off with the new disable-bigquery instance metadata key, while disable-mixer now controls only the Dataproc plugin.

Change

20261004.00_p0 Release

Change

Installed latest packages from upstream dependencies.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Security

Security fixes for the integrated portal and API specs in the Apigee Edge management UIs.

The Apigee Edge UIs for managing integrated portals and API specs were updated to patch vulnerabilities in underlying libraries and serving components. Functionality is unchanged, but some pages might show minor styling differences.

Application Design Center

Feature

Use the recommendeIAMroles API to identify a list of required APIs and Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles that you must configure before you deploy your application.

BigQuery

Feature

Iceberg external tables and Iceberg managed tables now support flexible column names by default. This feature is generally available (GA).

Feature

The gemini-embedding-2 model works well for embedding long strings, including multilingual and unstructured data. It supports a mix of text, images, audio, video, and PDF files. You can use this model in the AI.EMBED, AI.SIMILARITY, and AI.GENERATE_EMBEDDING functions. This model is generally available.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

This feature is in Preview.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports Assured Workloads control packages to help you meet regulatory, data residency, and data sovereignty requirements.

Specifically, the Cloud Workstations API (v1, v1beta, and v1alpha) supports the following Assured Workloads control packages:

  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP High
  • Data Boundary for FedRAMP Moderate
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 2 (IL2)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 4 (IL4)
  • Data Boundary for Impact Level 5 (IL5)
  • US Data Boundary and Support (AW Regional Controls - Premium)
  • EU Data Boundary with Access Justifications

For more information about compliance-supported regions for each control package and API fields that aren't intended for sensitive data, see Regulatory support in Cloud Workstations.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Z3 machine types that have 8 to 44 vCPUs can use Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes to synchronously replicate data across two zones.

For more information, see About Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability.

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Confidential Space

Announcement

A new Confidential Space image (260900) is available.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Deprecated

Starting on July 1, 2026, Identity Service for GKE is deprecated in GKE version 1.36 and earlier. This feature is also unavailable in organizations that were created on or after July 1, 2025. GKE version 1.37 and later don't support Identity Service for GKE. Before you upgrade clusters to 1.37 and later, disable this feature and migrate to Workforce Identity Federation.

For more information, see Identity Service for GKE deprecation.

Feature

GKE support for using the c4-standard-* machine types (up to 192 vCPUs) as Confidential GKE Nodes with Intel TDX is generally available. For more information, see the following pages:

  • To use this feature with GKE , see Encrypt workload data in-use with Confidential GKE Nodes.
  • To learn more about the feature from Compute Engine, see Confidential VM overview.
  • To see supported configurations, including machine support, see Supported configurations and its "Machine types, CPUs, and zones" section.

Google SecOps

Feature

[Spotlight Feature] Terraform and client libraries for multiple features using Chronicle API

Terraform providers and Google Cloud client libraries are now available for several Google SecOps features using Chronicle API including Feeds, Parsers, Rules, Findings Refinements, Retrohunts, Dashboards, Data Tables, Watchlists, Custom Lists, Environments, Environment Groups, Data Export, SOAR Domains, and SOAR Networks. For more information, see Terraform reference.

Terraform providers enable programmatic provisioning and management of Google SecOps resources as code, while Client Libraries enable developers to build custom integrations and automate Google SecOps workflows in their preferred programming languages. For more information, see Client libraries.

Guest Environment

Feature

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following features:

  • The managed workload identity certificate refresher is now a locally bundled extension. For more information, see Managed workload identities overview.
  • The guest telemetry extension is updated to version 1.1 and polls every 15 minutes instead of every 24 hours. However, it will only send data to the API every 24 hours, unless it detects a change in the system since the previous poll. The extension supports the following capabilities:
    • Running a command as the user associated with a discovered process.
    • Configuring regular expressions to match against the version command output.

Fixed

Version 20260921.00 of the guest agent is now available for all supported operating systems. This version introduces the following fixes:

  • The NetworkManager setup now no longer reloads the primary NIC when it applies changes to the network configuration of secondary NICs, unless necessary.
  • If the core plugin successfully rolls back any configurations, then it force-reloads the configurations to make sure that the instance re-obtains DHCP leases for secondary NICs.
  • The core plugin now respects the address-manager configuration flag and the corresponding metadata attribute.
  • The extensions manager now ignores install and remove requests from ACS for the core plugin and locally bundled extensions.
  • The extensions manager no longer logs that there are no local plugins to install when it's installing local plugins.
  • The metadata script runner now respects the sysprep_specialize configuration flag.

Knowledge Catalog

Feature

Data products in Knowledge Catalog now support Looker (Google Cloud core) assets. You can package, govern, and share Looker (Google Cloud core) dashboards, dashboard elements, Looks, Explores, and LookML projects, models, and views in a data product using Google Group mirroring and IAM access controls. This feature is generally available.

For more information, see About data products and Create data products.

Managed Service for Apache Spark

Change

Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Google Cloud Serverless for Apache Spark): Users may now specify short template names when creating a serverless session.

Network Intelligence Center

Feature

Flow Analyzer displays packet drops, allowing you to analyze packet loss in your traffic flows. For more information, see Display flows in packet drop mode.

Network Service Tiers

Feature

External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier in Preview. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

Virtual Private Cloud

Feature

Preview: External IPv6 addresses are now supported for Standard Tier. For more information, see IPv6 subnet ranges.

title: Never Trust File Uploads: Building a Secure S3 Pipeline
description:
File uploads look simple.

A user selects a file, your backend receives it, saves it to storage, and returns a URL.

Done, right?

Not really.

What if someone uploads a malicious file disguised as an image? What if hundreds of users upload large files at the same time? Or what if an infected PDF becomes available for everyone to download?

A simple upload feature can quickly become a security problem.

Let's look at how to build a safer file upload pipeline using S3, magic bytes, and ClamAV.

1. Stop sending files through your API server

A common approach is to receive files through your Node.js backend and then upload them to S3.

This works, but your API becomes a middleman.

Every upload uses server bandwidth and connections. If you're buffering files in memory, large uploads can also consume a lot of RAM.

A better approach is to use S3 presigned URLs.

Here's how it works:

  1. The client requests an upload URL from your API.
  2. Your API checks permission and generates a short-lived URL.
  3. The client uploads the file directly to S3.
  4. S3 stores the file in a private quarantine location.

Your API handles permissions, not the actual file transfer.

For example, using AWS SDK v3:

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { S3Client } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { createPresignedPost } from "@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post";

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: "us-east-1" });

export async function createUpload(userId: string) {
  // userId must come from the authenticated session
  const key = `quarantine/${userId}/${randomUUID()}`;

  const { url, fields } = await createPresignedPost(s3, {
    Bucket: "my-private-uploads",
    Key: key,
    Expires: 300,
    Conditions: [
      ["content-length-range", 1, 10 * 1024 * 1024],
    ],
  });

  return { url, fields };
}

This creates a presigned POST that allows uploads up to 10 MB and expires after five minutes.

The client sends the returned fields and file as multipart/form-data directly to S3.

The bucket stays private, and the backend should record the generated key against the authenticated user.

One important thing: a successful upload doesn't mean the file is safe.

We still need to inspect it.

2. Never trust file extensions or MIME types

Imagine someone uploads a file named profile.png.

Your backend checks:

if (file.mimetype === "image/png") {
  // Accept file
}

Looks fine, right?

The problem is that the MIME type usually comes from the client.

Anyone can rename a file or send a fake Content-Type header.

Instead, check the actual file content.

Check the magic bytes

Many file formats have recognizable binary signatures called magic bytes.

For example:

File Signature
PNG 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A
JPEG FF D8 FF
PDF 25 50 44 46 2D
ZIP 50 4B 03 04

In Node.js, the file-type package makes this easier.

import { fileTypeFromBuffer } from "file-type";

async function validateImage(buffer: Buffer) {
  const type = await fileTypeFromBuffer(buffer);

  const allowed = ["image/png", "image/jpeg"];

  if (!type || !allowed.includes(type.mime)) {
    throw new Error("Unsupported file format");
  }

  return type;
}

You don't need to download the entire file just to check its signature.

For supported formats, you can read a small part of the object using an S3 range request. The number of bytes needed depends on the format and detection library.

But remember, valid magic bytes don't mean a file is safe.

A valid PDF or image can still contain harmful content or exploit a vulnerable file parser.

That's why we need another layer.

3. Scan files before making them available

This is the part I wouldn't skip.

Never make an uploaded file available to users before it passes validation and scanning.

Instead, use a quarantine system.

Here's the flow:

Client
  |
  | Request upload URL
  v
Node.js API
  |
  | Generate presigned URL
  v
Client
  |
  | Upload directly
  v
Private S3 Quarantine
  |
  | Storage event
  v
Background Worker
  |
  | Check file size
  | Check magic bytes
  | Scan with ClamAV
  |
  +-- Failed --> Reject
  |
  +-- Passed --> Approved Storage
                       |
                       v
                Available to User

For malware scanning, we can use ClamAV, a free, open-source antivirus engine.

A background worker can download or stream the quarantined object to the scanner.

Here's a simplified example using the clamscan package:

import NodeClam from "clamscan";

const clam = await new NodeClam().init({
  clamdscan: {
    host: "clamav-service",
    port: 3310,
  },
});

export async function scanFile(
  fileStream: NodeJS.ReadableStream,
) {
  const result = await clam.scanStream(fileStream);

  if (result.isInfected !== false) {
    throw new Error("File rejected");
  }

  return true;
}

This example only shows the scanning step. The worker still needs to retrieve the correct S3 object, validate it, handle failures, and update the database.

If the scan fails, times out, or returns an unknown result, keep the file quarantined.

Don't approve it automatically.

Also, ClamAV reduces malware risk, but it cannot detect every possible threat.

4. Let background workers handle the heavy work

Virus scanning can take time.

You don't want users waiting for it inside an HTTP request.

Instead, use a background queue like BullMQ or AWS SQS.

When S3 receives a file, a storage event can trigger a job.

The worker validates the file, scans it, and updates its status.

A simple database lifecycle could look like this:

PENDING_UPLOAD
      |
      v
 QUARANTINED
      |
      v
   SCANNING
    /    \
   v      v
APPROVED REJECTED

The frontend can show "Processing your file" while scanning is in progress.

Make sure workers can safely retry jobs and handle duplicate events.

There's another important detail here.

Scan and approve the exact same object.

Otherwise, a file could be replaced after scanning but before approval.

Use unique storage keys and object versioning or other controls that prevent an unscanned replacement from being published.

5. A few security rules worth following

Even with these three layers, I'd still add a few protections:

  • Limit file sizes. Don't allow unlimited uploads.
  • Use random file names. Generate UUID-based storage keys instead of trusting user-provided paths.
  • Keep storage private. Approved files don't always need public URLs. Use authorized downloads when appropriate.
  • Limit upload requests. Add authentication, rate limits, and storage quotas.
  • Protect against ZIP bombs. Limit archive extraction size, file count, and nesting depth.
  • Serve files safely. Use correct response headers and avoid serving risky user content from your application's main origin.
  • Monitor failures. Track rejected uploads, scanner errors, and unusual upload activity.

And one underrated point: don't expose your ClamAV service directly to the internet. Keep it accessible only to trusted workers.

Final thoughts

File uploads are easy to build, but securing them takes a little more thought.

You don't need a complicated system from day one.

Start with three things:

1. Presign: Let clients upload directly to private object storage.

2. Validate: Check file size, format, and actual content instead of trusting filenames.

3. Scan: Run malware checks in the background before making files available.

These steps won't eliminate every security risk, but they'll give you a much safer foundation.

The main thing I've learned is simple:

Uploading a file and trusting a file should be two different steps.

How do you handle file uploads in your applications? Do you scan files before making them available, or use a different approach?

References

  • AWS S3 Presigned URLs
  • AWS S3 Presigned POST
  • ClamAV Documentation
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
