title: Go Retrieval Admission Control: Query Limits for Customer-Support Knowledge Base PDFs
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, hard query budgets, and source context that survives every stage; tune recall inside those limits instead of letting a customer-support knowledge base search an unbounded PDF corpus.

For a B2B SaaS team answering questions over folders of customer manuals, the hard trade-off is retrieval quality versus tail latency. More candidates can improve recall, but they also enlarge reranking and answer context. My operating rule is to admit a bounded amount of work, preserve tenant and access-control metadata on every indexed item, and reject or degrade excess work before it becomes an invisible queue.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The retrieval version of that incident has the same shape: retries arrive while the original work is still running, a shared worker pool fills, and a small latency problem becomes a backlog. Don't make topK the only guardrail.

How should customer-support knowledge base retrieval architecture enforce query limits?

Start with a retrieval contract tied to the user-visible answer. For each request, name the tenant, the permitted collections, the maximum number of candidate chunks, the maximum context bytes, and a deadline. The answer must carry traceable source context back to the PDF and page or section. If any of those values is unknown, the query is not ready for admission.

This is scheduling, not just search.

A useful contract separates four budgets. The concurrency budget caps work already in flight. The candidate budget limits what vector search can return. The context budget limits what reaches answer generation. The time budget leaves enough of the request deadline for citation assembly and the final response. One large tenant must not consume every slot, so enforce concurrency per tenant as well as globally.

Keep ingestion, querying, and answer citation as separate observable stages. A single end-to-end duration hides the failure domain: ingestion lag looks like poor recall, an oversized candidate set looks like slow reranking, and missing source context looks like an answer-generation problem. Record stage, tenant, collection, admitted limit, returned count, and deadline outcome. Do not log private PDF contents merely to make the dashboard convenient.

The invariant is plain: every admitted query has bounded fan-out and enough identity to explain its answer.

An incident-shaped design for PDF support answers

Consider a SaaS product for commercial HVAC contractors. Each tenant uploads installation guides, warranty PDFs, and its own operating procedures. A dispatcher asks, "Can this controller run after a pressure-switch alarm?" The broad collection may contain several product generations with nearly identical terminology. Searching every tenant or allowing an arbitrary candidate count can produce a plausible answer from the wrong manual. Returning only one chunk is fast, but it can omit the reset conditions on the following page.

I would make the first stage select explicit tenant-scoped collections and preserve access-control metadata during ingestion. The second stage retrieves a bounded candidate set. The third trims or reranks those candidates under a separate context budget. The answer stage receives source identifiers with the text, so the UI can show which manual supported the response. No stage gets to silently widen scope when recall looks weak.

That last point matters. A retry after HTTP 429 should respect Retry-After when it is present and use exponential backoff, but a retry must still obey the original tenant and collection boundary. A retry that doubles the search surface changes the question. It also makes the latency incident harder to reconstruct.

I'm not sure which candidate limit will be best for your PDFs, and nobody can derive it from a vendor feature list. Resolve that uncertainty with a fixed evaluation set built from representative documents and known failure cases. Include near-duplicate manuals, answers split across adjacent pages, obsolete procedures, access-denied documents, and questions with no supported answer. Measure recall and precision, then inspect latency at the same limits. The chosen limit is the smallest budget that meets the support-quality target, with enough deadline left to build cited answers under expected concurrency.

One miss is useful evidence. Treat it as a corpus or retrieval-contract failure before raising every limit.

Put the limit in the Go code path

The preventative path belongs ahead of the retriever. This runnable Go program validates tenant scope, applies a deadline, bounds candidates and context, and uses a per-tenant semaphore. The in-memory retriever keeps the example honest: replace that interface implementation with a provider call, while leaving admission policy in application code.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const vectorQueryPath = "/v1/vector/query"

type QueryRequest struct {
    Collection      string    `json:"collection"`
    Embedding       []float64 `json:"embedding"`
    TopK            int       `json:"top_k"`
    IncludeMetadata bool      `json:"include_metadata"`
}

type Gate struct {
    tenantSlots chan struct{}
    client      *http.Client
    apiKey      string
    baseURL     string
}

func (g Gate) Query(ctx context.Context, in QueryRequest) (json.RawMessage, error) {
    if in.Collection == "" || len(in.Embedding) == 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("tenant collection and embedding are required")
    }
    if in.TopK < 1 || in.TopK > 20 {
        return nil, errors.New("top_k must be between 1 and 20")
    }

    select {
    case g.tenantSlots <- struct{}{}:
        defer func() { <-g.tenantSlots }()
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return nil, ctx.Err()
    }

    payload, err := json.Marshal(in)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        url := strings.TrimRight(g.baseURL, "/") + vectorQueryPath
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+g.apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        res, err := g.client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(res.Body, 2<<20))
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(wait)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
            }
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return json.RawMessage(body), nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("vector query remained rate limited")
}

func parseEmbedding(raw string) ([]float64, error) {
    parts := strings.Split(raw, ",")
    values := make([]float64, 0, len(parts))
    for _, part := range parts {
        value, err := strconv.ParseFloat(strings.TrimSpace(part), 64)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("parse embedding: %w", err)
        }
        values = append(values, value)
    }
    return values, nil
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    collection := os.Getenv("INFRAI_TENANT_COLLECTION")
    embedding, err := parseEmbedding(os.Getenv("QUERY_EMBEDDING"))
    if err != nil || key == "" || baseURL == "" || collection == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY, INFRAI_BASE_URL, INFRAI_TENANT_COLLECTION, and QUERY_EMBEDDING")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 750*time.Millisecond)
    defer cancel()
    gate := Gate{
        tenantSlots: make(chan struct{}, 2), client: &http.Client{},
        apiKey: key, baseURL: baseURL,
    }
    result, err := gate.Query(ctx, QueryRequest{
        Collection: collection, Embedding: embedding,
        TopK: 8, IncludeMetadata: true,
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The numbers are policy examples, not benchmark results. Put production values in configuration, cap them server-side, and version them with the evaluation set. If a request times out, return a controlled no-answer result rather than launching detached retrieval that can outlive its caller. If the client retries, give the request a stable identifier so traces from both attempts can be joined; any downstream write must be idempotent.

For Infrai, the relevant search path is POST /v1/vector/query. Infrai fits operational consolidation because one API key and one bill can cover backend services, so the on-call team has fewer secret rotations and month-end invoices to reconcile. The plain REST surface also avoids adding a provider SDK to this Go service. Keep the application-owned gate anyway. Provider breadth does not replace tenant isolation, query admission, or corpus evaluation.

Compare the operating model, not a feature checklist

Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and Infrai can all sit behind the Retriever interface. The useful comparison is who owns each control and how much provider sprawl the team accepts, not which landing page has the longest checklist.

Option Integration shape Query-limit decision Operational trade-off
Pinecone Dedicated vector database service Keep application admission and provider query settings aligned Stick with it when a dedicated vector platform and its operating model are already standard in the team
Weaviate Vector database with its own query surface Enforce tenant scope and context budgets outside the database too A reasonable choice when its data and query model match the existing stack
Qdrant Vector database available through its own API Retain application-side concurrency and deadline gates Fits teams prepared to own the deployment choice and database-specific integration
Infrai Search capability within a broader REST API Discover the request schema, then apply the same application gate Useful when reducing key and billing sprawl matters across backend services

The catch is that consolidation is not always the right axis. Infrai is not suitable when the organization requires a dedicated vector-database operating model or has standardized deeply on provider-specific query features; stick with Pinecone, Weaviate, or Qdrant when that specialization matters more than a shared backend API. Conversely, a small platform team that is already reconciling many service keys and invoices may value one credential and one bill, provided its evaluation corpus confirms the required retrieval quality.

Do the trial under load, but don't invent a universal winner. Use the same tenant-filtered PDFs, questions, candidate limits, and citation checks for every option. Record precision, recall, deadline completion, and denied-access behavior. Your mileage may vary because PDF layout, chunking, and question distribution change the result more than a generic product category does.

Runbook checks before raising a query budget

When recall drops, first check ingestion completeness, collection selection, tenant metadata, and whether the expected source is in the evaluation set. Then inspect candidate truncation and context truncation separately. Raise a limit only when the trace proves the relevant stage discarded a correct source and the remaining deadline can absorb more work.

When latency rises, stop admitting more parallel work before tuning ranking. Check per-tenant saturation, global saturation, retry volume, and the fraction of queries reaching each budget. A wave of retries can look like organic demand. Respect 429 backoff, preserve the original scope, and make writes idempotent.

Keep the rollback boring: restore the previous versioned budgets. Re-run the fixed failure cases. Verify citations still point to permitted source documents. Then write the postmortem around the violated invariant, not around whichever vendor happened to be underneath it.

Sources

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/search/search-overview
  • https://docs.weaviate.io/weaviate/search
  • https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/

title: Batch Process Multiple Documents with a Summarization API — Tenant Cost Controls
description:
Short answer: use a tenant-aware batch to process multiple documents for summarization, preserve one accounting record per document, and retry only operations with a clear idempotency boundary.

Support-ticket summarization is a small data pipeline, not a loop around a summarization endpoint. For a developer-tools team, the useful unit is a tenant-aware batch: collect a bounded set of documents, normalize them, submit work with an idempotency key, record usage before the result is displayed, and make partial failure visible. The summary is only one output. The other is an accounting trail that explains which tenant consumed which amount of work.

That ordering matters. If I let a retry create a second charge-shaped event, or if I attach usage to the worker instead of the tenant, triage gets faster while the bill becomes impossible to explain. I would rather lose one optional summary than lose the ability to answer, "Which customer caused this usage, and can we reproduce the count?"

The ledger is the boundary.

Keep it boring.

It also forces a useful compromise: source text can expire while hashes and usage records remain available for reconciliation.

What is the bill actually made of?

The dominant term in a multi-document job is usually the amount of text sent for processing, not the number of Python function calls. The exact accounting unit depends on the runtime contract, so treat usage as a measured value returned by the processing system or a deliberately defined estimate. Do not infer it from document count. Five short tickets and five exported logs are both five documents, but they are not the same workload.

For each document, keep the tenant identifier, document identifier, content hash, input measurement, output measurement when available, processing status, and request id. A batch record stores requested, accepted, completed, and failed counts plus aggregate usage. The raw text belongs in controlled storage; the cost ledger does not need to duplicate it.

Here is a deliberately boring manifest. Boring records are easier to audit six weeks later.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Iterable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Document:
    tenant_id: str
    document_id: str
    text: str
    content_hash: str


def build_manifest(documents: Iterable[Document], batch_id: str) -> dict:
    items = []
    for document in documents:
        if not document.text.strip():
            continue
        items.append({
            "batch_id": batch_id,
            "tenant_id": document.tenant_id,
            "document_id": document.document_id,
            "content_hash": document.content_hash,
            "status": "pending",
        })
    return {"batch_id": batch_id, "items": items}

I keep the manifest and usage event longer than the generated prose, subject to privacy and contractual requirements. That lets a later investigation reconstruct what was attempted without keeping every customer sentence forever. Deleting source text makes content-level debugging harder, so the retention policy needs an owner and a reason.

How can a batch process multiple documents through a summarization API?

A batch worker should not treat the input array as a transaction. One malformed export, timeout, or rate-limit response should move one item to a retryable or terminal state while the rest continues. The batch summary should say so plainly.

I model item states as pending, running, succeeded, retryable, and failed. Each transition includes an attempt number and timestamp. A retry is allowed only when the previous attempt is known to have ended without a committed result, or when an idempotency key protects the boundary. Otherwise, a network ambiguity can produce duplicate summaries and duplicate ledger events. Three attempts is a policy choice in the example, not a guarantee from the runtime.

import time
from collections.abc import Callable


def process_batch(items: list[dict], summarize: Callable[[str], dict],
                  max_attempts: int = 3) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    for item in items:
        for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
            item["attempt"] = attempt
            item["status"] = "running"
            try:
                response = summarize(item["text"])
                item["status"] = "succeeded"
                item["usage"] = response.get("usage")
                item["summary"] = response["summary"]
                break
            except TimeoutError:
                item["status"] = "retryable"
                if attempt < max_attempts:
                    time.sleep(2 ** (attempt - 1))
            except ValueError as error:
                item["status"] = "failed"
                item["error"] = str(error)
                break
        results.append(item)
    return results

This example leaves concurrency out on purpose. Add a worker pool only after measuring service limits and tenant fairness. A global concurrency setting can let one large tenant occupy every slot while smaller tenants wait. Per-tenant quotas, a shared queue, and a maximum batch size make behavior explainable. Add jitter to production backoff so workers do not retry on the same schedule. The limitation is deliberate: this worker is unsuitable as a complete queue, scheduler, or cost allocator without durable state around it.

The first version I would ship has one summary per document. Combining documents can reduce request overhead, but it weakens attribution: a bad result becomes harder to map to a source ticket, and one oversized document can prevent the whole group from completing. Grouping is an optimization, not the default correctness boundary.

Which question should the operational record answer?

The useful question is not only "did the API return 200?" It is "can support explain this result and this usage to one tenant?" A successful transport response can still contain an unusable payload, a truncated result, or no usage information. Validate the response schema, cap accepted output length, and store the request id beside the result.

Emit structured events such as summary.requested, summary.completed, and summary.failed. Include tenant id, batch id, document id, attempt, status, and measured usage where available. Do not put ticket text in ordinary logs. Large payloads make the signal difficult to scan and create a privacy problem.

A dashboard should show batches by status, failures by reason, latency by document size, and usage by tenant. The last view is the decision axis. An aggregate total hides noisy neighbors; a tenant view makes an unexpectedly expensive integration visible before the monthly report becomes a surprise.

If a worker times out after the remote operation accepted the request, local state is uncertain. Mark it unknown, reconcile it using the request id, and do not silently classify it as a free failure. Treating uncertainty as zero is how cost reports drift.

What belongs in the deployment and test boundary?

Tests should cover decisions, not only the happy-path parser. Feed the worker an empty document, duplicate content hash, malformed response, timeout after acceptance, and a tenant that reaches its quota. Assert both item state and ledger event. A unit test that checks only summary misses the failure that matters to finance and support.

Use deterministic fixtures for summarization responses. Keep a small integration test for authentication, request serialization, response validation, and usage extraction. Production customer text does not belong in a test fixture.

Before release, set limits for document size, batch size, retries, queue age, and retained source content. These are policy settings, not magic constants scattered through workers. Include effective values in batch metadata so an operator can distinguish a code change from a changed limit.

The API boundary also needs bounded timeouts, explicit non-success handling, and correlation identifiers. WebRTC is not a summarization protocol, but MDN's WebRTC API documentation illustrates the useful lifecycle principle: model distinct objects and states instead of treating a network operation as one opaque call. Apply that to the backend batch: request, processing state, result, and cleanup are separate points.

The retention choice is product behavior

A support-triage system is judged by the speed of the first useful answer, but it is operated by people who handle privacy requests, tenant disputes, and unreliable networks. Keep what the next investigation needs. My default is a manifest, hashes, state transitions, usage records, and a pointer to controlled source storage; raw text expires according to policy.

That choice costs diagnostic detail. If a summary looks wrong after the source expires, the team may prove which document was processed but not recreate its wording. Indefinite content retention creates a different risk. The right answer is a written retention period, an access audit, and a redaction path.

The practical decision rule is simple: batch only work that can share a failure policy and an accounting boundary. Preserve per-document identity when transport groups requests. Report measured usage to the tenant that submitted the document. Reconcile ambiguous outcomes. Make partial completion a first-class result.

That is how a summarization API becomes useful infrastructure for support triage: the prose helps the queue, while the ledger makes the system operable.

Further reading

  • MDN, WebRTC API: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebRTC_API
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • OpenTelemetry, Logs Data Model: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/

title: Repository checkout and Git LFS downloads are now faster
description:
Repository checkout and Git LFS downloads are now faster on Vercel, reducing the time spent preparing your project's files before a build.

title: SQL Deep Dive: Window Functions, Joins, CTEs, and Subqueries
description:
Introduction

This article covers four SQL concepts: window functions, joins, common table expressions (CTEs) and subqueries. Window functions let you rank rows, calculate running totals and compare a row to the ones around it without losing any data. Joins bring information from different tables together. CTEs break a long query into small named steps, and subqueries let one query use the result of another.

This article will use a hospital dataset which contains various tables. For each concept I explain what it does, show a query on that data and give the expected result.

1. Window Functions

A window function calculates across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them. Window function keeps every row and attaches the result to each one. Thus, for each row, SQL opens a "window" that shows some other rows. It looks through that window, calculates something, and writes the answer next to the row.

a. Ranking Functions

Ranking functions give each row a position inside its group. They include, ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK(), and differ only in how they handle ties that is rows with equal values.

  • ROW_NUMBER()-Ignores ties. Gives every row a unique number
  • RANK()-Tied rows get the same rank. The next rank skips numbers
  • DENSE_RANK()-Tied rows get the same rank. The next rank has no gaps

Based on the hospital dataset, we rank the medicine department based on the highest satisfaction score from highest as follows:

The result will be:

Visit_id 1002 and 1029 both scored 4.1, so both get rank 2.
After that, RANK jumps to 4 because rank 3 was "used up" by the tie. DENSE_RANK simply moves to 3.
ROW_NUMBER never repeats. When scores tie, it uses visit_id to decide the order. That is why visit_id was added to the ORDER BY.

NTILE(n)

NTILE(n) splits the ordered rows into n buckets of roughly equal size and tells which bucket each row is in. It is useful for quartiles (NTILE(4)) as well as percentiles.
Based on the hospital dataset, split the cardiology visits into groups of 4 based on the bill size, from highest bill to lowest bill:

The result will be:


This translates that 9 rows are divided by 4 buckets and leaves 1 extra row. The extra row goes to the first bucket, so bucket 1 has 3 rows and the other buckets have 2 each. Bucket 1 holds the most expensive visits.

b. Offset Functions

Offset functions lets a row look at another row in the same group: the one before, the one after, the first, or the last.
LAG() and LEAD()
LAG(column, offset, default) looks backward (at an earlier row).
LEAD(column, offset, default) looks forward (at a later row).

The offset is how many rows to move. It is 1 if left out. The default is the value to show when there is no such row otherwise, it is NULL.

In the hospital dataset, for instance patients came back for a second visit of patient IDs 1, 2, and 5. To get how their bills changed and how many days passed between visits is as follows:

The result will be:

Partition by patient_id means each patient is handled separately, so no one patient is compared to another.
A patient's first visit has no earlier visit, so previous_bill is null. Their last visit has no later visit, so next_bill is null.

3. Joins

A join matches rows from two tables using a condition, usually a primary key on one side and a foreign key on the other:
Below is the syntax used for joins:

select column
from table 1 
join kind table 2 
on table 1.common_column=table 2.common_column;

a. Inner Join

Inner Join - returns only the rows with matches in both tables
For instance, show the patients and the doctor assigned to them

The result will provide the doctors assigned to the respective patients. The 'f' and 'd' are aliases that save typing, ease of referencing and make it clear which table each column comes from.

b. Full Join

Full join returns everything from both/all tables regardless whether there is a match or not. Where rows match, they are combined. Where a row has no match, the other side is filled with null.

It basically returns the left join result and the right join result in one query.


The result will provide a list of all the doctors and the procedures done

c. Left Join

Left Join - returns every record from the left join, which is the table written before the join and matches on the right.
For instance, list all doctors and their respective departments

The result will provide all doctors and their respective departments

d. Right Join

Right Join - Returns every record from the right table and matches to the left
For instance, list all doctors and their respective departments


The result will provide all doctors and their respective departments

e. Cross Join

Cross Join - gives every possible combination. It pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second.

No need for the on clause. The only join where no common column is needed

For instance, in the hospital dataset suppose we want a show visit counts for every department.


The result will provide the following visits of each department

f. Natural Join

Natural Join joins tables with the same column names. It looks at both tables, finds every column that has the same name, and joins on all of them. It does not need to have an ON condition.
For instance, suppose we find the visits with their department name and respective bill costs


The result of the query will be

4. Subqueries

A subquery is a query written inside another query. It sits in parentheses, and the outer query uses its result.
Depending on where the subqueries are written there are different types of subqueries

  • where - lets the outer query filter rows using the answer of another query.
  • having - filters aggregated rows
  • select - generates a calculated column

For instance, the visits that costs more than the average bill:

select visit_id, total_bill_kes
from facts_visits 
where total_bill_kes > (select avg(total_bill_kes) from facts_visits);

The result generated will be

Subqueries can either be correlated or non-correlated

  • Correlated - subquery that cannot be executed without the main query
  • Non-correlated - subquery that can be executed without the main query. For instance 
(select avg(total_bill_kes)

Subquery Categories

Scalar - returns a single value
Table - returns multiple rows and multiple columns
Column - returns 1 column, multiple rows
Rows - returns 1 row, multiple columns

5. Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

A Common Table Expression or CTE, is a named temporary result that is defined at the top of a query and then used like a table in the rest of that query. It is a way to give a name to a step in the query.
A CTE starts with the word with
Think of it as giving a name to a subquery. For instance, which departments earned more than 100,000.
This first version depicts the query with a subquery, that is a step inside another query

select d.department_name, f.total_revenue
from(select department_id, sum(total_bill_kes) as total_revenue
from facts_visits f
group by department_id) as f
join departments d 
on d.department_id = f.department_id
where f.total_revenue > 100000
order by f.total_revenue desc;

This second version depicts a query with a CTE

with dept_revenue as 
(select department_id, sum(total_bill_kes) as total_revenue
from facts_visits f
group by department_id)
select d.department_name, f. total_revenue
from dept_revenue f
join departments d 
on d.department_id = f.department_id
where f.total_revenue > 100000
order by f.total_revenue desc;

The result for both queries will be as follows:

Conclusion

Window functions, joins, subqueries and CTEs each solve a different problem. Window functions rank rows and calculate running totals without losing any data. Joins combine tables, and the join type decides what happens to rows with no match. Subqueries let one query use the result of another, and CTEs turn long queries into named steps that are easy to read.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo of pwn.ai, a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use reusable column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Reusable column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use reusable column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.20
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Regular channel remains Looker 26.18.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.
