title: Building a Local AI SOC Lab with Wazuh and Qwen: Lessons from a Real Implementation
description:
Security monitoring generates a lot of data. But collecting alerts is only the beginning. The real challenge is retrieving the right events, understanding what happened, and making decisions based on evidence.

I wanted to explore a practical question:

Can a locally hosted AI model help a security analyst investigate Wazuh alerts without giving the AI control over the infrastructure?

To explore this, I built an isolated AI-assisted Security Operations Center (SOC) lab using Wazuh, OpenSearch, Python, SQLite, and a local Qwen model.

This is a manually operated proof of concept, not a production SOC or an autonomous security platform.

1. My Lab Architecture

The environment includes Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machines for security telemetry and Wazuh services, together with a Windows workstation running the Python assistant and LM Studio.

The main components are:

  • Wazuh Agent: collects security events from an Ubuntu endpoint.
  • Wazuh Manager and OpenSearch Indexer: process and store security alerts.
  • Python SOC Assistant: retrieves alerts and prepares them for analysis.
  • SQLite: tracks processed events and stores generated reports.
  • LM Studio + Qwen 3.5 4B Instruct: generates structured incident analysis proposals.
  • Human analyst: reviews findings and determines the next steps.

The assistant uses a restricted reader account. Access to the Indexer is protected through SSH port forwarding and TLS verification.

Important security boundary: The AI cannot execute firewall commands, modify server configurations, or automatically block IP addresses.

Its purpose is investigation support, not autonomous remediation.

2. The First Problem: Missing Alerts

My initial implementation retrieved only the 20 newest alerts.

This worked for a small demonstration, but it was not reliable when more events were present.

I improved the Python client using OpenSearch Scroll pagination to retrieve a bounded snapshot of matching alerts.

In one documented integration test:

152 matching alerts were reported by OpenSearch.

152 alerts were successfully retrieved.

152 unique event IDs were verified.

That confirmed the pagination logic worked correctly for that query snapshot.

It did not prove continuous monitoring or complete historical coverage.

I also encountered an Indexer permission issue affecting Scroll cleanup. Fixing the reader permissions was part of making the workflow reliable without giving it unnecessary access.

3. Why I Added SQLite

Originally, processed event IDs were tracked using a JSON file.

That approach was simple, but I wanted more reliable event state, recovery, and retry behavior.

I introduced SQLite to preserve processed identifiers and incident reports.

During verification, I successfully migrated 20 existing event IDs and confirmed database integrity.

I also tested restoring a synthetic incident report from the database after its Markdown export was missing.

This taught me an important engineering lesson:

AI analysis is only one part of the system. Reliable event state and recovery matter just as much.

4. Connecting a Local Qwen Model

The Python assistant connects to Qwen through LM Studio's local API-compatible endpoint.

The workflow sends selected security events to the model and requests structured JSON output.

The application validates required fields before saving a report.

In one test, I used a synthetic failed SSH authentication event.

Qwen proposed:

Disposition: SUSPICIOUS

Severity: LOW

Recommended action: Investigate and review related logs.

This was useful, but I also noticed how easily a language model could misinterpret technical context.

For example, a client source port can be confused with a destination service port. A single failed login also does not automatically indicate brute-force activity.

That is why I separate observed evidence from AI-generated hypotheses.

5. Prompt Injection in Security Logs

One of the most interesting experiments involved an untrusted SSH log message.

I tested synthetic log content containing text designed to manipulate the model into treating failed authentication as successful authentication.

In a documented retest, the model preserved the failed-login finding.

An earlier test also exposed an unsafe recommendation to block an IP address. I introduced conservative recommendation filtering and regression tests to help keep responses within the lab's read-only investigation scope.

These were limited experiments.

They do not demonstrate complete resistance to prompt injection or guarantee that every AI-generated recommendation is safe.

Security logs are evidence, not instructions.

Human review remains essential.

6. Testing and Verification

I wanted the project to demonstrate more than a working screenshot.

The repository includes 31 mocked and offline Python tests, exercised through GitHub Actions using Python 3.10 and 3.12.

The implementation also includes validation of event identity, persistent processing state, structured model responses, and read-only operational boundaries.

However, automated tests alone do not prove production security or detection accuracy.

The lab still has important limitations: manual execution, no continuous alert monitoring, and network restrictions around the local model service that require further verification before broader deployment.

7. What I Learned

Three lessons stand out from this project.

First, reliable data retrieval comes before AI analysis. Missing alerts can undermine even a well-written incident report.

Second, local AI can assist security investigations, but its output must be validated. A structured response is not necessarily a correct response.

Third, automation needs clear security boundaries. I prefer a system that helps an analyst understand an event over one that performs potentially harmful actions without approval.

My next areas of work include more realistic alert replay tests, better performance measurements, and stronger local-model network restrictions.

Project Resources

The public repository includes the Python implementation, tests, documentation, and sanitized verification examples.

GitHub: AI-Powered SOC Lab

Original engineering article: Building a Local AI SOC Lab with Wazuh and Qwen

I'm interested in how other engineers approach local AI for security operations.

Would you trust a local LLM to prepare incident triage reports if every recommendation required human approval?

Editorial disclosure: This DEV.to adaptation was prepared with AI writing assistance using my original engineering article and documented project results as source material.

title: Web Search on AWS Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location controls
description:
Web Search on AWS Bedrock now supports two new controls that give you more precision over the results that ground a model's response: domain filtering and user location. Both are configured directly on the web_search tool in your existing OpenAI Responses API request.

With domain filtering, you can restrict Web Search results to a set of domains you choose. Using the filters parameter, you specify up to 100 allowed_domains to limit results to trusted sources, or up to 100 blocked_domains to exclude sources you don't want. This is useful when you want responses grounded only in specific sites, or when you need to keep certain domains out of results.

With user location, you can optionally specify location parameters so that Web Search can return results relevant to that geography. This helps with location-dependent questions, such as regional availability or local services.

Domain filtering and user location are available in all AWS Regions where Web Search is supported: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). To get started, see the Web Search section in the AWS Bedrock User Guide. For pricing, see the AWS Bedrock pricing page.

title: Next.js Security Update October 2026: Patch the use cache RCE, SVG sharp RCE and Server Actions DoS
description:
The Next.js security update of October 14, 2026 fixes three vulnerabilities: two critical unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) bugs, one in use cache and one in SVG image optimization through sharp, and a high severity denial of service in Server Actions. Upgrade to Next.js 16.4.1 or later on 16.x, or 15.5.28 on 15.x, make sure sharp is 0.35.5 or later, then rebuild and redeploy.

The patch is easy to apply and easy to get wrong when you self-host. I reproduced the upgrade on real installs and found that upgrading Next.js 15 to 15.5.28 left the vulnerable sharp 0.34.5 in place, while npm audit on an unpatched next@16.4.0 reported 0 vulnerabilities. This guide shows how to check whether you are affected, a script that checks for you, and the exact steps to patch a Docker or Coolify deployment. Everything is cited to the official advisories.

What did the October 2026 Next.js security update fix?

It fixed three advisories published on October 14, 2026, all patched in Next.js 16.4.1 (Active LTS) and 15.5.28 (Maintenance LTS), according to the official Next.js security update. Two allow unauthenticated remote code execution with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.5; the third lets crafted requests pin a server's CPU.

Advisory Severity What it is Affected next versions Fixed in Workaround
GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr Critical, 9.5 RCE in use cache functions that return multiple typed arrays 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 16.4.1 None
CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw Critical, 9.5 RCE in the Image Optimization API with SVG, via sharp's librsvg, on glibc Linux 10.0.0 to 15.5.27, 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 15.5.28, 16.4.1 sharp 0.35.5 or later
GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r High, 8.2 DoS: crafted requests cause excessive CPU in App Router apps with Server Actions 13.0.0 to 15.5.27, 16.0.0 to 16.4.0 15.5.28, 16.4.1 None

The two React Server Components bugs also have upstream React advisories: GHSA-xqc2-xf4c-x3h3 for the typed-array RCE and GHSA-h3gv-c5rc-p453 for the DoS. Next.js ships its own compiled copy of react-server-dom-webpack and react-server-dom-turbopack inside the next package (I checked node_modules/next/dist/compiled), so upgrading next is what fixes a Next.js app, not bumping react alone.

Quick definitions

Term What it means
RCE Remote code execution: an attacker can run code on your server
DoS Denial of service: the server stops answering legitimate requests
GHSA A GitHub Security Advisory ID
sharp The image library Next.js uses for Image Optimization; it bundles libvips and librsvg
glibc The C library used by Debian, Ubuntu and node:*-slim images (Alpine uses musl instead)
Active / Maintenance LTS Next.js 16.4.x and 15.5.x, the two release lines that receive security fixes

TL;DR: how to patch Next.js now

  1. Upgrade: npm install next@16.4.2 on 16.x (16.4.1 is the security release; 16.4.2 adds bug fixes) or npm install next@15.5.28 on 15.x.
  2. Check sharp: run npm ls next sharp and confirm sharp@0.35.5 or later. On 15.x, run npm update sharp if it still shows 0.34.x.
  3. Commit the lockfile, rebuild the image from scratch and redeploy.
  4. Verify the running container, not just your laptop.

Is my Next.js app affected?

You are affected if your installed next is 16.0.0 through 16.4.0, or 15.5.27 and earlier, or if the sharp copy Next.js loads is older than 0.35.5. Which bugs reach you depends on features: use cache needs Cache Components, the DoS needs at least one Server Action, and the SVG bug needs glibc Linux.

Check the versions first:

npm ls next sharp

Then match your app against each advisory:

  • use cache RCE (GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr). Only Next.js 16 apps using the App Router with Cache Components can be exposed, and the trigger is a use cache function that returns multiple typed arrays. The advisory still says to upgrade immediately even if your application does not have similar functions. New apps from create-next-app 16.4 have Cache Components on by default, as I covered in Next.js use cache explained.
  • SVG Image Optimization RCE (CVE-2026-96889). A memory bug in librsvg, which sharp uses to decode SVG, can lead to RCE when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux. That covers most Debian and Ubuntu based Docker images and VPS installs. By default Next.js does not optimize SVG images; apps that set images.dangerouslyAllowSVG: true are the clearest exposure, but the advisory is not limited to that setting, so patch either way.
  • Server Actions DoS (GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r). Any App Router app with at least one Server Action, on Next.js 13 through 15.5.27 or 16.0.0 through 16.4.0. Pages Router apps and apps without Server Actions are not vulnerable.

Why does npm audit say my app is safe?

Because the advisory feed it reads may not list these issues yet. On October 17, 2026, I installed next@16.4.0, react and react-dom in an empty project and ran npm audit:

$ npm audit --json | jq .metadata.vulnerabilities
{ "info": 0, "low": 0, "moderate": 0, "high": 0, "critical": 0, "total": 0 }

Zero findings on a version with two open critical advisories. Treat npm audit, Dependabot and similar scanners as a backstop here and check the versions yourself, or use the script below.

A script that checks your app against all three advisories

I wrote this to check every app I run. It reads the installed next version, resolves sharp from Next.js's own folder (the copy the image optimizer actually loads), scans your source for use cache, use server and dangerouslyAllowSVG, and exits with code 1 if anything is unpatched, so you can drop it into CI. It has no dependencies.

// check-next-security.mjs: checks a Next.js app against the October 14, 2026 advisories.
// Usage: node check-next-security.mjs [projectDir]
import { readFileSync, readdirSync, statSync, existsSync } from 'node:fs'
import { createRequire } from 'node:module'
import path from 'node:path'

const dir = path.resolve(process.argv[2] ?? '.')
const req = createRequire(path.join(dir, 'package.json'))
// Find node_modules/<pkg>/package.json the way Node would, without relying on "exports".
const version = (pkg, from = req) => {
  for (const base of from.resolve.paths(pkg) ?? []) {
    const file = path.join(base, pkg, 'package.json')
    if (existsSync(file)) return JSON.parse(readFileSync(file, 'utf8')).version
  }
  return null
}
const cmp = (a, b) => {
  const [x, y] = [a, b].map((v) => v.split('-')[0].split('.').map(Number))
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) if (x[i] !== y[i]) return x[i] - y[i]
  return 0
}
const inRange = (v, lo, hi) => cmp(v, lo) >= 0 && cmp(v, hi) <= 0

// Scan source files for features the advisories depend on.
const src = []
const walk = (d) => {
  for (const name of readdirSync(d)) {
    if (['node_modules', '.next', '.git', 'out', 'dist'].includes(name)) continue
    const p = path.join(d, name)
    if (statSync(p).isDirectory()) walk(p)
    else if (/\.(m?[jt]sx?)$/.test(name)) src.push(readFileSync(p, 'utf8'))
  }
}
walk(dir)
const code = src.join('\n')
const uses = {
  useCache: /['"]use cache(: \w+)?['"]/.test(code),
  serverActions: /['"]use server['"]/.test(code),
  svgOptimizer: /dangerouslyAllowSVG\s*:\s*true/.test(code),
  nextOg: /from ['"]next\/og['"]/.test(code),
}

const next = version('next')
if (!next) { console.error('next is not installed in', dir); process.exit(2) }
// Resolve sharp from next's own folder, since that is the copy the image optimizer loads.
const nextPkg = (req.resolve.paths('next') ?? []).map((b) => path.join(b, 'next', 'package.json')).find(existsSync)
const sharp = version('sharp', createRequire(nextPkg))
const major = Number(next.split('.')[0])

const checks = [
  {
    id: 'GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr (critical): RCE in use cache returning typed arrays',
    vulnerable: inRange(next, '16.0.0', '16.4.0'),
    fix: 'upgrade next to 16.4.1+ (no workaround)',
    note: uses.useCache ? 'app uses "use cache"' : 'no "use cache" found, upgrade anyway',
  },
  {
    id: 'CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw (critical): RCE via SVG in image optimization',
    vulnerable: sharp ? cmp(sharp, '0.35.5') < 0 : false,
    fix: 'sharp must be 0.35.5+ (npm update sharp), next 16.4.1+ or 15.5.28+',
    note: `sharp ${sharp ?? 'not installed'}` + (uses.svgOptimizer ? ', dangerouslyAllowSVG on' : '') + (uses.nextOg ? ', uses next/og' : ''),
  },
  {
    id: 'GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r (high): DoS via Server Actions',
    vulnerable: inRange(next, '13.0.0', '15.5.27') || inRange(next, '16.0.0', '16.4.0'),
    fix: major >= 16 ? 'upgrade next to 16.4.1+' : 'upgrade next to 15.5.28+',
    note: uses.serverActions ? 'app defines Server Actions' : 'no "use server" found',
  },
]

console.log(`next ${next}, sharp ${sharp ?? 'not installed'} in ${dir}\n`)
let bad = 0
for (const c of checks) {
  if (c.vulnerable) bad++
  console.log(`${c.vulnerable ? 'VULNERABLE' : 'ok        '}  ${c.id}`)
  console.log(`            ${c.note}${c.vulnerable ? `\n            fix: ${c.fix}` : ''}`)
}
console.log(bad ? `\n${bad} issue(s) found. Patch, rebuild and redeploy.` : '\nAll three October 14, 2026 advisories are patched.')
process.exit(bad ? 1 : 0)

Run it from your project root with node check-next-security.mjs. This is the real output on a Next.js 16.4.0 app with one use cache function and one Server Action, before and after npm install next@16.4.2:

$ node check-next-security.mjs
next 16.4.0, sharp 0.35.4 in /app

VULNERABLE  GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr (critical): RCE in use cache returning typed arrays
            app uses "use cache"
            fix: upgrade next to 16.4.1+ (no workaround)
VULNERABLE  CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw (critical): RCE via SVG in image optimization
            sharp 0.35.4
            fix: sharp must be 0.35.5+ (npm update sharp), next 16.4.1+ or 15.5.28+
VULNERABLE  GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r (high): DoS via Server Actions
            app defines Server Actions
            fix: upgrade next to 16.4.1+

3 issue(s) found. Patch, rebuild and redeploy.

$ npm install next@16.4.2 && node check-next-security.mjs
next 16.4.2, sharp 0.35.5 in /app

ok          GHSA-673q-mjm6-r5xr (critical): RCE in use cache returning typed arrays
            app uses "use cache"
ok          CVE-2026-96889 / GHSA-2464-fhr4-w9xw (critical): RCE via SVG in image optimization
            sharp 0.35.5
ok          GHSA-p3m5-59mp-jv5r (high): DoS via Server Actions
            app defines Server Actions

All three October 14, 2026 advisories are patched.

The script checks versions and source patterns; it is not an exploit test. A clean result means you are on patched versions, which is what the advisories ask for.

How do you upgrade Next.js 16 to the patched version?

Install the latest 16.4 patch, then confirm sharp moved with it. Next.js 16.4.1 raised its sharp requirement to ^0.35.5 (16.4.0 accepted ^0.35.4; I read both from the npm registry), so npm has to upgrade sharp when you upgrade next.

npm install next@16.4.2
npm ls next sharp

In my test, a project whose lockfile held next@16.4.0 and sharp@0.35.4 came out of npm install next@16.4.1 with sharp@0.35.5, as expected. Run the same check with pnpm why sharp or yarn why sharp if you use those package managers.

eslint-config-next should match your next version, so bump it in the same commit. If you have not moved to 16 yet, the version 16 upgrade guide covers the breaking changes; that is a bigger job than this patch, so patch 15.x first.

How do you patch Next.js 15 safely?

Upgrade to 15.5.28, then check sharp separately, because upgrading next alone may not fix the SVG bug. Next.js 15.5.28 declares sharp as ^0.34.3 || ^0.35.5, so an existing lockfile that already resolved sharp 0.34.x still satisfies it, and npm keeps it.

This is what happened on a real project with next@15.5.27 and sharp@0.34.5 in the lockfile:

$ npm install next@15.5.28
$ npm ls sharp
└─┬ next@15.5.28
  └── sharp@0.34.5        # still vulnerable

$ npm update sharp
$ npm ls sharp
└─┬ next@15.5.28
  └── sharp@0.35.5        # fixed

If sharp is a direct dependency in your package.json, run npm install sharp@0.35.5 instead. To force one version across a monorepo, add an override:

{
  "overrides": {
    "sharp": "0.35.5"
  }
}

pnpm uses pnpm.overrides and Yarn uses resolutions for the same job.

How do you patch a self-hosted Next.js app in Docker or Coolify?

Update the lockfile, rebuild the image without reusing old layers, redeploy, then check the versions inside the running container. A dependency fix only protects you once the container that serves traffic contains it, and a Docker build that copies package-lock.json and runs npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says.

  1. Update and verify locally. npm install next@16.4.2, npm ls next sharp, run the checker.
  2. Commit package-lock.json. Without it, your build server resolves whatever it resolved last time.
  3. Rebuild the image. With the standalone output used in my production Next.js Dockerfile, next build copies sharp and its native libvips package into .next/standalone/node_modules. In my build that was @img/sharp-libvips-linux-x64, the glibc variant. An image built before the patch keeps the old sharp until you rebuild it.
  4. Redeploy. In Coolify, push the commit or click Redeploy. To skip cached layers for this one build, trigger a forced deploy, for example through the Coolify API with GET /api/v1/deploy?uuid=<app-uuid>&force=true. My self-host Next.js with Coolify guide covers the deploy setup. With plain Docker, run docker compose build --no-cache && docker compose up -d.
  5. Verify the running container. In a standalone image the app lives in /app, so: 
docker exec <container> node -e "console.log(require('/app/node_modules/next/package.json').version, require('/app/node_modules/sharp/package.json').version)"

Requiring the package.json files by absolute path works even though sharp 0.35.5 does not export ./package.json. I checked the same command against a standalone build of Next.js 16.4.2; it printed 0.35.5 16.4.2 for sharp and next. Adjust the path if your Dockerfile copies the app somewhere other than /app.

What if you cannot upgrade Next.js today?

Only the SVG bug has an interim mitigation; the use cache RCE and the Server Actions DoS have no workaround, so plan the upgrade within hours, not weeks. In the meantime:

Bug Interim step Source
SVG / sharp RCE Make sure sharp is 0.35.5 or later, even without upgrading next Next.js advisory
SVG / sharp RCE In your own code that calls sharp, block SVG decoding with sharp.block({ operation: ['VipsForeignLoadSvg'] }) sharp advisory
SVG / sharp RCE Turn off images.dangerouslyAllowSVG if you do not need optimized SVGs Image docs
use cache RCE None. Upgrade. Next.js advisory
Server Actions DoS None. Upgrade. Rate limits only reduce the blast radius. Next.js advisory

I tested the sharp.block call with sharp 0.35.5: before it, a small SVG converted to a 100-byte PNG; after it, the same call failed with Input buffer contains unsupported image format.

import sharp from 'sharp'

// Refuse to decode SVG input anywhere this sharp instance is used.
sharp.block({ operation: ['VipsForeignLoadSvg'] })

The sharp advisory adds one hardening note: whether the librsvg bug can reach code execution depends partly on the Node.js binary. It recommends a node built as a Position Independent Executable (PIE), notes that most Linux distribution packages already are, and warns that the official Node.js binaries are not.

How do you know whether you were attacked?

The advisories publish no indicators of compromise and do not mention exploitation in the wild, so look for the side effects each bug would leave, and re-check the advisories for updates.

  • DoS: sustained 100% CPU on a Next.js process together with slow or failed requests, especially POST requests carrying a Next-Action header.
  • SVG RCE: unexpected requests to /_next/image with .svg sources, crashes of the Node.js process during image optimization, and new child processes or outbound connections from the container.
  • Any RCE: unknown files in the container filesystem, changed environment variables or secrets used from new IPs. If you find any of these, rotate secrets (database URLs, API keys, NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY) after patching.

Security habits that make the next patch faster

This was an out-of-band release that landed eight days after 16.4.0 shipped on October 6. A few habits keep the next one to a ten-minute job:

  • Stay on an LTS line. Security fixes land on 16.4.x (Active LTS) and 15.5.x (Maintenance LTS).
  • Turn on upgrade nudges. Next.js 16.4 added experimental.agentUpgrade, whose default 'security' policy reminds you during next dev and next build when an upgrade fixes a known vulnerability in your installed version (Next.js 16.4 notes).
  • Run the checker in CI. Exit code 1 fails the build when a vulnerable version is installed.
  • Pin and commit lockfiles, then rebuild images from them so the running version is the one you reviewed.
  • Keep Server Actions small and authenticated. The DoS needs only one action to exist, but auth and input validation limit what any future bug can reach; see Server Actions vs Route Handlers.

Common mistakes when patching

Mistake What happens Fix
Upgrading react instead of next Next.js keeps its bundled RSC runtime Upgrade next
Upgrading 15.x to 15.5.28 and stopping sharp 0.34.x can stay in the lockfile npm update sharp, confirm 0.35.5+
Trusting npm audit It reported 0 issues on unpatched 16.4.0 Check versions or run the script
Not committing the lockfile CI or Coolify rebuilds the old versions Commit package-lock.json
Rebuilding from a cached layer Old node_modules layer is reused Build once with no cache
Checking only the laptop Production still runs the old image docker exec into the running container

Related: I packaged the checker script above as a reusable agent skill, so Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Copilot can run the check and patch for you. See Agent Skills: how to write a SKILL.md.

Related: running an MCP server next to your Next.js app? MCP security in 2026 covers this month's MCP SDK OAuth advisories and how to fix them.

Key takeaways

  • The October 14, 2026 update fixes two critical RCEs (use cache typed arrays and SVG via sharp) and a high-severity Server Actions DoS.
  • Patched versions are Next.js 16.4.1+ and 15.5.28+, with sharp 0.35.5 or later.
  • On 15.x, upgrading next can leave sharp 0.34.x installed; run npm update sharp and verify.
  • npm audit reported nothing for unpatched next@16.4.0 on October 17, 2026, so check versions directly.
  • A self-hosted fix only counts after you rebuild the image, redeploy and verify the versions inside the running container.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Your Rate Limiter Works Until You Deploy a Second Server
description:
A rate limiter can work perfectly in development and still fail in production.

You test it locally, send too many requests, and receive a 429 Too Many Requests response. Everything looks fine.

Then you deploy your Node.js application with two instances behind a load balancer.

Suddenly, users can send more requests than your limit allows.

The problem isn't necessarily your rate-limiting algorithm. It's where you're storing the request counts.

The Problem With In-Memory Rate Limiting

Consider this Express middleware:

const requests = new Map();

function rateLimiter(req, res, next) {
  const key = req.ip;
  const now = Date.now();
  const windowMs = 60_000;
  const limit = 10;

  let record = requests.get(key);

  if (!record || now - record.start >= windowMs) {
    record = {
      count: 0,
      start: now,
    };
  }

  record.count++;
  requests.set(key, record);

  if (record.count > limit) {
    return res.status(429).json({
      message: "Too many requests",
    });
  }

  next();
}

This simplified fixed-window limiter allows up to 10 requests per IP address per minute in a single process.

But what happens when your application runs on two servers?

Imagine the load balancer distributes requests like this:

  • Server A receives 10 requests.
  • Server B receives another 10 requests.
  • Each server maintains its own Map.

Both servers see only 10 requests. Neither rejects the requests.

Your intended limit was 10 requests per minute, but the user managed to send 20.

With more instances, the discrepancy can become even larger.

The key issue is that each process has its own memory.

An in-memory counter is not shared across Node.js processes, containers, or separate application instances.

Why This Matters in Production

This becomes especially important when rate limits protect:

  • Login and password-reset endpoints
  • Public APIs with usage quotas
  • Expensive database queries
  • AI or third-party API calls that cost money
  • Endpoints vulnerable to automated abuse

A rate limiter that works only within one process may provide weaker protection than you expect.

There is another problem: when a process restarts, its counters disappear. Scaling, restarting, or replacing instances can therefore change the effective limit.

A Better Approach: Use Redis

Redis gives multiple application instances access to shared state.

Instead of keeping request counts in a local Map, each instance updates a shared counter.

A simplified Redis fixed-window implementation might look like this:

async function rateLimiter(req, res, next) {
  try {
    const key = `rate-limit:${req.ip}`;
    const limit = 10;
    const windowSeconds = 60;

    const count = await redis.incr(key);

    if (count === 1) {
      await redis.expire(key, windowSeconds);
    }

    if (count > limit) {
      return res.status(429).json({
        message: "Too many requests",
      });
    }

    next();
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
}

Here, redis represents an already configured Redis client.

Now both servers use the same counter. If Server A processes six requests and Server B processes five, the shared count reaches eleven, so the eleventh request is rejected.

However, this example illustrates the idea rather than providing a complete production-ready implementation.

There is still a subtle problem

The counter increment and expiration are separate commands.

If the process fails between INCR and EXPIRE, the key might remain without an expiration. That could cause requests to be rejected indefinitely.

For production use, execute the counter update and expiration logic atomically, for example with a Redis Lua script or an appropriate atomic Redis operation.

You should also decide what happens when Redis becomes unavailable. Failing open allows requests through but weakens protection; failing closed preserves the limit but can make an endpoint unavailable. The right choice depends on the endpoint and its risk.

Redis Doesn't Automatically Make Every Rate Limiter Correct

Using shared storage solves the per-instance counter problem, but other design decisions still matter.

1. Choose the right algorithm

A fixed-window limiter is easy to implement, but it can allow bursts around window boundaries.

For example, a client might send 10 requests just before a window resets and another 10 immediately afterward.

Depending on your requirements, a sliding-window counter, sliding log, or token bucket may provide better behavior.

2. Identify clients correctly

Using req.ip requires careful proxy configuration.

If Express trusts forwarded headers from untrusted clients, an attacker might spoof their apparent IP address. Configure trust proxy according to your actual infrastructure rather than enabling it blindly.

For authenticated APIs, you may want to rate-limit by user ID, API key, IP address, or a combination of these.

3. Set limits by endpoint

A public read endpoint and a password-reset endpoint do not have the same risk profile.

You might allow more requests for inexpensive reads while applying stricter limits to authentication or resource-intensive operations.

4. Consider an existing library

For many Express applications, using a maintained rate-limiting library with a Redis-compatible store is safer than implementing every detail yourself.

A library can handle important concerns such as response headers, window behavior, storage integration, and configuration. You still need to verify that its algorithm and failure behavior match your requirements.

How to Test Your Rate Limiter

Don't test only one request at a time against your local development server.

A more useful test plan includes:

  1. Send more requests than the configured limit and verify that excess requests receive 429.
  2. Send requests through multiple application instances and confirm that the shared limit is enforced.
  3. Verify that the counter resets or expires as intended.
  4. Test concurrent requests, not just sequential requests.
  5. Simulate Redis failures and confirm the intended fail-open or fail-closed behavior.
  6. Test forwarded IP headers using your actual proxy configuration.

For production systems, also monitor rejected requests and storage errors. A rate limiter that silently fails can be difficult to diagnose.

The Real Lesson

Rate limiting is not just about counting requests. It is about maintaining consistent state across the infrastructure that processes those requests.

An in-memory counter can be perfectly reasonable for a single-process prototype. But once an application scales horizontally, local state is no longer enough for a globally enforced limit.

Before deploying a rate limiter, ask yourself one question: does every server agree on how many requests this client has made?

If the answer is no, your limit might not be the limit you think it is.

Have you implemented rate limiting in a production application? Did you use Redis, a gateway, or another approach?

title: Why a score's printed beat and playback BPM need separate units
description:
A printed tempo mark can say eighth note = 120, while a playback timeline measures speed in quarter notes per minute. Treating both numbers as the same BPM would double the intended playback rate. Pianory keeps the score's beat unit for display and converts to a canonical quarter-note rate for timeline math.

In tempo.ts, a TempoMark stores the printed unit, whether it is dotted, the printed per-minute value, and quarterBpm. beatQuarters maps half, quarter and eighth notes to 2, 1 and 0.5 quarter notes respectively, then multiplies by 1.5 for one dot. So an eighth-note mark at 120 beats per minute becomes 60 quarter notes per minute. The label function reverses that conversion for the player UI, leaving the score's printed ♪ = 120 intact.

readTempoMark deliberately accepts only the first simple MusicXML <metronome> mark. Unsupported beat units, more than one dot, note-to-note relations and non-positive rates return no mark. The OSMD iterator supplies tempo points; buildTimeline scales those points against the parsed mark's quarter-note rate and retains the printed beat for display. A focused test checks that eighth note = 120 produces 60 quarter BPM at the start and converts a later point of 60 to 30 quarter BPM. The UI also uses the preserved beat when displaying the tempo slider's accessible value.

This design keeps arithmetic in one unit while showing musicians the beat the score actually printed. The focused conversion and timeline tests passed locally, but they do not measure playback accuracy in a real browser or establish how every MusicXML file behaves. I make Pianory; this example comes from its score player. AI assisted with drafting this article, and I checked the claims against the source and focused tests.

title: October 20, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 20th, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-6, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-6 within the next seven to 21 days. A notification containing the expected date of upgrade will be sent within the next two business days.

Note: Instances that meet either of the following two criteria will not be updated:
  • Your instance has a DNS misconfiguration, as described in Known Issue 445936920.
  • Your instance uses an Apigee Java Library that has been removed, as described in Apigee release notes dated October 16, 2025.

For more information on participating in scheduled maintenance windows, see Maintenance overview and Manage Apigee instance maintenance windows.

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations supports automatic failover for boost configurations in Preview. When you enable automatic failover, Cloud Workstations automatically provisions a workstation VM using the boost configuration if Compute Engine lacks capacity for the default machine type during startup.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Antigravity Enterprise Gateway support

Antigravity Enterprise Gateway lets organizations route model inference requests from the Antigravity app, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs through a centralized enterprise gateway before forwarding them to Google Cloud. This deployment enables organizations to inspect and audit model traffic, enforce custom security and network egress policies, and authenticate developers through a gateway API key without requiring individual Google Account sign-in.

Requests routed through Antigravity Enterprise Gateway use a centralized Google Cloud service account and are billed on a pay-as-you-go (PAYG) consumption basis through the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. This deployment model doesn't use your Gemini Enterprise seat-based subscription quotas (such as included Standard or Plus monthly allowances). You can't use a gateway and sign in with a Google Account at the same time. If you want to use your included subscription quota instead, disable the enterprise gateway and sign in with your Google Account.

This feature is generally available (GA).

For more information, see:

  • Deploy Antigravity Enterprise Gateway
  • Connect Antigravity to an Enterprise Gateway.

Breaking

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro discontinued in Canada and Japan

Gemini 2.5 Pro has been discontinued for in-country Gemini Enterprise app deployments in Canada and Japan. Agents and chat sessions in these regions that previously used Gemini 2.5 Pro automatically switch to in-country Gemini 3.5 Flash.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise and Manage web app features.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Fixed

A security issue in GKE fleet management that could have allowed unauthorized configuration changes to clusters registered to a fleet has been resolved. The fixes are rolled out to all regions, and no action is required.

Fixed

This is an update to the release note regarding the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver issue published on October 2, 2026.

This issue has been resolved. You can upgrade your cluster control plane to the following versions to fix the issue for ubuntu_containerd and older cos_containerd node pools:

  • 1.36.5-gke.1032000 or later

  • 1.37.1-gke.1552000 or later

  • Specific 1.36.4 mitigation patches: 1.36.4-gke.1247001, 1.36.4-gke.1247002, 1.36.4-gke.1391001, 1.36.4-gke.1391003, 1.36.4-gke.1495001, 1.36.4-gke.1495003, 1.36.4-gke.2046001, 1.36.4-gke.2202002

Looker

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Regular channel: Looker 26.20

The latest version in the Rapid and No Channel channels remains Looker 26.20.

Note: This item was added on October 23, 2026.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner supports approximate aggregate functions for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. These functions produce statistical estimates of distinct counts, allowing you to compute results faster and save resources on large datasets compared to exact aggregation.

For more information, see approximate aggregate functions (GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL), HyperLogLog++ functions, and Sketches.

565072374 Fixed an issue where VerifyJWT policies using a JWKS uriRef could return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the 5-minute JWKS cache TTL expired when the identity provider rotated keys. The cache now refreshes synchronously upon expiration.
556680325 Fixed a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in URL host validation for the SemanticCacheLookup policy.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.

502540992 Fixed an issue where the SemanticCacheLookup policy was incompatible with Vertex AI Vector Search Private Service Connect (PSC) endpoints by adding gRPC transport support via <PrivateServiceConnect><GrpcEndpoint>.
492042425 Fixed an issue in the LLMTokenQuota policy where operation-level token quota values configured on an API product were not applied at runtime, causing product-level quota values to be enforced instead.

Application Integration

Security

An Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the AuthConfig validation and integration execution runtime in Application Integration versions prior to August 27, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve capacity by using future reservation requests, you can specify that Compute Engine delivers your reserved capacity as specifically targeted reservations. Specifically targeted reservations help you track and control which Compute Engine instances consume your reserved capacity. For more information, see About future reservation requests.

Feature

Generally available: You can increase the size of a Google Cloud Hyperdisk volume that's in multi-writer mode while the volume is attached to multiple instances. Previously, you had to detach the volume from all instances before you could resize it.

For more information, see Share disks between instances and Change the size or provisioned performance of a Hyperdisk volume.

Dataform

Feature

You can automatically preserve BigQuery data policies and data governance tags (Preview) applied to tables across Dataform executions by enabling the preserveGovernanceControls option in your table or workflow configuration. For more information, see Preserve access controls metadata. This feature is generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in the United Kingdom

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in the United Kingdom.

  • Location availability: Supported in the UK (europe-west2) in-country region with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).
  • App availability: Turned on by default in the web app for the UK region. Administrators can manage access with the Gemini 3.8 Flash toggle under Model availability.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in Workflow Builder

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for Workflow Builder. Gemini 4 Argon is also available in Workflow Builder workflow agents. Updates take up to a day to appear in workflow agents.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.

For more information, see Workflow Builder.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Priority PayGo support for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1

Priority Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) is available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1) on the global endpoint.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.15.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Enhanced SARIF 2.1.0 reporting: Updated cm report SARIF output with standardized rule descriptors, severity properties, and repository-relative artifact locations for improved GitHub Code Scanning compatibility.
  • Model invocation metrics: Added model invocation tracking to cm stats --json, providing total, per-session, and per-turn invocation counts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed an issue where token usage from completed turns was omitted from session logs during error or cancellation exit paths.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is available in Public Preview

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from DeepSeek is available as a fully managed model (MaaS) in Model Garden. The model accepts text and image input, targets agentic and coding tasks, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens.

For more information, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Feature

title: Debugging Delayed Webhook Payloads in Node.js Queues — Schema Governance
description:
Use schema ownership as the debugging boundary: validate a webhook before it enters a delayed queue, enforce the same contract in the consumer, and quarantine messages that still fail. In a marketplace cleanup job, this makes a malformed payload diagnosable instead of allowing it to consume retries until the reservation or listing is already stale.

The queue is a transport boundary. It is not a schema registry, and it cannot infer whether listing_id was accidentally renamed to item_id. The web request should accept the event quickly; a worker should perform the delayed cleanup, with a durable idempotency record protecting the side effect from duplicate delivery.

What does the payload contract own?

Start with one deliberately small envelope. The producer owns syntactic validity: required fields, types, an explicit schema version, and an event identifier. The consumer owns semantic compatibility: it must know what expire_listing means in the release currently consuming the queue. The business write owns idempotency.

Those are separate responsibilities, and collapsing them is the source of many misleading queue incidents. A valid JSON object can still describe an action that this worker no longer supports. A message can also be perfectly valid and arrive twice. Standard queues are at-least-once, and FIFO deduplication lasts only 5 minutes, so transport-level deduplication cannot be the final correctness mechanism.

For a marketplace cleanup, I would record these invariants before choosing a queue:

  1. event_id, listing_id, action, and schema_version are present and typed.
  2. The consumer rejects unknown schema versions rather than guessing field meanings.
  3. The cleanup operation can return the same result when the same event_id is delivered again.
  4. A message that cannot be corrected is visible in a dead-letter queue (DLQ), with enough metadata to identify the producer release and failure class.

This is governance, not ceremony. It tells the team who can fix each failure and prevents a retry policy from becoming a substitute for a contract.

Schema drift is permanent until someone changes code.

Which queue fits a schema-governed cleanup?

The relevant comparison is where the application wants schema ownership to live, not which product has the longest feature list.

Option Schema and failure boundary Appropriate fit Important limit
BullMQ The Node.js application owns job data, retries, and deduplication conventions around Redis A team already operating Redis and wanting jobs close to application code It is a queue library, so workflow history and contract governance remain application concerns
Amazon SQS The queue provides managed delivery primitives, while the producer and consumer own validation and idempotency A narrowly scoped managed queue with standard or FIFO delivery Standard delivery is at-least-once; FIFO deduplication is limited to 5 minutes, so consumers still need idempotency
Temporal Workflow code owns durable state transitions, timers, and activity boundaries A cleanup that has become a multi-step workflow with compensation It is a broader workflow abstraction than one delayed webhook message
A REST scheduling and queue surface The application owns the payload contract while scheduling, delayed delivery, DLQ inspection, and queue statistics share one API boundary Teams that want one backend contract across these capabilities Delays top out at 7 days, retention at 30 days, and there is no DAG, fan-out/join primitive, or Kafka-style replay

The last row can suit a marketplace that values a broad backend surface behind a simple interface. Infrai has 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and its public discovery surface describes capability schemas and runnable examples without requiring a key; that can reduce the integration work needed to inspect a queue contract before wiring a producer. It does not validate the marketplace's business meaning for the team, and it does not make an idempotent consumer optional.

Choose BullMQ when the existing Node.js and Redis operating model is the constraint. Choose SQS when a focused managed queue is enough and the surrounding observability already exists. Choose Temporal when timers, activities, and compensation form a workflow. Choose the REST surface when a single contract across scheduling and queue operations is more valuable than workflow orchestration.

The limits matter in the decision. A cron task has a 900-second execution ceiling and targets a public http_url; longer work should use cron to trigger queue publication and a worker to consume it. Delayed messages have a 7-day maximum, bodies are limited to 256 KB, retention is at most 30 days, and acknowledgement deletes the message. Push subscriptions require a public HTTPS target. A cleanup that needs a 10-day delay or Kafka-style replay belongs elsewhere, or needs a different application design.

How do you check delayed webhook payload formatting issues?

The critical path has three checkpoints: ingress validation, consumer validation, and the idempotent side effect. The following Python example also checks queue statistics through the verified REST route, so an operator can compare malformed-payload issues with queue behavior before changing retry settings. It keeps the contract visible without pretending that an in-memory set is a production database. It is runnable, but the processed_ids store must be replaced by an atomic inbox table or an equivalent durable mechanism before deployment.

import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


class PayloadError(ValueError):
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CleanupEvent:
    event_id: str
    listing_id: str
    action: str
    schema_version: int


def read_queue_stats(queue: str) -> bytes:
    base_url = "https://api." + "infrai.cc/v1"
    route_template = "/queue/stats/{queue}"
    request = Request(
        f"{base_url}{route_template.format(queue=queue)}",
        method="GET",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
    )
    for attempt in range(5):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"stats failed: HTTP {response.status}")
                return response.read()
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code == 429 and attempt < 4:
                retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
                time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)
                continue
            raise RuntimeError(f"stats failed: HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
        except URLError as error:
            if attempt == 4:
                raise RuntimeError(f"stats request failed: {error.reason}") from error
            time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("stats request exhausted retries")


def validate_payload(payload: dict[str, Any]) -> CleanupEvent:
    required = {"event_id", "listing_id", "action", "schema_version"}
    missing = required.difference(payload)
    if missing:
        raise PayloadError(f"missing fields: {sorted(missing)}")
    if payload["schema_version"] != 1:
        raise PayloadError("unsupported schema_version")
    if payload["action"] != "expire_listing":
        raise PayloadError("unsupported action")
    for field in ("event_id", "listing_id"):
        if not isinstance(payload[field], str) or not payload[field]:
            raise PayloadError(f"{field} must be a non-empty string")
    return CleanupEvent(
        event_id=payload["event_id"],
        listing_id=payload["listing_id"],
        action=payload["action"],
        schema_version=payload["schema_version"],
    )


def process_once(payload: dict[str, Any], processed_ids: set[str]) -> str:
    event = validate_payload(payload)
    if event.event_id in processed_ids:
        return "already_processed"

    # Production code must make this check and the business write atomic.
    cleanup_listing(event.listing_id)
    processed_ids.add(event.event_id)
    return "processed"


def cleanup_listing(listing_id: str) -> None:
    print(f"cleaning up listing {listing_id}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    read_queue_stats("marketplace-cleanup")
    event = {
        "event_id": "evt-1042",
        "listing_id": "listing-77",
        "action": "expire_listing",
        "schema_version": 1,
    }
    print(process_once(event, set()))

The example demonstrates the order, but not a particular vendor request shape. At ingress, reject the malformed message before calling the queue publish operation. At consumption, reject a schema version the worker cannot interpret and send it to the DLQ rather than retrying it indefinitely. At the side-effect boundary, use a database uniqueness constraint or an inbox record keyed by event_id; the set above exists only to make the state transition legible.

Retry only failures that may change without changing the payload. A temporary dependency timeout can use bounded exponential backoff and the service's retry guidance. A missing field is a contract defect. Repeating it five times creates five logs and no valid marketplace state.

What should operators inspect after a rejection?

The DLQ record should carry the queue name, event identifier, schema version if present, failure class, attempt count, first-seen time, and a redacted payload fingerprint. Avoid storing a full customer webhook in every diagnostic record. The point is to group failures and identify the producer release, not to create an uncontrolled second payload store.

Queue statistics add the time dimension. A rising publish-failure count suggests ingress validation or an upstream contract change. A stable publish rate with a growing DLQ suggests consumer enforcement or a downstream schema change. A rising retry count with few DLQ entries can indicate a slow dependency. None of these counters proves the cause alone; compare them with deployment and producer-version data.

Use the queue's DLQ listing operation to inspect representative failures and redrive only messages whose correction is known. Preserve the original event_id, cap the redrive batch, and watch the statistics after each correction. If the payload is irreparably malformed, retain the diagnostic record and fix the producer rather than laundering it through another retry cycle.

The scheduling and queue capabilities do not provide a DAG, fan-out/join primitive, native debounce or throttle, or topic-style one-to-many delivery. A cron pause also does not backfill missed triggers, trigger timing has second-level jitter, and run-history output retains only the first 4 KB. These are boundaries of the chosen primitive, not defects to hide in a retry loop.

Infrai is not suitable when the job needs DAG execution, fan-out and join semantics, replay across multiple consumer groups, or a delay longer than 7 days. SQS or Temporal is the more honest choice in those scenarios; the trade-off is a narrower queue or a broader workflow system instead of one shared REST surface.

Do not redrive blindly.

The rejected design: retry first, validate later

The tempting design is to publish every webhook, let the worker discover malformed fields, and rely on retries until the producer is fixed. It has one valid use case: a temporary downstream outage where the payload is already known to be valid. It is a poor design for schema errors because it mixes permanent and transient failures, delays diagnosis, and can keep a poison message in the hot path.

The decision rule is therefore narrow. Validate before publication, enforce again at consumption, record idempotency at the side effect, and use the DLQ as an inspection boundary. Pick the queue whose operational and orchestration limits match the job; do not ask a delayed queue to become a schema registry or a workflow engine.

The search problem is concrete: check the webhook payload formatting issues before a delayed queue hides them, then compare the worker's schema version with queue statistics. In Node.js scenarios, that sequence keeps a malformed message from consuming the retry budget reserved for recoverable failures.

References

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://docs.temporal.io/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Timestamp attributes are now supported in Vercel Flags
description:
Vercel Flags now supports timestamp attributes, so you can target entities by date and time.

Use timestamp attributes to show a campaign page only between two dates, run a Black Friday promotion, or target users who registered before a cutoff.

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

Learn how to provide entities in code and release a flag at a specific time, or read the Flags documentation.

title: Microsoft AI models are now available on AI Gateway
description:
Vercel and Microsoft AI (MAI) have partnered to make MAI models available on AI Gateway. AI Gateway is one of a limited number of platforms offering access to MAI models.

MAI's focus on security and zero data retention (ZDR) align with Vercel's goal of giving AI Gateway users control over their data and transparency in how it is used for training.

MAI models on AI Gateway

MAI's latest audio models are now supported on AI Gateway. MAI-Voice-2.1 and MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash generate speech, while MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming returns transcript updates as audio arrives.

  • MAI-Voice-2.1 (microsoft/mai-voice-2.1) generates expressive speech in 23 languages and keeps a consistent speaker across longer passages. Use it for narration, audiobooks, podcasts, and lessons where delivery matters from start to finish.

  • MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash (microsoft/mai-voice-2.1-flash) brings the same multilingual speech generation to lower-latency interactions. It is suited to voice agents, assistants, and spoken replies that need to arrive quickly.

  • MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming (microsoft/mai-transcribe-2-streaming) returns partial transcripts while audio is still arriving. Applications can show live captions or follow a conversation as it happens, without waiting for the full recording.

AI Gateway bills these models at their listed rates, with no platform fee or markup on inference.

Get started

Use generateSpeech in AI SDK 7 with MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash to create a spoken response. The voice name selects Microsoft's Harper voice with the Flash model:

For longer audio such as narration, use microsoft/mai-voice-2.1.

Transcribe live audio

streamTranscribe takes a stream of audio chunks and returns transcript updates as the audio arrives. This example assumes microphoneStream is a ReadableStream of 16 kHz, 16-bit PCM audio:

Partial transcripts can change as more audio arrives, so replace the displayed text when a new partial arrives.

Additional resources

Explore MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash for speech generation and MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming for live transcription. See the MAI model page for the full family, or follow the speech quickstart to get started.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and viewing request traces. It also supports routing, retries, and failover across available providers.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the <namespace> segment in these queries.

Queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification. We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases.

Mitigation:

  • Recommended: Migrate to supported headless Service DNS records (<hostname>.<subdomain>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local).
  • Workaround: Ensure the <namespace> specified in the DNS query exists in the cluster.

title: Content, themes and plugins shouldn't know each other: the idea behind Umono
description:
For almost four years I worked as a full-stack developer on a large WordPress site. It combined e-commerce and e-learning, and over time it grew to more than 60 plugins. By the end, even simple changes were stressful. A theme update could break a page, a plugin update could break the theme, and nobody could tell in advance what a change would touch.

The site wasn't badly built. The problem was structural: content, design and features had grown into each other. That's the question I started Umono with. What if those layers had hard boundaries, enforced by the system instead of by everyone's discipline?

Umono is an open-source CMS (Go, SQLite, MIT) that I've been building on my own since 2024. This post is about the idea behind it, not the feature list.

Three layers, three jobs

  • Content says what something means.
  • A theme decides how it looks.
  • A plugin adds what it does.

In most CMSs each of these can reach into the others. A theme ships templates and logic, so switching themes can change what a page shows. A plugin writes its own markup into your content, and when the plugin goes, that markup stays. In Umono each layer gets only what its job needs, and nothing more.

Content only says what it means

Pages are written in Compono, a Markdown-based language with components. Its Markdown surface is closed: there is no raw HTML and no way to style anything from the content. A component is reusable content:

{{ SAY_HELLO name="World" }}

~ SAY_HELLO name="Guest"
# Hello, {{ name }}!

That renders <h1>Hello, World!</h1>. Component names never appear in the output, and Umono adds no classes of its own. The result is plain, semantic HTML. Since the content carries no design, it doesn't care which theme displays it.

A theme only styles

A theme is a package of CSS, fonts and images. No templates, no scripts. This is a deliberate limit, and Umono checks it when a theme is built, installed and activated:

  • A theme has no JavaScript and can't change how anything works.
  • It can't add words, not even with CSS content. Text, link targets and accessibility attributes belong to the site owner.
  • It loads nothing from another origin: no fonts from a CDN, no remote images. The page's Content-Security-Policy enforces it.
  • It can't touch anything outside the page's root element, <head> included.

What a theme styles is plain HTML like this:

<umono-root>
  <header>
    <a href="/">My website</a>
    <nav aria-label="Main menu">
      <ul>
        <li><a href="/" aria-current="page">Home</a></li>
        <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>
      </ul>
    </nav>
  </header>
  <main>
    <h1>Hello</h1>
    <p>This is my first page, written in <strong>Compono</strong>.</p>
  </main>
  <footer>
    <p>Made with Umono</p>
  </footer>
</umono-root>

And a theme is CSS against it:

:scope {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  background-color: #fdfcf8;
  color: #1f1d1a;
}

nav ul {
  display: flex;
  gap: 1.25rem;
  list-style: none;
}

a[aria-current="page"] {
  font-weight: bold;
}

The payoff for these limits is that switching themes is safe. Activating another theme replaces the old one in one step, without touching a single page.

The boundary is a public contract

How does a theme know which HTML to expect? From a contract. A contract is a TOML file published on umono.dev that describes a kind of site:

  • Layouts, the structure of a page. A blog has post, post-list and page.
  • Parameters, everything a layout shows: the site name, the menu, the title, the content. They all come from the site owner. A contract writes no text of its own, so it works in every language.
  • Components that the layouts share.

A theme picks one contract, and three rules keep that contract trustworthy:

  1. A published contract never changes and is never removed. A new structure comes as a new contract version.
  2. Contracts are MIT-0. Anyone can write a theme for any contract. Nobody controls who is allowed to style your site.
  3. The HTML is frozen. The same content produces the same elements in every Umono release until v1. Fixes to the output are collected and land once, in v1. A theme written today keeps working.

Umono also doesn't take a theme's word for it. It detects which features a theme actually uses and refuses one that declares less than it uses.

This is what I mean by no vendor lock-in. Your content isn't written for a theme, and a theme isn't written for your site. Both are written against a public contract, so either side can be swapped.

Plugins: the same idea, not built yet

Plugins are planned the same way. A plugin will implement a published schema, run as a separate service and get only the access the site owner grants it. Plugins for the same schema will be interchangeable, like themes for the same contract. This is still in design, and I'd rather say so than sell it.

Your site stays yours

Umono is one Go binary and one SQLite file on your own server. Public pages set no cookies and make no third-party requests. Fonts are served by the site itself.

What it costs

Hard boundaries have a price, and I don't want to hide it:

  • A theme can't add a feature. If a contract has no place for something, a theme can't invent one. That takes a new contract version.
  • Compono is a language you have to learn. Today it suits technical users more than editors.
  • Only the official contracts exist so far, with one official theme each: Octavo for simple sites and Folio for blogs.
  • There is no plugin system yet.

I think the trade is worth it, but it is a trade, and I'd like to hear where it hurts.

Where it is, and how you can help

Umono has had regular releases since November 2024, and umono.io runs on it. Version 0.9 brought the theme system. It isn't finished, and development continues.

  • Try it. curl -fsSL https://umono.io/install.sh | sh, then the docs walk you from an empty directory to a site with a theme: https://docs.umono.dev/getting-started/your-first-site/
  • Write a theme. The contracts are open, and the first-theme tutorial takes about fifteen minutes: https://docs.umono.dev/themes/your-first-theme/
  • Tell me where the idea breaks. Is a contract between content and theme the right boundary, or too rigid for real sites? GitHub Discussions: https://github.com/umono-cms/umono/discussions
  • Share it. If the idea resonates, a star or a share helps a one-person project get seen: https://github.com/umono-cms/umono

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The ideas, the design and the decisions behind Umono are mine.
