title: What is iroh?
description:
Originally published at Agent Terminal's blog.

iroh is the open-source networking library behind Agent Terminal's remote access. Here is what it does, who runs its relays, and what they can see.

  1. Dial by key. Devices are named by a public key, called an endpoint ID, not an IP address.
  2. Try direct. iroh tries a direct connection first.
  3. Fall back to relay. If a network blocks the direct path, traffic goes through a relay.

What a relay sees: both devices' IP addresses, and encrypted packets, which it passes along.

What it can't see: what you type, or what your terminal shows.

With n0's relays, n0's lookup service also keeps a record of which relay each device is on.

What iroh is

iroh is an open-source networking library that connects one device to another by its public key, called an endpoint ID, instead of its IP address. It tries a direct connection first and falls back to a relay server, and every connection is encrypted end to end with QUIC.

A library is code inside an app, not something you install. iroh is written in Rust, licensed under MIT or Apache 2.0, and built by a company called n0.

The precise version

  • An endpoint ID is the public half of an Ed25519 key pair. The app creates the pair itself; there is no sign-up.
  • Connections use QUIC with TLS 1.3, through n0's own QUIC implementation, noq, which supports multipath: a connection can move between Wi-Fi and mobile data.
  • To be found, an endpoint publishes a signed record (Pkarr) with its endpoint ID and its home relay's URL to a DNS server, run by n0 by default. Publishing to the Mainline DHT is opt-in, and devices on the same network can find each other directly.

Sources: What is iroh, Endpoints, Address lookup, the iroh repository.

Why your phone can't just reach your PC

Every device online has an IP address, like a street address. Your PC at home usually does not have its own: the router shares one public address among the whole house. That is NAT (network address translation).

The router is a one-way door: devices inside can reach out, but its firewall drops any incoming connection that is not a reply. And addresses change, for example when your phone moves from Wi-Fi to mobile data.

Diagram on the original post: a phone away from home sends a connection toward the home router. The router drops it, because it is not a reply to anything the PC sent, so the PC behind the router never sees it. Caption: the router lets replies in, not new connections from outside.

Instead of opening a port to the whole internet, iroh gets both devices to open the door from their own side.

How iroh connects

  1. Find. Your phone looks up which relay the PC's endpoint ID is connected to.
  2. Go direct. Through that relay, the devices swap addresses, then send packets to each other at the same moment. Each router sees what looks like a reply and lets it in: hole punching.
  3. Fall back. If some network still blocks it, traffic keeps flowing through the relay instead.

Diagram on the original post, in two parts. 1. Direct, when it works: the phone and the PC connect to each other. 2. Otherwise, via a relay: encrypted traffic goes from the phone to a relay server and on to the PC, and the relay forwards encrypted packets it cannot read. Caption: the relay carries traffic only when a direct path fails.

What the relay can and can't see

The relay passes your traffic along but cannot read it: it is encrypted for the other device's key. It does see both devices' IP addresses. And with n0's relays, n0's lookup service keeps a record of which relay each device is on.

More detail on the direct path

iroh runs NAT traversal inside the QUIC connection itself, through an extension (n0_nat_traversal) modelled on a QUIC NAT traversal draft, so the connection details stay encrypted. Both sides send UDP datagrams to each other's public addresses at the same time. The relay is the meeting point; it does not take part in the punch. Devices reach relays over WebSockets.

Sources: NAT traversal, Relays, Iroh 1.0.

Who n0 is, and what the public relays are

n0 (n0, inc.) is the company that builds iroh, in the open on GitHub. It also runs a set of public relays that iroh uses unless an app sets its own. According to n0 and our in-app notice, these relays are:

  • Free, and shared by every app built on iroh.
  • Not guaranteed: no uptime promise, and speed limits n0 does not publish, so a relayed connection can be slow, drop, or not connect at all when they are busy or down.
  • For recent versions only: n0 supports only recent iroh releases on them, so an out-of-date app may stop connecting.

n0's docs call them suitable for development and testing, and offer paid relays for production.

For Tailscale users

The ideas are familiar: go direct, hole-punch through NAT, fall back to a relay (Tailscale's are called DERP) that cannot decrypt what it forwards. The difference is scope. Tailscale puts a whole device on a private network every app can use; iroh connects one app to its peers.

iroh Tailscale
What it is A library inside one app A client that joins the device to your tailnet (tsnet embeds it in a Go program)
Encryption QUIC with TLS 1.3 WireGuard
Identity A key the app creates; no account An account; a coordination server shares devices' public keys
Relays iroh relays: n0's public set, paid, or your own DERP: Tailscale's, or your own

Neither is better in general: Tailscale for one private network with access rules, iroh for an app that reaches its own other half with no setup.

How Agent Terminal uses it

The desktop app on your Windows PC or Mac runs an iroh endpoint; the phone dials its endpoint ID once you pair by scanning a QR code.

  • Same Wi-Fi, or a direct path: no relay is used.
  • Free plan, away from home: the free plan relies on n0's public relays, with no account: a free service run by n0, not by us, with no promise of uptime or speed. Expect it to be slow, to drop, or not to connect at all; we have no control of n0's side.
  • Pro: remote access you can rely on, through Agent Terminal's dedicated relays (plans). If Pro ends, it falls back to the public relays.
  • Your own relay: run one and set it on the desktop.

Inside the iroh connection it is still SSH, end to end between your phone and your PC, and the desktop accepts public keys only (how to check). Reaching the PC lets nobody in without a paired key.

Questions

Is it safe?

A relay cannot read your session: it is iroh's encryption on the outside and SSH on the inside, and the desktop checks every key itself. What a relay does learn is both devices' IP addresses. Any relay sees them, so the choice is whose: n0's on the free plan, ours with Pro, or your own.

Do I need an account?

No, not for the free plan. An account is only for Pro.

What if n0's relays are down or slow?

On the same Wi-Fi, or wherever the devices connect directly, nothing changes. On the free plan a relayed connection can be slow, drop, or not connect at all until they recover, and we have no control of that; Pro uses Agent Terminal's dedicated relays instead. Keep Agent Terminal up to date, since n0 supports only recent iroh versions.

Can I run my own relay?

Yes. n0 publishes the relay as open source (how). Run it on a server you control, then set it on the desktop.

Your PC's terminals, on your phone. Free and self-sustained on your own Wi-Fi, no account. Windows and macOS.

Download Agent Terminal

Checked against iroh's documentation, n0's blog and Tailscale's documentation on 20 October 2026. Written by Edward, from the team that builds Agent Terminal, which uses iroh.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

Read more

title: Heroku alternatives in 2026: five options compared, with real dyno math
description:
The best Heroku alternatives in 2026 are Ownkube, Render, Railway, Fly.io and DigitalOcean App Platform. Ownkube is the closest swap if you want the Heroku workflow (push a repo, get a URL, add Postgres) at a lower total: the small production stack priced below comes to about $178 a month on Heroku and about $57 on Ownkube. Render is the most Heroku-like in pricing shape, Railway has the fastest setup, and Fly.io suits apps spread across continents. Heroku is still a good place to be for some teams, so this post also covers when to stay.

Our picks

If you want Pick
The Heroku workflow, Postgres and a cache, at a lower full-stack total Ownkube
Fixed instance prices that read like a dyno price list Render
The fastest setup and a big template catalog Railway
Low latency on several continents Fly.io
To stay next to your existing DigitalOcean resources DigitalOcean App Platform
Salesforce integration and the add-on marketplace you already use Stay on Heroku

The Heroku alternatives at a glance

Prices are approximate list prices from each provider's pricing page, as of October 2026.

Alternative Billing model Smallest always-on service Managed Postgres Cache Best for
Ownkube Prepaid wallet, metered per minute or a flat box per app Metered from cents, or a Spark 1 box at $5 a month From $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB Valkey from $2 a month Personal software and small teams
Render Workspace plan plus flat instances $7 a month (0.5 CPU, 512 MB) From $6 a month Key Value from $10 Steady services
Railway Metered per second Whatever it uses, from cents Metered service Metered service Fast setup
Fly.io Machines per second $2.19 a month (256 MB) Managed from $38 a month Bring your own Global apps
DigitalOcean App Platform Flat container tiers $5 a month From $15.15 a month Managed, priced separately DigitalOcean users
Heroku Flat dynos plus add-ons Basic dyno, $7 a month (512 MB) Essential-0 from $5 a month Key-Value Mini $3 Salesforce-centric teams

Why people look for a Heroku alternative

Memory per dollar. A Standard-1X dyno is $25 a month for 512 MB, and Standard-2X is $50 for 1 GB. The same $25 buys 2 GB on Render. Once a team runs a few web dynos and workers, that ratio becomes most of the bill.

There is no free tier. The cheapest dyno is Eco at $5 a month, and it sleeps after 30 minutes of inactivity. Basic at $7 stays up.

Add-ons add up. Logging, search, monitoring and the cache are each a separate add-on with its own price. A real app collects several.

The roadmap is quiet for small teams. New work at Heroku centers on Salesforce and enterprise buyers, which leaves small apps further from the middle of the roadmap.

The alternatives, one by one

Ownkube

Ownkube is a cloud for personal software, and it keeps the part of Heroku people liked. You connect a GitHub or GitLab repo, every push builds and deploys, and the app gets an *.ownkube.app hostname with TLS. A Dockerfile is optional. Web apps, workers, cron jobs, Postgres and a Valkey cache sit side by side on one canvas.

Where Heroku sells add-ons, Ownkube includes the basics: logs, CPU and memory metrics, request rates, alerts and rollback to recent builds come with every app. The Marketplace deploys open-source apps such as n8n, Directus, Metabase and Umami with their database already connected.

Billing is a prepaid wallet. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, Personal ($5 a month) and Team ($20 a month) load credit each month, and unused credit never expires. Apps meter CPU and memory per minute on actual use (about $18 per vCPU and $4.50 per GiB a month), or sit on a flat box like a dyno (Spark from $5, Core from $58). Postgres runs on a database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, with 7-day backups on paid plans. See managed Postgres pricing across eight providers for how that compares.

The trade-offs: Ownkube Compute runs in two regions (Mumbai and Germany), there is no add-on marketplace for third-party services, and custom domains are not on Compute yet. When an app has to move into your own or a customer's AWS account, the same app ships there with no rewrite, and its logs, metrics and health checks come with it.

Render

Render is the most common Heroku replacement because the pricing shape matches: a flat price per instance, plus a workspace plan. You get more memory per dollar, and Postgres scales in smaller steps. See Render vs Heroku.

Railway

Railway meters usage per second and has excellent onboarding and templates. It is a good fit for many small, mostly idle services. See Railway alternatives for its trade-offs.

Fly.io

Fly.io runs Machines in dozens of regions. It is the pick when latency on several continents matters, and its managed Postgres from about $38 a month is the line to check. See Fly.io pricing explained.

DigitalOcean App Platform

Flat container tiers from $5 a month and managed databases from about $15. A sensible move if your other infrastructure is on DigitalOcean.

A small production stack, priced

Two web processes at 1 GB, one 512 MB worker, a Postgres with 4 GB of memory and 20 GB of data, and a small cache. Heroku and Ownkube figures assume the apps run all month; the Ownkube web and worker lines assume an average of a quarter of a vCPU each, since metered CPU follows actual use.

Line Ownkube Heroku
Web 2 apps, metered, about $18 2 x Standard-2X, $100
Worker Metered, about $4 Standard-1X, $25
Postgres DB 4 box $28 plus 20 GB at $0.25, $33 Standard-0, $50
Cache Cache 0.25 box, $2 Key-Value Mini, $3
Total about $57, plus bandwidth about $178

Heroku figures are approximate, as of October 2026. A busier app moves the Ownkube compute lines up; a Core box fixes them at a flat price if you prefer. Run your own sizes on the homepage calculator.

When to stay on Heroku

Stay if your team runs on Salesforce and uses Heroku Connect or the data integrations. Stay if your app depends on several third-party add-ons that would each need a new home. Stay if the bill is small, stable and nobody has time to migrate, since a working app on a known platform is worth something.

A quick checklist before you switch

  • List every add-on and decide where each one goes.
  • Export Postgres with pg_dump and test the restore on the new platform.
  • Copy config vars into environment variables.
  • Check whether a Procfile process maps to a web app, a worker or a cron job.
  • Keep the Heroku app running until the new one has served real traffic.

FAQ

What is the cheapest Heroku alternative?

For a full stack with Postgres and a cache, Ownkube comes out cheapest in our comparison. For a single tiny process, Fly.io's 256 MB Machine at about $2 a month is hard to beat. Price the whole app, since the database and cache are where totals diverge.

Does Heroku have a free tier in 2026?

No. The cheapest option is the Eco dyno at $5 a month, which sleeps after 30 minutes of inactivity. Ownkube Compute has no free tier either: Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, and that credit never expires.

Do I need a Dockerfile to move from Heroku?

No. Ownkube builds from your repo with automatic build, the way Heroku buildpacks did, and uses your Dockerfile if you have one. The migration guide walks through each step.

Reference: for the side-by-side breakdown, see Ownkube vs Heroku in the docs.

Where Ownkube fits

Move off Heroku when the dyno and add-on lines cost more than the workflow is worth to you. Stay when Salesforce integration is the reason you are there. Ownkube is built for personal software and small teams: push a repo, get a URL, run Postgres from $4 a month, and keep the credit you do not spend. Deploy my first app.

title: Cloud Computing Made Simple: Understanding IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
description:
Introduction

Have you ever wondered how apps like Netflix, Gmail, and Spotify work without you having to install or manage complicated servers?

The answer often involves cloud computing.

Cloud computing allows you to use computing resources over the internet instead of owning and maintaining all the physical hardware yourself.

But when you explore cloud computing, you will quickly encounter three terms: IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

They sound complicated, but the ideas behind them are surprisingly simple.

Let's break them down using everyday examples, real-world services, and one analogy that makes the differences easy to remember.

First, What Is Cloud Computing?

Before discussing IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, let's understand cloud computing.

Imagine you want to watch a movie. You don't need to build a cinema, buy all the equipment, and hire people to operate it. You can simply subscribe to a streaming service and watch the movie over the internet.

Cloud computing works similarly.

Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet instead of requiring you to own and manage all the physical equipment yourself.

These services can include:

  • Servers that run applications.
  • Storage for files and photos.
  • Databases that store information.
  • Platforms for developing software.
  • Applications you can use directly through a browser.

Cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud offer many of these resources.

The important thing to understand is that not every cloud service gives you the same level of control or responsibility.

That brings us to IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

1. IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

IaaS gives you access to computing infrastructure, such as virtual servers, storage, and networking, without requiring you to purchase the physical hardware.

Think of it as renting an empty apartment.

The building, electricity connections, and basic infrastructure are provided for you. However, you are responsible for furnishing the apartment and making it suitable for your needs.

With IaaS, the cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, while you manage much of the software running on it.

What are you responsible for?

Depending on the service, you typically manage:

  • The operating system.
  • Your applications and code.
  • Application configuration.
  • Many security settings and software updates.
  • The data and software you deploy.

The provider manages the physical servers, data center, and underlying infrastructure.

Real-world examples

  • Amazon EC2: Rent virtual servers to run your applications.
  • Azure Virtual Machines: Create and manage virtual machines in Microsoft's cloud.
  • Google Compute Engine: Run virtual machines on Google Cloud.

When would you use IaaS?

Imagine you are building a website that needs a customized server environment.

You want to choose the operating system, install specific software, configure the server, and control how your application runs.

IaaS gives you that flexibility without requiring you to buy a physical server.

In simple terms: IaaS gives you the building blocks, and you decide how to use them.

2. PaaS — Platform as a Service

PaaS provides a platform for building, testing, deploying, and running applications without requiring you to manage the underlying servers and operating systems yourself.

Think of it as renting a fully equipped kitchen.

The kitchen already has an oven, refrigerator, worktops, and cooking equipment. You don't need to install everything before you start cooking.

You can focus on preparing the meal instead of managing the kitchen infrastructure.

With PaaS, developers can focus more on writing and improving code while the provider handles much of the underlying platform.

What are you responsible for?

Typically, you focus on:

  • Writing application code.
  • Building application features.
  • Managing application data.
  • Configuring the application.
  • Testing and improving your software.

The provider manages much of the underlying infrastructure and platform, including the operating system and runtime environment.

The exact division of responsibilities depends on the service.

Real-world examples

  • Google App Engine: Build and run applications without managing the underlying servers.
  • Azure App Service: Host web applications and APIs using a managed platform.
  • Heroku: Deploy applications using a platform that handles much of the infrastructure management.

When would you use PaaS?

Imagine you are developing an online shopping application.

You want to write the code, connect a database, and deploy the application without spending your time configuring virtual machines and maintaining operating systems.

PaaS can simplify that process.

In simple terms: PaaS gives you a ready-to-use platform so you can focus on building your application.

3. SaaS — Software as a Service

SaaS provides a complete software application that you can use over the internet.

Think of it as ordering a meal at a restaurant.

You don't buy the kitchen, install the equipment, or prepare every ingredient yourself. You simply order your meal and enjoy it.

SaaS works similarly. The provider operates and maintains the software, and you use the finished application.

What are you responsible for?

As a typical user, you mainly manage:

  • Your account and access permissions.
  • Your settings and preferences.
  • The information you enter or upload.
  • How you use and share data within the application.

The provider manages the application and its underlying infrastructure, although your organization may still have important security and data-management responsibilities.

Real-world examples

  • Gmail: Send and receive emails through a web-based service.
  • Microsoft 365: Use applications and collaboration tools such as Word and Excel.
  • Salesforce: Manage customer relationships and sales activities.
  • Dropbox: Store, synchronize, and share files.

When would you use SaaS?

Imagine you need to send emails, collaborate with colleagues, or manage customer information.

You don't want to develop an email system or maintain the servers behind a customer management application.

You simply want software that works.

SaaS lets you use an existing application without building and maintaining it yourself.

In simple terms: SaaS gives you the finished product, ready to use.

One Kitchen Analogy to Remember Them All

Let's imagine you want to prepare a meal.

There are three ways you could approach the task.

IaaS: Rent the kitchen infrastructure

You rent a kitchen with the essential infrastructure in place.

You choose and install the equipment and decide how to organize the cooking environment.

This resembles IaaS because you get the infrastructure but retain significant control over what runs on it.

PaaS: Use a fully equipped kitchen

You walk into a kitchen where the equipment is already installed and ready to use.

You bring your recipe and ingredients, then focus on preparing the meal.

This resembles PaaS because the platform is ready, allowing you to focus on building and running your application.

SaaS: Order a prepared meal

You order a meal from a restaurant.

Someone else manages the kitchen, equipment, and cooking process. You simply enjoy the finished meal.

This resembles SaaS because you use a complete application instead of building or maintaining it yourself.

Here's the easiest way to remember the difference:

  • IaaS: You manage more of the environment.
  • PaaS: You focus on building the application.
  • SaaS: You use the finished application.

IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS: What's the Difference?

Feature IaaS PaaS SaaS
Full name Infrastructure as a Service Platform as a Service Software as a Service
What you get Computing infrastructure Application development platform Complete software application
Main focus Infrastructure and configuration Building and deploying applications Using software
Control High over virtual infrastructure Focused on the application Primarily application settings and usage
Server management Mostly your responsibility at the operating-system level and above Mostly handled by the provider Handled by the provider
Coding required Depends on what you build Usually required to build applications Usually not required to use the software
Example Amazon EC2 Azure App Service Gmail
Best suited for Teams needing infrastructure control Developers wanting to simplify deployment Individuals and businesses needing ready-made software

The main difference is how much you manage yourself versus how much the cloud provider manages for you.

Generally, IaaS offers more control, PaaS reduces infrastructure management, and SaaS provides a complete application.

Remember that these are general patterns. Actual responsibilities vary by service.

Are There Other Cloud Service Models?

Not at all!

IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS are the three traditional cloud service models, but cloud computing also offers many other specialised services.

Think about it this way: sometimes you need to rent an entire kitchen, sometimes you need a kitchen where you can prepare your own meals, and sometimes you simply want to order food.

But what if you only need storage, a database, or someone to perform one specific task?

Cloud computing works similarly. You can access specific resources and capabilities without having to manage everything yourself.

Here are some other cloud service models worth knowing.

1. FaaS — Function as a Service

FaaS lets you run small pieces of code in response to events without managing servers directly.

For example, imagine users upload photos to your application. You want each photo to be resized automatically.

A function could run whenever a new photo is uploaded.

Examples:

  • AWS Lambda
  • Azure Functions
  • Google Cloud Run functions

FaaS is commonly associated with serverless computing. Serverless doesn't mean there are no servers; it means the provider manages much of the server infrastructure for you.

2. DBaaS — Database as a Service

DBaaS provides a managed database so you don't have to handle all the setup, maintenance, backups, and infrastructure yourself.

For example, an online store needs to store customer details, orders, and product information. A managed database service can handle much of the database administration.

Examples:

  • Amazon RDS
  • Azure SQL Database
  • Google Cloud SQL

3. STaaS — Storage as a Service

STaaS provides storage over the internet so you can save and retrieve files or data without maintaining your own storage infrastructure.

For example, a company might store backups, images, videos, and documents in cloud storage.

Examples:

  • Amazon S3
  • Azure Blob Storage
  • Google Cloud Storage

4. NaaS — Network as a Service

NaaS provides networking capabilities through cloud-based services.

Businesses can use it to connect offices, manage network access, or establish secure connections without building and managing every networking component themselves.

Examples of related offerings include cloud-managed networking and network security services.

The precise features depend on the provider and service.

5. AIaaS — Artificial Intelligence as a Service

AIaaS lets businesses and developers use AI capabilities through hosted services and APIs rather than building and operating every AI component themselves.

For example, a developer might add text analysis, image recognition, or a generative AI chatbot to an application.

Examples:

  • Amazon Bedrock
  • Azure AI services
  • Google Cloud's Vertex AI

These additional models describe particular capabilities offered as services. They can overlap with IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS rather than forming one mutually exclusive list.

Which Cloud Service Model Should You Choose?

The right choice depends on what you want to accomplish.

Choose IaaS if:

  • You need substantial control over your computing environment.
  • You want to configure virtual machines and operating systems.
  • You have the skills and resources to manage your software environment.

Choose PaaS if:

  • You want to build and deploy applications.
  • You want to spend less time managing servers.
  • You prefer a managed platform for development.

Choose SaaS if:

  • You need a ready-to-use application.
  • You don't want to build the software yourself.
  • You want the provider to manage most of the application's underlying technology.

For many organizations, the answer isn't just one model. A company might use SaaS for email, PaaS to host an application, and IaaS for workloads that need more control.

Conclusion

Cloud computing becomes much easier to understand when you stop focusing on the acronyms and start thinking about what you receive and what you are responsible for managing.

Remember the kitchen analogy:

  • IaaS: You get the kitchen infrastructure and manage more of the environment.
  • PaaS: You get a kitchen ready for your work and focus on creating the meal.
  • SaaS: You order the finished meal and simply use the service.

Once you understand that distinction, it becomes easier to recognize the different cloud services you encounter in real projects.

You don't need to memorize every cloud product. Start by asking one simple question:

"Am I renting the infrastructure, building an application on a platform, or using software that's already built?"

That question will help you identify the model in many everyday situations.

What about you? Have you used IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS in a project? Share your experience in the comments. I will love to hear which model you find most useful!

title: October 09, 2026
description:
Access Approval

Feature

Database Migration Service is generally available (GA).

Access Transparency

Feature

Database Migration Service is generally available (GA).

BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Data Engineering Agent is now available in the asia-northeast1 (Tokyo) regional endpoint and supports the gemini-3.5-flash model. For more information, see Where Gemini in BigQuery processes your data.

This feature is Generally Available (GA).

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Note: Near real-time sync upon Knowledge Catalog (KC) enablement isn't available for existing instances created before April 18, 2026. For more information, see the release note from October 14, 2026.

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running MySQL version 8.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

For more information, see Enable the integration of Knowledge Catalog on an existing Cloud SQL instance.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Feature

Note: Near real-time sync upon Knowledge Catalog (KC) enablement isn't available for existing instances created before April 18, 2026. For more information, see the release note from October 14, 2026.

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).

This feature is available for instances running PostgreSQL version 14.0 or later on the new network architecture. If Knowledge Catalog integration is already enabled on the instance with once-a-day updates, you can deactivate and re-enable the integration to switch to near real-time updates.

For more information, see Enable the integration of Knowledge Catalog on an existing Cloud SQL instance.

Datastream

Feature

Datastream now supports replicating SQL Server GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY spatial data types.

For more information, see the following:

  • Map SQL Server data types to Datastream unified types
  • Data type mappings in BigQuery

Gemini

Announcement

Sale of Gemini Code Assist subscriptions is ending. Starting October 9, 2026, new Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions can no longer be purchased. Existing subscriptions will continue to auto-renew through the rest of 2026, but auto-renewal will end in 2027. For more information, see Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions.

For alternative AI developer tools, use Antigravity, which is available through eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions and through Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

Announcement

Sale of Gemini Code Assist subscriptions is ending. Starting October 9, 2026, new Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions can no longer be purchased. Existing subscriptions will continue to auto-renew through the rest of 2026, but auto-renewal will end in 2027. For more information, see Gemini Code Assist Standard and Enterprise subscriptions.

For alternative AI developer tools, use Antigravity, which is available through eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions and through Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.

Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka

Change

The format for bootstrap addresses and broker URLs has changed for new Managed Service for Apache Kafka clusters. To learn how to get a cluster's bootstrap address, see View a Managed Service for Apache Kafka cluster.

Looker

Announcement

Beginning October 5, 2026, the following features will be automatically enabled for Looker (original) instances running Looker 26.18. Feature enablement for Looker (Google Cloud core) will be announced separately.

Feature

Looker now includes built-in support for the Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) dialect. The Dremio 26.0+ (Arrow Flight SQL) uses the bundled Apache Arrow Flight SQL JDBC driver, so that you don't have to install unpackaged custom JDBC driver JAR files. See the Dremio documentation page for more information.

Feature

The AI-Assisted Quick Starts feature, called Starter questions in the new Explore experience, is now generally available.

Feature

The new Diagnose & Repair tool evaluates your LookML project repository across eight diagnostic test checks in either your personal development environment or the shared production environment. When issues are found, Looker can automatically perform repairs (such as removing stale lock files, fixing file permissions, or repairing corrupted object indexes) or rebuild damaged repositories while safeguarding uncommitted changes on a dedicated recovery branch.

Feature

Looker Continuous Integration (CI) now includes the Style Validator, which enforces LookML coding standards, naming conventions, and structural best practices across your LookML project. You can run the Style Validator with the default built-in ruleset or customize rule severities, file exclusions, path overrides, and custom rules by adding an lkmlstyle.yaml configuration file to your project repository.

Feature

Now available in preview, Conversational Analytics agentic workflows support scheduled agentic workflows in addition to triggered agentic workflows. You can use scheduled agentic workflows to schedule recurring deliveries of AI-generated insights summaries, data tables, visualizations, and PDF reports to email or Slack by using natural language. Recipients can select Investigate in a workflow notification to open a private, persistent conversation with the data agent.

Users and admins can manage workflows on the updated Manage Workflows user page and Manage Workflows admin page, respectively, and Looker admins can monitor scheduled workflow runs and troubleshoot errors on the new Workflow Executions admin page.

Workflows that were created in versions earlier than Looker 26.14 appear on the Legacy Workflows tab and must be recreated.

Feature

Now available in preview, Looker Data Apps are freeform canvas dashboards that are built by local AI coding agents, such as Gemini CLI, Claude Code, or Cursor, from natural-language prompts. Data Apps give you complete visual layout control (including absolute positioning, overlapping elements, and custom web components) while remaining bound to Looker's governed LookML semantic layer and user permissions.

Change

In Conversational Analytics, the default question mode is now Fast rather than Thinking. Fast mode is intended for answering quickly, and it directly maps your query to underlying LookML definitions without generating reasoning steps. You can still select Thinking mode from the question mode drop-down menu when asking complex, multi-step analytical questions about Explores or dashboards.

Change

The Modern User Interface preview feature toggle now defaults to ON.

Change

The Modern visualization theme now supports map charts (static map points and regions), word cloud charts, and donut multiples. While support for donut multiples was previously documented, it is now officially available with this release. These additions expand the range of visualization options that are available with the modern theme.

Feature

Looker now supports connections to the ClickHouse 26+ dialect. ClickHouse 26+ uses modernized JDBC drivers and introduces support for symmetric aggregates. See the ClickHouse documentation page for more information.

Feature

Enhanced observability metrics, including user engagement and estimated token usage data on the Token usage tab of the Conversational Analytics System Activity dashboard, are now generally available (GA). This launch also adds a Daily Token Utilization visualization and supports token usage observability for Conversational Analytics data agents that are published to Gemini Enterprise. (Note: This item was added on October 20, 2026.)

Model Armor

Feature

Model Armor includes enhanced prompt injection and jailbreak protection for Workspace data. This capability improves detection accuracy and minimizes false positives when screening Workspace content, such as emails, documents, and files.

This capability is available on multi-region endpoints in the US (us) and EU (eu) for templates and floor setting configured with filter version v3 or later, including the Stable and Latest aliases.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports global access. You can enable this feature when creating a Secure Web Proxy instance to make sure that clients from any Google Cloud region can connect to your proxy.

With global access, you can route your outbound traffic through specific regions to meet regulatory compliance or cost requirements. You can also use this option to simplify your network administration by managing outbound traffic from a centralized location.

This feature is available in Preview.

Security Command Center

Feature

Using gcloud CLI, the securitycenter REST API, or client libraries, you can configure Pub/Sub and BigQuery continuous export to receive notifications when findings are deleted from Security Command Center due to data retention policies.

For more information, see the following:

  • Enable finding notifications for Pub/Sub
  • Stream findings to BigQuery for analysis
  • Enable real-time notifications

Sensitive Data Protection

Change

If you set InfoType.version to legacy when including the MEDICAL_ID infoType in your InspectConfig, Sensitive Data Protection now includes MEDICAL_RECORD_NUMBER findings as type MEDICAL_ID in the scan results.

title: Cron Job Trigger Approach: Combining Worker-Based Queues for 24-Hour Report Generation
description:
Short answer: let the cron-like scheduler create a small, idempotent sweep command, and let a worker queue own the long-running report job. Keep reservation expiry separate from report rendering. The important boundary is not the timer; it is the retry contract. A repeated trigger must enqueue equivalent work, a repeated worker delivery must not send a second email, and a delayed report must never extend a reservation that has already crossed its fixed hold window.

For a B2B SaaS daily report email, I would set the report's schedule and the reservation's expiry policy independently. A 24-hour hold is a business rule, not a queue timeout. The scheduler can wake every 5 minutes, discover due work, and enqueue a stable job key. Workers can then spend minutes on report generation without making the scheduler wait. This combining approach gives the platform team a tractable SLO: for example, 99.9% of due reports accepted within 10 minutes, with report delivery latency measured separately from trigger latency.

That is the whole boundary.

The incident lesson: the timer was innocent

The bounded failure scenario is familiar: a daily sweep starts while yesterday's report is still rendering. The sweep sees the same account again, submits another job, and a retry after a worker timeout submits a third. Meanwhile, a reservation created for a fixed hold window is still eligible in one code path because the renderer copied an old status into its output. The scheduler did what it was asked to do. The missing invariant was elsewhere.

I treat a trigger as a request to reconcile state, never as proof that work has happened exactly once. That distinction survives process restarts, overlapping sweeps, queue redelivery, and a database failover. The durable record needs a business key such as (account_id, report_date), a reservation version or expiry timestamp, and a send state that can be checked atomically. A queue message is a delivery mechanism; it is not the source of truth.

The preventative path is deliberately boring:

  1. Read due report rows using a bounded query and claim them with a lease or compare-and-swap update.
  2. Enqueue a job containing the immutable report key, not a large snapshot of mutable account data.
  3. Let the worker re-read current state, render, and record an idempotency result before acknowledging delivery.
  4. Retry transient failures with a bounded policy; send permanent validation failures to an operator-visible dead-letter path.

The same rule applies to reservation expiry. A sweep may issue expire(reservation_id, expected_version). If the row is already expired, the operation succeeds as a no-op. If its version changed, the worker reloads and decides again. It does not resurrect the reservation because an earlier message arrived late.

How should I combine a cron job trigger with a worker-based queue?

A scheduler should own time and discovery. It should not own report computation, outbound HTTP calls, or email delivery. Its run duration should be predictable enough to fit inside the trigger interval, and its query should be resumable when the due set is larger than one process can inspect. A cursor, a partition key, or a database-side claim can provide that boundary; a loop that loads every account into memory cannot.

A worker-based queue owns the expensive and failure-prone part. It can apply concurrency limits, back pressure, timeouts, and per-tenant fairness while the scheduler remains available for the next sweep. I would make the job payload small and versioned. These are report-generation tasks, so the payload should identify work rather than attempt to carry every input needed to perform it:

package reports

import "time"

type ReportJob struct {
    AccountID  string
    ReportDate string
    Schema     int
    CreatedAt  time.Time
}

func (j ReportJob) Key() string {
    return j.AccountID + ":" + j.ReportDate
}

The identifier is not a magic guarantee. It must be enforced by a unique constraint or an equivalent atomic state transition. If the queue hands the same job to two workers, both may render; only one should be allowed to commit the send decision. Where the email provider cannot offer an idempotency contract, an outbox record and a send ledger reduce duplicates, but they cannot make an external side effect perfectly transactional with the database. That limitation belongs in the design review.

How do retries avoid extending the hold window?

Retry policy needs two clocks. The first is the business deadline: expires_at for the reservation. The second is the operational deadline: how long the report job may be retried before it becomes an incident or a dead-letter item. Mixing them is how a transient queue outage silently changes business behavior.

At each attempt, the worker should compare the current time with the stored expiry and compare the stored version with the job's expected version. The update must be conditional. In SQL terms, the intended shape is an atomic update with predicates for identity, version, and state; the exact syntax depends on the database. A successful update returns one affected row. Zero rows means the worker must inspect current state, not blindly retry the same mutation.

package reservations

import "context"

type Store interface {
    ExpireIfDue(ctx context.Context, id string, version int64) (bool, error)
}

func Expire(ctx context.Context, store Store, id string, version int64) error {
    changed, err := store.ExpireIfDue(ctx, id, version)
    if err != nil {
        return err // The queue may retry a transient storage failure.
    }
    if !changed {
        // Already expired, cancelled, or updated: all are terminal here.
        return nil
    }
    return nil
}

This advice does not apply unchanged to a job whose effect is intentionally cumulative, such as appending an audit event for every attempt. There, the attempt identifier belongs in the event identity and deduplication rules. It also does not remove the need for an email provider's delivery semantics; it only prevents the platform from treating an at-least-once queue as exactly-once execution.

Build or buy: compare the operational boundary

The choice is less about the word cron and more about which failure handling the team is prepared to operate. A managed scheduler plus a managed queue can reduce control-plane maintenance, while a self-hosted scheduler and queue can offer more direct control over persistence, topology, and upgrade timing. Neither choice supplies the reservation invariant automatically.

Decision area Managed components Self-hosted components
On-call load Less scheduler and broker maintenance; provider limits become part of the design More patching, capacity planning, failover drills, and operational ownership
Retry semantics Must verify documented delivery, visibility, and redelivery behavior Can tune behavior deeply, while owning every edge case and upgrade
Lock-in APIs and event formats may become migration constraints Fewer service-specific dependencies, but more internal platform code
Cost model Often tracks executions, retention, or throughput Tracks infrastructure, people, and the capacity headroom needed for bursts
Team fit Useful when the team needs to focus on report logic and SLOs Useful when queue behavior is a core platform capability

I would reject a design that cannot answer three questions in a review: what happens when the sweep runs twice, what happens when a worker acknowledges after the email call but before recording success, and what happens when a reservation changes between enqueue and execution? The answers should be testable state transitions, not an assumption about a vendor's exactly-once label.

Testing the boundary before production

The highest-value tests are not happy-path timer tests. Freeze time and run two scheduler instances against the same due rows. Deliver one job twice. Kill a worker after the external send and before the database commit. Advance the clock beyond expires_at, then deliver a job created before expiry. Verify that the reservation remains terminal and that the report ledger records one logical send decision.

Load tests should vary the due-set size, worker concurrency, report duration, and retry delay independently. A capacity plan that uses only average report duration will fail during the morning burst; reserve headroom for the longest permitted retry backlog and for database claim contention. Alert on age of the oldest due item, queue depth, retry rate, dead-letter count, duplicate-send conflicts, and the percentage of reservations whose expiry transition misses its SLO.

The practical result is a narrow, defensible architecture: a short periodic reconciliation creates durable work, workers perform slow computation, and every state-changing operation is conditional and repeatable. The scheduler provides time. The database provides truth. The queue provides delivery attempts. Keeping those responsibilities separate is what makes a daily report system recoverable when the boring failures arrive. It also makes capacity planning concrete: the trigger path needs headroom for due-row discovery, while the worker path needs headroom for report duration, retries, and the largest expected burst, and those are different resources with different alerts.

The failure is visible sooner.

Sources

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html
  • https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/

title: Building a Mobile App in the UAE: 6 Decisions That Matter More Than the Feature List
description:
Most mobile app briefs we see start with a feature list. Login, profile, notifications, payments, a dashboard, maybe a chat screen. The list is usually fine. It is also the least important part of the brief.

What decides whether an app ships on time, gets used, and keeps working a year later is a handful of choices made in the first few weeks. Often nobody writes them down, because nobody realised they were choices.

If you are planning an app for a business in the UAE, these are the six worth settling before anyone opens a design tool.

1. Which platform do your users actually carry?

The UAE is not a typical market. iPhone share is high, especially among the customers many Dubai businesses want most. But Android is strong in other segments, and some audiences are mostly Android.

What to do: look at your own data before you look at market reports. Your website analytics, your support tickets, your existing customers. If you have to launch on one platform first, choose based on who pays you, not who is loudest in the meeting. We wrote a longer breakdown of this in Android or iOS first in the UAE?.

2. Native, Flutter or React Native?

For most business apps, a cross-platform framework gets you to both stores with one codebase and one team. Native still wins for heavy graphics, deep hardware access, or when you already have strong iOS and Android teams in house.

What to do: decide based on your team and your next three years, not on which framework is trending. Who will maintain this after launch? What does your web team already know? If they write React, React Native is a short step. If you are starting fresh, Flutter is a serious option. Our comparison is here: Flutter vs React Native.

3. Arabic, right-to-left, and local details

Adding Arabic late is expensive. Right-to-left layouts affect every screen, every icon that points somewhere, and every form. Retrofitting it after launch usually means redesigning half the app.

What to do: decide on day one whether Arabic is in version one, version two, or never. Even if it ships later, build the layouts so they can flip. The same goes for local details people notice immediately: phone number formats, Emirates ID fields, addresses that don't fit Western templates, and weekend and prayer times if your app deals with scheduling.

4. Payments and where your data lives

If your app takes money, the payment provider shapes more of the build than most people expect: which cards and wallets work, how refunds flow, what the checkout looks like. Apple Pay is close to expected in the UAE. Some sectors also have firm rules about where customer data is stored.

What to do: pick the payment gateway before the checkout is designed, and confirm early which cloud region your backend runs in. For retail and marketplace apps, this is most of the hard work. More on that in our guide to e-commerce app development in Dubai.

5. Build the smallest version that tells you something

The most common way an app project fails is not bad code. It is a year spent building features nobody tested with a real user.

What to do: define the first release as the smallest thing that answers your biggest question. Will people sign up? Will they pay? Will they come back next week? Monkify, a wellness product we built from nothing, went from idea to a live platform and around $1M in annual recurring revenue in its first year. That happened because each release was small enough to learn from.

6. Who runs the app after launch?

Launch day is the start of the work, not the end. iOS and Android release major updates every year. Store policies change. Crashes show up on phones you never tested. Users ask for things.

What to do: agree before you start who handles releases, monitoring, store reviews and fixes. Is it your team, the agency, or a mix? Docupet already had a successful web platform but no spare engineers for mobile. We built and ran their iOS and Android apps end to end in React Native, so their own team could stay focused on the product that was already earning.

A simple checklist before you brief anyone

Before you talk to an agency or hire developers, write one line for each of these:

  • Which platform first, and why (with your own data)
  • Cross-platform or native, and who maintains it
  • Arabic and RTL: version one, later, or not at all
  • Payment provider and data region
  • What the first release needs to prove
  • Who owns the app after launch

If you can answer all six, the feature list will mostly sort itself out. If you can't, those are the first conversations to have, with whoever you hire.

Choosing who builds it

Whether you are in Dubai or Abu Dhabi, the partner you pick should ask you about these six things before they quote a price. If they go straight to screens and a timeline, they are quoting the feature list, not your project. You can see how we approach it on our mobile app development page.

What is the one decision you wish you had made earlier on your last app project?

Originally published on LinkedIn by Latent Digital Solutions FZCO. Learn more at latentdigitalsolutions.com.
