title: Nodejs Express Session End: Revoke Tokens Before Closing the Channel
description:
Ending a classroom poll is a delivery-guarantee problem, not a button-state problem. Revoke every issued token, disconnect the remaining clients, and only then delete the channel. Record the session end time in the same application workflow for attendance reporting. If deletion happens first, authorized clients can keep retrying; the orderly sequence makes those reconnect attempts fail authorization instead of bringing state back into play.

TL;DR: Put shutdown behind one idempotent Express command. Keep attendance persistence in your application, and hide realtime operations behind a narrow adapter so the provider can change without rewriting the session lifecycle. The hard guarantee is the order, not the vendor SDK.

How should Nodejs Express end a session and revoke tokens?

The boundary starts when the server accepts an instructor's end-session command. It ends only after credentials can no longer authorize a reconnect, connected users have been removed, the channel has been deleted, and the attendance record contains an end time. A browser showing “poll closed” proves none of that.

This distinction matters during fan-out. Twenty-five students may receive the closing UI update at slightly different moments, while a laptop wakes from sleep and another client retries a dropped connection. The server therefore owns closure. Clients observe it.

One REST API can fit at that boundary because application code calls a small port whose contract stays fixed while the service behind it moves. Infrai uses one REST API for multiple backend capabilities under one key, with consistent conventions, so swapping the vendor behind a capability doesn't change application code. Its public discovery surface exposes capability request schemas and runnable TypeScript examples without requiring a key. I recommend trying it for the realtime teardown portion of a small Node.js system when you want that provider boundary; keep the attendance write in your database, where it belongs.

Do not confuse a convenient boundary with a transaction. The sequence crosses the application database and a realtime system, so the handler must be safe to repeat. No hype. Just explicit state transitions.

Build the orchestration before the provider adapter

The following client is runnable with Node.js 20+ and TypeScript. Pass revokeRequest and disconnectRequest objects validated against the public discovery schemas. Their fields aren't duplicated here because the schema is the contract; guessing them in a blog post would make the sample brittle.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";

type EndSessionInput = {
  sessionId: string;
  channel: string;
  revokeRequest: unknown;
  disconnectRequest: unknown;
};

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  return 250 * 2 ** attempt;
}

async function call(
  path: string,
  method: "POST" | "DELETE",
  operationId: string,
  body?: unknown,
): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const request = new Request(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
      method,
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": operationId,
      },
      body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
    });
    const response = await fetch(request);

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await new Promise((resolve) =>
        setTimeout(resolve, retryDelay(response, attempt)),
      );
      continue;
    }

    throw new Error(`${method} ${path} failed: ${await response.text()}`);
  }
}

export async function endSession(input: EndSessionInput): Promise<string> {
  const operationId = `end-session:${input.sessionId}`;

  await call(
    "/realtime/token/revoke",
    "POST",
    `${operationId}:tokens`,
    input.revokeRequest,
  );
  await call(
    "/realtime/user/disconnect",
    "POST",
    `${operationId}:users`,
    input.disconnectRequest,
  );
  await call(
    `/realtime/channel/delete/${encodeURIComponent(input.channel)}`,
    "DELETE",
    `${operationId}:channel`,
  );

  return new Date().toISOString();
}

The Express handler should look up the session, return its existing endedAt on a duplicate command, call endSession, then persist the returned timestamp. The stable operation IDs make remote retries idempotent. The client also inspects non-success bodies and backs off on 429, honoring Retry-After when it is expressed as seconds.

There is one uncomfortable edge: the process can stop after deleting the channel but before recording endedAt. Production code should drive the workflow from a durable command or outbox and resume incomplete steps with the same operation IDs. Picture an instructor ending a 25-student poll as the process restarts: the resumed command repeats completed remote writes, finishes the missing database write, and produces one final attendance timestamp. The ordering remains unchanged. Storing the end time first would make attendance look final while students could still reconnect.

Retries aren't optional.

Delivery guarantees decide the design

The shutdown path is a small state machine: active, credentials revoked, clients disconnected, channel deleted, attendance finalized. Each transition must tolerate repetition because the caller cannot distinguish “the server did nothing” from “the server completed the work but the response was lost.”

Keep the issued token IDs with the session record. Keep the connected-user snapshot as input to the command, then let the adapter make disconnect calls safe to repeat. Most importantly, never allow channel deletion to jump ahead of revocation. Deleting first leaves clients retrying with credentials that remain valid.

Fast fan-out is secondary here. Correct denial on reconnect is the real finish line.

This also clarifies what the adapter should not own. It should not calculate attendance, decide who may end a class, or translate database records into reports. It owns three verbs and their retry behavior. That narrow surface is what makes a future provider swap plausible rather than a rewrite disguised as configuration.

Compare the boundary, not the feature checklist

Ably, Pusher Channels, Socket.IO, and Liveblocks can all appear beside a unified REST provider in a realtime shortlist, but they imply different ownership boundaries. Evaluate the exact teardown contract in a proof of concept; product names alone do not establish equivalent token revocation or channel-lifecycle semantics.

Option Boundary to evaluate Better fit when
Unified REST provider A capability adapter discovered from published schemas You want one HTTP surface and expect the provider behind a capability to change
Ably A hosted realtime product with its own authentication and channel model A specialist realtime platform should own more of the delivery layer
Pusher Channels A hosted channels API and client ecosystem Your application maps cleanly to its channel abstraction
Socket.IO A server and client library you operate as part of the Node.js stack You need control over deployment and connection behavior and will carry the operating burden
Liveblocks A collaboration-focused platform Presence and collaborative application state are more central than a thin poll fan-out boundary

This is not a ranking. There is a real limitation and trade-off: for a poll that will grow into collaborative documents or rich presence, Liveblocks deserves the first test. For a team that needs protocol-level control and already runs stateful Node.js infrastructure, Socket.IO may be the honest choice. Infrai is not a fit when those deeper specialist models matter more than portability. It is strongest here when the clean, swappable REST boundary matters, and one key spans 295 routes across 20 backend modules; that reduces credential integration work for a solo operator, but it should never override delivery semantics.

Run the same teardown acceptance test against every candidate: issue credentials, connect multiple clients, end the session, attempt a reconnect with an old credential, and verify that the stored end time is present. The evidence you need is whether the old credential fails and the channel stays gone, not a marketing claim about scale.

Operational checks before shipping

Authorize the instructor before enqueueing the end command. Give the command a stable ID derived from the classroom session, retain the token IDs needed for revocation, and emit structured status for each transition without logging credentials. Set a finite retry budget; a tight loop on rate limits turns a controlled shutdown into load amplification.

Watch the awkward paths. A sleeping browser may reconnect late. Two instructors may press End within milliseconds. An HTTP response may vanish after the remote action succeeds. The idempotent command and fixed transition order cover all three without treating the client as the source of truth.

Finally, test reporting separately from transport. Attendance consumers need a recorded ISO 8601 end time, while realtime clients need failed authorization after closure. Those are related outcomes, not the same outcome, and monitoring should make either missing result visible.

The decision rule is compact: use a specialist when you need its deeper realtime or collaboration model; use a narrow REST adapter when provider replaceability is the higher-value constraint. If the latter boundary fits your system, start with the provider documentation and obtain the live request schemas from discovery before writing the adapter.

Sources

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation
  • Liveblocks documentation
  • Infrai official documentation

title: Zentro v0.10.0: Open-Core SQL IDE Built with Go + Wails
description:
I've been building Zentro, a desktop SQL IDE (Windows, macOS, Linux) that's organized around projects rather than loose connections. It supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SQLite, and it's written in Go + Wails on the backend with React + TypeScript on the frontend, shipping as a single executable.

With v0.10.0 (released 2026-10-23), the core is now open source under GPL-3.0-only: https://github.com/ZentroIDE/Zentro

What "open core" means here (and what it doesn't)

To be precise, because this is easy to oversell:

  • Open (GPL-3.0): the free core of the IDE, in the public repo. The git history there starts at this release.
  • Closed (commercial): Pro is a separate layer on top, under a commercial license. Its source is not in the public repo.
  • So Zentro is not fully open source. It's open core, similar in spirit to how JetBrains or Grafana split things. ## Two downloads
Zentro (official) Zentro Community Edition (CE)
Contents Free core + Pro features (unlocked by a plan or the 30-day trial) Free core only, built from the public source
Where zentro-ide.com/downloads and GitHub releases GitHub releases only (zentro-ce-*)
Updates In-app auto-update None, download new versions manually
Built by Private release system, Windows binaries code-signed GitHub Actions in the public repo, from the release tag; unsigned

Most people should pick the official build: it's free, needs no account, and includes the Pro trial. CE is for people who want a binary built publicly from source they can read. Since CE is unsigned, Windows SmartScreen and macOS Gatekeeper will warn on first launch. CE has no Pro code and no updater.

Pro trial and the AI assistant

  • 30-day Pro trial for everyone, started inside the app, no card, no invite. It replaces the old early-access program.
  • The AI assistant with your own API key (BYOK) is completely free, including the MCP server for external agents. Only the query statistics panel is Pro.
  • The data-protection rule for AI (the model only sees schemas you allow, ADR 0017) applies to every plan.

What else is new in v0.10.0

  • Activity panel & background jobs: CSV import and whole-table export run as cancellable jobs with live progress; a Jobs tab and a Server Sessions tab (view and kill sessions on the database itself).
  • Bigger AI assistant: new chat with history and streaming; SQL checking, query plan explanations, schema comparison across environments, impact lookup when changing a schema, table/index stats; MCP server for outside agents.
  • SSH tunnels and per-connection TLS control (minimum TLS version, legacy ciphers when a server needs them).
  • Driver-specific connection strings (postgres://, mysql://, sqlserver://) with examples and correct defaults.
  • Integrated terminal (local or SSH) in the bottom panel.
  • ERD: auto-layout (dagre), minimap, pan/zoom shortcuts, layout reset.
  • SQL editor: custom SQL grammar, schema-aware highlighting (tables, columns, aliases), a Colors page with preview, a T-SQL-aware formatter.
  • Keyboard navigation: explorer tree and results grid, tab jumping via command palette, chord shortcuts, Enter/F2 to edit cells. Ctrl+Tab now jumps to the most recently used tab, browser-style.
  • Security: paid plans are only granted from verified, signed entitlements.

Try it / tell me what's broken

  • Download: https://zentro-ide.com/downloads
  • Source: https://github.com/ZentroIDE/Zentro
  • Docs: https://docs.zentro-ide.com This is a one-person project. Contributions need a CLA, and for larger PRs please open an issue first. Bug reports and ideas go in the repo's Issues and Discussions.

title: Laravel Sanctum vs Passport for Mobile Apps (2026)
description:
For a mobile app that talks to its own Laravel API, use Sanctum. It issues one revocable token per device from a login endpoint you control, supports abilities and expiry, and has nothing to configure beyond a trait. Passport is a full OAuth2 server, and the only mobile cases that need one are apps you do not own asking for access to your users’ data, or other servers authenticating as themselves.

That is the short answer, and it matches what the Laravel docs say. The rest of this article is the reasoning, the parts of each package that matter once the app is in production, and the code for the places where Sanctum’s simplicity leaves a gap. It is one part of a larger guide to Laravel as a backend for mobile apps, which covers versioning, response shape, pagination, and push alongside authentication.

What Sanctum Actually Is

Sanctum is two separate features in one package, and only one of them applies to a native app.

  • API tokens. Modelled on GitHub personal access tokens. createToken() on the user writes a row to personal_access_tokens with a SHA-256 hash of a random string and returns the plain text once. The client sends it as a Bearer header and Sanctum looks the hash up on every request. Tokens can carry abilities, which work like scopes, and an optional expiry.
  • SPA cookie authentication. No tokens at all. A browser frontend on the same top-level domain logs in through the normal web guard and Sanctum lets the session cookie authenticate API routes, with CSRF protection intact. The statefulApi() middleware decides which origins get this treatment.

A mobile app uses the first feature only. There is no browser, no cookie jar worth trusting, and no CSRF problem, so the cookie half of Sanctum does not apply. The docs are explicit that API tokens are for mobile apps and third parties while first-party SPAs should use the cookie flow; the mistake worth avoiding is doing it the other way round.

What Passport Actually Is

Passport is a complete OAuth2 authorization server built on league/oauth2-server. It registers the /oauth/authorize and /oauth/token endpoints, stores clients and their redirect URIs, issues RSA-signed JWT access tokens together with refresh tokens, and implements the standard grants: authorization code (with or without PKCE), client credentials, device authorization, and the older password and implicit grants, which are off unless you turn them on.

The important word is server. Passport exists so that other applications can obtain access to your API on a user’s behalf, with the user approving a scope list on a consent screen you render. When the only client is your own app, every one of those moving parts is still present and still has to be configured, deployed, and kept secure, but none of them is doing anything you need.

Why Mobile Apps Almost Always Want Sanctum

Your own iOS or Android app is a first-party client. The user types their credentials into a screen you built, so there is no delegation to model and no third party to keep at arm’s length. What the app needs from the token system is narrower than OAuth2 and more specific:

  • One token per installed device, named so the user can recognise it in a sessions list.
  • The ability to revoke one device without logging out the others, and all of them at once on a password reset.
  • A token that survives app restarts for weeks, not minutes, because re-login on a phone costs you users.
  • Optionally, a token that can do less than the user can, so a stolen token from a read-only screen cannot place orders.

Sanctum covers each of these with a line or two. The login endpoint below follows the shape in the docs, with an expiry and abilities added, and device_name supplied by the app from the device model or a user-chosen label.

<?php
// routes/api.php
Route::post('/auth/login', function (Request $request) {
    $request->validate([
        'email' => ['required', 'email'],
        'password' => ['required'],
        'device_name' => ['required', 'string', 'max:100'],
    ]);

    $user = User::where('email', $request->email)->first();

    if (! $user || ! Hash::check($request->password, $user->password)) {
        throw ValidationException::withMessages([
            'email' => ['The provided credentials are incorrect.'],
        ]);
    }

    $expiresAt = now()->addDays(30);

    $token = $user->createToken(
        $request->device_name,
        ['orders:read', 'orders:write', 'profile:read'],
        $expiresAt,
    );

    return response()->json([
        'token' => $token->plainTextToken,
        'expires_at' => $expiresAt->toIso8601String(),
    ]);
})->middleware('throttle:login');

Returning expires_at alongside the token is a small addition that pays for itself later: the app can decide when to rotate without parsing anything, and support can see at a glance why a device was signed out.

Abilities are enforced on routes with the two middleware Sanctum ships, Laravel\Sanctum\Http\Middleware\CheckAbilities and CheckForAnyAbility. They are not aliased by default in Laravel 11 and 12, so register them once in bootstrap/app.php.

<?php
// bootstrap/app.php, inside withMiddleware()
$middleware->alias([
    'abilities' => CheckAbilities::class,  // token must have every listed ability
    'ability' => CheckForAnyAbility::class, // token must have at least one
]);

// routes/api.php
Route::get('/orders', [OrderController::class, 'index'])
    ->middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'abilities:orders:read']);

Route::post('/orders', [OrderController::class, 'store'])
    ->middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'abilities:orders:write']);

// Inside a policy, combine the token check with ownership
return $user->id === $order->user_id && $user->tokenCan('orders:write');

Revocation is a delete. Logout removes the current device’s row; a password reset, email change, or “sign out everywhere” removes them all. Because only hashes are stored, a leaked database does not yield usable tokens, though you should still rotate after an incident.

<?php
// Logout: only this device
Route::post('/auth/logout', function (Request $request) {
    $request->user()->currentAccessToken()->delete();

    return response()->noContent();
})->middleware('auth:sanctum');

// Password reset listener: every device, then the user logs in again
class RevokeTokensOnPasswordReset
{
    public function handle(PasswordReset $event): void
    {
        $event->user->tokens()->delete();
    }
}

// A sessions screen: revoke one named device the user picked
$request->user()->tokens()->where('id', $request->integer('token_id'))->delete();

What You Give Up: Refresh Tokens and Rotation

Sanctum has no refresh tokens. A token is valid until it expires or is deleted, and the default is that it never expires, because expiration in config/sanctum.php is null. That default is fine for a developer’s personal access token and wrong for a phone that can be lost, so the first production decision is to set it.

<?php
// config/sanctum.php: minutes, applies to every token without its own expiry
return [
    'expiration' => 60 * 24 * 30,
];

// routes/console.php: expired rows stay in the table until this runs
Schedule::command('sanctum:prune-expired --hours=24')->daily();

Once tokens expire you need an answer to “what happens on day 31?” Forcing a re-login is acceptable for some products and a churn problem for others. The alternative is rotation: an authenticated endpoint that issues a replacement with the same name and abilities and deletes the token that called it, in one transaction so a crash between the two statements cannot leave the user with zero tokens or two.

<?php
Route::post('/auth/token/rotate', function (Request $request) {
    $user = $request->user();
    $current = $user->currentAccessToken();
    $expiresAt = now()->addDays(30);

    $fresh = DB::transaction(function () use ($user, $current, $expiresAt) {
        $token = $user->createToken($current->name, $current->abilities, $expiresAt);
        $current->delete();

        return $token;
    });

    return response()->json([
        'token' => $fresh->plainTextToken,
        'expires_at' => $expiresAt->toIso8601String(),
    ]);
})->middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'throttle:rotate']);

On the client, call it when expires_at is within a few days, on app foreground, and store the new token before discarding the old one. Two details keep this honest. The endpoint requires a valid token, so an expired token cannot be refreshed; that is the trade-off versus an OAuth2 refresh token, which outlives the access token by design. And the endpoint needs its own rate limiter, because a captured token can otherwise be renewed forever by whoever holds it. If a long-lived credential that survives access token expiry is a hard requirement, that is a genuine reason to look at Passport.

When Passport Is the Right Choice

Three situations call for a real OAuth2 server, and they are about who the client is rather than how large the app is.

  • Apps you do not own. A partner’s app, a customer’s integration, or a public developer platform where someone else’s code asks for access to your users’ accounts. The user has to see what is being requested and approve it, and the client must never see the user’s password. That is the authorization code grant with PKCE.
  • Machine-to-machine. A reporting job, a warehouse system, or another one of your services calling the API as itself rather than as a user. That is the client credentials grant.
  • Real refresh semantics. A short-lived access token plus a longer-lived refresh token, with both lifetimes set centrally and refresh tokens revocable on their own.

Setup starts with php artisan install:api --passport, then passport:keys on each environment to generate the RSA key pair that signs tokens. The user model takes Passport’s HasApiTokens trait and the OAuthenticatable interface, and the api guard in config/auth.php switches to the passport driver. Scopes and lifetimes live in a service provider.

<?php
// app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php
class AppServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider
{
    public function boot(): void
    {
        Passport::tokensCan([
            'orders:read' => 'Read your order history',
            'orders:write' => 'Place orders on your behalf',
            'profile:read' => 'Read your profile',
        ]);

        Passport::defaultScopes(['profile:read']);

        Passport::tokensExpireIn(CarbonInterval::hours(1));
        Passport::refreshTokensExpireIn(CarbonInterval::days(30));
        Passport::personalAccessTokensExpireIn(CarbonInterval::months(6));

        // Opt-in only, and the docs no longer recommend it. Leave it out
        // for a first-party mobile app; use Sanctum for that instead.
        // Passport::enablePasswordGrant();
    }
}

For a mobile app that belongs to someone else, create a public client, which has no secret, since a secret compiled into an app binary is not a secret. The app opens the authorization URL in a system browser sheet (ASWebAuthenticationSession on iOS, Custom Tabs on Android), receives the code on its redirect URI, and exchanges it together with the code verifier.

<?php
// Create the PKCE client once; Passport prints its client ID
// php artisan passport:client --public

// The mobile client builds the challenge from a random 43-128 char verifier
$codeVerifier = Str::random(128);
$codeChallenge = strtr(rtrim(base64_encode(hash('sha256', $codeVerifier, true)), '='), '+/', '-_');

// Step 1: open in the system browser
$authorizeUrl = 'https://api.example.com/oauth/authorize?'.http_build_query([
    'client_id' => $clientId,
    'redirect_uri' => 'com.partner.app://oauth/callback',
    'response_type' => 'code',
    'scope' => 'orders:read profile:read',
    'state' => $state,
    'code_challenge' => $codeChallenge,
    'code_challenge_method' => 'S256',
]);

// Step 2: exchange the code; no client_secret for a public client
$response = Http::asForm()->post('https://api.example.com/oauth/token', [
    'grant_type' => 'authorization_code',
    'client_id' => $clientId,
    'redirect_uri' => 'com.partner.app://oauth/callback',
    'code_verifier' => $codeVerifier,
    'code' => $code,
]);

// Protect routes by scope with auth:api and the scope middleware
Route::get('/orders', [OrderController::class, 'index'])
    ->middleware(['auth:api', CheckToken::using('orders:read')]);

// Machine-to-machine routes use the client as the resource owner instead
Route::get('/reports/daily', DailyReportController::class)
    ->middleware(EnsureClientIsResourceOwner::using('reports:read'));

Passport does not ship a mobile SDK, and the challenge and exchange above would normally run in Swift or Kotlin; the PHP form is here because it is the same algorithm and lints. The server side is the routes Passport registers plus the consent view you provide through Passport::authorizationView().

Passport Costs You Should Price In

  • Token size. Access tokens are RSA-signed JWTs that encode the client, user, scopes, and expiry, and come out around a kilobyte. A Sanctum token is the row ID, a pipe, and a 40-character random string. Per request that is noise; across a screen that fires a dozen calls on a cellular connection it is measurable, and it is the kind of thing that shows up when you profile a slow list.
  • Key management. passport:keys writes a private and public key to storage/. They must not be in git, every server that validates tokens needs the public key, and rotating the pair invalidates every token signed by the old one. Most teams load them from PASSPORT_PRIVATE_KEY and PASSPORT_PUBLIC_KEY environment variables, or point Passport::loadKeysFrom() at a mounted secrets path.
  • Revocation sets a flag rather than deleting the row. Expiry is encoded inside the signed token, so the expires_at column is informational and cannot be edited to shorten a token. To cut one off you call $token->revoke(), and separately $token->refreshToken?->revoke(), otherwise the client simply refreshes. Revoked and expired rows accumulate until passport:purge runs, so schedule it.
  • More tables, more grants, more surface. Five tables instead of one, a consent screen to design, redirect URI validation to get right, and the discouraged password and implicit grants sitting one method call away from being enabled by a well-meaning teammate. 
<?php
// Revoke one connection, access and refresh token together
$token = Passport::token()->find($tokenId);
$token->revoke();
$token->refreshToken?->revoke();

// Password reset: every token the user has issued to any client
$user->tokens()->each(function (Token $token) {
    $token->revoke();
    $token->refreshToken?->revoke();
});

// routes/console.php
Schedule::command('passport:purge')->hourly();

Decision Table

Concern Sanctum Passport
Client you own (iOS, Android, Flutter) Yes, the intended use Works, but over-built
Third-party apps with user consent No Authorization code + PKCE
Machine-to-machine Long-lived token on a service user Client credentials grant
Token format Opaque id|random, hash stored RSA-signed JWT, about 1 KB
Refresh tokens None; rotate with a custom endpoint Built in, separate lifetime
Scopes Abilities per token Scopes declared with tokensCan()
Expiry Config minutes or per-token date; null by default tokensExpireIn(); one year by default
Revocation Delete the row revoke() token and refresh token
Secrets to manage None beyond APP_KEY RSA key pair per environment
Database One table Clients, codes, tokens, refresh tokens, device codes
Housekeeping sanctum:prune-expired passport:purge

Migrating Between Them

The constraint that shapes every mobile migration applies here too: installed app builds keep using whatever token they were issued, for as long as users keep them. You cannot swap the guard on a Tuesday. Plan for a window where both guards accept requests.

Passport to Sanctum is the common direction, usually when a team discovers it adopted OAuth2 for one client it owns. Install Sanctum and add a second guard (sanctum is already a driver), publish a new login endpoint that issues Sanctum tokens, and ship an app build that uses it. Existing builds keep calling the Passport routes until their tokens expire; shorten tokensExpireIn() ahead of the switch so that window is weeks rather than a year. Protect shared routes with auth:sanctum,api so either guard can authenticate during the overlap. Once your build adoption analytics show the old builds are gone, remove the Passport guard, its routes, and the tables.

Sanctum to Passport happens when a partner programme arrives. The snag is that both packages ship a trait called HasApiTokens with the same method names, so one User model cannot simply use both. The cleanest path is to move the first-party app onto Passport as well, either through the PKCE flow in a system browser sheet or through Passport’s own createToken() for personal access tokens, which has a similar signature but mints a JWT. The same overlap window applies, with the Sanctum guard kept alive until old builds have gone. If the partner surface is small, it is worth asking first whether a separate, narrowly scoped Passport resource server in front of the same database would cost less than migrating your own app.

Either way, the migration is mostly a guard switch plus patience. The code that changes is the login endpoint, the route middleware, and the token-revocation paths listed above; business logic should not know which package authenticated the request.

Sources

  • Laravel docs: Sanctum, Passport
  • league/oauth2-server: which grant should I use?
  • RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange
  • RFC 8252: OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps

Where This Fits

Pick Sanctum, set an expiry, add the rotation endpoint, and spend the time you saved on the controls that fail security reviews more often than the token library does: ownership checks on every lookup, rate limits on login, and logs that can answer who read what. Those are worked through in the Laravel API security checklist. If you would rather have someone build the auth layer and the API around it, see backend API development.

title: 84% of abandoned v0 apps run a known-exploited Next.js
description:
A field note on what happens to AI-built apps after the builder walks away, measured on October 21, 2026, the day Next.js 15 left security support.

Of 274 abandoned v0-built apps whose Next.js version we could read, 231 (84%) declare a version inside the React2Shell range, the remote code execution flaw CISA has listed as actively exploited since December 5, 2025. 226 of them run the exact same version: Next.js 15.2.4. Only 3 run Next.js 16, and none runs the current patched release.

The date matters for a second reason. Next.js 15 was released on October 21, 2024, and the Next.js support policy keeps a major in Maintenance LTS for two years. Since October 21, 2026, the policy sends security fixes to Next.js 16 only. That leaves 271 of the 274 apps on a major outside its support window, on top of the 231 already in a known-exploited range.

This note explains how we measured it, why so many apps landed on one version, what the numbers do and do not prove, and what to do if one of these apps is yours.

1. What we measured

We wanted apps that were generated by an AI builder, deployed, and then left alone. v0 makes that population easy to find without guessing: projects it syncs to GitHub carry a recognizable notice in their README. We searched public GitHub repositories with that notice, created between January and August 2025, whose last push was before October 1, 2025, and that list a live homepage. That gave 398 apps, each untouched for more than a year.

For each one we fetched the homepage and the JavaScript files it links, exactly what any visitor's browser downloads. An App Router build of Next.js declares its own version in that code (a line of the form window.next = { version: "15.2.4", appDir: true }), and that self-reported version is what we recorded. We sent no exploit, no crafted request and no login attempt, and we are not publishing any app's address.

Result Apps
Sampled (v0 notice, created Jan to Aug 2025, no push since Sep 30, 2025) 398
Still serving a page 304
Next.js version readable from the served code 274
Version inside the React2Shell range (CVE-2025-55182, on CISA KEV) 231
On Next.js 14, out of support since October 2025 39
On Next.js 15, out of support since October 21, 2026, already patched for React2Shell 1
On Next.js 16, the only supported major 3
On the current patched release (16.4.2) 0

The other 94 apps were gone or unreadable: 69 answered 404 (a deleted deployment), 7 answered 402 (a paused Vercel project), and the rest timed out, no longer resolved, or ran a build whose version we could not read.

2. Why one version dominates: the exact pin

The concentration on 15.2.4 is not a coincidence, and it is not about people choosing an old version. We opened the package.json of sampled repositories, and the generated projects of that period declare "next": "15.2.4" with no range operator. An exact pin means a fresh install, a rebuild or a redeploy all produce the same 15.2.4 forever. Nothing upstream can move the app forward. Only a person editing that line can.

That turns a normal software habit into a trap. In a hand-maintained project, an exact pin is a deliberate choice somebody revisits. In a generated project, it is a snapshot of the day the model wrote the file, and the builder who accepted it usually never opened package.json at all. The 35 apps on 14.2.16 show the same pattern from an earlier template: one version, pinned, frozen.

Then the builder moved on. Every app in this sample was created in a burst of experimentation in 2025 and has not received a single commit in over a year. The deployment kept running anyway, because hosting a small app costs nothing and nobody turns it off. The app outlived the attention of the person who made it, and the version it was generated with became its permanent version.

3. What React2Shell is, and what the numbers do not prove

CVE-2025-55182, known as React2Shell, is unauthenticated remote code execution in React Server Components, which the Next.js App Router uses. It affects every Next.js 15 release line and 16.0 until that line's patch (15.2.6 for the 15.2 line), and CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on December 5, 2025. Its one precondition, the App Router, is stated on the same line as the version we read, which is why a version in range is a meaningful signal and not a guess.

It is still not proof that any of these apps can be compromised today, and we want to be precise about why:

  • Most of these apps sit behind Vercel's firewall. 266 of the 274 are hosted on vercel.app, where Vercel deployed firewall rules against React2Shell for every project. Vercel itself says those rules cannot guarantee protection against all possible variants of an attack and that upgrading is the fix, and researchers have found ways around some WAF defenses. A firewall rule is a mitigation in front of vulnerable code, not a patch to it.
  • The version is self-reported. It is what the served code declares, which is the version that was built. We did not test whether the flaw can be triggered, and we will not.
  • The sample is v0 projects on public GitHub. Builders who kept their repositories private, or who used other tools, are not in it. We think the mechanism (exact pins plus abandonment) generalizes, but the 84% figure describes this population.

What the numbers do show is the gap between how long an AI-built app keeps running and how long anyone maintains it. The fix for React2Shell has existed for more than ten months, and 84% of this population never received it.

4. The second problem started on October 21

Even the apps outside the exploited range are not in a safe place. Next.js 14 left its support window in October 2025, and 37 of the 39 apps on it run a version below the fix for the March 2025 middleware authorization bypass, which matters for any app that checks sign-in in middleware.

Since October 21, 2026, Next.js 15 joins it. The October 14 security release, two critical fixes and one high, was the last that 15.x was owed under the support policy. Vercel has made exceptions for severe flaws before (it shipped 14.2.35 in December 2025, after 14 had left support), but an exception only helps an app that installs it. A pinned, abandoned app misses every patch equally: the ones that ship for its line and the ones that never will.

5. If one of these apps is yours

The cheapest fix is often the right one. An app you no longer use should not be running. Delete the deployment or pause the project, and the exposure is gone along with everything else it might hold (an API key in its code, a database it still talks to).

For an app you want to keep:

  • Upgrade Next.js to 16. The official upgrade guide covers the breaking changes, and a codemod handles most of them. A generated app is usually small enough that this takes minutes, not days.
  • Replace the exact pin with a range ("next": "^16.4.2"), so a rebuild picks up patch releases.
  • Turn on automated dependency updates (Dependabot or Renovate) in the repository, so the next advisory arrives as a pull request instead of as nothing.
  • Check what the live app actually serves, not what you remember deploying.

MacroCyber reads the Next.js version an App Router site serves and flags it when it falls inside a range CISA lists as exploited, as a signal to verify, alongside the AI-era exposures it was built for (open Supabase and Firebase databases, leaked AI keys, exposed MCP servers). You can scan any site free, or give your coding agent the same check with our MCP server so it can scan what it just deployed and confirm its own fix. If your app runs on Supabase, the Supabase exposure check covers the other common way abandoned AI-built apps leak.

6. Method details

  • Population: public GitHub repositories whose README carries v0's sync notice, found through GitHub's repository search, one query per creation month from January to August 2025, restricted to repositories last pushed before October 1, 2025 and listing a homepage. Four repositories that had been pushed after that date by the time we read them were excluded.
  • Reading: one GET of the homepage and of the Next.js JavaScript files it references, with a user agent naming MacroCyber, on October 21, 2026. The version is the one the App Router runtime declares in the served code.
  • Matching: versions were matched with the same advisory table the MacroCyber scanner uses, so the article and the product cannot disagree.
  • Publication: aggregate figures only. No app is named.

This note reflects data read on October 21, 2026. Versions, hosting protections and support dates change, so check the current Next.js advisories before acting on any single figure.

Originally published on macrocyber.co. Written with AI assistance from data we collected on October 21, 2026, and checked against it.

title: Relationships in a Relational Database: MySQL vs NebulaGraph from 1 Million to 500 Million Rows
description:
About three years ago I started to build what was really a graph inside a relational database. My thinking at the time was quite simple: every connection between two nodes is a kind of many-to-many relationship, so if I have a table for the nodes and a table for the relationships between them, it should work. When we got to around 500 million rows, nodes and relationships together, the system completely collapsed. We were running it on the largest virtual machine we could get on AWS, which cost about 15 to 20 thousand dollars per month, and a simple query to find one relationship between two nodes was taking about 15 minutes.

After that we moved to graph databases, first ArangoDB, then Neo4j, and now we are using NebulaGraph (I wrote about the move from ArangoDB to NebulaGraph in an earlier article). The same kind of query now takes a few seconds, and at most 7 to 10 seconds, depending on how well the query is optimised.

A story from production is not something you can check, so for this article I built a benchmark that anyone can run on their own machine: the same graph loaded into MySQL and into NebulaGraph, the same questions asked to both, and every answer compared before any timing is trusted. All of the code and the raw results are on GitHub: MehdiMohseni82/graph-vs-relational-benchmark.

The benchmark confirms part of that story, but it also separates two things that the story mixes together, and I think that difference is the most useful thing in this article.

The model most of us start with

When a SQL developer models a graph, the first design is almost always the same, and it's the design I used three years ago. There is one table for the things, and one table for the relationships, where each row says that one node is connected to another node.

CREATE TABLE nodes (
  id   BIGINT      NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE edges (
  src BIGINT NOT NULL,
  dst BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (src, dst)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

ALTER TABLE edges ADD INDEX ix_edges_dst_src (dst, src);

This is not a bad design, and I want to be fair to it. In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, so all the relationships of one node are stored next to each other, and the reverse index (dst, src) does the same for the other direction. Finding the direct neighbours of a node is one index lookup, and it is very fast. The problem doesn't start with one hop, it starts when the question needs many hops.

The questions

The benchmark asks questions that are very common in real systems, for example in fraud detection, recommendations, access control or any knowledge graph. A relationship always counts in both directions.

  1. The relationship question: are node A and node B related, and if yes, how many hops apart are they, up to 6 hops? This is the "simple relationship" query from my own story.
  2. The neighbourhood question: how many different nodes can be reached from this node in 1, 2, 3 or 4 hops?
  3. The neighbourhood without hubs: the same question, but the search may never enter a hub, a node with more than 1,000 relationships. I added this one after looking at a real identity graph, where a few placeholder values are connected to almost everything, and every useful search has to walk around them.

In MySQL 8 the natural way to ask a multi-hop question is a recursive CTE. This is the query for the neighbourhood question:

WITH RECURSIVE reach (id, depth) AS (
    SELECT @start, 0
    UNION
    SELECT e.dst, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.src = r.id WHERE r.depth < @hops
    UNION
    SELECT e.src, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.dst = r.id WHERE r.depth < @hops
)
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT id) FROM reach WHERE depth > 0;

And this is the query for the relationship question, which is almost the same:

WITH RECURSIVE reach (id, depth) AS (
    SELECT @a, 0
    UNION
    SELECT e.dst, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.src = r.id WHERE r.depth < @maxHops
    UNION
    SELECT e.src, r.depth + 1 FROM reach r JOIN edges e ON e.dst = r.id WHERE r.depth < @maxHops
)
SELECT MIN(depth) FROM reach WHERE id = @b;

In NebulaGraph the first two questions are written in nGQL, and they are much shorter, because traversal is the main job of the language:

GO 1 TO 4 STEPS FROM 42 OVER related BIDIRECT YIELD DISTINCT id($$) AS v | YIELD COUNT(*) AS n;

FIND SINGLE SHORTEST PATH FROM 42 TO 1337 OVER related BIDIRECT UPTO 6 STEPS YIELD path AS p | YIELD length($-.p) AS len;

Why the recursive CTE gets so expensive

It's important to understand what the CTE actually does, because the reason is not that MySQL is slow. Every recursive step joins the whole result of the previous step with the edges table again, twice, once for each direction. UNION removes duplicate rows, but a row here is the pair (id, depth), not the node alone. That means a node that was reached at depth 2 is reached again at depth 4, because you can walk to a neighbour and come straight back, and every time it is expanded again. The CTE has no memory of "I have already visited this node", it only knows "I have not produced this exact row yet".

The relationship question has a second problem, which is even bigger. A recursive CTE cannot stop when it finds B. It first builds every node within 6 hops of A, at every depth, and only after that the outer SELECT looks for B in the result. So the cost of the question "are these two nodes related?" does not depend on how close they are, it depends on how big the neighbourhood of A is.

The third method: a breadth-first search in C

I also added a third method, because I think it is the most honest comparison. It is the solution that a good SQL developer would build after the CTE becomes too slow: keep the same MySQL tables, but do the breadth-first search in C#, one level at a time, with a HashSet of visited nodes and a bidirectional search for the shortest path.

public async Task<long?> ShortestPathAsync(long a, long b, int maxHops, TimeSpan timeout)
{
    if (a == b) return 0;
    var deadline = DateTime.UtcNow + timeout;
    var seenFromA = new HashSet<long> { a };
    var seenFromB = new HashSet<long> { b };
    var frontierA = new List<long> { a };
    var frontierB = new List<long> { b };

    for (int length = 1; length <= maxHops; length++)
    {
        bool expandA = frontierA.Count <= frontierB.Count;
        var (frontier, seen, other) = expandA
            ? (frontierA, seenFromA, seenFromB)
            : (frontierB, seenFromB, seenFromA);
        if (frontier.Count == 0) return null;

        var next = new List<long>();
        foreach (var neighbour in await NeighboursAsync(frontier, deadline, Queries.MySqlNeighboursOf))
        {
            if (other.Contains(neighbour)) return length;
            if (seen.Add(neighbour)) next.Add(neighbour);
        }
        if (expandA) frontierA = next; else frontierB = next;
    }
    return null;
}

NeighboursAsync sends the frontier to MySQL in batches of 2,000 ids and reads the neighbours in both directions with one query per batch:

SELECT dst FROM edges WHERE src IN ({0})
UNION ALL
SELECT src FROM edges WHERE dst IN ({0});

For the third question the BFS uses the same query with one extra condition per direction, NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM hubs h WHERE h.id = e.dst), so MySQL never returns a hub. The CTE gets the same condition inside its recursion. The exact queries are in the repository.

The setup

Everything runs in Docker on one machine, and the repository has a runbook and a script that runs one size from empty databases to the final table.

  • Hardware: Mac Studio, Apple M3 Ultra, 96 GB RAM. Docker had 80 GB of memory and 24 CPUs, and nothing else was running.
  • The same memory for both engines: MySQL 8.4 in a 30 GB container with a 24 GB InnoDB buffer pool. NebulaGraph 3.8 with 30 GB in total: the storage service in a 24 GB container with a 16 GB RocksDB block cache, and the graph service in a 6 GB container. One storage node and 36 partitions.
  • Loading: MySQL with LOAD DATA INFILE and the reverse index built after the load. NebulaGraph with nebula-importer from exactly the same CSV files, followed by a compaction.
  • The data: a deterministic generator in C#. Every node gets on average 9 relationships, and half of the targets come from a skewed distribution, so some nodes become hubs. The sizes are 1M, 10M, 100M and 500M rows, nodes and relationships together, which is the way I counted the rows in my own system.
  • The measurement: 10 cases per question, one warm-up run and 3 measured runs, and the tables show the median. Half of the pairs for the relationship question are close to each other, the other half are two random nodes. The timeout is 15 minutes per query.
  • Validity: after every size the run checks that no container was killed or restarted, that the kernel killed nothing for lack of memory, that no query returned an engine error, and that all methods returned the same answers. Every size passed.

Results: the relationship question

Size (rows) MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C# NebulaGraph
1M 5.68 s 1.1 ms 2.1 ms
10M 1.2 min 1.6 ms 18.7 ms
100M 9.7 min, 2 of 10 timed out 1.5 ms 8.6 ms
500M no answer in 15 minutes (10 of 10) 2.7 ms 23.6 ms

This is the result from my story. At 500 million rows the recursive CTE didn't answer a single one of the ten pairs within 15 minutes, while the other two methods answered in milliseconds. The pairs were between 2 and 6 hops apart, so this is not a question of a long path, it's the CTE building the whole 6-hop neighbourhood before it looks for B.

But look at the other two columns. The bidirectional search in C#, on the same MySQL tables, was faster than NebulaGraph at every size. So for this question, the problem was not the relational database. It was the recursive CTE.

Results: the neighbourhood question

Size (rows) MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C# NebulaGraph
1M 180 ms 177 ms 72.4 ms
10M 2.65 s 508.5 ms 288.1 ms
100M 10.61 s 1.70 s 1.13 s
500M 3.18 s 579.6 ms 529.1 ms

These are 4 hops. At 1, 2 and 3 hops all three methods answer in at most about 130 ms at every size, and at 1 and 2 hops in a few milliseconds or less.

Two things are worth explaining here. First, NebulaGraph is the fastest at every size, but the BFS in C# is never far behind, between 1.1 and 2.4 times slower, and the CTE is between 2.5 and 9.4 times slower than NebulaGraph.

Second, 500M is faster than 100M for every method, which looks wrong. It isn't: the time of this query depends on how many nodes it reaches, not on the size of the table. With 10 million nodes, the median start node reached 3.9 million nodes in 4 hops, but with 50 million nodes the median start node reached 2.3 million, because the same number of relationships is spread over five times more nodes. Less work, less time, for all three engines in the same way.

Results: a graph with hubs

The graph above is friendly. Real graphs often have hubs, and in an identity graph a single placeholder value, like a default phone number, can be connected to hundreds of thousands of records. So I generated a second graph: 1 million nodes with on average 50 relationships, plus 20 hubs connected to about 630,000 nodes each. 904 nodes have more than 1,000 relationships. It's 63.5 million rows, and the timeout here is 5 minutes.

The first thing this graph shows is why hubs matter: from a median start node, 2 hops reach 999,991 of the 1,000,000 nodes. Every search goes through a hub, and after that it has the whole graph.

Question MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C# NebulaGraph
relationship, up to 6 hops no answer in 5 minutes (10 of 10) 0.5 ms 1.1 ms
neighbourhood, 2 hops 8.49 s 1.07 s 575.6 ms
neighbourhood, 3 hops 3.6 min 20.58 s 5.95 s
neighbourhood, 4 hops no answer in 5 minutes (10 of 10) 20.59 s 11.27 s

Here the difference between the BFS in C# and NebulaGraph becomes real: when a query touches the whole graph, NebulaGraph is 1.8 to 3.5 times faster. The BFS has to pull every level of the search over the network into the application, batch by batch, and NebulaGraph does the same work next to the data.

But nobody wants the whole graph. The useful question on this graph is the third one, the neighbourhood that walks around the hubs:

Hops MySQL recursive CTE MySQL + BFS in C#
2 6.8 ms 5.5 ms
3 2.55 s 479.6 ms
4 2.6 min 22.91 s

Avoiding the hubs, the median start node reaches about 12,000 nodes in 2 hops and 730,000 in 3 hops, so this is still a big search, but it is one the user actually asked for.

This question shows the most about NebulaGraph, because I couldn't write it as one nGQL statement that is both correct and usable:

  • GO 1 TO 3 STEPS ... WHERE NOT "hub" IN tags($$) runs, but it returned more nodes than the SQL version. In our check on a small graph it found 5,821 nodes at 2 hops where the correct answer was 463, because the filter doesn't stop the walk from going through a hub.
  • MATCH with a condition that no node on the path is a hub returns the correct answer, but it enumerates paths, and on a 20,000-node test graph the 4-hop version used up the 1 GB the graph service had in that test.

What an application does in this case is to walk one GO step per level from C# and remove the hubs between the levels. That is the same small graph engine in the application as the BFS on MySQL, just on top of a different database. I measured a version of it, but my implementation filtered the hubs with WHERE NOT "hub" IN tags($$) in every step, which makes NebulaGraph read the tags of every destination node, and a version that filtered in C# was about twice as fast in a small test. Because I don't have a fair measurement of that approach at full size, I leave NebulaGraph out of this table rather than show a number that makes it look worse than it is.

What the numbers say

I think the honest summary has three parts.

The recursive CTE is what breaks. In every table it is the slowest method, from about 1.2 times slower on the smallest searches to several thousand times slower on the relationship question, and at 500M rows it didn't answer a single relationship question within 15 minutes. It can't remember visited nodes, can't search from both sides and can't stop early. The query in my story was this kind of relationship question, and the benchmark suggests that the way such a query is written matters at least as much as where the data lives.

A breadth-first search on MySQL is a real alternative, and for paths it was the fastest. With the same tables and the same indexes, the BFS in C# answered the relationship question in under 3 milliseconds at every size, faster than NebulaGraph's FIND SHORTEST PATH, and on the 4-hop neighbourhood it stayed within 2.4 times of NebulaGraph on the normal graph. On the hub-avoiding question it was more than five times faster than the CTE at 3 hops. But it's important to be clear what it is: you are writing a small graph engine inside your application, with the visited set, the frontier, the batching, the bidirectional search and the timeouts, and every new kind of question means more code.

A graph database pays off when the traversal itself is big. On the hub graph, when a query really had to walk a large part of the graph, NebulaGraph was 1.8 to 3.5 times faster than the BFS, because it does the work next to the data instead of pulling every level into the application. It also gives you a language where the first two questions are one line each. What it didn't give me, in this test, is a single statement for a traversal that has to avoid certain nodes, and that is exactly the kind of question real graphs need.

Limits of this benchmark

  • It runs on one machine with local disks and one NebulaGraph storage node. NebulaGraph is designed to spread partitions over many machines, and this test doesn't measure that at all. If your graph doesn't fit on one machine, that is a different question, and a benchmark on one machine can't answer it.
  • The data is generated. It has the right shape (skewed degrees, hubs), but it is not production data with production query patterns and other traffic.
  • The MySQL schema and queries are the common approach, not the only one. If you can make the relational side faster, a pull request with the numbers is very welcome.

When a relational database is still the right choice

If your queries are one or two hops, for example "the orders of this customer" or "the members of this group", a relational database with the right indexes is very fast, much simpler to operate, and you already have it. In every table above, 1 and 2 hops on the normal graph stayed in the range of a few milliseconds for all three methods.

In my view, the signal to look at a graph database is the shape of the questions, not the number of rows. When you start to write recursive CTEs, first replace them with a search in your application: in this benchmark that alone turned minutes into milliseconds. When the traversals become large, when the business keeps asking new kinds of graph questions, or when the graph grows beyond one machine, that's the point where a graph database earns its place.

Run it yourself

The repository has everything needed to reproduce these numbers: the Docker Compose file for MySQL and NebulaGraph, the C# generator, the C# benchmark with all methods, the runbook with the validity checks, and the raw CSV of every single run.

title: Gemini 4 Argon now available on AI Gateway
description:
Gemini 4 Argon from Google is now available on AI Gateway.

Gemini 4 Argon is built for coding, agentic work, and complex reasoning. It has a 1M token context window, accepts text, image, PDF, and video input, and supports tool calling.

On coding tasks, Gemini 4 Argon builds features, fixes bugs, and researches unfamiliar codebases, carrying longer tasks through multiple steps. The model also reads dense diagrams, spreadsheets, layout-heavy documents, and video, which suits tasks like a financial analysis spread across several spreadsheet tabs. Beyond code, it handles work in finance, health, and law, and hard problems in math and science. Gemini 4 Argon uses thinking levels (low, medium, and high) instead of thinking budgets.

Call Gemini 4 Argon through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Set the thinking level with reasoning in the AI SDK or reasoning_effort in Chat Completions, and see reasoning for the other controls.

Use google/gemini-4-argon as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select google/gemini-4-argon in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Gemini 4 Argon in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

title: BlackX UEFI Bootkit Discovered Bypassing Secure Boot: Analysis
description: Security researchers have uncovered an advanced UEFI bootkit tracked as BlackX, capable of hijacking system firmware and neutralizing Windows Secure Boot protections at the pre-boot level. By achieving ring -2 / SMM execution privileges, BlackX establishes undetectable persistence that survives full operating system reinstallations and drive reformatting. Our latest low-level firmware security analysis explores the attack vector used by BlackX, hardware platform vulnerabilities, and recommended firmware hardening and revocation steps for enterprise defenders. Read the full technical security breakdown on our official security portal.

title: Laya decision model now available on AI Gateway, free through October 31
description:
Laya from Convai Innovations is free to use on AI Gateway for 1 month through October 31, 2026 via Boundless.

Laya is an evaluation/decision model that evaluates shared context against yes/no, choice, or scoring questions and returns structured answers with probabilities. For example, use it to:

You can call Laya through the AI SDK evaluation API, the native HTTP API, the TypeSafe-compatible API, or the AI CLI with convaiinnovations/laya or convaiinnovations/laya-free:

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets
