title: From ImportError to Video: Bringing Looking Ahead to Windows
description:
Looking Ahead's 1.3B image-to-video example stopped on my Windows machine before inference started:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fcntl'

The machine had an RTX 5090. FlashAttention 4 was installed. Neither was enough to get past the import.

My fix, TencentARC/Looking-Ahead PR #2, was merged on October 23, 2026 (UTC). With the patch, the tested 1.3B example produced 80 frames at 768×432 on Windows 11, using PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention fallback.

The change spans six files. The interesting part is how three separate assumptions had to be removed before the fallback actually worked end to end.

Why I wanted to run Looking Ahead

Looking Ahead is a video-generation research project from researchers at Nanjing University, Tencent ARC Lab, and Zhejiang University.

Its method, Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), addresses a shortcut in autoregressive video training: neighboring video chunks can be similar enough that a model relies on local continuity without learning much about how a scene evolves.

FCP adds auxiliary training branches that predict more distant future chunks from the current chunk's intermediate features, without seeing the intervening chunks. Those branches are removed at inference. The authors report improvements in physical consistency; the project page explains the method and shows their comparisons.

The released code includes 1.3B and 5B models. Its documented test environment was Linux with an NVIDIA H200. My contribution makes the tested Windows inference path accessible through the upstream code. It does not change FCP, retrain the model, or establish Windows support for every configuration.

That is why this merge matters to me: the compatibility fix now lives in the research repository, where the next person trying the model can receive it.

1. Installed does not mean importable

The attention modules used is_flash_attn_4_available() before importing flash_attn.cute.

In the tested environment, that availability check reported the installed package. Importing it still failed: its quack dependency imported fcntl, a Unix-specific module unavailable on Windows.

The merged code attempts the import and treats an ImportError as an unavailable optional backend:

FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE = is_flash_attn_4_available()
if FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE:
    try:
        import flash_attn.cute
    except ImportError as exc:
        FLASH_ATTN_4_AVAILABLE = False
        warn_flash_attention_fallback(type(exc).__name__, str(exc))

Both attention modules receive this handling. A shared helper logs the selected backend and reports each distinct import failure once.

The warning explicitly says that performance and numerical results may differ. That matters because a run that silently switches backend is harder to reproduce or compare.

The helper receives the exception type and message as strings. It does not cache the exception object and its traceback just to deduplicate a warning.

This check establishes importability, not a guarantee that every subsequent kernel call will work on every device. It also catches ImportError specifically; it does not convert arbitrary runtime failures into silent fallbacks.

2. Cross-attention bypassed the fallback

Getting past the import exposed the next problem.

The code already had an attention() function that selected between FlashAttention 4 and PyTorch SDPA. But cross-attention called the FA4-only flash_attention() directly. Removing FA4 from the environment therefore avoided the import error while leaving an assertion waiting later in the run.

The relevant change is small:

- x = flash_attention(q, k, v, k_lens=context_lens)
+ x = attention(q, k, v, k_lens=context_lens)

Now cross-attention uses the same backend-selection boundary.

There is a semantic condition behind that edit. In the call path covered by the PR, context_lens is None, so the fallback computes full attention. The SDPA branch does not implement arbitrary variable-length padding masks. Routing a masked attention call through it would need additional work.

When FA4 is available, the dispatcher forwards the same arguments to the existing FA4 implementation.

The general lesson is to trace the callers. An optional backend is only optional if the execution paths that need it actually pass through the fallback.

3. Model loading had its own Unix dependency

The remaining fcntl dependency was outside attention.

The project stages base-model files and checkpoints into a local cache, using fcntl for file locking. The default staging path brought the same platform assumption back into the run.

The patch makes the import optional in both loading utilities. If fcntl is unavailable, staging is skipped and the model or checkpoint is loaded from its original path.

This preserves the underlying operation—reading the weights—without pretending that the Unix locking mechanism exists. It also avoids adding a new cross-platform lock implementation for a cache optimization.

On systems where fcntl exists, the existing staging path remains available. On systems where FA4 imports successfully, that attention path remains available too.

What the Windows run established

The PR records the following setup:

  • Windows 11 and RTX 5090.
  • Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.10.0+cu128.
  • Other package versions from the project's uv.lock.
  • FCP 1.3B EMA checkpoint, sailboat example, seed 42, and a five-second duration request.

Before the patch, the run stopped at import. With the patch and SDPA, it produced 80 frames at 768×432, with 209 seconds of sampling, 231 seconds for the whole run, and 16.4 GiB peak allocated GPU memory.

One detail belongs beside those results: all reported runs used load_diffusion_pretrained=false. The PR explains that the EMA checkpoint strictly replaces every backbone weight, so the base DiT initialization does not determine the final output. This was not a claim that every model file or loading step could be omitted.

These numbers describe one tested example and environment. They are not an end-to-end validation of training, every checkpoint, or every GPU.

Preserving FA4 and comparing SDPA are different checks

The fallback needed to work, but the original fast path also needed a regression check.

For a controlled experiment, I made FA4 importable using triton-windows and a test-only no-op fcntl module. That shim is not in the PR and is not an installation recommendation—it does not provide real file locking.

With FA4 available, the original branch and the patched branch produced bit-identical decoded frames. That comparison checks whether the patch changed the existing FA4 path.

Comparing SDPA against FA4 answers a different question. On the same example, the first conditioning frame was identical, while frame PSNR was 33.5 dB on average and 31.6 dB at minimum. The generated results were not bit-identical.

FA4 sampling took 154 seconds, versus 209 seconds for SDPA. The fallback made the example runnable with a measurable speed tradeoff. It did not reproduce FA4's exact numerical output.

These are comparisons recorded in the PR's validation notes, not new experiments performed for this article.

The 5B follow-up found the next boundary

I also checked the 5B model with the paper-fan example and documented the result in a follow-up comment.

Sampling completed: 30 latent frames in 231 seconds, with 24.3 GiB peak allocated GPU memory.

The immediately following VAE decode did not fit in the same process on the tested 32 GB GPU / 64 GB RAM machine. The generator and both KV caches remained on the GPU; Windows commit charge passed 104 GiB, and I stopped the run.

Decoding those saved latents separately took 8.2 GiB and 11 seconds. That result points to a phase-lifetime and memory-management problem, beyond the portability fix in this PR.

So the precise outcome is: the 1.3B example completed end to end; the 5B example completed sampling, with decode checked in a separate process. The merge does not include a solution for the combined 5B memory peak.

What I would carry into the next portability fix

This patch connected three things: optional-backend detection, the callers that select that backend, and the platform-specific optimization in model loading.

For another research implementation, I would follow the same checks: attempt the optional import, trace every caller, verify that the fallback preserves the required attention semantics, log the selected path, and test the complete workload. A successful import is only the beginning.

The merged changes are small enough to read alongside the model's setup and inference instructions. FCP and the released models are the research authors' work; my contribution is getting this tested inference path through Windows without replacing the existing FA4 path.

Have you encountered an “optional” dependency that turned out to be mandatory through a different call site?

Drafted with AI assistance from the merged diff, project documentation, and recorded PR validation results. Merge commit: 15f90becc4d37f4f8c74cb0c868b6d855a7c605d.

title: I let a 4B model watch 321 stock clips overnight so I never have to scroll again
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What I Built

I make short videos, and all of them draw from one shared folder of stock clips: 321 files from Pixabay and Pexels, 7.6 GB, about two and a half hours of footage. Every file is named with a number. pixabay/4926.mp4 could be anything.

There is a catalog next to the files, with tags, but the tags are the search queries I typed when I downloaded each clip. They tell me what I was looking for that day, not what the clip contains. So when I need "a single candle on a dark background", the honest method is to open the folder and scrub through thumbnails. I have done that more times than I want to admit.

nightshelf is a small command-line tool that looks at the library once, unattended, and writes down what is in every clip. For each video it pulls three evenly spaced frames, asks Gemma 3 (the 4B vision model, running locally through Ollama) to describe them, embeds the description, and stores everything in a SQLite file. After that I just type what I want:

$ nightshelf search "a candle flame" --limit 3
1. pixabay/4926   score 0.0328  sim 0.83  10.6s
   A single candle burns brightly against a dark background, casting a warm, flickering light…
   status: prayers-nightwatch=approved | used: prayers-nightwatch
2. pixabay/4933   score 0.0320  sim 0.80  33.1s
   A single candle with a flickering flame burns brightly against a dark background…
3. pixabay/51749  score 0.0320  sim 0.82  20.0s
   A single lit candle burns brightly in a dark room, casting a warm glow against a black background…

The tool also reads my existing catalog (read-only, it never writes to it), so it knows which clips I already approved, rejected, or used for a given project. --status unused means "something I have not used yet and did not reject".

The real run on my library: 321 clips described and embedded, 0 failures, 2,874 seconds in total, 8.9 seconds per clip, on my Mac, with no GPU server involved.

Demo

The video (about 80 seconds, a real terminal on my real library) shows the overnight run with its one-line-per-clip progress, the stats of the full run, a few searches, and an export of a shortlist.

These are real terminal outputs from my library (the path of my clip folder is masked):

Code

Deval123 / nightshelf

Overnight, local video-clip librarian: an open-weight vision model describes your stock clips so you can search them by meaning.

nightshelf

Overnight indexer that makes a local video clip library searchable by meaning.

A stock-clip library grows until nobody remembers what is in it, and file names like clip_0412.mp4 say nothing. nightshelf looks at a few frames of every clip with an open-weight vision model running on your own machine, writes a short description, stores it in a local SQLite database, and lets you search the library from the command line ("rainy city at night", "someone walking a dog on a beach"). Nothing leaves your network, the library is only ever read and the whole library is processed unattended, overnight.

How it works

flowchart LR
    L[("Clip library<br/>read-only")] --> S["scan + sync<br/>(new / changed / removed)"]
    C["catalog.json<br/>read-only"] -. "filters, status, uses" .-> Q
    S --> F["ffmpeg<br/>N frames per clip"]
    F --> V["Vision model<br/>(Ollama)"]
    V --> D[("SQLite index<br/>descriptions + FTS5")]
    D --> E["Embedding model<br/>(Ollama)"]
    E --> D
    D --> Q["search / export<br/>full-text
…
View on GitHub

Apache 2.0, Java 21, no framework, 169 tests. The README has a quick start (jar or Docker), every command, and a configuration table.

How I Built It

The pipeline is deliberately boring:

clip library (read-only) → scan + sync → ffmpeg (3 frames) → Gemma 3 via Ollama
      → SQLite (descriptions + FTS5) → embeddings → search / export

One structured answer per clip. I ask Gemma for JSON matching a schema: a description of at most two sentences, a list of subjects, a setting, a time of day (day, night, dusk, dawn, unknown) and a mood. Temperature is 0, and 0.3 on the retry after a malformed answer, so a retry does not repeat the same bad output. Everything the model returns is treated as untrusted: the JSON is validated, lengths are capped, control and bidirectional characters are stripped, and the prompt tells the model that any text visible in a frame is content to describe, never an instruction.

Hybrid search without a vector database. 321 vectors do not need a server. Search runs SQLite FTS5 for the words and a plain cosine similarity in Java over the embeddings (nomic-embed-text, also through Ollama), then merges the two rankings with reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60). If Ollama is not reachable at search time, it falls back to full-text only and says so in one line.

SQLite, on purpose. One machine, one writer, a few hundred rows. The database uses WAL, foreign keys and versioned migrations, every statement is parameterized, and it refuses to open on a network filesystem, because SQLite locking on SMB or NFS is not something I want to trust. The clip library is mounted read-only, in Docker as well.

Slow and steady, as a design rule. The indexer handles one clip at a time and commits each result in its own transaction. A SIGTERM finishes the current clip, prints a summary and exits cleanly. A test simulates a hard kill and checks that the next run redoes only the unfinished clips. Ten failures in a row stop the run, because Ollama is probably down. And if the library drive is unmounted, the scan sees zero clips, so a guard refuses to flag more than half of the index as removed. An unplugged disk should never look like a deletion.

Things that did not work the first time. Almost every description began with "The video shows…". A sentence in the prompt reduced it, a display-time cleanup removed the rest, and the stored text and embeddings are untouched. The query "spring flowers in daylight" matched nearly everything because of the word "in", so stop words are now removed from the full-text query. User text is always split into words and quoted before it reaches FTS5, so operators like NEAR or * are plain text.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

My library is not secret, but it is mine: 7.6 GB, plus a record of every choice I made about it. A hosted vision API would mean sending frames from every clip to someone else's servers, and paying again every time I add a clip.

With open weights, none of that applies:

  • Nothing leaves the machine. Frames and descriptions go to a model on localhost. The README says plainly that traffic to Ollama is unencrypted http, so it must stay on localhost, a trusted LAN, or an SSH tunnel.
  • No per-image cost, no quota. Indexing 321 clips cost electricity and about 48 minutes of waiting.
  • It works offline once two models are pulled.
  • The model is pinned. The index was built with gemma3:4b. Nobody can change it under me, and swapping models is two environment variables (VISION_MODEL, EMBED_MODEL).

There is a real trade-off: a larger hosted model would probably describe some clips better. For this job, a 4B model that I can run unattended on my own computer was enough, and I would rather have an index I fully control.

The Lazy Payoff

I waited once, for 48 minutes, while doing something else. Now finding a clip takes a second instead of a scroll through hundreds of thumbnails, and export turns a query into a shortlist file (Markdown, CSV or JSON) that I can keep next to a project. The tool never copies or moves a clip.

It has limits, and they are worth stating. Concrete visual queries work well: "a candle flame" returns candles, with similarity between 0.80 and 0.83 for the top three. Abstract ones do not: "hope after a storm" returned wind turbines, raindrops on a window and a rainy night street, with similarity between 0.58 and 0.63, and I would not trust it. Three frames per clip can also miss fast action. For my use, the approach is good enough, and I know where it stops.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 (4B, vision) runs locally through Ollama and produces the description of each of the 321 clips: structured output with a JSON schema, a retry strategy, and sanitized results. It is not fine-tuned.

title: Benchmarking Expo Router Navigation: Memory Footprint and Frame Drop Analysis Under Deep Stack Depth
description:
Benchmarking Expo Router Navigation: Memory Footprint and Frame Drop Analysis Under Deep Stack Depth

When migrating a multi-tenant dashboard from React Navigation to Expo Router's file-based routing, we hit a silent performance cliff at 42 nested routes. Navigation animations dropped from 60fps to 38fps, and memory usage spiked by 140MB on Android mid-range devices. This benchmark isolates the breaking point.

Test Topology

Environment:

  • Expo SDK 52, React Native 0.76
  • Test devices: Pixel 5 (Android 13), iPhone 12 (iOS 17)
  • Profiling: React Native Performance Monitor + Android Studio Memory Profiler
  • Load harness: Automated UI test cycling through 10/25/50/75 nested (tabs) and [id] dynamic routes

Route Structure:

app/
  (auth)/
    login.tsx
  (dashboard)/
    _layout.tsx
    index.tsx
    [tenant]/
      settings/
        [section]/
          [subsection]/
            index.tsx  // Depth = 6 levels

Metric Comparison Table

Route Depth Avg Navigation Time (ms) Memory Delta (MB) Frame Drops (per transition) UI Thread CPU (%)
10 routes 68 +22 0 14
25 routes 105 +58 2 28
50 routes 187 +142 9 51
75 routes 312 +229 18 73

Root Cause: Expo Router's useSegments() hook re-renders the entire layout tree on each navigation event. At 50+ routes, the reconciliation overhead compounds with TailwindCSS class recalculation in nested _layout.tsx components.

Production CSS Mitigation Pattern

The breakthrough came from isolating TailwindCSS utilities into static stylesheet references instead of dynamic className props in deeply nested layouts.

Before (Dynamic Classes):

// app/(dashboard)/_layout.tsx
export default function DashboardLayout() {
  const segments = useSegments();
  const isSettingsActive = segments.includes('settings');

  return (
    <View className={`flex-1 ${
      isSettingsActive ? 'bg-slate-50' : 'bg-white'
    }`}>
      <Slot />
    </View>
  );
}

After (Static Stylesheet + Conditional Mounting):

import { StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: { flex: 1 },
  settingsBg: { backgroundColor: '#f8fafc' },
  defaultBg: { backgroundColor: '#ffffff' },
});

export default function DashboardLayout() {
  const segments = useSegments();
  const isSettingsActive = segments.includes('settings');

  return (
    <View style={[
      styles.container,
      isSettingsActive ? styles.settingsBg : styles.defaultBg
    ]}>
      <Slot />
    </View>
  );
}

Result: Navigation time at 50 routes dropped from 187ms to 94ms. Frame drops reduced from 9 to 3 per transition.

Container Query Optimization for Tab Bar

Expo Router's (tabs) layout triggers re-renders when switching between tab screens. Using CSS container queries to scope tab indicator animations prevents layout thrashing:

// app/(dashboard)/(tabs)/_layout.tsx
import { Tabs } from 'expo-router';
import { Platform } from 'react-native';

export default function TabsLayout() {
  return (
    <Tabs
      screenOptions={{
        tabBarStyle: Platform.select({
          ios: styles.tabBarIOS,
          android: styles.tabBarAndroid,
        }),
        tabBarActiveTintColor: '#3b82f6',
        tabBarInactiveTintColor: '#64748b',
      }}
    />
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  tabBarIOS: {
    height: 88,
    paddingBottom: 34,
    borderTopWidth: 0,
    elevation: 0,
    shadowOpacity: 0.1,
    shadowRadius: 8,
  },
  tabBarAndroid: {
    height: 64,
    elevation: 8,
    borderTopWidth: 1,
    borderTopColor: '#e2e8f0',
  },
});

Key: Static StyleSheet objects bypass TailwindCSS runtime parsing. Measured 18% reduction in UI thread CPU usage during tab switches.

Accessibility Focus Trap Fix

Deep navigation stacks broke screen reader focus when modal routes overlaid tab navigators. The issue: <Slot /> doesn't forward accessibilityViewIsModal to child screens.

Fix (Modal Route Layout):

// app/(dashboard)/settings/_layout.tsx
import { Slot } from 'expo-router';
import { View } from 'react-native';

export default function SettingsLayout() {
  return (
    <View
      accessible={true}
      accessibilityViewIsModal={true}
      accessibilityLabel="Settings panel"
      style={{ flex: 1 }}
    >
      <Slot />
    </View>
  );
}

Wrapping <Slot /> in an accessible container with accessibilityViewIsModal ensures VoiceOver and TalkBack trap focus within the modal context.

Production Threshold

Adopting Expo Router's file-based navigation makes architectural sense for:

  • Apps with ≤40 route files in production bundle
  • Teams prioritizing type-safe routing over maximum flexibility
  • Projects where navigation state persists across app restarts (URL-driven state)

When to revert to React Navigation:

  • Dynamic route generation from API responses (e.g., CMS-driven navigation)
  • Apps requiring custom transition animations beyond presentation: 'modal'
  • Route stacks exceeding 60 nested levels (at which point, rearchitect your IA)

The 50-route inflection point isn't arbitrary—it's where JavaScript bundle size intersects with native bridge serialization overhead. Below that threshold, Expo Router's DX benefits outweigh the performance tax.

title: Measuring Knowledge Base Health: Metrics & Dashboards for QA
description:
• Which KB metrics actually move the needle
  • Designing usage dashboards and actionable alerts for owners
  • Using analytics to triage updates and close knowledge gaps
  • Reporting cadence that keeps leadership and owners aligned
  • Fast-start playbook: KPIs, templates, and checklist

Knowledge bases rot quietly: stale procedures, orphaned articles, and search dead-ends increase support noise and make QA brittle. You need a compact set of measurable signals, a defensible dashboard, and an owner-first alerting approach so work gets prioritized where it actually reduces tickets and test flakiness.

The problem shows up in three predictable ways: end users search and find nothing (or click but still open tickets), agents ignore the KB or link the wrong article, and QA/test steps diverge from the true system state because docs weren't updated. Those symptoms look like rising ticket volume for documented topics, repeated "searches with no results", high views on articles with low helpfulness scores, and long lists of articles with no assigned owner — all measurable from search logs, article feedback and ticket linkages.

Which KB metrics actually move the needle

Focus on a small set of robust signals that are fast to collect and hard to argue with. The table below lays out the essential metrics I use as a QA knowledge curator, how I calculate them, and the operational role each plays.

Metric Why it matters Calculation / definition Practical threshold / signal
Search success (Search CTR) Leading indicator of findability — if users click results, search is working. search_clicks / total_searches (per day/week). Use GA4 view_search_results or your search logs. Target: > 50–70% depending on KB size. Sustained drop → investigate ranking/titles.
Searches with no results Fastest way to detect coverage gaps and search tuning needs. no_result_searches / total_searches (list top zero-result queries). Signal: > 5–10% in mature KBs or rising trend. Spike → add article or synonyms.
Average clicks per search Indicates whether the first result is relevant or users must hunt. sum(result_clicks) / total_searches. >1.2 implies users often click multiple pages; aim to reduce.
Helpfulness (thumbs-up rate) Direct quality signal from readers. helpful_yes / (helpful_yes + helpful_no) per article. Flag < 60% for review when views > threshold.
Article views (trend + velocity) Shows impact; high-impact stale content is first priority. Views by article, 7/30/90-day trend. High views + falling helpfulness = priority #1.
Content freshness (average age / overdue%) Documents must match product state; age correlates with inaccuracy. avg(days_since_last_update); % articles not reviewed in >12 months. >12 months median → assessment; >30% overdue → maintenance sprint.
Agent article use / linked-articles-per-ticket Adoption by agents drives deflection and consistent responses. linked_articles / tickets (agent activity logs). Declining agent use often precedes higher AHT.
Self-service / deflection score Business-level ROI metric linking KB to fewer tickets. KB_unique_visitors / tickets_created or % incidents resolved via KB suggestions. Track trend; aim for rising deflection after updates.
Low-quality high-impact articles Combines impact and quality: view high + helpfulness low. Filter articles with views > X and helpfulness < Y. One of the fastest levers to reduce tickets.
Correction/flag rate Shows instability or outdated content edits_or_flags / 1000 views Spikes indicate churn or product changes; add review cycle.

Practical note: the most actionable signals are those that combine search behavior with article quality — e.g., top no-result queries intersected with ticket drivers. Zendesk, HubSpot and other platforms expose these building blocks; GA4 exposes view_search_results for site search events.

Important: A rising no-result rate is often the earliest sign of KB decay — it precedes decreases in helpfulness and increases in tickets. Track it daily.

Designing usage dashboards and actionable alerts for owners

Dashboards must answer three questions at a glance: are people finding answers; is the content useful; are we reducing tickets. Avoid a dashboard that merely lists everything — design for action.

Recommended dashboard layout (left-to-right, top-down):

  • Headline row: KB Health Score (single number + 30/90-day trend sparkline) and current deflection.
  • Search panel: total searches, search success (CTR), no-result %, average clicks per search, search latency. Include a table of top zero-result queries with counts.
  • Quality panel: Top 10 articles by views, their helpfulness %, and days_since_update. Highlight articles with high views + helpfulness < 60%.
  • Owner panel: items assigned to owners, overdue reviews, and open content requests (priority backlog).
  • Impact panel: deflection trend, AHT for KB-assisted tickets, and tickets opened for topics linked to KB articles.

Alert recipes for content owners (deliverable, low noise):

  • Alert A — Owner action required: an article owned by X has helpfulness < 60% AND > 500 views in last 30 days → notify owner (Slack/email).
  • Alert B — Search gap spike: daily no_result_rate > baseline + 3σ or > 10% → open an "investigate" ticket in backlog.
  • Alert C — Stale high-impact content: article days_since_update > 365 AND views_last_90d > threshold → assign review task.
  • Alert D — Agent adoption drop: linked-articles-per-ticket declines >15% month-over-month → schedule training/QA sync.

Example alert payload (JSON webhook) for Slack:

{
  "alert": "Stale high-impact article",
  "article_id": 1234,
  "title": "Configuring X in Prod",
  "views_90d": 1345,
  "helpfulness": 48,
  "days_since_update": 408,
  "owner": "alice@example.com",
  "next_action": "Please review or retire within 7 days"
}

Implementation notes:

  • Source your alerts from the canonical dataset (search logs + article metadata + ticket links). GA4 view_search_results is a reliable pipeline for searches; Zendesk / Guide Explore provides article metrics and linkages.
  • Use scheduled queries (BigQuery / Snowflake) or platform-native alerts (Looker, Tableau, Zendesk Explore) to reduce duplication and ensure a single source of truth.

Using analytics to triage updates and close knowledge gaps

Analytics should feed a priority backlog, not a to-do list of every low-value edit. Use a simple, repeatable triage framework I call IMPACT:

  1. Impact (traffic + ticket volume)
  2. Miss (search gaps / zero-result signal)
  3. Precision (helpfulness / feedback)
  4. Age (content freshness)
  5. Confidence (owner / subject-matter availability)
  6. Time-to-fix (estimate)

Translate IMPACT into a numeric priority score. Example scoring (illustrative):

  • Normalize metrics to 0–1 (min-max per dataset).
  • PriorityScore = 0.45*NormalizedViews + 0.25*NormalizedNoResultCount + 0.20*(1 - Helpfulness) + 0.10*NormalizedAge

Articles with PriorityScore > 0.7 enter the "update in next sprint" bucket; 0.5–0.7 are "review"; <0.5 are lower priority. Use thresholds as governance, not absolutes.

Sample SQL (BigQuery / GA4-like) to compute no_result_rate per day:

WITH searches AS (
  SELECT
    DATE(event_timestamp) AS day,
    event_params.value.string_value AS search_term,
    COUNT(1) AS attempts
  FROM `project.ga4_events_*`,
  UNNEST(event_params) AS event_params
  WHERE event_name = 'view_search_results'
    AND event_params.key = 'search_term'
  GROUP BY day, search_term
),
results AS (
  -- imaginary table of search_result_clicks populated by your search engine
  SELECT day, search_term, SUM(result_clicks) AS clicks
  FROM `project.search_clicks`
  GROUP BY day, search_term
)
SELECT
  s.day,
  SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(r.clicks,0)=0 THEN s.attempts ELSE 0 END) / SUM(s.attempts) AS no_result_rate
FROM searches s
LEFT JOIN results r
  ON s.day = r.day AND s.search_term = r.search_term
GROUP BY s.day
ORDER BY s.day DESC;

Use the top zero-result search_term output to create new backlog cards and to decide whether to add articles, retitle pages, or tune synonyms/redirects.

Contrarian insight from practice: chasing low-traffic, perfect grammar in every article stalls value. Prioritize the high-exposure failures — the articles people hit most that still fail them. A targeted refresh of 10–20 such pages often yields measurable deflection within 60–90 days.

Reporting cadence that keeps leadership and owners aligned

Establish rhythms that match stakeholder needs — rapid operational cadence for owners, summary cadence for managers, and strategic cadence for execs.

  • Daily (automated): owner alerts and a "today's top 5" digest posted to owner Slack channels. This is action-focused and should only surface items requiring action within 72 hours.
  • Weekly (owner + support lead): 30–45 minute triage to assign the top 10 priority items; convert high-impact fixes into a sprint backlog. Keep the meeting tactical and time-boxed.
  • Monthly (ops / QA manager): one-page KB health snapshot with KB Health Score, deflection trend, top 10 zero-result queries, and progress on the backlog. This is the unit of operational reporting.
  • Quarterly (product + leadership): present trend lines, major root causes (product ambiguity, search tuning, taxonomies), and resourcing requests (e.g., 2 FTEs for a quarter to refresh high-impact docs). Tie recommendations to expected ROI (reduction in tickets, AHT improvements). KCS measurement suggests using triangulated signals rather than single metrics when making investment cases.

Sample monthly KPI snapshot (one paragraph at top, then bullets):

  • One-line summary: "KB Health Score 74 (↑5 pts MoM), deflection +6% MoM, top 3 gaps remain X/Y/Z."
  • Bulleted details: search metrics, backlog progress, owner compliance rate, and estimated monthly ticket savings.

Process governance that sticks:

  • Assign clear owners and SLAs (e.g., an owner must respond to alerts within 7 business days).
  • Record decisions: update/retire/redirect/merge. Keep a changelog on each article (audit trail).

Fast-start playbook: KPIs, templates, and checklist

This is a compact, executable checklist to go from zero to a working KB health practice in 4 weeks.

Week 0 — foundation

  1. Define canonical data sources: search logs, article metadata (owner, last_updated), article feedback, ticket dataset. Map fields and owners.
  2. Create canonical metric definitions document (names + SQL/ETL) — share with data team.

Week 1 — dashboard + alerts

  1. Build a minimum dashboard: headline score, search panel, quality panel, owner queue. Use Looker/Tableau/PowerBI or vendor dashboards (Zendesk Explore, HubSpot Insights).
  2. Implement two alerts: (A) no-result spike; (B) stale high-impact article.

Week 2 — backlog intake and triage

  1. Populate backlog from: top zero-result queries, top low-helpfulness high-views, and top ticket drivers not covered.
  2. Run first weekly triage; assign owners and SLAs.

Week 3 — measure impact

  1. Track deflection and ticket volume for updated articles; measure AHT for KB-assisted issues. Report weekly.
  2. Iterate thresholds and owner SLAs based on noise/false positives.

Templates & snippets

Priority backlog scoring (Python-like pseudocode):

# normalized values are 0..1
priority = 0.45 * norm_views + 0.25 * norm_no_result_hits + 0.20 * (1 - helpfulness) + 0.10 * norm_age

Owner alert rule (pseudo SQL condition):

-- select articles that should trigger owner alert
SELECT article_id, title, views_30d, helpfulness, days_since_update, owner
FROM kb_articles
WHERE views_30d > 500
  AND helpfulness < 0.60
  AND owner IS NOT NULL;

Dashboard widget checklist:

  • Single-value widget: KB Health Score with sparkline (30/90d).
  • Line chart: no_result_rate daily (last 90d).
  • Table: Top 20 zero-result queries with search volume.
  • Table: Top 20 high-views low-helpfulness with owner and days_since_update.
  • Bar chart: Deflection trend (monthly).
  • Owner view: My assigned tasks / overdue reviews with direct links.

Governance checklist (use as policy):

  • Each article must have an owner and last_reviewed date.
  • Articles with no owner & views > threshold → auto-assign to team lead and flag.
  • Every content owner receives a weekly digest with actionable items only.
  • Quarterly audit: retire or archive articles with zero views for 18+ months unless business-critical.

Closing paragraph

Make the KB measurable, visible, and governed: triage by impact not by age, automate noise-free alerts to owners, and tie outcomes to support metrics like deflection and AHT. A focused dashboard and a small set of defensible KPIs turn a reactive pile of documents into a reliable operational lever that improves QA consistency and reduces support load.

Sources:
Using the metrics that matter to improve your knowledge base - Zendesk guide on article views, search analytics, helpfulness, and Explore reports used for KB measurement and self-service scoring.

Analyze knowledge base performance - HubSpot documentation on KB metrics (views, helpfulness, search terms, and content insights) and the Insights/Analyze tools.

Automatically collected events - Analytics Help (GA4) - GA4 view_search_results event and search_term parameter guidance for tracking internal site search.

Introduction - Consortium for Service Innovation (KCS Measurement Matters) - KCS measurement philosophy and principles for governance and continuous improvement.

How to Measure Knowledge Management Success: KPIs, Dashboards and Real ROI - Practitioner guidance on KM metrics, dashboards, and translating KB analytics into operational impact.

Acting on Your Site Search Analytics - Practical examples of site-search metrics to act on and how to prioritize search improvements.

How to Avoid ‘No Results’ Pages - Guidance on zero-result queries, why they matter, and remediation strategies (synonyms, fallback content).

title: Managed Postgres pricing in 2026: eight providers compared
description:
Managed Postgres is priced in more ways than almost any other cloud product. Some providers sell a fixed instance with storage on top, some include storage up to a cap, one meters memory by the hour, and one wraps the database in a $25 platform plan. That makes two quotes hard to compare at a glance. This post prices the same two databases on eight providers, using list prices read from each provider's pricing page on 2026-10-13. The numbers match our managed Postgres cost calculator, where you can try any size.

TL;DR

  • For a small database (1 GB of memory, 10 GB of storage), monthly prices run from $9 on Heroku Essential-1 to about $41 on Fly.io Managed Postgres. Ownkube is $10.50.
  • For a mid-size database (4 GB of memory, 50 GB of storage), the range runs from $40.50 on Ownkube to $296 on Fly.io, which has no plan between 2 GB and 8 GB.
  • Heroku's Essential plans are the cheapest small option, with shared memory and a hard 10 GB storage cap on Essential-1.
  • Neon and Railway bill by usage, so a quiet database costs less than the always-on figures here. Fly.io includes high availability in every plan, which is part of why it costs more.

How do providers price managed Postgres?

Four models show up across the eight providers:

  • Fixed instance plus storage. You pick a memory size and pay a flat monthly price, then pay per GB of disk. Ownkube, Render and Fly.io work this way.
  • Fixed instance with storage included. The plan price covers a set amount of disk. Heroku includes storage up to each plan's cap. DigitalOcean includes the low end of a storage range and charges for more in 10 GiB steps.
  • Usage-based. Neon bills compute in CU-hours (one CU is about 4 GB of memory) plus storage. Railway bills memory and CPU by the minute plus volume storage.
  • Platform plan plus compute. Supabase Pro costs $25 a month and includes $10 of compute credit and 8 GB of disk. Larger compute sizes and extra disk add to that.

The storage rate is easy to skim past. It ranges from $0.125 per GB on Supabase to $0.35 per GB on Neon, which matters more as the database grows.

What does a 1 GB and a 4 GB database cost on each provider?

Provider 1 GB memory, 10 GB storage 4 GB memory, 50 GB storage
Ownkube $10.50 (DB 1) $40.50 (DB 4)
Heroku $9.00 (Essential-1, shared memory) $50.00 (Standard-0)
Railway $13.50 (usage) $49.50 (usage)
DigitalOcean $15.15 (1 GiB node) $60.90 (4 GiB node)
Render $22.00 (0.5c-1g) $70.00 (1c-4g)
Neon $22.85 (Launch, 0.25 CU always on) $94.88 (Launch, 1 CU always on)
Supabase $25.25 (Pro + Micro) $80.25 (Pro + Medium)
Fly.io $40.80 (Basic) $296.00 (Launch, 8 GB)

List prices in USD per month, read from each provider's pricing page on 2026-10-13. Railway assumes 0.1 vCPU of average database CPU; each extra 0.1 vCPU adds about $2. Neon is modelled always on. Single instance unless noted. Taxes and bandwidth excluded.

Why is Heroku the cheapest small database?

Heroku Essential-1 costs $9 a month with 10 GB of storage included, and nothing on this list beats it at that size. The trade is in the plan shape. Essential databases run on shared memory with no stated allocation, and storage is a hard cap: Essential-1 stops at 10 GB, and the next step is Essential-2 at $20 for 32 GB. Above that, Heroku moves to the Standard plans, which start at $50 for 4 GB of memory and jump to $200 for 8 GB.

So Heroku is a good fit for a small database that will stay small. Once you need a guaranteed memory size or more than 32 GB of data, the price steps are large. Our Heroku pricing and alternatives guide covers the rest of the Heroku bill.

What do Neon and Railway cost when the database is quiet?

Less than the table shows. Both bill by usage, and the table prices them as if the database runs all month.

Neon scales compute to zero after a period without queries, so a database that serves a few hours of traffic a day pays for those hours plus storage. The always-on figure ($22.85 at 0.25 CU) is the ceiling for that size. Neon also gives you branching, which makes a copy of the database for each pull request.

Railway bills the memory the database process holds and the CPU it uses. Postgres keeps its buffers in memory, so the memory line tends to stay near the allocation. The CPU line is where a quiet database saves money.

On fixed-instance providers, including Ownkube, the price stays the same whether the database is busy or idle.

Why does Fly.io cost more?

Fly.io Managed Postgres includes high availability, backups and connection pooling on every plan, and the $38 Basic price pays for all three. If you need a standby from day one, compare Fly against the high-availability price elsewhere. On Ownkube, for example, each standby bills as another database box plus its own storage, so a primary with one standby costs about twice the single-instance figure.

The plan ladder also matters at the 4 GB size. Fly's plans go from Starter (2 GB) to Launch (8 GB), so a 4 GB requirement lands on the 8 GB plan.

What does Supabase include for $25?

Supabase Pro is a platform plan: Postgres plus authentication, file storage, realtime and edge functions, with $10 of compute credit that covers the Micro size. If you use those features, the $25 buys much more than a database. If you only use Postgres behind your own API, you are paying for the bundle. Our Supabase alternatives post walks through that decision.

How does Ownkube price Postgres?

Ownkube runs Postgres 17 or 18 on database boxes: a flat monthly price for the memory size, plus storage.

  • Boxes: DB 0.5 at $4, DB 1 at $8, DB 2 at $12, DB 4 at $28, DB 8 at $54 and DB 16 at $104 a month.
  • Storage: $0.25 per GB per month from the first GB, on the volume you provision.
  • Backups: on the Personal and Team plans, storage includes 7-day backups with point-in-time restore. Backups are off by default and you turn them on per database.
  • High availability: a primary plus up to two standbys with automatic failover, on Team. Each standby bills as its own database box, and storage bills per replica.

Pay as you go accounts can run databases up to DB 2, with no backups. Personal costs $5 a month, loads $5 of wallet credit, and unlocks every size and backups. Everything draws one prepaid wallet, and unused credit never expires.

A database on Ownkube sits next to your app in the same region, on the same bill. Our guide to adding a managed Postgres database shows the setup, and the Postgres hosting page covers versions and connection details.

When is another provider the better choice?

  • The database is small and will stay small. Heroku Essential is cheaper than Ownkube at 1 GB, as long as shared memory and a storage cap are fine for you.
  • You want branching or scale to zero. Neon is built for that workflow.
  • You need high availability on the smallest plan. Fly.io includes it from Basic. On Ownkube, standbys are a Team feature.
  • You need a region outside Europe and South Asia. Ownkube databases run in the Mumbai and Germany regions today. DigitalOcean, Render and Fly.io cover far more locations.
  • You use Supabase's auth, storage and realtime. Keep Supabase; replacing all of it is real work.

FAQ

What is the cheapest managed Postgres in 2026?

For a 1 GB database with 10 GB of storage, Heroku Essential-1 at $9 a month, followed by Ownkube at $10.50 and Railway at about $13.50. For a 4 GB database with 50 GB of storage, Ownkube at $40.50, followed by Railway at about $49.50 and Heroku Standard-0 at $50. Prices are list prices checked on 2026-10-13.

Is Neon cheaper than Supabase?

It depends on how often the database is busy. Always on, a 1 GB Neon database costs about $22.85 against $25.25 on Supabase Pro. If the database sleeps for much of the day, Neon drops well below that. Supabase includes auth, storage and realtime in its $25, which Neon does not.

Does managed Postgres pricing include backups?

It varies. On Ownkube, 7-day backups with point-in-time restore are included in the storage price on Personal and Team. Fly.io includes backups on every plan, and Render offers point-in-time recovery on paid instances. Check each provider's retention window, since a day of backups and a week of point-in-time restore are very different safety nets.

How much storage should I plan for?

Plan for your data plus its indexes plus room to grow. On Ownkube and Render you pay per GB provisioned. On Heroku a database that crosses its plan's cap needs a plan change, and DigitalOcean adds storage in 10 GiB steps up to each plan's maximum. Our calculator lets you price any storage size.

Where Ownkube fits

Ownkube is a developer platform that runs your app and its Postgres side by side on one prepaid wallet. Database boxes start at $4 a month, storage is $0.25 per GB with 7-day backups included on Personal and Team, and at the 4 GB size priced here it has the lowest list price of the eight providers. Deploy my first app.

title: Node.js Realtime Delivery Latency — 4 Connection Health Metrics for Patient Alerts
description:
Short answer: in Node.js, measure realtime delivery latency by publishing a server timestamp and message ID with every typing indicator or read receipt, then have each client report when it observed that event. Track the resulting delay distribution alongside connection health, reconnects, and receipt coverage; alert on a sustained trend, not one slow phone.

For a healthtech notification flow, the deciding constraint is fan-out. A successful publish says little about the last browser in a care team, and server timing cannot include the final network hop, a suspended tab, or work queued on the client. The useful measurement boundary ends at the screen that received the event.

My recommendation is to try Infrai for the realtime publish and metrics-reporting boundary when a small team also expects to add adjacent backend capabilities: its 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind one key and a consistent REST contract, so the next capability does not require another credential lifecycle. One credential and one bill also remove reconciliation work from this already multi-part telemetry path. The supporting advantage is practical during instrumentation: its public discovery surface returns request and response schemas, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. This is a breadth and operating-cost argument, not a claim that its network is faster.

Infrai's second verified advantage is operational: one API key, one wallet, and one consolidated bill cover the publishing and reporting sides of this loop, while the plain REST API needs no SDK to install. Its self-describing public discovery surface needs no key, returns full request and response JSON Schema, billing details, and runnable examples, and every documented capability has examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, those are concrete maintenance reductions: a solo team can generate both adapters from current schemas, reuse one HTTP retry policy and one credential rotation path, and avoid maintaining separate vendor libraries, keys, and invoice reconciliation for realtime delivery and its metrics. The benefit grows when the same application later needs another backend module, because the integration machinery remains the same even though the capability changes.

Infrai also specifies per-call cost, vendor, and latency metadata consistently on its native and OpenAI-compatible surfaces. That makes downstream spend and vendor routing observable through one metadata shape, which is useful when this experiment compares the full operating bill rather than a published unit price.

That friction compounds.

The workflow uses one API key, one wallet, and one bill across realtime publication and metric reporting. That avoids separate credentials and invoice reconciliation for the two halves of the measurement loop. It is also one plain REST API with no SDK to install, so the Node.js publisher and metric reporter can share the platform's built-in HTTP client, error handling, and retry policy instead of carrying two vendor libraries through upgrades.

There is a second operational reason for this workload: idempotency is a platform convention, not an endpoint afterthought. The discovery data marks 171 of 294 capabilities as idempotent, and the convention specifies an Idempotency-Key, a deterministic server fallback, and a 24-hour default deduplication window. That matters when a 429 or broken connection leaves the publisher unsure whether a read receipt was accepted. The client still has to reuse the same key across retries, as the example does.

How should Node.js measure realtime delivery latency and connection health?

Typing indicators are disposable state. Read receipts are not. Treating them as identical creates an attractive dashboard that hides the actual product contract.

For a typing event, freshness wins: an event that arrives after the user stopped typing can be discarded. For a read receipt, the client should apply an idempotent state transition keyed by message and reader, because reconnection and retry can produce another observation. Neither rule turns publish acknowledgement into delivery proof.

I would define four measurements before choosing a provider:

  1. Observed delay: client receive time minus the publish timestamp, summarized with percentiles rather than an average.
  2. Receipt coverage: distinct intended clients reporting an observation divided by intended clients for a sampled event.
  3. Heartbeat age: time since the client last demonstrated a healthy connection.
  4. Reconnect rate: reconnect attempts per active client over a fixed window.

The first metric answers speed. The next three explain confidence in that answer. If receipt coverage falls, a flattering latency percentile may merely describe the clients that remained connected.

There is a clock caveat. Client receive time and server publish time live on different clocks, so raw subtraction includes clock skew. Record a client clock-offset estimate from a small request-response exchange, keep the uncorrected value for diagnosis, and reject impossible values from alert aggregation. For stricter measurement, send a server timestamp periodically and estimate offset from the midpoint of the round trip. It is an estimate, not truth.

A focused TypeScript measurement loop

The simple approach is to start a timer around the server's publish call. That measures provider acceptance latency. It does not measure delivery, and it gets less representative as fan-out grows.

The following dependency-free TypeScript sketch measures at the recipient. It keeps transport details behind two tiny interfaces, so the same code can sit above a hosted realtime service, WebSocket gateway, or Server-Sent Events connection. The reporter batches observations to control downstream metric volume; a read receipt can be fully observed while high-frequency typing events are sampled.

import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

type RealtimeEvent = {
  id: string;
  channel: string;
  kind: "typing" | "read";
  publishedAtMs: number;
  actorId: string;
  messageId?: string;
};

type DeliveryObservation = {
  eventId: string;
  clientId: string;
  kind: RealtimeEvent["kind"];
  observedDelayMs: number;
  rawDelayMs: number;
  connectionAgeMs: number;
  observedAtMs: number;
};

interface ObservationReporter {
  report(observation: DeliveryObservation): Promise<void>;
}

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function postInfrai(url: string, body: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  const idempotencyKey = randomUUID();
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
      const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
        ? retryAfter * 1_000
        : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
      continue;
    }

    const result: unknown = await response.json();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Infrai ${response.status}: ${JSON.stringify(result)}`);
    }
    return result;
  }
  throw new Error("Infrai retry budget exhausted");
}

export async function publishCareEvent(
  publishBody: Record<string, unknown>,
  event: Omit<RealtimeEvent, "id" | "publishedAtMs">,
): Promise<RealtimeEvent> {
  const stamped: RealtimeEvent = {
    ...event,
    id: randomUUID(),
    publishedAtMs: Date.now(),
  };
  await postInfrai(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish",
    { ...publishBody, data: stamped },
  );
  return stamped;
}

export async function observeCareEvent(
  reporter: ObservationReporter,
  event: RealtimeEvent,
  clientId: string,
  connectedAtMs: number,
  estimatedClockOffsetMs: number,
): Promise<void> {
  const observedAtMs = Date.now();
  const rawDelayMs = observedAtMs - event.publishedAtMs;
  const observedDelayMs = rawDelayMs - estimatedClockOffsetMs;

  if (!Number.isFinite(observedDelayMs) || observedDelayMs < 0) return;

  const observation = {
    eventId: event.id,
    clientId,
    kind: event.kind,
    observedDelayMs,
    rawDelayMs,
    connectionAgeMs: observedAtMs - connectedAtMs,
    observedAtMs,
  };

  await reporter.report(observation);
  await postInfrai(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/metrics/report",
    observation,
  );
}

Pass publishBody fields from the current public discovery schema rather than freezing undocumented fields into the adapter. The example adds only the measured event under data; before running it, confirm that field against discovery as well. Authentication is Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY, and the adapter surfaces non-2xx response bodies while backing off on HTTP 429 and honoring Retry-After.

Do not report every keystroke from every client. A deterministic sampler based on event ID keeps a stable subset across retries. Keep every read-receipt observation where the audit value warrants it, aggregate typing observations into short windows, and attach only low-cardinality dimensions such as event kind, client platform, and region. Patient IDs and message IDs belong in controlled diagnostic storage, not metric labels.

Why averages fail this experiment

Suppose a care-team notification fans out to 12 intended sessions. Ten arrive quickly, one arrives much later, and one disconnected session never reports. The mean over the ten reports erases both tails: the delayed clinician and the absent device. No invented threshold fixes that modeling error.

Store a histogram of observed delay and a separate coverage ratio. Review p50, p95, and p99 over a rolling window, split by event kind and client platform. Then compare those distributions with heartbeat age and reconnect rate. A rising p95 with stable coverage points toward slower delivery; falling coverage with a normal p95 points toward connection loss or clients unable to report.

One sample proves nothing.

Alert when several adjacent windows depart from the service objective, and require enough samples for a percentile to mean anything. The exact window, minimum count, and threshold must come from the clinical workflow's tolerance and measured baseline. A typing indicator may expire quietly. A read receipt may need a durable reconciliation path in the application data model. Realtime telemetry should reveal that difference rather than flatten it.

Effective cost also changes with fan-out. Count publish operations, delivered messages if the provider bills that way, client observation writes, retained diagnostic records, and the engineer time spent maintaining authentication, schemas, dashboards, and retries. Downstream metric cardinality can dominate a design that looked inexpensive at the publish boundary. Sampling and aggregation are product decisions as much as telemetry decisions.

Where each provider fits

No public feature page can establish which service will be fastest for your users. Run the same instrumented workload in the regions, browsers, mobile states, and fan-out sizes you expect. Product architecture still narrows the shortlist.

Option Useful fit for this experiment Boundary to evaluate
Infrai A small team that values one REST contract across realtime, metrics, and later backend modules Use discovery for exact schemas; validate delivery behavior and regional fit with the client-reported experiment
Ably Teams that want a realtime specialist with documented message ordering, delivery semantics, and connection-state behavior Map its guarantees to ephemeral typing versus durable receipt requirements, then measure the actual client path
Pusher Channels Teams that want a focused hosted channels model with presence and client events Plan the separate metrics pipeline and test how reconnect behavior affects coverage
PubNub Workloads that benefit from a specialist publish/subscribe network plus presence and message persistence options Decide which events merit persistence and account for the resulting delivery and storage workload
AWS AppSync Events AWS-centered systems that want managed serverless WebSocket events integrated with AWS identity and operations Include cloud coupling, authorization design, and observability assembly in the operating bill

Ably is the stronger candidate when explicit realtime protocol semantics and specialist tooling are the main purchase. Pusher Channels can be easier to reason about when the scope stays narrowly channel-oriented. PubNub deserves evaluation when presence, persistence, and wide publish/subscribe distribution drive the design. AppSync Events makes sense when the team already operates inside AWS and accepts that coupling.

Infrai's advantage is different: breadth behind one surface. It is a sensible shortlist entry when adding the metrics side of this experiment, and later capabilities, would otherwise mean more integrations, keys, and billing paths. A specialist is the better choice if its delivery guarantees, regional topology, connection controls, or protocol-specific tooling match a hard requirement that the broader surface does not document.

What to measure before copying this choice

Run a replayable test matrix before committing. Vary fan-out, payload size, client platform, network state, and foreground versus suspended execution. For each cell, capture observed-delay percentiles, receipt coverage, heartbeat age, reconnect rate, duplicated observations, and metric ingestion volume. Keep provider acceptance time too, but label it correctly.

Test read receipts and typing indicators separately. Confirm that stale typing events expire at the application boundary, duplicate read observations converge to one state, and a reconnecting client cannot make the dashboard look healthier by omitting missed events. Then estimate the full operating bill from the workload: realtime traffic, reporting traffic, telemetry retention, cardinality, and integration ownership. Price per call is only one input, and it changes.

The decision rule is compact: choose the option whose measured delivery distribution and coverage meet the workflow objective, whose guarantees fit each event type, and whose complete operating burden a small team can sustain. If the unified boundary fits that result, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before implementing adapters.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Ably: Message ordering and delivery guarantees
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub: Message persistence
  • AWS AppSync Events
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: The one-line way to add live chat to a hosted storefront or a custom-built site
description:
One <script> tag, placed in the single layout file every page renders through, loaded async, with a guard so client-side navigation doesn't load it twice. That's the whole answer.

The rest of this post is the five places people get it wrong.

The line 

<script async src="EMBED_SRC" data-site="YOUR_SITE_KEY"></script>

Two values, both issued for your site: EMBED_SRC and YOUR_SITE_KEY. Copy them from the snippet you were given — don't retype them from a screenshot, and don't hand-edit the source URL.

Put it immediately before </body>. Not in <head>: async helps, but there's no reason for the widget to compete with your largest contentful paint for bandwidth.

Where it goes — once

Static site

The footer partial — whatever your build includes on every page. One file, one paste.

Single-page app

The root layout: the _app file, App.vue, layout.tsx, the component that wraps every route. Not the router outlet, and not individual pages.

Hosted storefront

The theme's main layout file — the single file every page renders through. One paste covers product pages, collections, cart, and checkout.

If you find yourself pasting it into three templates, stop. You now have three places to update the site key.

Guard against the double load

Frameworks remount layouts on some navigations. Check before injecting:

<script>
  (function () {
    if (window.__chatEmbedLoaded) return;
    window.__chatEmbedLoaded = true;
    var s = document.createElement('script');
    s.async = true;
    s.src = 'EMBED_SRC';
    s.setAttribute('data-site', 'YOUR_SITE_KEY');
    document.body.appendChild(s);
  })();
</script>

Same two values, one flag. Verify it below.

Give the widget something to work with

A one-line embed can't guess what the visitor is asking about. Whatever the embed accepts as page context — the current URL, an order reference, a hashed user id — set it before the loader runs, and only the keys the snippet documents.

Why this matters more than it sounds: the point of the handoff. Rules answer the questions you've already written answers for, AI covers the long tail in between, and a human steps into the same conversation when both run out. If the human arrives without the page URL and the order number, their first message is asking for them.

The shop side of that handoff is publicly demoable without a signup, so you can see what the agent's console actually looks like mid-conversation before you install anything. And the client notifies you even when it's in the background, so "someone is waiting" doesn't depend on you keeping a tab in front of you.

Add the embed origin to your CSP

If you ship a Content-Security-Policy, the embed is a new origin and it will be blocked silently. Take the scheme and host of EMBED_SRC, strip the path, and call that EMBED_ORIGIN:

Content-Security-Policy:
  script-src 'self' EMBED_ORIGIN;
  connect-src 'self' EMBED_ORIGIN;
  frame-src EMBED_ORIGIN;

Do this before you paste, not after you've spent an afternoon on a blank corner of the screen.

Verify in sixty seconds

  1. DevTools → Network, filter by EMBED_ORIGIN: the request appears on the home page.
  2. Navigate to five different pages: still exactly one request per load.
  3. Console: no CSP violation, no 404 on the source.
  4. Resize to a mobile viewport: the launcher is visible and doesn't cover your add-to-cart or form submit button.
  5. Trigger a soft navigation (client-side route change): still exactly one request.

If step 2 or 5 shows two, the guard above is missing or the tag is in two templates.

Why one line is the right unit

The embed is the install, not the product. Rules, AI answers, and the human handoff live in the conversation layer, not in the snippet — which means you can ship the widget today and add rules next week once you've seen what people actually ask. That split is also why the install stays one line when the logic grows.

The same install is documented here — aumcreate.com/aumchat. If the site happens to be WordPress, there's an installer plugin and you paste nothing at all.

Pitfalls, in order of frequency

  • Inside a conditional block. The tag ends up only on the pages where that condition held. Put it in the layout, unconditionally.
  • In <head> with no async. Blocks parsing. If you must keep it in the head, keep async and move it down when you can.
  • Re-injected on every route change. No flag, no guard, three widgets stacked in the corner.
  • CSP added later. Everything worked in staging because staging had no policy.
  • Site key hardcoded in three templates. You'll find out when you rotate it.

title: My webhook catcher taught me that testing Stripe callbacks locally is a lie you tell yourself
description:
I built a webhook catcher because every agent developer hits the same wall: you're wiring up a payment flow, a GitHub integration, or some internal service, and you need a public HTTPS URL that actually receives POSTs. Ngrok works until your laptop sleeps. Deploying a throwaway function to some cloud costs more than the test is worth.

So I made an ephemeral webhook receiver: one call creates a single-use HTTPS URL, senders need no credentials, it stores up to 100 events for 24 hours, then deletes itself. In-memory, no database, no cleanup cron.

The lesson came from watching my own test suite. I was testing a Stripe-like flow end to end: fire a webhook, read it back, assert the payload shape. Worked perfectly until I added a retry loop — the sender retries on timeout, which my catcher intentionally doesn't simulate, so every test "passed" while my real integration would have collapsed under the first network blip.

The fix wasn't in the catcher. It was in my mental model of what a webhook receiver is for. It's not a mock. It's a mirror. If you're testing retry logic, durability, ordering guarantees — those are properties of the sender and your consumer, not the pipe. The catcher's job is to be a dumb, reliable pipe so you can see exactly what your consumer receives, byte for byte, headers included.

That distinction shaped the API. No filtering, no transformation, no "helpful" normalization. Store the raw body, the headers, the timestamp. Let the agent decide what matters. I've used it for Stripe webhook shapes, GitHub push events, and once for debugging why an internal service's JSON was arriving as form-encoded — the catcher showed me the Content-Type lie in one call.

If you're building anything that receives callbacks, point your sender at a fresh hook, do your real work, then read back what actually arrived. The gap between what you sent and what landed is where the bugs live.

I packaged it as https://x402.freeq.one/tools/webhook_catch.html

title: I built a static site generator in Rust because Astro felt slow
description:
Most frameworks feel slow to me. I was using Astro for my blog, and even Astro, which is supposed to be fast, felt slow. Then one day it hit me: why not write a really fast static site generator in Rust, the language that makes everything fast?

That's how agno started. It's a single 4.2 MB binary with no Node.js and no bundler.

Performance blew past my expectations. On the same corpus, cold builds are 3.9-12.8x faster than Hugo and 16.7-185x faster than Astro. I tested it with up to 10,000 posts, and the speed never let me down, it kept surprising me. The full methodology and caveats are in the README.

It has everything I personally need, but that is not the finish line for me, and I'm still working on it.

You can try it with cargo install agno.

Repo: https://github.com/agnogad/agno

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports Secure Compute
description:
Vercel Sandbox now supports Secure Compute, connecting sandboxes to a team's dedicated network. Public-internet traffic exits through the network's static IPs, and sandboxes can reach private resources in an AWS VPC through VPC peering.

You can attach a sandbox to your network in your code or via the CLI.

In your code, pass an existing Secure Compute network ID when creating a sandbox:

In the CLI, append --network-id and your network id value when you run the sandbox create command.

Existing sandboxes can attach to or change networks with sandbox.update(). The change takes effect on the next session. A running session keeps its current network until it stops.

Available to Enterprise teams with Secure Compute.

Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

title: October 02, 2026
description:
Apigee X

Announcement

On October 2, 2026, we released an updated version of Apigee (1-18-0-apigee-6).

Note: Rollouts of this release began today and can take four or more business days to complete across all Google Cloud zones. Your instances might not have the features and fixes available until the rollout is complete.

Security

Bug ID Description
564386425 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Apigee ingress gateway (ASM) to patch security vulnerabilities.
561666530 Security fix for Apigee. Upgraded the Prometheus library to patch the following vulnerabilities:

  • CVE-2026-42151
  • CVE-2026-42154
  • CVE-2026-44903
  • CVE-2026-40179
N/A Security fix for Apigee infrastructure.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Issue

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.

Workaround: For cos_containerd node pools, upgrade the node pool to a version with the required kernel support (for example, 1.34.6-gke.1154000 or later, 1.35.3-gke.1389000 or later, or match the control plane).
