title: Keeping tags attached when files move: watched folders in AssetHoard 0.2.4
description:
A file manager knows where a file is. An asset library also knows what you said about it: its tags, its category, which bundle it belongs to and which projects use it. The moment someone renames that file in Explorer or Finder, those two views of the world disagree.

AssetHoard is a local-first desktop asset manager for indie game devs, built in Rust and Tauri. Watched folders let you point it at directories you already organise by hand, and it keeps the library in step. Version 0.2.4 rewrites how watched folders handle files that change underneath them.

The cases that break naive watching

A file watcher reports events. Turning those events into "this is the same asset as before" is where it gets interesting.

Renames and moves. The event stream for a move is not always a tidy rename. Moves across directories, or batches of them from a sync tool, can arrive as separate removals and creations. In 0.2.4 the asset is the thing being preserved, so tags, category, bundle and project links follow the file to its new path. Mirrored bundles move with their folders.

Case-only renames. Renaming Rock.png to rock.png is a real rename, but a case-insensitive comparison sees no change at all. These now keep their metadata too.

Changes made while the app was closed. There are no events to listen to when nothing is running. AssetHoard now recognises moves made while it was closed. Existing libraries are catalogued in the background after the update.

Saving over a file. Plenty of tools save by writing a new file and replacing the old one. To a watcher, that looks like a deletion. AssetHoard now waits briefly before marking anything missing, so a save does not flag the asset.

Disconnected drives. An unplugged external drive is not a deleted library. Assets on a disconnected drive or network share are paused rather than marked missing, and if the drive comes back under a different letter, AssetHoard picks it up again.

Nested watched folders. Watch Assets/ and also Assets/Characters/, and two watchers claim the same files. The rule now is that the innermost watched folder owns its files, and you get a preview with exact counts before anything moves.

The limit: network drives

Live rename and move tracking depends on the operating system sending file change events. Network drives over SMB or UNC paths do not provide them, so they do not get live tracking. They still pause cleanly when they disconnect.

Also in 0.2.4

  • 3D model thumbnails generate around 20x faster on import.
  • Most image thumbnails are now generated after import, so imports finish much sooner.
  • Re-importing a changed file updates the existing asset instead of creating a duplicate.
  • The search index is reused on launch instead of rebuilt, and text search no longer waits for image search.

Everything else is in the 0.2.4 release notes, and setup is covered in the watched folders docs. AssetHoard is free to download during the open beta.

If you have built file watching into a desktop app, I would like to hear how you handled renames and saves that replace files.

title: Queue depth lies when one Service Bus queue serves every customer
description:
Here's the design question that keeps coming back on our SaaS platform: one queue, shared by every customer, sitting between the cloud product and whatever the customer runs on-prem. Is that one queue enough? Scalable enough, reliable enough? I think the answer is yes for a surprisingly long time. What I don't think survives is the dashboard most teams put on top of it.

Start with the plumbing, because the on-prem link is where the decision actually gets made.

There are two ways to get the cloud talking to a customer's data centre. You can have the cloud call in over HTTP, a trigger that hits an endpoint on their side. Or you can put a broker in the middle, Service Bus say, and let the on-prem agent reach out and pull. I'm firmly in the second camp. Customers' firewall teams will say no to inbound holes. They rarely object to an outbound connection on 443 from one agent. And an HTTP trigger has an ugly failure mode: when the customer's site is down for maintenance, your caller either blocks, retries in a tight loop, or drops the call. A queue just holds the message.

That last point is the whole value. The queue turns "the customer is offline" from an incident into a backlog.

Now the multi-tenant part. A single queue for all customers is cheap and simple, and the usual objection is noisy neighbours: one customer bulk-loads fifty thousand messages and everyone behind them waits. That's real. But it's a fairness problem, not a capacity problem, and the two get different fixes. Capacity you buy: Premium tier, more messaging units, partitioning. Fairness you design: session IDs keyed on tenant, so ordering holds per customer and a slow consumer for one tenant doesn't block the others' sessions.

Sessions have a cost. A session-enabled queue means every receiver has to accept a session before it reads anything, and a tenant's session is locked to one receiver at a time. That caps single-tenant throughput at what one receiver can chew through. For most B2B integration traffic that's fine. For a tenant who really does send in bursts, give them their own queue. I'd rather have a shared default and a handful of promoted exceptions than start with queue-per-tenant and own a thousand entities in the deployment pipeline.

So far so ordinary. Here's where I think teams get hurt.

They wire up an alert on active message count. Over 5,000, page someone. It feels right. It's wrong in a multi-tenant queue, and wrong in a specific way: it measures the sum of everybody, and the sum hides the one person who is actually broken.

Picture it. Customer A's on-prem agent lost its credentials on Tuesday afternoon. Their messages pile up, 300 of them. Total queue depth is 300 on a queue that normally runs at 2,000 during business hours. No alert. Nothing looks unusual. Customer A finds out their data hasn't synced for two days when they phone support on Thursday.

Depth fails you in both directions. A big batch from a healthy tenant trips the alarm while every message is being consumed on time. A stuck tenant stays under the threshold forever because the rest of the queue is quiet.

The metric I want instead is the age of the oldest unprocessed message, per tenant. A stuck tenant shows up in minutes, because their oldest message keeps getting older while every other tenant's resets constantly. A bulk load from a healthy tenant shows high depth but a low, flat age. Age separates "busy" from "broken", and depth cannot.

Getting it isn't free. Service Bus doesn't hand you per-session oldest-age as a built-in metric, so you stamp the enqueue time and the tenant ID on every message, and emit the delay from the consumer when it completes one. That gives you processing latency per tenant, which is already useful. For the stuck case, where nothing is completing at all, you need a second signal: a small scheduled check that peeks the head of the queue and flags any tenant with a message older than your threshold. Peek doesn't lock anything, so it's safe to run every minute. Messy, yes. Still much cheaper than the Thursday phone call.

Dead-letter needs the same treatment. A total dead-letter count of 40 means nothing until you know 38 of them belong to one tenant whose payloads started failing schema validation after a release. Tag it, group by tenant, alert on a tenant crossing a number rather than the queue crossing one.

I'll admit the counterpoint with some weight behind it: per-tenant tracking adds cardinality, and metrics platforms bill on it. If you have ten thousand tenants, per-tenant time series is its own cost problem. Fine. Track the top offenders, or sample. But even at that scale, I'd take the oldest-age-by-tenant on the worst twenty over a perfect global depth chart.

On reliability, the answer to "one queue for all customers" comes down to three choices, and none is exotic. Turn on duplicate detection, since the on-prem agent will retry and you don't want a customer's order processed twice. Set max delivery count deliberately, because the default of 10 means a poison message cycles ten times before dead-lettering, and in a session queue that stalls the whole tenant while it does. And make the on-prem consumer idempotent regardless, because duplicate detection only covers the window you configured.

Where does that leave the original question? One queue is fine to start. HTTP triggers into customer networks are the thing I'd avoid. But the part that deserves your design time isn't the topology at all. It's whether, on a quiet Tuesday, you would find out that one customer has been silently stuck since lunch.

If your current alert can't answer that, the queue is not the thing to fix.

title: node2shell: How to Check If Your Node.js App Is Exposed and Patch It
description:
node2shell is the nickname for CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The Node.js project fixed it on 21 October 2026, and the fix is a runtime upgrade. Here's how to check and patch, based on the advisories listed at the end.

What node2shell is

The Node.js security release describes an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder. If an attacker can supply Brotli data that your app decompresses with node:zlib, they can corrupt process memory. Node.js says this can lead to a crash, memory disclosure or remote code execution. It affects the 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines, and Node.js credits OpenAI Codex Security with reporting it.

Severity ratings differ by source:

  • The Node.js advisory rates it high.
  • The CVE record gives it 9.2 (critical) on CVSS 4.0 and places the root bug in Google's Brotli library, versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0.
  • Singapore's Cyber Security Agency calls it critical, citing a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

Imperva's Red Team says it got code execution against the official Node.js 24.22.0 image, through both the built-in fetch() and Express 5 / body-parser 2 request parsers. It says 24.22.1 rejected the same input.

Where http2shell fits in

http2shell is not a second bug. Aikido Security uses the name for the same CVE now that it is known to reach beyond Node.js. It lists fixes for Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, libbrotli, curl/libcurl, Bun, Envoy and Istio. On 23 October, Aikido said patches were not yet available for every affected service.

Am I exposed?

Vercel's advisory explains that Node.js doesn't decode Brotli by itself. Your app is exposed when your code or a library decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. That data can come in a request body or in a response your app fetches.

1. Check the runtime version.

node -v

The fixed versions are 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 (or newer in the same line). Anything older in those lines is affected. Node.js 20 is end-of-life and won't get a fix, according to Vercel.

2. Look for paths that decode Brotli. Imperva's tests found Express 5 and body-parser 2 decode Brotli request bodies when their parsers are configured:

npm ls express body-parser

Also look for fetch() calls to servers you don't control and direct zlib Brotli use (brotliDecompress).

3. Check containers and CI, not just your laptop. Imperva warns that a package inventory can miss an older Node binary inside a container image:

docker run --rm your-image:tag node -v

How to patch

With nvm:

nvm install 24
nvm use 24
node -v   # should print v24.22.1 or newer

For Docker, rebuild on a base image with a fixed Node version and redeploy. For distro packages, Aikido notes vendors may backport the fix without changing the version number, so check your distribution's security notice.

On a managed platform, check the provider's notice. Vercel says it manages patch versions for 22.x and 24.x, but projects on 20.x must move to 22.x or 24.x and redeploy.

Python and Bun users get their own fixes, per Aikido:

pip show Brotli brotlicffi
pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1"      # or "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0"
bun --version                        # 1.4.4 or later is fixed

Aikido notes that requests, httpx and aiohttp use these packages automatically when installed, and that pip-audit and Dependabot weren't flagging it as of 23 October, so check by hand.

If you can't upgrade today

Vercel and Imperva both added WAF rules, but both say that doesn't replace patching. A WAF also can't see Brotli responses your app fetches from other servers. As a stopgap, Aikido suggests rejecting requests whose Content-Encoding includes br before any decoder runs. For outbound traffic, it suggests disabling or rejecting Brotli response decoding.

Sources

  • Node.js: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Security Releases
  • CVE.org: CVE-2026-111497
  • Cyber Security Agency of Singapore: Critical Vulnerability in Node.js (AL-2026-154)
  • Vercel: Node.js security advisory, Brotli decoder RCE
  • Imperva: Node2Shell, From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution
  • Aikido Security: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell

For more research-based AI and tech news, see AI News by AIFix at ainews.useaifix.com, and useaifix.com for help keeping sites and workflows in shape.

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox
description:
A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

Snapshot restoration time now counts toward creation instead of the first operation. Creation is about 50 ms longer at p50, with a larger increase possible for uncached snapshots. The total time through the first operation remains the same.

This change applies automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. See the Sandbox.create() documentation for details.

Read more

title: Closing a Modal Is Not One Operation
description:
Once open() returns a Promise, modal lifecycle design becomes observable API behavior: resolve, dismiss, remove, animate, and tear down are no longer interchangeable.

A promise-based modal API looks wonderfully small:

const result = await modal.open(someModal, input);

The complexity is simply hidden below the call site.

What happens when:

  • the modal completes successfully?
  • the modal explicitly rejects because the operation failed?
  • the user presses Escape?
  • the caller dismisses the modal programmatically?
  • all modals are closed at once?
  • the provider unmounts?
  • the UI needs a 200 ms exit animation?
  • two different pieces of code try to settle the same modal?

Once an interaction is represented by a Promise, these are not merely rendering details.

They are part of the API contract.

close(result) and dismiss() should mean different things

Suppose a rename modal has this result:

type RenameResult =
  | {
      status: "renamed";
      name: string;
    }
  | {
      status: "cancelled";
    };

The modal can explicitly complete with:

close({
  status: "renamed",
  name,
});

or:

close({
  status: "cancelled",
});

Both values are valid domain results.

From the caller's point of view:

const result = await modal.open(renameModal, input);

resolves with a RenameResult.

But now imagine the caller does this:

const handle = modal.open(renameModal, input);

handle.dismiss();

Should that resolve to:

{ status: "cancelled" }

automatically?

Not necessarily.

The library cannot assume that every modal has a cancelled variant.

Even if it does, a programmatic lifecycle interruption may mean something different from the user intentionally selecting "Cancel."

That suggests an important separation:

close(result)
    ↓
successful completion with TResult


dismiss()
    ↓
lifecycle interruption

In react-modal-manager, dismissal rejects the pending operation with ModalDismissError.

Why lifecycle dismissal belongs on the rejection channel

Consider a modal that must return a selected account:

type AccountPickerResult = {
  accountId: string;
};

There is no natural fake value to return if the modal disappears.

Resolving with undefined weakens the type:

Promise<AccountPickerResult | undefined>

Adding a cancellation variant changes the domain contract even if cancellation is not conceptually a result.

Silently leaving the Promise pending is worse.

Rejection provides a separate channel:

try {
  const result = await modal.open(accountPickerModal, input);

  await selectAccount(result.accountId);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ModalDismissError) {
    return; // lifecycle interruption
  }

  throw error;
}

The successful path stays:

Promise<TResult>

while interruption remains explicit.

reject(error) is a third semantic channel

Once close(result) and dismiss() are separate, there is still another case:

the modal operation itself failed.

For that, a lifecycle API can expose:

reject(error);

This is different from both successful completion and abandonment:

close(result)
    -> resolve with TResult

reject(error)
    -> reject because the operation failed

dismiss(reason)
    -> reject because the interaction was abandoned

In react-modal-manager, non-Error rejection values are normalized to ModalRejectError, while lifecycle dismissal uses ModalDismissError.

The distinction matters because callers may want to react differently:

try {
  const result = await modal.open(importModal, input);
  await processImportResult(result);
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ModalDismissError) {
    return;
  }

  reportFailure(error);
}

A single "close" operation cannot express all three semantics without smuggling meaning into arbitrary result values.

Domain cancellation can still be a valid result

This does not mean "Cancel" must always reject.

If cancellation is a meaningful outcome of the interaction, model it:

type RenameResult =
  | {
      status: "renamed";
      name: string;
    }
  | {
      status: "cancelled";
    };

Then the Cancel button can call:

close({
  status: "cancelled",
});

The key distinction is ownership of the decision.

The modal intentionally produced a valid result.

That is different from the lifecycle being interrupted externally.

The built-in confirm() is a good example.

Its normal UI actions resolve with typed results:

{ confirmed: true }
{ confirmed: false, reason: "cancel" }
{ confirmed: false, reason: "dismiss" }

So pressing Escape in the built-in confirmation UI resolves as:

{
  confirmed: false,
  reason: "dismiss",
}

That UI action intentionally calls close(result).

By contrast, these manager-level operations reject with ModalDismissError:

handle.dismiss();
modal.dismiss(instanceId);
modal.closeAll();

Provider teardown does the same for still-pending operations.

The important rule is therefore not:

Escape always rejects.

It is:

a component may model a user action as a valid domain result, while lifecycle-level interruption remains a rejection.

A Promise can still expose instance control

Sometimes awaiting the result is enough:

const result = await modal.open(renameModal, input);

Sometimes the caller needs to control the specific instance later.

For example:

const handle = modal.open(progressModal, {
  title: "Generating report...",
});

// Observe the handle's rejection before programmatic dismissal.
const completion = handle.catch((error: unknown) => {
  if (!(error instanceof ModalDismissError)) {
    reportFailure(error);
  }
});

try {
  await generateReport();
} finally {
  handle.dismiss();
  await completion;
}

A useful API can therefore return a Promise-like handle:

const handle = modal.open(renameModal, input);

console.log(handle.instanceId);

try {
  // The caller may dismiss this instance from another event.
  const result = await handle;
  processRenameResult(result);
} catch (error) {
  if (!(error instanceof ModalDismissError)) {
    throw error;
  }
}

// Elsewhere, while the handle is still pending:
// handle.dismiss();

This preserves the ergonomic async API while still exposing instance-level lifecycle control.

Conceptually:

interface ModalHandle<TResult>
  extends Promise<TResult> {
  readonly instanceId: string;
  dismiss(): void;
}

The exact implementation can vary, but the design goal is useful:

do not force the caller to choose between awaiting the operation and controlling its instance.

Every instance gets one logical settlement

Promise settlement is idempotent at the JavaScript level, but lifecycle state still needs clear rules.

Imagine:

  1. the user clicks "Save";
  2. close(result) runs;
  3. an Escape event fires during the same frame;
  4. dismiss() also runs.

The abstraction must guarantee a single logical outcome.

A modal instance should move from pending to settled once.

Conceptually:

          ┌─ resolve(result)
pending ──┤
          └─ reject(dismissal)

after settlement:
additional settlement attempts do nothing

This matters because callbacks around settlement can affect more than the Promise:

  • removing state;
  • starting animations;
  • releasing registry references;
  • restoring focus;
  • logging;
  • triggering caller code.

The lifecycle therefore needs its own once-only transition, not merely reliance on JavaScript's Promise behavior.

In the current design, the first close(result), reject(error), or dismiss(reason) wins. Later settlement attempts for that instance are ignored.

"Promises ignore the second resolve" is not a complete lifecycle design.

Promise settlement and visual removal run on different clocks

Exit animation introduces another subtlety.

Suppose the user clicks Save.

The application should be able to continue immediately:

const result = await modal.open(...);

navigateToNextStep(result);

But visually, the modal may need to fade out for 150 ms.

If Promise settlement waits for the animation, application logic becomes coupled to presentation timing.

If the modal disappears immediately, the animation cannot run.

The solution is to separate:

logical settlement

from:

visual removal

For example:

open
  ↓
close(result)
  ↓
Promise resolves immediately
  ↓
status = "closing"
  ↓
exit transition
  ↓
instance removed

In react-modal-manager, closeDelayMs supports this separation.

The caller gets the result without waiting for CSS.

The renderer gets time to animate the closing instance.

Expose semantic status; let the renderer decide the animation

A renderer can use lifecycle status:

function AppModalRenderer({
  children,
  modal,
}: ModalRendererProps) {
  return (
    <div
      data-status={modal.status}
      className="modal-shell"
    >
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

Then CSS can react to:

.modal-shell[data-status="closing"] {
  opacity: 0;
}

The modal manager does not need to know which animation library is used.

It only needs to expose enough lifecycle information for the presentation layer to respond.

This is a useful boundary:

manager:
  semantic lifecycle

renderer:
  visual lifecycle

Provider teardown must terminate pending operations

Provider-owned state creates another lifecycle edge case.

Consider:

<ModalProvider>
  <Feature />
</ModalProvider>

Feature opens a modal:

const pending = modal.open(someModal, input);

Then the entire provider unmounts before the modal completes.

What should happen to pending?

Leaving it unresolved would create a dangling Promise.

Resolving it with a fabricated result would violate the result contract.

A lifecycle dismissal is the natural outcome.

In the current react-modal-manager contract, provider teardown rejects pending operations with ModalDismissError.

The same principle applies to operations such as closing all active instances.

Every pending operation must have a defined termination path.

Caller unmount is not provider unmount

A subtler case appears when the component that opened a modal disappears while the provider remains mounted.

Consider:

<ModalProvider>
  <Page />
</ModalProvider>

Page opens a modal, then Page unmounts because navigation changes.

Should the modal be dismissed automatically?

Not necessarily.

The provider owns the lifecycle, so the modal can legitimately outlive the component that initiated it.

That is useful for operations whose lifetime belongs to a broader application scope.

But sometimes the caller does own the interaction.

In that case, cleanup should be explicit.

And if the caller can launch more than one modal concurrently, tracking only the latest handle is not enough.

function RenameLauncher() {
  const modal = useModalManager();
  const pending = useRef(
    new Set<ModalHandle<RenameReportResult>>(),
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const handles = pending.current;

    return () => {
      for (const handle of handles) {
        handle.dismiss();
      }

      handles.clear();
    };
  }, []);

  async function handleClick() {
    const handle = modal.open(renameReportModal, {
      reportId: "report-1",
      currentName: "Draft",
    });

    pending.current.add(handle);

    try {
      const result = await handle;

      if (result.status === "renamed") {
        await renameReport({
          reportId: "report-1",
          name: result.name,
        });
      }
    } catch (error) {
      if (!(error instanceof ModalDismissError)) {
        throw error;
      }
    } finally {
      pending.current.delete(handle);
    }
  }

  return <button onClick={handleClick}>Rename</button>;
}

Why a Set?

Because this is incorrect when repeated launches are possible:

pending.current = modal.open(...);

A second click replaces the first handle. Cleanup would dismiss only the latest modal and leave the earlier Promise pending.

Tracking every active handle makes the ownership policy match the actual concurrency model.

This is an important architectural point:

caller cleanup is optional policy, not hidden library behavior.

If the operation should survive the caller, do not dismiss it in caller cleanup. If the caller owns the operation, track and terminate every pending instance it created.

Dismiss an instance, not merely a modal definition

Once multiple instances can exist, "close modal X" is not always precise enough.

The same modal definition might be opened twice:

const first = modal.open(renameModal, firstInput);
const second = modal.open(renameModal, secondInput);

A definition identifies a kind of modal.

It does not necessarily identify an active instance.

That is why an instance identifier matters:

first.instanceId;
second.instanceId;

The handle can remain bound to exactly the lifecycle that created it:

first.dismiss();

This avoids ambiguity and becomes especially useful for:

  • stacked modals;
  • concurrent operations;
  • progress dialogs;
  • timeout-driven dismissal;
  • external commands.

Bridge design-system close events into lifecycle semantics

A design-system dialog can have its own closing behavior.

For example, a user clicks an overlay and the underlying dialog component reports:

onOpenChange(false)

That needs to reach the lifecycle manager.

A renderer can bridge the event:

function ShadcnRenderer({
  children,
  modal,
}: ModalRendererProps) {
  const manager = useModalManager();

  return (
    <Dialog
      open={modal.status === "open"}
      onOpenChange={(open) => {
        if (!open) {
          manager.dismiss(modal.instanceId);
        }
      }}
    >
      <DialogContent>
        {children}
      </DialogContent>
    </Dialog>
  );
}

The design system detects presentation-level dismissal.

The modal manager converts that event into lifecycle semantics.

The pending Promise then terminates consistently with other dismissal paths.

Integration note: This is a conceptual renderer sketch, not a drop-in shadcn/ui integration. A provider-wide renderer wraps both custom modals and built-in confirmation content. If a child already renders its own <Dialog> or <dialog>, wrapping it in DialogContent can create nested dialog semantics and conflicting focus management. Use content-only modal components with this renderer and supply a compatible custom confirmModal when needed. The renderer also needs an explicit strategy for Radix exit animations and closeDelayMs; closing immediately via open={false} does not by itself prove that the visual exit matches the manager's removal delay.

Strict Mode changes how teardown must be implemented

React 18 and 19 development Strict Mode can replay effects.

That creates a trap for provider-owned lifecycle state.

A naïve cleanup implementation might interpret the development-only effect cleanup as final provider disposal and reject every pending modal — even though React immediately remounts the same owner as part of replay.

The lifecycle therefore needs to distinguish:

temporary Strict Mode cleanup

from:

final provider disposal

The current implementation defers final teardown and cancels it when the same lifecycle owner immediately remounts.

This is not merely a test convenience. It preserves the public guarantee that provider teardown terminates pending work without making development Strict Mode behave differently from a real mounted application.

The larger lesson is useful beyond modals:

when asynchronous resources are owned by a React provider, effect cleanup is not always equivalent to permanent ownership loss.

If callers can observe it, it is part of the API

It is tempting to treat all of this as internal implementation detail.

But callers observe the consequences.

They observe whether:

await modal.open(...)

resolves, rejects, or never settles.

They observe whether programmatic dismissal is possible.

They observe whether a closing animation delays business logic.

They observe what happens when the owning provider disappears.

Therefore lifecycle semantics are part of the contract, even if internal data structures are not.

Think in two state machines

A simplified model could look like:

                  close(result)
               ┌───────────────► settled: resolved
               │
open ─► pending
               │
               └───────────────► settled: rejected
                    dismiss()


visual state:

open
  ↓
closing   (optional)
  ↓
removed

The two models interact, but they answer different questions.

Promise state answers:

Has the operation completed?

Visual state answers:

Should the modal still be rendered?

That separation is what makes exit animations possible without delaying application control flow.

Final thoughts

The first version of a promise-based modal API often focuses on this:

const result = await openModal();

The difficult part comes next.

You have to define:

  • what counts as a valid result;
  • what counts as operational failure;
  • what counts as lifecycle dismissal;
  • whether a particular Cancel/Escape action resolves or rejects;
  • who can dismiss an instance;
  • whether the caller or provider owns its lifetime;
  • how concurrent instances are tracked;
  • what provider teardown does;
  • how Strict Mode replay interacts with cleanup;
  • whether promises settle before or after exit animations;
  • how repeated settlement attempts are handled.

Those decisions determine whether the abstraction remains predictable under real application pressure.

A modal is not finished merely because it disappeared from the screen.

Its operation and its visual instance each have a lifecycle.

Once those lifecycles are designed separately, await modal.open(...) can stay simple without making the underlying semantics vague.

If you like the approach, drop a ⭐️ on the GitHub repo and let me know what you think in the comments! 👇

title: JDBC Explained: Drivers, Statements and Best Practices
description:
The first time I had to save data from a Java program into a database, I was sure there would be a different library for every database. One for MySQL, one for Oracle, one for PostgreSQL, each with its own commands to learn.

It turns out Java solved this problem a long time ago, with one standard called JDBC. You learn it once, and the same code works with almost any relational database. You mostly just swap one small jar file and one line of text.

In this post, we'll learn what JDBC is, what a JDBC driver does (and which one to use for each database), the steps of every JDBC program, a complete working example with an explanation of each line, the different execute methods, the three kinds of statements and when to use each, and the best practices that keep your code safe and fast. The example uses an in-memory database called H2, so you don't need to install anything to try it.

Table of contents

  • What is JDBC?
    • The problem JDBC solves
    • The main pieces of JDBC
  • JDBC drivers
    • The four driver types
    • Drivers for popular databases
    • Adding a driver with Maven
    • Anatomy of a JDBC URL
  • Steps for working with JDBC
  • Your first JDBC program
    • The complete code
    • Explaining the code
    • What happens behind the scenes
  • Types of execute methods
    • executeQuery
    • executeUpdate
    • execute
    • executeBatch
  • Types of statements
    • Statement
    • PreparedStatement
    • CallableStatement
    • SQL injection and why it matters
    • Choosing the right statement
  • Working with ResultSet
  • Transactions
  • Best practices
    • Close resources with try-with-resources
    • Use PreparedStatement for every query with input
    • Use a connection pool
    • Handle SQLException properly
    • Keep credentials out of your code
    • Other good habits
  • Which one should I use?
  • Common mistakes
  • Quick recap
  • Try it yourself

What is JDBC?

JDBC stands for Java Database Connectivity. It's a standard API (a set of classes and interfaces) that lets a Java program connect to a relational database, send SQL commands and read the results. It's part of Java itself, in the packages java.sql and javax.sql.

The problem JDBC solves

Every database has its own way of talking over the network. MySQL speaks one protocol, Oracle another, PostgreSQL a third. Without a standard, you'd have to learn each one and rewrite your code to switch databases.

JDBC fixes this with a middle layer. Your code talks only to JDBC's standard interfaces. A small library from the database vendor, called a driver, translates those calls into the database's own language.

   YOUR JAVA CODE
        |   uses standard interfaces: Connection, Statement, ResultSet
        v
   JDBC API   (java.sql and javax.sql, part of Java SE)
        |
        v
   JDBC DRIVER   (a jar file from the database vendor)
        |   speaks the database's own protocol over the network
        v
   DATABASE   (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, H2 ...)

Because your code depends only on the standard interfaces, switching databases usually means changing the driver jar and the connection URL. (Your SQL itself may still need small changes, since each database has its own dialect for some features.)

The main pieces of JDBC

You'll meet these names again and again:

  • DriverManager: finds the right driver for a URL and opens a connection.
  • DataSource: a more modern way to get connections. It's what connection pools implement, and it's preferred in real applications.
  • Connection: your session with the database. You use it to create statements and to control transactions.
  • Statement, PreparedStatement, CallableStatement: objects that send SQL to the database.
  • ResultSet: the rows that come back from a query.
  • SQLException: the exception thrown when anything goes wrong with the database.

All of these (except the driver itself) are interfaces. The driver provides the real classes behind them.

JDBC drivers

A JDBC driver is a library that implements the JDBC interfaces for one specific database. It knows how to open a network connection to that database, log in, send SQL and read the results. You add it to your project like any other library.

The four driver types

JDBC drivers are traditionally grouped into four types:

  • Type 1, JDBC-ODBC bridge: used the old ODBC standard on your computer to reach a database. It was removed from Java in version 8, so you won't use it.
  • Type 2, native-API driver: partly Java and partly native code, and it needs the database's client software installed on the machine. It's used in a few special cases (for example, Oracle's OCI driver).
  • Type 3, network-protocol driver: talks to a middleware server, which then talks to the database. It's rare today.
  • Type 4, thin driver (pure Java): written entirely in Java and talks to the database directly over the network. No extra software to install. This is the type you'll use almost every time, and all the drivers in the next section are Type 4.

Drivers for popular databases

Here are the common ones, with the Maven dependency (groupId:artifactId), the driver class name and an example URL:

  • MySQL
    • Dependency: com.mysql:mysql-connector-j
    • Driver class: com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
    • URL: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/school
  • MariaDB
    • Dependency: org.mariadb.jdbc:mariadb-java-client
    • Driver class: org.mariadb.jdbc.Driver
    • URL: jdbc:mariadb://localhost:3306/school
  • PostgreSQL
    • Dependency: org.postgresql:postgresql
    • Driver class: org.postgresql.Driver
    • URL: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/school
  • Oracle
    • Dependency: com.oracle.database.jdbc:ojdbc11 (use ojdbc8 for Java 8)
    • Driver class: oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver
    • URL: jdbc:oracle:thin:@//localhost:1521/XEPDB1
  • SQL Server
    • Dependency: com.microsoft.sqlserver:mssql-jdbc
    • Driver class: com.microsoft.sqlserver.jdbc.SQLServerDriver
    • URL: jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=school
  • H2 (a small, pure-Java database, great for learning and tests)
    • Dependency: com.h2database:h2
    • Driver class: org.h2.Driver
    • URL: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb (in memory) or jdbc:h2:~/school (a file)
  • SQLite
    • Dependency: org.xerial:sqlite-jdbc
    • Driver class: org.sqlite.JDBC
    • URL: jdbc:sqlite:school.db

A few notes:

  • The driver class names are only needed in old-style code (we'll see why in a moment). It's still useful to recognize them in error messages.
  • Always check the vendor's documentation for the current version and options. For example, newer SQL Server drivers encrypt the connection by default, so local development often needs extra URL settings such as trustServerCertificate=true (use that only for development, never in production).

Adding a driver with Maven

If you use Maven (see my Maven post), add the dependency in your pom.xml. We'll use H2 for this post's examples:

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
    <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
    <version>2.4.240</version>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Two things to notice:

  • Use the newest version you can find on Maven Central. 2.4.240 is just the version I used.
  • The scope is runtime, because your code uses only the standard java.sql interfaces. The driver is needed to run the program, but not to compile it. That's the kind of "runtime" scope we saw in the Maven post.

For another database, swap in its dependency from the list above.

Anatomy of a JDBC URL

A JDBC URL tells DriverManager which database to reach and where it lives:

   jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/school?useSSL=true
    |     |        |        |     |        |
    |     |        |        |     |        +-- optional settings (key=value)
    |     |        |        |     +----------- database (schema) name
    |     |        |        +----------------- port
    |     |        +-------------------------- host (the machine running the database)
    |     +----------------------------------- sub-protocol: which database/driver
    +----------------------------------------- always "jdbc"

The exact format changes slightly from database to database (see the list above), but the idea is always jdbc: + the database type + the location.

Steps for working with JDBC

Every JDBC program follows the same steps:

   1. Add the driver          put the driver jar on the classpath (Maven dependency)
          |
          v
   2. Register the driver     happens automatically in modern JDBC
          |
          v
   3. Open a Connection       DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password)
          |
          v
   4. Create a statement      createStatement() or prepareStatement(sql)
          |
          v
   5. Execute the SQL         executeQuery(), executeUpdate() or execute()
          |
          v
   6. Process the results     loop over the ResultSet, or read the update count
          |
          v
   7. Handle exceptions       catch SQLException
          |
          v
   8. Close everything        ResultSet, then Statement, then Connection

A quick note on step 2. In older tutorials, you'll see this line before connecting:

Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver");

You don't need it anymore. Since JDBC 4.0 (Java 6), every driver jar announces itself in a file, and Java finds and registers it automatically as soon as it's on the classpath. Just add the jar, and DriverManager will find it.

Your first JDBC program

We'll build a program that connects to an in-memory H2 database, creates a table, inserts two rows and reads them back. You need nothing installed except the H2 dependency above.

The complete code 

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;

public class JdbcDemo {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:h2:mem:testdb";
    private static final String USER = "sa";
    private static final String PASSWORD = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD)) {

            createTable(conn);
            insertStudent(conn, 1, "Asha", 88);
            insertStudent(conn, 2, "Ravi", 72);
            printStudents(conn);

        } catch (SQLException e) {
            System.err.println("Database error: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    private static void createTable(Connection conn) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "CREATE TABLE student (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50), marks INT)";
        try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
            stmt.executeUpdate(sql);
        }
    }

    private static void insertStudent(Connection conn, int id, String name, int marks)
            throws SQLException {
        String sql = "INSERT INTO student (id, name, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
        try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
            ps.setInt(1, id);
            ps.setString(2, name);
            ps.setInt(3, marks);
            int rows = ps.executeUpdate();
            System.out.println("Inserted " + rows + " row(s): " + name);
        }
    }

    private static void printStudents(Connection conn) throws SQLException {
        String sql = "SELECT id, name, marks FROM student ORDER BY id";
        try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
             ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql)) {
            while (rs.next()) {
                int id = rs.getInt("id");
                String name = rs.getString("name");
                int marks = rs.getInt("marks");
                System.out.println(id + " | " + name + " | " + marks);
            }
        }
    }
}

Output:

Inserted 1 row(s): Asha
Inserted 1 row(s): Ravi
1 | Asha | 88
2 | Ravi | 72

Explaining the code

Let's go through it piece by piece.

The three constants. URL, USER and PASSWORD describe where the database is and how to log in. jdbc:h2:mem:testdb means "an H2 database that lives in memory, named testdb." sa is H2's default user, with an empty password. (For a real database, you'd never write the password in your code. More on that in the best practices.)

DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD). This asks Java to find a driver that understands the URL, then opens a connection to the database. It returns a Connection, your session with the database. It throws SQLException if the database can't be reached, the login fails or no driver matches.

try (Connection conn = ...). This is try-with-resources. Anything declared in the parentheses is closed automatically when the block ends, even if an exception happens. So we never need to write conn.close() ourselves. (An in-memory H2 database disappears when its last connection closes. Since we use one connection for the whole program, our data stays.)

conn.createStatement(). This creates a Statement object, a messenger that carries plain SQL text to the database.

stmt.executeUpdate(sql). This sends SQL that changes something (here, a CREATE TABLE). It returns the number of rows affected, which is 0 for this kind of command.

conn.prepareStatement(sql) with the ? marks. This creates a PreparedStatement. The ? characters are placeholders for values we'll supply later. Then we fill them in with setInt and setString. The numbers start at 1, not 0: 1 is the first ?, 2 is the second, and so on. executeUpdate() sends the command and returns how many rows were inserted (1).

stmt.executeQuery(sql) and ResultSet. This sends a SELECT and returns a ResultSet, the rows that came back. The loop while (rs.next()) moves to the next row each time, and returns false when there are no more rows. Inside the loop, rs.getInt("id") and rs.getString("name") read the columns of the current row by name.

catch (SQLException e). Almost every JDBC call can throw this checked exception, so the compiler makes us deal with it. Here we simply print the message.

The small helper methods. Putting each job in its own method keeps main short and makes each step easy to read and reuse.

What happens behind the scenes

When you call DriverManager.getConnection(...), a lot happens in a few milliseconds:

   getConnection("jdbc:h2:mem:testdb", "sa", "")
        |
        v
   DriverManager asks each registered driver: "Do you accept this URL?"
        |        (drivers register themselves when their jar is on the classpath)
        v
   The matching driver opens a network connection (TCP) to the database,
   sends the user name and password, and waits for the database to accept them
        |
        v
   You get back a Connection object  (a real class from the driver,
   used through the standard java.sql.Connection interface)

Then, when you run a query:

   stmt.executeQuery("SELECT ...")
        |  the driver sends the SQL text over the network
        v
   DATABASE: parses the SQL, plans how to run it, runs it
        |  sends the rows back (often in chunks)
        v
   ResultSet: a cursor that points at one row at a time; rs.next() moves it

Opening a connection is expensive: it needs a network round trip, a login and some setup. Sending SQL is much cheaper. That's why connection pools (covered in the best practices) are so important.

Types of execute methods

A statement can send its SQL in four main ways. The right one depends on what kind of SQL you're sending:

   METHOD           USE IT FOR                          RETURNS
   executeQuery     SELECT                              ResultSet
   executeUpdate    INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and DDL     int (rows affected)
   execute          unknown SQL, or several results     boolean (true = a ResultSet)
   executeBatch     many statements at once             int[] (one count for each)

(DDL means commands that change the structure, like CREATE TABLE.)

executeQuery

Use it for a SELECT. It returns a ResultSet and can never return an update count.

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT name FROM student ORDER BY id")) {
    while (rs.next()) {
        System.out.println(rs.getString("name"));
    }
}

Asha
Ravi

If you pass something that isn't a query (like an INSERT) to executeQuery, you get an SQLException.

executeUpdate

Use it for INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and for DDL commands like CREATE TABLE. It returns an int: the number of rows affected.

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
    int rows = stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE student SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks < 80");
    System.out.println("Rows updated: " + rows);
}

Rows updated: 1

Only Ravi (72) matched, so one row changed. For DDL, it returns 0. If you ever expect more than about two billion affected rows, there's also executeLargeUpdate, which returns a long.

execute

Use it when you don't know in advance what the SQL does, or when it might produce several results (some stored procedures do). It returns a boolean:

  • true means the first result is a ResultSet. Get it with getResultSet().
  • false means the first result is an update count. Get it with getUpdateCount(). 
static void run(Connection conn, String sql) throws SQLException {
    try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
        boolean hasResultSet = stmt.execute(sql);

        if (hasResultSet) {
            try (ResultSet rs = stmt.getResultSet()) {
                int count = 0;
                while (rs.next()) {
                    count++;
                }
                System.out.println("Query returned " + count + " row(s)");
            }
        } else {
            System.out.println("Update count: " + stmt.getUpdateCount());
        }
    }
}

run(conn, "SELECT * FROM student");
run(conn, "DELETE FROM student WHERE id = 99");

Query returned 2 row(s)
Update count: 0

The same method handled both a query and an update, because execute told us which kind of result we got. In everyday code, executeQuery and executeUpdate are clearer, so reach for execute only when you need its flexibility.

executeBatch

Use it to send many statements in one trip to the database. Sending 1000 inserts one by one means 1000 network round trips. A batch sends them together, which is much faster. You add statements with addBatch(), then send them all with executeBatch():

String sql = "INSERT INTO student (id, name, marks) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setInt(1, 3);  ps.setString(2, "Meera"); ps.setInt(3, 95); ps.addBatch();
    ps.setInt(1, 4);  ps.setString(2, "Kabir"); ps.setInt(3, 64); ps.addBatch();
    ps.setInt(1, 5);  ps.setString(2, "Zoya");  ps.setInt(3, 81); ps.addBatch();

    int[] counts = ps.executeBatch();
    System.out.println(Arrays.toString(counts));
}

[1, 1, 1]

(This needs import java.util.Arrays;.) The returned array holds one count for each statement. Some drivers return the special value Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO (which is -2) instead, meaning "it worked, but I can't tell you how many rows." For very big batches, send them in chunks of a few hundred or thousand rows.

From here on, our table has five students: Asha, Ravi, Meera, Kabir and Zoya.

Types of statements

JDBC has three kinds of statement objects. They differ in how they build and send SQL.

   Statement            plain SQL text, no parameters
        ^
        |  extends
   PreparedStatement    SQL with ? placeholders, precompiled, safe with user input
        ^
        |  extends
   CallableStatement    calls stored procedures and functions

Statement

A Statement sends a complete SQL string exactly as you wrote it. It has no placeholders.

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement()) {
    stmt.executeUpdate("CREATE TABLE course (id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(50))");
}
  • Good for: fixed SQL that has no input from users, like creating tables, running a fixed report or a one-off admin command.
  • Watch out: every time you run it, the database has to read and plan the SQL again. And if you build the SQL by joining in user input, you open the door to SQL injection (next).

PreparedStatement

A PreparedStatement takes SQL with ? placeholders. The database compiles it once, and you supply the values separately with setInt, setString, setObject and similar methods.

String sql = "SELECT name, marks FROM student WHERE marks >= ?";
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ps.setInt(1, 80);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        while (rs.next()) {
            System.out.println(rs.getString("name") + " " + rs.getInt("marks"));
        }
    }
}

Asha 88
Meera 95
Zoya 81

(Ravi is at 77 after our earlier update, and Kabir at 64, so neither matches.)

Why it's better for most work:

  • Safe from SQL injection, because values are never mixed into the SQL text.
  • Faster when repeated, since the database (or driver) can reuse the prepared plan.
  • Handles types and special characters for you. A name like O'Brien just works, with no manual escaping.
  • Supports batches easily, as we saw.

One limit: placeholders can only stand for values. You can't use ? for a table name, a column name or an SQL keyword.

CallableStatement

A CallableStatement calls a stored procedure or function, which is a piece of code saved inside the database itself. It uses a special call syntax that JDBC translates for each database:

try (CallableStatement cs = conn.prepareCall("{call get_student_count(?)}")) {
    cs.registerOutParameter(1, Types.INTEGER);
    cs.execute();
    int count = cs.getInt(1);
    System.out.println("Students: " + count);
}

This assumes your database already has a procedure named get_student_count with one output parameter. Notes:

  • registerOutParameter declares a parameter that the procedure fills in (an OUT parameter). Parameters you send in are IN parameters, set with setXxx as usual. A parameter can also be both (INOUT).
  • For a function that returns a value, the syntax is {? = call my_function(?)}.
  • CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement, so everything you know about placeholders still applies.
  • How you write procedures differs a lot between databases, but the Java side stays the same.

SQL injection and why it matters

SQL injection happens when user input becomes part of the SQL itself. Watch what happens with a nasty input:

String userInput = "x' OR '1'='1";

// UNSAFE: Statement with the input joined into the SQL
String unsafeSql = "SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = '" + userInput + "'";
System.out.println(unsafeSql);
try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(unsafeSql)) {
    int count = 0;
    while (rs.next()) {
        count++;
    }
    System.out.println("Statement returned " + count + " row(s)");
}

// SAFE: PreparedStatement with a placeholder
try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = ?")) {
    ps.setString(1, userInput);
    try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        int count = 0;
        while (rs.next()) {
            count++;
        }
        System.out.println("PreparedStatement returned " + count + " row(s)");
    }
}

SELECT * FROM student WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'
Statement returned 5 row(s)
PreparedStatement returned 0 row(s)

The input was meant to be a name. But with the plain Statement, the quote characters changed the meaning of the SQL. '1'='1' is always true, so the query returned every row. In a login form, the same trick lets someone in without a password. With the PreparedStatement, the whole input is treated as one plain value to compare to a name, so nothing matched.

   Statement (joined text):      [ SQL + user input ]  ---->  database parses it ALL as SQL
   PreparedStatement:            [ SQL with ? ]  ---->  database parses and plans it
                                 [ value ]       ---->  value is handled as DATA only

Many drivers don't allow several commands in one string by default, so the ; DROP TABLE trick is often blocked. But data leaks and login bypasses still work, so don't count on that. The rule is simple: never build SQL by joining in user input.

Choosing the right statement

  • Statement: fixed SQL with no outside input (DDL, a fixed report, quick scripts).
  • PreparedStatement: the default choice. Use it for any SQL that has values, anything with user input, anything you run repeatedly and any batch.
  • CallableStatement: when you need to call a stored procedure or function.

If you're ever unsure, use PreparedStatement. It's almost never the wrong answer.

Working with ResultSet

A ResultSet is like a cursor that starts before the first row. Each call to next() moves it down one row and returns true, or false when you run out:

   before first row
        |
        v   rs.next()  -->  row 1     (true)
        |   rs.next()  -->  row 2     (true)
        |   rs.next()  -->  row 3     (true)
        v   rs.next()  -->  after last (false)

So you must call next() before you read anything. If you skip it, you'll get an error like "before start of result set."

Reading columns:

  • By name: rs.getString("name"). This is clearer and survives column reordering.
  • By position: rs.getString(2). Column numbers start at 1.
  • Pick the getter that matches the column: getInt, getLong, getDouble, getString, getBoolean, getBigDecimal (best for money), and so on.
  • For dates and times, use the modern java.time types: rs.getObject("birth_date", LocalDate.class).

A subtle trap is NULL. getInt returns 0 for a NULL column, which is indistinguishable from a real zero. To keep a NULL as a NULL, read it as an object:

Integer marks = rs.getObject("marks", Integer.class);   // stays null if the column is NULL

Or call rs.wasNull() right after reading.

You can also inspect the shape of a result with metadata:

try (Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
     ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery("SELECT id, name, marks FROM student")) {
    ResultSetMetaData meta = rs.getMetaData();
    for (int i = 1; i <= meta.getColumnCount(); i++) {
        System.out.println(meta.getColumnName(i) + " : " + meta.getColumnTypeName(i));
    }
}

ID : INTEGER
NAME : CHARACTER VARYING
MARKS : INTEGER

(The type names depend on the database. H2 also shows column names in uppercase.)

By default, a ResultSet is forward-only and read-only: you move down once, and you can't edit rows through it. You can ask for scrollable or updatable result sets with createStatement(type, concurrency), but that's rarely needed. A ResultSet is also tied to its statement: closing the statement closes the result set.

Transactions

A transaction is a group of SQL commands that must succeed together or not at all. The classic example is moving money: subtract from one account, add to another. If the first step works and the second fails, you must undo the first.

By default, JDBC runs in auto-commit mode: every statement is committed (made permanent) the moment it runs. For a multi-step job, turn it off and commit yourself:

conn.setAutoCommit(false);
try {
    debit(conn, 1, 500);     // UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1
    credit(conn, 2, 500);    // UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2
    conn.commit();           // both changes become permanent together
} catch (SQLException e) {
    conn.rollback();         // undo everything since the last commit
    throw e;
} finally {
    conn.setAutoCommit(true);
}

   setAutoCommit(false)
          |
     step 1 ---- step 2 ---- step 3
          |                    |
       all OK?              something failed?
          |                    |
       commit()            rollback()
     (permanent)         (as if nothing happened)

Transactions give you the ACID guarantees: Atomic (all or nothing), Consistent (rules stay true), Isolated (other users don't see half-finished work) and Durable (committed data survives a crash). If you forget commit() after turning off auto-commit, your changes are lost when the connection closes.

Best practices

Close resources with try-with-resources

Connection, Statement and ResultSet all hold real resources (network sockets, memory on the database server). If you forget to close them, they leak, and eventually the database runs out of connections. Always use try-with-resources, which closes everything for you in reverse order, even when exceptions happen:

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql);
     ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
    // use rs
}   // closed automatically: rs, then ps, then conn

Avoid the old style with finally blocks, null checks and nested try/catch. It's long and easy to get wrong.

Use PreparedStatement for every query with input

Never build SQL by joining text with user input. Always use ? placeholders, and set the values with the right setXxx method. We saw why in the SQL injection section. It also gives you speed and correct handling of quotes and types for free.

Use a connection pool

Opening a new connection for every request is slow. A connection pool opens a fixed set of connections once and lends them out. When you call close() on a pooled connection, it isn't really closed. It goes back to the pool for the next user.

Popular pools include HikariCP. You create the pool once, when the application starts, and share it:

HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
config.setJdbcUrl(System.getenv("DB_URL"));
config.setUsername(System.getenv("DB_USER"));
config.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));
config.setMaximumPoolSize(10);

DataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config);   // create once, reuse everywhere

try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {    // borrowed from the pool
    // use conn
}                                                        // returned to the pool

Notice the code uses the standard DataSource interface. That's why frameworks and servers prefer it to DriverManager: you can swap in a pool without changing your database code.

Handle SQLException properly

Don't swallow it with an empty catch. SQLException carries more than a message:

try (PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO student VALUES (?, ?, ?)")) {
    ps.setInt(1, 1);                  // id 1 already exists
    ps.setString(2, "Duplicate");
    ps.setInt(3, 50);
    ps.executeUpdate();
} catch (SQLException e) {
    System.err.println("Message : " + e.getMessage());
    System.err.println("SQLState: " + e.getSQLState());
    System.err.println("Code    : " + e.getErrorCode());
}

Message : Unique index or primary key violation: ...
SQLState: 23505
Code    : 23505

(H2 shown. Other databases word the message differently.)

  • getSQLState() is a standard 5-character code. 23505 means a duplicate key, and the first two digits show the category (23 is "integrity constraint violation"). This is the safest value to write logic against.
  • getErrorCode() is a number specific to the database vendor.
  • Log the full exception for developers, but show users a friendly message. Raw database errors can reveal table names and other details an attacker could use.

Keep credentials out of your code

Never hard-code passwords in source files, and never commit them to Git. Read them from environment variables, a config file outside the repository or a secrets manager:

String url = System.getenv("DB_URL");
String user = System.getenv("DB_USER");
String password = System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD");

Also give the application's database user only the permissions it needs (for example, no permission to drop tables), and use an encrypted connection (TLS) when the database is on another machine.

Other good habits

  • Select only what you need. Name the columns instead of SELECT *, and add WHERE and limits, so you don't pull huge amounts of data.
  • Use batches for bulk inserts and updates, in chunks.
  • Use transactions for anything that must succeed as a unit, and keep them short.
  • Use java.time types (LocalDate, LocalDateTime) with setObject and getObject, instead of the older java.util.Date and java.sql.Date.
  • Separate database code from business logic. Put SQL in its own classes (often called DAOs or repositories), so the rest of the program doesn't depend on JDBC details.
  • Set timeouts. stmt.setQueryTimeout(30) stops a stuck query from hanging forever.
  • Don't use Class.forName for modern drivers. Just keep the driver jar on the classpath.
  • Use column names in ResultSet reads for clarity, unless performance on huge result sets proves otherwise.

Which one should I use?

  • Statement or PreparedStatement? PreparedStatement whenever there's any input value or any repetition. Statement only for fixed, input-free SQL like DDL.
  • CallableStatement? Only to call stored procedures or functions.
  • executeQuery, executeUpdate or execute? executeQuery for SELECT, executeUpdate for everything that changes data or structure, and execute only when the kind of result is unknown or there may be several. Use executeBatch for bulk work.
  • DriverManager or DataSource? DriverManager is fine for learning and small scripts. Use a pooled DataSource in real applications.
  • Get columns by name or by index? Name, for readability. Index is a little faster and fine for tiny queries.
  • JDBC directly, or a framework? Plain JDBC is perfect for learning, small tools and cases where you want full control. For bigger applications, tools built on top of JDBC (like Spring's JdbcTemplate, jOOQ or JPA with Hibernate) remove repetitive code. They all use JDBC underneath, so understanding it makes every one of them easier.
  • Auto-commit or manual transactions? Auto-commit for single statements. Manual commit and rollback whenever several statements belong together.

Common mistakes

  1. "No suitable driver found." The driver jar isn't on the classpath, or the URL is wrong. Check the dependency (and its scope) and the exact URL format for your database.
  2. Joining user input into SQL. "... WHERE name = '" + name + "'" is an SQL injection bug waiting to happen. Use PreparedStatement with ?.
  3. Not closing resources. Leaked connections, statements and result sets slowly exhaust the database. Use try-with-resources.
  4. Off-by-one and cursor mistakes. Parameter and column positions start at 1, and a ResultSet must be advanced with next() before you read it.
  5. Using the wrong execute method. Calling executeQuery with an INSERT, or executeUpdate with a SELECT, throws an SQLException. Match the method to the SQL, or use execute.
  6. Transaction surprises. With auto-commit on, a half-finished multi-step job leaves half the changes saved. With auto-commit off, forgetting commit() throws all the changes away.

Quick recap

  • JDBC is Java's standard API (java.sql and javax.sql) for talking to relational databases. Your code uses the interfaces, and a vendor's driver does the translation.
  • Drivers come in four types, but you'll use Type 4 (pure Java): mysql-connector-j, postgresql, ojdbc11, mssql-jdbc, h2, sqlite-jdbc and others. Add the right one with Maven, usually in runtime scope.
  • A JDBC URL looks like jdbc:<database>://host:port/name. Since JDBC 4, drivers register themselves, so Class.forName is no longer needed.
  • The steps: add the driver, open a Connection, create a statement, execute the SQL, process the results, handle SQLException and close everything.
  • Execute methods: executeQuery (SELECT, returns a ResultSet), executeUpdate (changes data, returns a row count), execute (unknown or multiple results, returns a boolean) and executeBatch (many statements at once).
  • Statements: Statement (plain, fixed SQL), PreparedStatement (placeholders, safe, faster, the default) and CallableStatement (stored procedures).
  • Joining user input into SQL causes SQL injection. PreparedStatement prevents it.
  • A ResultSet is a cursor: call next() first, and columns start at 1. Watch out for NULL values.
  • Use transactions (setAutoCommit(false), commit, rollback) when several statements must succeed together.
  • Best practices: try-with-resources, PreparedStatement for all input, a connection pool, careful SQLException handling, credentials outside the code and small, focused queries.

Try it yourself

Here's a small practice idea: build a StudentDao class with five methods: insert, findById, findAll, updateMarks and delete, all using PreparedStatement and try-with-resources, against the H2 table from this post. Then add a insertAll(List<Student>) method that uses a batch, and a method that moves marks from one student to another inside a transaction, rolling back if either update fails.

For a bonus experiment, switch to a real database. Install MySQL or PostgreSQL (or run one in Docker), swap the H2 dependency for the right driver, and change only the URL, user and password. The rest of your code should run unchanged, and that's the whole point of JDBC. Then put your connection settings in environment variables, and add a HikariCP pool.

If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

title: Building accessibility into a canvas-based product
description: Building on a canvas unlocks performance that a traditional HTML web app can't touch. It also strips away any accessibility the browser gives you for free. Here's how we built it back in.

title: Bring multimodal semantic search to the edge with EmbeddingGemma 2
description: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a new 740M open-weight multimodal model that maps text, images, video, and audio into a unified vector space for privacy-first, on-device retrieval. Developers can easily integrate these capabilities cross-platform using MediaPipe Tasks or optimize fine-grained performance across CPU, GPU, and NPU accelerators with LiteRT. The model enables ultra-low-latency local solutions like search-as-you-type media retrieval, keyframe video moments finding, and zero-shot intent routing.

title: Sorta — An AI Downloads Butler Built with Local Gemma
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady
My downloads folder can get messy pretty quickly, so for the Hacktoberfest Week 3 challenge, I decided to build something that could help me organize it.

I made Sorta, a small AI-powered app that suggests where a downloaded file could belong based on its filename.

What I Built

Sorta is built with Python, Streamlit, Ollama, and Gemma 3 1B.

I enter or select a filename, and Gemma suggests a folder category. I can review the suggestion in the app before deciding what to do with the file.

This is an early prototype: Sorta currently previews folder suggestions. It does not automatically move files, and its undo feature is not implemented yet.

Instead of having to think through a folder category for every download, Sorta gives me a quick suggestion to review. I haven’t measured a specific time saving yet, but I wanted to explore how AI could make this small, repetitive task easier.

Demo

codesnippet-lab / Sorta-AI

A local AI-powered downloads organizer that uses Gemma to suggest folders for your files—without sending filenames to a cloud AI.

Sorta — AI Downloads Butler 🪄

Sorta is a file-organization assistant that uses a locally running Gemma model to suggest folders for your files. You can review the suggestions before taking any action.

Features

  • Upload multiple files in a Streamlit interface
  • Use local Gemma AI through Ollama to suggest folders
  • Preview the proposed organization
  • Keep the user in control: this prototype does not move, rename, or delete files

Built with

  • Python
  • Streamlit
  • Ollama
  • Gemma 3 1B

Run locally

1. Install Ollama

Install Ollama for your operating system: https://ollama.com/download

2. Download Gemma

Open a terminal and run:

ollama pull gemma3:1b

Ensure Ollama is running.

3. Set up Sorta

From the project folder:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

4. Launch the app

streamlit run app.py

Open the local URL printed in your terminal.

Privacy and safety

Sorta sends filenames to the locally running Gemma model to generate…

View on GitHub

Code

Github Repository:https://github.com/codesnippet-lab/Sorta-AI

How I Built It

I used Gemma 3 1B through Ollama, with the model running on my own computer. For this prototype, the filename is sent to the local model rather than a hosted AI API.

Using an open model gave me a chance to experiment with AI locally and connect it to an app I built myself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

As a first-year Computer Science student who’s still learning development, this project helped me practice connecting a local AI model to a Python interface and handling the model’s response.

My next steps are to add safe, user-approved file organization and implement a real undo feature.

Thanks for checking out my project! I’d appreciate feedback and ideas for improving Sorta.
