title: firmware-auditor: Zero-Emulation Static Security Analysis for Firmware Rootfs in CI/CD
description:
Security assessments for IoT devices and embedded Linux systems have long relied on two main approaches: manual static inspection or full dynamic emulation (QEMU, Unicorn, Firmadyne, FirmAE).

Dynamic analysis is invaluable for verifying vulnerabilities, but plugging emulated environments into automated CI/CD pipelines often leads to:

  1. High execution overhead and slow feedback loops.
  2. Architecture incompatibilities: custom NVRAM, vendor peripherals and proprietary SoC hardware are exactly where generic emulators tend to break.
  3. Flaky automation that stalls pull requests.

To bridge this gap I built firmware-auditor: a fast, zero-emulation static analysis framework for unpacked root filesystem images.

The Core Idea: Reproducible Static Posture

When you have an unpacked SquashFS, ext4 or UBIFS rootfs, many security posture indicators can be checked entirely offline, without executing a single target binary:

  • ELF binary hardening: are binaries built with modern mitigations, or exposed to classic exploitation techniques?
  • Filesystem hygiene and secret exposure: did the build bake private SSH keys, a readable /etc/shadow or world-writable scripts into production?
  • Actionable DevSecOps gates: can the pipeline fail (exit 1) on critical issues and emit standardized, machine-readable results?

Here is what a run looks like. This is a test rootfs with intentionally planted flaws, not a real firmware image:

rootfs     : test_rootfs
duration   : 0.007s (workers=1)
severity   : >= info
analyzers  : binary_hardening 1.0.0 ok (0 findings, 0.004s)
             filesystem_hygiene 1.0.0 ok (5 findings, 0.002s)

SUMMARY BY SEVERITY
CRITICAL   5 ####################
HIGH       0
MEDIUM     0
LOW        0
TOTAL      5

FINDINGS BY RULE (4 rule(s), 5 finding(s))
SEVERITY RULE         COUNT LOCATION SAMPLE     TITLE
CRITICAL FWK-PERM-001     1 etc                 World-writable directory
CRITICAL FWK-KEY-001      1 etc/id_rsa          Private key material in the firmware image
CRITICAL FWK-PERM-002     2 etc/id_rsa; shadow  World-writable file in a sensitive tree
CRITICAL FWK-PERM-004     1 etc/shadow          Password hash database readable by any user

Architecture

The framework is written in Python 3.10+ with a modular design built around isolation and reproducibility:

firmware_auditor/
├── analyzers/
│   ├── base.py                 # Base analyzer & Finding contract
│   ├── binary_hardening.py     # ELF checks (NX, PIE, Canary, RELRO)
│   └── filesystem_hygiene.py   # Secrets, permissions, credentials
├── core/
│   ├── pipeline.py             # Concurrent runner, fault isolation
│   └── reporter.py             # Console, JSON and SARIF v2.1.0
└── tests/                      # pytest suite (Ubuntu & Windows)

Each analyzer runs behind a fault-isolation boundary with a timeout guard, so one broken analyzer or a malformed binary doesn't take down the whole scan.

1. ELF Hardening Inspections

Using pyelftools, the engine parses ELF headers directly:

  • NX / DEP: checks the PT_GNU_STACK flags for an executable stack. A missing PT_GNU_STACK header is also treated as an executable stack, since that is the default on several architectures common in firmware (ARM, MIPS).
  • PIE / ASLR: ET_DYN alone is not enough, because shared libraries are ET_DYN too. The engine separates PIE executables from .so files by checking for PT_INTERP and the DF_1_PIE flag in DT_FLAGS_1. ET_EXEC means a fixed load address.
  • Stack canaries: looks for __stack_chk_fail in .dynsym and .symtab.
  • RELRO: checks PT_GNU_RELRO for Partial RELRO, and for Full RELRO also requires immediate binding (DT_BIND_NOW, DF_BIND_NOW in DT_FLAGS, or DF_1_NOW in DT_FLAGS_1).

2. Filesystem Hygiene

Instead of running arbitrary regex over the entire filesystem, the module targets specific security attributes:

  • Checks permission masks (st_mode) on sensitive Unix paths (/etc, /bin, /sbin).
  • Detects unshadowed or empty password hashes in authentication files.
  • Identifies raw private key material without leaking the secret into CI logs or reports.

Note: permission checks need an extraction that preserves Unix modes (unsquashfs, tar, WSL or Linux). A rootfs copied onto NTFS loses this information, and permission findings will not be reliable.

3. Native SARIF Support for GitHub Code Scanning

firmware-auditor outputs SARIF v2.1.0 instead of a proprietary report format, so findings can show up directly under Security > Code scanning on GitHub:

firmware-auditor /path/to/extracted/rootfs \
  --format sarif \
  --output report.sarif \
  --fail-on high

GitHub Actions example 

name: firmware-audit
on: [pull_request]

permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write

jobs:
  audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install firmware-auditor
        run: |
          git clone https://github.com/RichJJ98/firmware-auditor
          pip install ./firmware-auditor

      - name: Extract rootfs (preserving permissions)
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y squashfs-tools
          sudo unsquashfs -f -d rootfs firmware.squashfs

      - name: Run audit
        run: firmware-auditor rootfs --format sarif --output report.sarif --fail-on high

      - name: Upload SARIF
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: report.sarif

The if: always() on the upload step matters: with --fail-on high the audit step exits non-zero, and without it the findings would never reach the Code scanning tab.

Limitations (What It Does Not Cover)

Static analysis has blind spots, and it is better to say so upfront:

  • Not a replacement for dynamic analysis. It won't confirm exploitability or find runtime and logic vulnerabilities.
  • No CVE matching of bundled library versions (yet).
  • Possible false negatives on canaries: stripped or statically linked binaries may not expose __stack_chk_fail.
  • Needs an already unpacked rootfs. Extraction (binwalk, unsquashfs, etc.) is a separate step, and encrypted or proprietary containers are out of scope.
  • Permission checks depend on extraction fidelity (see the note above).

Open Source & Next Steps

firmware-auditor is released under the MIT License, and the test suite runs in CI on both Linux and Windows.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/RichJJ98/firmware-auditor

If you work with embedded devices, IoT security or DevSecOps pipelines, clone it, try it on your own firmware images and contribute new rule modules. Feedback, issues and pull requests are very welcome.

title: Node.js Report Scheduling: Combining Cron Jobs with Worker-Based Long-Running Tasks
description:
A cron process should create one durable scheduling record and exit. A worker queue should own report generation, subscriber fan-out, retries, and delivery state. That boundary keeps a slow daily shipment report from turning a timer into an accidental job runner, while still leaving room to choose latency or cost deliberately.

Short answer: run the scheduler at a fixed time, claim the day with an idempotency key, enqueue one report job, and let workers split the resulting shipment update into subscriber-sized deliveries. The scheduler needs a small timeout. The report worker needs a lease, bounded concurrency, durable progress, and a clear rule for permanent failure.

The concrete case here is a fintech operation that sends a daily shipment-status report by email to many subscribers. Report generation may scan a large event range; the final update may fan out to thousands of recipients. The report is one logical job, but delivery is many independently retryable jobs. Treating those as one unit is the first design mistake.

How should I combine a cron job trigger with a worker-based queue?

The clock is not a guarantee that work happened. It is only a request to start work. This combining of a cron trigger with worker-based execution is useful because the two components have different failure boundaries. I define these invariants before choosing a queue library or storage engine:

Keep it boring.

The queue is the boundary.

  • At most one report run is active for a tenant and report date, unless an operator explicitly starts a replacement.
  • A worker may execute a job more than once, but a subscriber must not receive an unbounded number of copies because of a retry.
  • A generated report is retained long enough for delivery retries, and its status is observable without reading worker logs.
  • One slow subscriber cannot hold the report-generation lease forever.
  • A failure has a category: retryable, permanent, or awaiting operator action.

The identifier should be derived from stable business data, such as tenant_id + report_date + report_type, rather than from the scheduler attempt. Otherwise two timer invocations create two valid-looking reports. A uniqueness constraint at the persistence boundary is more convincing than a promise that the cron process will never overlap.

Here is the decision record I use for the critical path:

Boundary Option Latency benefit Cost or failure trade-off
Timer to queue enqueue one run key Low scheduler overhead Requires durable deduplication
Report to delivery fan out child jobs Slow recipients are isolated More queue records and state transitions
Retry policy bounded exponential delay Absorbs short outages Delays visibility of a bad dependency
Result storage immutable artifact plus status row Delivery can resume Retention and access controls become explicit work

This is a latency-versus-cost decision, not a contest between cron and queues. More parallel delivery reduces wall-clock time but increases connection pressure, provider calls, and duplicate-delivery exposure.

Why should cron stop before the report is finished?

A timer process has a narrow responsibility: determine the intended run, record it, and publish a message. It should not wait for a database scan, render a large attachment, or send email. A long-lived cron invocation makes timeout semantics ambiguous: did the process die before enqueueing, after enqueueing, or after the work completed but before acknowledging it? Those are long-running tasks, so the trigger should return before the expensive work begins.

A generic Node.js scheduler can hand the durable parts to a queue client like this. The interface is intentionally abstract; the important detail is the stable key and the separation between schedule time and execution time.

from datetime import date


def schedule_daily_report(store, queue, tenant_id: str, run_date: date) -> None:
    run_key = f"shipment-report:{tenant_id}:{run_date.isoformat()}"

    created = store.insert_run_if_absent(
        key=run_key,
        tenant_id=tenant_id,
        report_date=run_date,
        status="queued",
    )
    if created:
        queue.publish(
            topic="report.generate",
            key=run_key,
            payload={
                "run_key": run_key,
                "tenant_id": tenant_id,
                "report_date": run_date.isoformat(),
            },
        )

The insert and publish operations need a defined relationship. If they cannot share a transaction, use an outbox record in the same transaction as the run row, then have a small publisher relay unsent outbox records. That adds storage and a relay, but it closes the gap where the run exists and the message does not. A queue's acknowledgement alone cannot repair that gap.

How do workers survive retries and partial fan-out?

The report worker claims a run with a lease, reads the required event range, writes an immutable artifact, and records the artifact checksum or version. It then creates delivery jobs keyed by (run_key, subscriber_id). The fan-out step is a state transition, not a loop whose progress lives only in memory.

I use a lease such as 15 minutes only when the report can make progress or renew it; a fixed lease that outlives the worker's real liveness delays recovery. A reaper can return expired work to the queue, but it must not assume that an expired lease means the old worker stopped. The delivery write needs its own idempotency key, and the email boundary needs an explicit duplicate policy because a process can lose its acknowledgement after sending.

def deliver_one(store, mailer, delivery_id: str) -> None:
    delivery = store.claim_delivery(delivery_id, lease_seconds=900)
    if delivery is None:
        return

    if delivery.status == "sent":
        return

    try:
        mailer.send(
            recipient=delivery.recipient,
            artifact_ref=delivery.artifact_ref,
            idempotency_key=delivery.idempotency_key,
        )
        store.mark_sent(delivery_id)
    except TemporaryDependencyError as error:
        store.release_for_retry(delivery_id, reason=str(error))
    except PermanentDeliveryError as error:
        store.mark_failed(delivery_id, reason=str(error))

The code cannot make an external email provider transactional with the database. That is a real failure boundary. If the send succeeds and the process crashes before mark_sent, a retry may send again. The practical answer is to use provider-supported idempotency where available, or make the message tolerate duplicates and expose the duplicate risk to operations. Claiming exactly-once delivery without controlling both sides is a misleading label.

Which failure modes deserve a separate alarm?

A queue depth alarm is not enough. A growing queue can mean a report scan is slow, delivery is throttled, or workers are repeatedly receiving poison messages. Those require different actions.

Track schedule lag, time from run creation to artifact completion, fan-out count, retry age, lease expirations, permanent failures, and delivery-provider responses. Keep the run key in every log and metric. The useful question at 09:30 UTC is not “are workers up?” but “which tenant and report date cannot reach a terminal state, and at which boundary?”

Security belongs in the same record of decisions. A report worker that fetches a callback URL, attachment, or remote logo must validate the destination and restrict network access; an attacker should not be able to turn report generation into a server-side request forgery primitive. The OWASP guidance distinguishes allowlisting approaches for trusted destinations from broader controls, and the right choice depends on whether destinations are fixed or user-supplied.

Do not let retries amplify that risk. A permanent validation error should move to a review state, not be retried every minute. Conversely, a transient database connection failure should not be marked permanent merely because the first attempt exceeded a short worker timeout.

When is a single scheduled worker enough?

A queue with separate generation and delivery jobs has a price: more rows, more instrumentation, more deployment coordination, and more operational states. For one tenant, a small report, and a recipient list that fits comfortably inside the execution budget, one scheduled worker can be the better design. It should still persist a run key and an outcome; simplicity does not remove the need for recovery.

Choose the split when report duration is variable, subscribers have uneven delivery behavior, or a missed retry has business consequences. Choose the simpler worker when the work is short, the recipient set is small, and the team can inspect and replay one run without reconstructing hidden progress. My decision rule is to buy parallelism only where it removes a measured bottleneck or isolates a failure boundary. Otherwise it is operational interest on a system that has not earned the complexity.

The durable architecture is therefore modest: a timer creates intent, an outbox protects publication, a worker materializes one report, and child jobs make fan-out independently recoverable. Latency improves through controlled concurrency; cost stays visible through queue volume, storage retention, and provider calls. The design is credible because it names what it cannot guarantee.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457

title: Node.js Update: Patch the Node2Shell RCE Tonight — Self-Hosted Fix Guide (CVE-2026-111497)
description:
The only sane advice this week: patch tonight. On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, Node.js shipped security releases for the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines. By Thursday, a working proof of concept was public — researchers had demonstrated remote code execution on the official Node.js 24.22.0 Docker image using crafted Brotli data. Today, The Hacker News carried the story wider. The vulnerability has a nickname now: Node2Shell.

If you self-host, this one matters more than most Node advisories. Node.js isn't just a runtime on your server — it is inside your containers. Your dashboards, automation and media tooling ship a Node runtime that a host package audit won't find. This guide is a runbook: find every Node in your stack, then fix each one — including the three traps that catch self-hosters.

Honest-testing note: We did not reproduce any exploit — no exploit or PoC instructions here, only defensive checks. Every fact below is quoted or derived from the official Node.js advisory, Imperva's research, Singapore's CSA advisory, or The Hacker News' coverage.

What Node2Shell actually is

Node2Shell is CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in Node.js's bundled Brotli decoder. The official advisory: "A flaw in Node.js can cause Node.js Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write permits remote code execution." It affects the 26.x, 24.x and 22.x lines; the fixed builds are 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4. Reported by OpenAI Codex Security — Khai Tran and Sylvie Mayer; fixed by mcollina and aduh95.

Two things to get right on severity. Node.js's own words: "The highest severity issue fixed in this release is HIGH." Separately, Singapore's CSA scored the same CVE at CVSS v3.1 9.8 — the CSA's score, not the Node.js project's rating. Per CSA: "Successful exploitation of this out-of-bounds write vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely or disclose sensitive information from the memory of affected systems. Exploitation requires an affected application to decompress attacker-controlled Brotli-compressed data."

Imperva's research identified three paths: (1) incoming request bodies with Brotli encoding — Express 5 (versions 5.0.0–5.3.0) and body-parser 2.x (2.0.0–2.3.0) decompress these; (2) outbound fetch() calls decoding Brotli responses from servers you don't control; (3) direct use of node:zlib. Imperva demonstrated RCE against the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image and confirmed the fixed 24.22.1 rejected the same input. No in-the-wild exploitation was reported as of October 22 — a window-of-opportunity story, which is exactly when patching pays off.

This release also fixed ten vulnerabilities total (four high, three medium, three low) — TLS hostname-check bypasses, a dns.resolve NUL-truncation bug, and bundled updates (c-ares, ca-cert with the eMudhra Intermediate CA compromise, OpenSSL, SQLite, Undici). More reasons to update Node.js everywhere it hides.

Step 0 — Are you exposed? Audit every Node in your stack

Start with the Node you know about, on the host:

node -v
# If it prints v22.23.4, v24.22.1 or v26.12.1 (or newer), the host runtime is fixed.

Then the Node you forgot about — inside your containers. A package inventory misses a runtime bundled in an image, so query the image itself:

docker run --rm my-app-image node --version
# Repeat for every Node-based app image in your compose stacks

Critical detail: check the running container, not just the pulled image — an old running container survives an image update:

docker exec my-app-container node --version
# or, for compose: docker compose exec app node --version

Make a list: every container older than 22.23.4 / 24.22.1 / 26.12.1 on its line, plus anything on an end-of-life line. That's your patch queue for tonight.

Step 1 — Re-pull and verify (the image-publisher lag trap)

The lag trap: Your app's Docker image is not fixed until its maintainer rebuilds it on node ≥22.23.4 / ≥24.22.1 / ≥26.12.1. Updating your image tag or restarting the container changes nothing if the publisher hasn't rebuilt yet. Never assume a re-pull fixed it — verify.

Before touching anything, snapshot first — the same snapshot-first discipline as our SafePay ransomware NAS survival guide. Then, for each Node-based app in your patch queue:

cd /path/to/your/compose/stack
docker compose pull          # get the publisher's latest build
docker compose up -d         # recreate containers on the new image
docker compose exec app node --version   # verify the RUNNING container is fixed

Two failure modes. First, a cached digest: if the version still shows old after the pull, confirm the digest actually changed (docker images --digests) — pinned digests and cached layers redeploy the old image silently. Second, the publisher may not have rebuilt yet — check the project's release notes. Same patch-tonight discipline as our GitLab CVSS-10 RCE guide: the vendor's fix and your deployment of it are two different events.

Step 2 — Fix the pin trap

If you build your own images, check your base-image pins. Aikido's warning, in spirit: a Dockerfile pinned to node:24.22.0 stays vulnerable no matter how often you rebuild it — rebuilding on the old pin changes nothing. So:

# In your Dockerfile, change:
#   FROM node:24.22.0-alpine
# to the fixed patch on your line:
#   FROM node:24.22.1-alpine
# Then rebuild:
docker build --no-cache -t my-app:latest .
docker run --rm my-app:latest node --version

Move to 24.22.1, 22.23.4 or 26.12.1 (or later) on whichever line you run. Same careful sequencing as our n8n 3.0 breaking-changes walkthrough — line jumps need release-note reading; patch bumps within a line are tonight's safe, fast move.

Step 3 — The EOL trap

The official advisory is blunt about end-of-life lines: "It's important to note that End-of-Life versions are always affected when a security release occurs." Per third-party guides (Aikido and others), lines like 20.x and earlier, plus odd lines 23.x/25.x, receive no fix — that detail comes from third-party analysis, not the official page.

The homelab killer: check your image's base. If any image you run is still built on an EOL Node line, no re-pull will ever fix it. Two moves: migrate the app to an image built on a supported line (22.x or 24.x), or — if the app can't move tonight — pull it off the public internet and sandbox it behind your VPN. Verify each project's Dockerfile or release notes yourself rather than trusting memory.

Can't patch tonight? A bridge-only stopgap

The official advisory offers no workaround in Node.js itself — patching is the fix. For the container you genuinely can't update tonight, reduce inbound exposure at the reverse proxy by rejecting Brotli request bodies. A bridge only: it does nothing about Brotli responses your app fetches, so don't treat it as protection.

For Nginx Proxy Manager, add to the proxy host's Custom Nginx Configuration:

# Node2Shell stopgap — TEMPORARY, remove after patching
if ($http_content_encoding ~* "br") {
  return 415;
}

For Caddy (in the site's handle block):

# Node2Shell stopgap — TEMPORARY, remove after patching
@brotli header Content-Encoding br
respond @brotli 415

Legitimate browsers sending Brotli request bodies will get a 415 — acceptable for one night on most homelab services, since Brotli request bodies are rare. Schedule the real node js security update for the morning and remove the rule once you're patched.

A note on Bun

If any self-hosted app runs on Bun rather than Node.js: Bun before 1.4.4 is affected, and Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix (per Aikido's FAQ). bun --version on the host or in the container tells you where you stand — update it the same way you'd update Node.js.

Verify the fix

Close the loop the same way you opened it — confirm the running state, not your intent:

# Host runtime
node -v
# Every patched container, checked live:
docker compose exec app node --version
docker exec my-other-app node --version

Expected: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (or newer) on each app's line. Anything still old goes back on the queue — or gets the stopgap and an off-internet sandbox until it can be patched.

One last operator caveat: if you run Watchtower or similar auto-updaters, exclude or pin images prone to major version jumps — the same discipline every nodejs docker update demands — so tonight's fix doesn't arrive as tomorrow's breaking change. Patch the runtime, verify the running container, then sleep.

Companion read: our Plex2Shell compromise check and patch guide covers the same patch-tonight workflow for Plex servers.

Node2Shell FAQ — quick answers

Which Node.js versions fix Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497)?

The October 21, 2026 releases: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1 for the 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. End-of-life lines (per third-party guides, 20.x and earlier) get no fix — the official advisory states end-of-life versions are always affected.

Is Node2Shell being exploited in the wild?

No in-the-wild exploitation was reported as of October 22, per The Hacker News — but a working proof of concept was publicly demonstrated on October 22. Patch now, while the window is open.

How do I check if my Docker containers run a vulnerable Node version?

Query the image directly — docker run --rm <image> node --version — since a host package audit misses runtimes bundled inside images. Then verify the running container with docker exec <container> node --version, because an old running container survives an image update.

My app image still reports the old Node version after updating — what now?

Three checks: (1) confirm the image digest actually changed after the pull — a cached or pinned digest redeploys the old image; (2) check the project's release notes — the publisher may not have rebuilt on the fixed base yet; (3) check your Dockerfile pins — a Dockerfile pinned to node:24.22.0 stays vulnerable no matter how often you rebuild it.

Does blocking Brotli at my reverse proxy fully protect me?

No. Rejecting Content-Encoding: br request bodies at the proxy only covers one attack path. It does nothing about Brotli responses your app fetches from servers you don't control, or direct node:zlib use. A temporary bridge for the night — the real fix is the Node.js update.

Is Bun affected by Node2Shell?

Bun before 1.4.4 is affected; Bun 1.4.4 includes the fix (per Aikido's FAQ). Run bun --version on the host or in the container and update the same night.

Originally published on The Homelab Fixer.

title: folderblog 0.2.7: Your blog can be a podcast now
description:
folderblog turns a folder of Markdown into a live blog the moment you save. Four releases since the last word here, 0.2.4 through 0.2.7, and the big one is 0.2.6: the same folder can now publish a podcast, with a proper feed, hosted audio, and a way for an AI agent to help without ever publishing on its own.

Podcasts from a folder

Put episodes in podcast/, one folder per episode, each with its MP3 (or an MP4 if it's a video show). folderblog builds the show page, a page for every episode, and /podcast/feed.xml. Turn it on with:

folderblog podcast on

The feed is ready for Apple Podcasts and Podcasting 2.0: every episode gets a permanent guid, and you can add transcripts, chapters, people, and optional Lightning tips. Episodes stay out of your main blog feed unless you set in_main_feed, so readers who only want posts don't get audio in their reader.

Audio hosted on Cloudflare R2

Audio files are too big to live comfortably next to your HTML, so folderblog uploads them to Cloudflare R2 when the site deploys. The site isn't published until the upload succeeds, which means the feed never points at a file that isn't there yet. folderblog podcast setup walks you through it. It works with an r2.dev address or your own domain, and a custom domain is recommended. Your keys are kept outside the blog folder, so they never end up in git or on the site.

An MCP server for AI agents

folderblog mcp starts an MCP server, so an AI agent can draft, check and publish episodes for you. It only publishes after you say yes. If you'd rather do it yourself, folderblog podcast publish --episode SLUG does the same thing from the terminal. The watcher and a publish take turns, so they never build or deploy at the same time.

Templates to copy

New blogs now come with a templates/ folder holding a sample post and a sample podcast episode. Each one lists every front matter field with a short note on what it does, so you don't have to dig through the guide to remember what draft or image does. To add the folder to a blog you already have, run folderblog templates.

Blogs keep up with updates by themselves

0.2.7 is the small one that makes the rest easier. After you install a new version, restart the service:

systemctl --user restart folderblog

The first time it starts, it adds any sample files your blogs don't have yet, like the new templates/ folder, and refreshes the generated part of AGENTS.md. It logs what it changed. It never turns a feature on, and it never touches your design, blog.toml or your posts. A sample file you delete stays deleted.

Two fixes along the way

  • 0.2.4: draft: true in front matter now really hides a post or page from the live site, as the guide always said. Before, those were still built and listed. They now behave like files in drafts/: visible in folderblog preview and build --drafts, never in real builds.
  • 0.2.5: if you use GoatCounter, 404 pages are now counted as events named after the missing URL instead of page views, so broken links show up on their own instead of looking like visits.

Grab it

System Command
Arch / Omarchy sudo pacman -U folderblog-bin-0.2.7-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst
Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install ./folderblog_0.2.7-1_amd64.deb
Fedora / RHEL / openSUSE sudo dnf install ./folderblog-0.2.7-1.x86_64.rpm
autonomix-cli autonomix-cli add https://github.com/ninepointlabs/folderblog

The packages and a plain tarball are on the v0.2.7 release. New to folderblog? Start with the guide, or run folderblog guide.

title: Making every harness durable
description:
Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike.

Running harnesses in the cloud

Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products.

These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt.

In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work.

Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.

Making every harness durable

We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness, which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code. It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts.

With durable-harness, you can:

  • Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel

  • Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance

  • Make your local harness workflow durable

  • Build your own durable harness

Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn

Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back.

What happens if its function times out while CI is still running?

Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.

Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.

With durable-harness, a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.

Logs and queues

durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World, the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.

It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.

After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:

  • Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens.

  • Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them.

  • Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check.

Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it.

Pick your harness

fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.

For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs.

Runs everywhere

Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.

Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World.

durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:

  • On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World.

  • In development, it uses files on your machine.

  • On your own servers, it uses Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, or Turso.

Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres.

For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:

Check the self-hosting docs for more details.

See every session in Agent Runs

Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.

Tools

An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.

Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools:

  • A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically.

  • A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice.

The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund:

For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on.

Files

When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations.

To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options:

  • virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox.

  • virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn.

  • sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work.

Compare the three side by side in the docs.

Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read, write, edit, and bash, and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace:

For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace, and for fx, pass it to fxTools(). Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true. Each harness guide lists its built-in tools.

Documents

Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session.

Tools can edit documents through io.docs, and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves:

Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI:

In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result.

Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure.

Wrapping up

Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness, a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface.

durable-harness is open source on GitHub.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open Small Language Model for Local Voice Agents, Game Characters and Robots

To set it up, point the proxy entrypoint in vercel.toml at your proxy:

Your middleware is an ASGI or WSGI app that runs separately from your main app, with only the packages in the vercel.proxy dependency group of your pyproject.toml. Add the packages your middleware imports to that group:

The vercel-proxy package provides utilities for writing routing middleware on Vercel, including a Proxy app that routes requests by path:

Requests that match no route continue to your app unchanged.

title: Railway alternatives in 2026: six options compared, and when to switch
description:
The best Railway alternatives in 2026 are Ownkube, Render, Fly.io, Northflank, DigitalOcean App Platform and Coolify. Ownkube is the closest swap if your worry is the bill: you load a prepaid wallet, apps draw it down per minute, and credit you do not spend rolls over. Render suits steady services with fixed prices, Fly.io suits apps spread across continents, and Coolify suits people happy to run their own server. Railway is still one of the nicest ways to ship a container, so this post also covers when to stay.

Our picks

If you want Pick
A bounded bill and a full stack (Postgres from $4, a cache from $2) Ownkube
A few steady, busy services at flat prices Render
Low latency for users on several continents Fly.io
Kubernetes power without running Kubernetes Northflank
To run the server yourself Coolify
To stay next to your existing DigitalOcean resources DigitalOcean App Platform

The Railway alternatives at a glance

Prices are approximate list prices from each provider's pricing page, as of October 2026. They move, so read the table as the shape of each model.

Alternative Billing model Smallest service Managed Postgres Best for
Ownkube Prepaid wallet, metered per minute or a flat box per app Metered from cents, or a Spark 1 box at $5 a month Yes, from $4 a month Personal software and small teams who want a bounded bill
Render Workspace plan plus flat instances, postpaid $7 a month (0.5 CPU, 512 MB) Yes, from $6 a month Steady services with predictable line items
Fly.io Per-second machines, postpaid $2.19 a month (shared-cpu-1x, 256 MB) Yes, managed from $38 a month Global, multi-region apps
Northflank Per-second compute, postpaid $2.70 a month (0.1 shared vCPU, 256 MB) Yes Teams that want Kubernetes power without running it
DigitalOcean App Platform Flat container tiers, postpaid $5 a month Yes, from $15.15 a month Teams already on DigitalOcean
Coolify Free software, you pay for the server Whatever your server costs You run it Developers happy to operate the box

Render, Fly.io, Northflank and DigitalOcean keep Railway's postpaid model and change the pricing shape. Coolify moves the platform onto a server you run. Ownkube changes the billing direction: you load a wallet first and usage draws it down. For Render and Northflank in more depth, see Railway vs Render vs Northflank.

Why people look for a Railway alternative

The reasons show up on the invoice or in the roadmap, rarely in the demo.

The postpaid surprise bill. Railway meters usage by the second and bills it after the fact. That works when someone watches the dashboard daily. It bites when a test service runs all month, or a traffic spike meters against a card faster than an alert reaches you.

Credit that resets each month. Railway's plans include a monthly usage allowance scoped to the cycle. A quiet month does not bank credit you can spend later.

The old free plan is gone. What remains is about $1 of credit a month after a one-time trial credit. For a lot of side projects, the free plan was the reason to be there.

The roadmap is moving upmarket. Like most of the category, Railway is building for Pro and Enterprise buyers. That is a healthy move for the company, and it puts the one-developer project further from the center of the roadmap.

The alternatives, one by one

Ownkube

Ownkube is a cloud for personal software. You deploy web apps, workers, cron jobs, Postgres and a Valkey cache onto Ownkube Compute with no cloud account to set up. Connect a GitHub or GitLab repo (a Dockerfile is optional) or pick an app from the Marketplace, and it gets an *.ownkube.app hostname with TLS.

Billing is a prepaid wallet. Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up; Personal ($5 a month) and Team ($20 a month) load that much credit each month and raise the limits. Usage draws the wallet down per minute, and unused credit rolls over and never expires. Each app either meters CPU and memory on actual use (about $18 per vCPU and $4.50 per GiB a month) or sits on a flat box (Spark from $5, Core from $58). Databases run on boxes from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB of storage, caches from $2. For the full-stack math, we priced a web app, Postgres and a cache on seven platforms.

Idle web apps, databases and caches can sleep. A sleeping app meters nothing, a sleeping database bills only its storage, and the next request wakes it. You can also set a monthly budget that either emails you or pauses everything.

The trade-offs: two regions today (Mumbai and Germany), no GPU, and custom domains are not on Ownkube Compute yet, so apps use their *.ownkube.app hostname. When an app later has to run inside your own or a customer's AWS account, the same app ships there with no rewrite, and its logs, metrics and health checks come with it.

Render

Render bills a workspace plan (from $0, Pro at $25 a month) plus a flat price per instance. A 1 CPU, 2 GB service is $25 a month whether it idles or not, which is easy to forecast and expensive for mostly idle apps. Its free instances spin down after 15 minutes idle, and free Postgres expires after 30 days. See Render pricing explained.

Fly.io

Fly.io runs Machines in many regions and bills them per second while they run. It is the strongest pick when latency on several continents matters. Managed Postgres starts around $38 a month, which changes the math for small apps. See Fly.io pricing explained.

Northflank

Northflank bills compute per second and offers GPU, job runners and an option for platform teams to run it in their own cloud. It is closer to a Kubernetes control panel than a quick-start platform, which is the point for teams that want that power.

DigitalOcean App Platform

App Platform has flat container tiers from $5 a month and managed databases from about $15. It fits best when your Droplets, Spaces and databases already live on DigitalOcean.

Coolify

Coolify is free, open-source software that turns a server you rent into a small platform. You pay only for the server, and you also patch it, back it up and debug it at 2am. See the self-hosted PaaS comparison.

Railway vs Ownkube

Ownkube Railway
Pricing structure Metered, or a flat box, chosen per app Metered usage, per second
Billing method Prepaid wallet the plan loads and usage drains Plan credit, then postpaid to your card
Credit rollover Unused wallet credit rolls over and never expires Monthly allowance resets each cycle
Entry plan Pay as you go from a $5 top-up; Personal $5 a month $5 plan with $5 of usage
Managed Postgres Database box from $4 a month plus $0.25 per GB Metered like any other service
Idle apps Sleep and meter nothing; databases bill only storage Optional sleep for serverless services
At zero balance Apps pause with data kept, resume on top-up, deleted after 7 days paused Billing continues on the card
Custom domains Not on Compute yet Yes
GPU No Yes

Railway figures are approximate, as of October 2026.

When to stay on Railway

Stay if developer experience is what you value most. Railway's onboarding, templates and project graph are among the best in the category, and Ownkube's dashboard is younger. Stay if you need GPU workloads or a custom domain on every app today. Stay if your bill is steady and someone already watches it.

A quick checklist before you switch

  • Price the whole app (web, worker, Postgres, cache, egress), not the web process alone.
  • Check where your users are and whether two regions cover them.
  • List the domains you serve today and whether an *.ownkube.app hostname works for now.
  • Export the database with pg_dump and test a restore before you cut over.
  • Decide whether you want a hard ceiling on spend or an alert.

FAQ

Is there a Railway free tier?

Railway's free plan is about $1 of credit a month after a one-time trial credit. Ownkube Compute has no free tier: Pay as you go starts with a $5 top-up, and that credit never expires.

Does Railway credit expire?

Railway's plan credit is scoped to the billing cycle and resets. Ownkube's wallet credit rolls over to the next month and never expires. More in does Railway credit roll over or expire.

Railway vs Ownkube cost: which is cheaper?

On compute alone the two are close: Railway's per-second CPU lands near Ownkube's metered CPU, and Ownkube's memory rate is lower. The gap opens with the database and cache. Take a 1 vCPU / 1 GiB web app, a 1 GiB / 10 GB Postgres and a small cache: that lands around $44 to $56 a month on Railway against roughly $27 on Ownkube. Treat those as illustrative (approximate, as of October 2026) and run your own sizes on the homepage calculator.

Can I move from Railway without a Dockerfile?

Yes. Ownkube builds straight from a GitHub or GitLab repo with automatic build, and uses your Dockerfile when there is one.

Reference: for the side-by-side breakdown, see Ownkube vs Railway in the docs.

Where Ownkube fits

Move off Railway when the postpaid meter or the monthly reset is what costs you. Stay if polished onboarding, GPU or custom domains matter most today. Ownkube is built for personal software and small teams: ship in seconds, load a wallet instead of exposing a card, and keep the credit you do not spend. Deploy my first app.

title: Everything Within a 30-Minute Walk: Practical Geospatial Queries with PostGIS, H3 and Isochrones
description:
Hôm nay trên Hacker News có một project tên "Local Wikipedia" đạt hơn 1100 điểm. Ý tưởng rất đơn giản: Wikipedia, nhưng chỉ hiện các bài về những địa điểm cách bạn khoảng nửa tiếng đi bộ. Đọc xong mình nghĩ ngay tới phía kỹ thuật bên dưới, vì câu hỏi "cái gì ở gần tôi?" là loại query mà gần như dev nào cũng sẽ gặp: app giao đồ ăn, tìm quán cà phê, chấm công theo vị trí, gợi ý phòng trọ gần trường. Nhiều team ở Việt Nam vẫn làm bằng cách lưu lat/lng dạng FLOAT, kéo hết về application rồi tính khoảng cách trong vòng lặp. Với 500 record thì không sao. Với 2 triệu POI thì server khóc. Bài này đi qua 3 cấp độ, từ "bán kính đường chim bay" tới "thật sự đi bộ được trong 30 phút", kèm code chạy được.

Cấp độ 1: Bán kính đường chim bay với PostGIS

Đầu tiên phải đổi "30 phút đi bộ" thành con số. Tốc độ đi bộ trung bình khoảng 4.5–5 km/h, nên 30 phút ≈ 2.5 km. Đây là khoảng cách đường thẳng, nên nó luôn lớn hơn khoảng cách thực tế. Tạm thời cứ chấp nhận vậy.

Đừng tự viết công thức Haversine trong SQL. Dùng PostGIS (mình đang dùng PostGIS 3.5 trên PostgreSQL 17), lưu cột kiểu geography và đánh index GiST:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS postgis;

CREATE TABLE places (
  id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  geom    GEOGRAPHY(Point, 4326) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX places_geom_gist ON places USING GIST (geom);

-- Lưu ý: ST_MakePoint nhận (longitude, latitude), KHÔNG phải (lat, lng)
INSERT INTO places (name, geom) VALUES
  ('Hồ Hoàn Kiếm', ST_MakePoint(105.8522, 21.0287)::geography),
  ('Văn Miếu',     ST_MakePoint(105.8355, 21.0293)::geography);

-- Mọi địa điểm trong bán kính 2.5 km, sắp xếp theo khoảng cách
SELECT id, name,
       round(ST_Distance(geom, me)::numeric) AS meters
FROM places,
     (SELECT ST_MakePoint(105.8480, 21.0245)::geography AS me) p
WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, me, 2500)
ORDER BY geom <-> me
LIMIT 50;

Có vài điểm mình thấy người mới hay sai:

  • Thứ tự tham số là (lng, lat). Google Maps hiển thị lat, lng nên ai cũng copy ngược. Kết quả là điểm của bạn rơi xuống đâu đó ở Nam Cực.
  • Dùng ST_DWithin, đừng dùng ST_Distance(...) < 2500 trong WHERE. ST_DWithin dùng được index, còn ST_Distance trong WHERE sẽ scan toàn bộ bảng.
  • geography tính bằng mét trên mặt cầu, còn geometry SRID 4326 tính bằng độ. Nếu viết ST_DWithin(geom, me, 2500) với geometry thì nghĩa là 2500 độ, tức cả Trái Đất.
  • Toán tử <-> là KNN, dùng index để sắp xếp theo khoảng cách. Nó cực nhanh khi đi kèm LIMIT.

Chạy EXPLAIN ANALYZE thì bạn sẽ thấy Index Scan using places_geom_gist. Với khoảng 1 triệu điểm, query này thường mất dưới 10ms.

Cấp độ 2: Khi không có PostGIS, dùng H3 để chia lưới

Có lúc bạn không dùng được PostGIS: data nằm trong Redis, DynamoDB, Elasticsearch không có geo, hoặc bạn cần cache kết quả theo khu vực. Lúc đó cách làm là chia bản đồ thành ô (spatial index). Hai lựa chọn phổ biến là Geohash (ô chữ nhật) và H3 của Uber (ô lục giác). Mình thích H3 hơn vì các ô lân cận đều cách tâm gần như bằng nhau, không bị méo ở góc như ô vuông.

flowchart LR
    A[User location lat/lng] --> B[h3.latlng_to_cell res 8]
    B --> C[grid_disk k ô xung quanh]
    C --> D[Lookup các cell ID trong DB/Redis]
    D --> E[Lọc chính xác bằng Haversine]
    E --> F[Sort và trả kết quả]

Ví dụ với h3 4.x (pip install h3==4.1.2):

import math
import h3

RES = 8  # cạnh ô khoảng 530m ở resolution 8

def haversine_m(lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2):
    r = 6_371_000
    p1, p2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
    dp = p2 - p1
    dl = math.radians(lng2 - lng1)
    a = math.sin(dp / 2) ** 2 + math.cos(p1) * math.cos(p2) * math.sin(dl / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * r * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))

# Lúc ghi: tính sẵn cell cho mỗi địa điểm, lưu thành 1 cột có index
def index_place(place):
    place["h3"] = h3.latlng_to_cell(place["lat"], place["lng"], RES)
    return place

# Lúc đọc: lấy các ô lân cận rồi lọc chính xác
def nearby(places_by_cell, lat, lng, radius_m=2500):
    center = h3.latlng_to_cell(lat, lng, RES)
    edge = h3.average_hexagon_edge_length(RES, unit="m")
    k = math.ceil(radius_m / (edge * 1.5)) + 1
    candidates = []
    for cell in h3.grid_disk(center, k):
        candidates.extend(places_by_cell.get(cell, []))
    result = [
        (p, haversine_m(lat, lng, p["lat"], p["lng"])) for p in candidates
    ]
    return sorted([x for x in result if x[1] <= radius_m], key=lambda x: x[1])

Pattern ở đây là lọc thô bằng cell → lọc tinh bằng công thức. Cột h3 chỉ là một string hoặc int64 bình thường, nên database nào cũng index được. Thêm một lợi ích: cell ID làm cache key rất tốt. Hai người đứng cách nhau 100m trong cùng một ô sẽ dùng chung kết quả cache.

Cấp độ 3: "Đi bộ được" chứ không phải "đường chim bay"

Đây là chỗ phân biệt một app làm cho có với một app làm tốt. Ở Hà Nội hay Sài Gòn, một quán cách bạn 800m theo đường thẳng có thể nằm bên kia sông, bên kia đường ray, hoặc bên kia một cái hẻm cụt, và đi bộ mất 25 phút. Câu trả lời đúng là isochrone: một polygon bao trọn mọi điểm bạn tới được trong X phút trên mạng lưới đường thực tế.

Công cụ open-source mình hay dùng là Valhalla, chạy trên dữ liệu OpenStreetMap. Tự host bằng Docker:

# Tải dữ liệu OSM Việt Nam (~300MB) từ Geofabrik
mkdir -p valhalla_data && cd valhalla_data
wget https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/vietnam-latest.osm.pbf

# Chạy Valhalla, lần đầu build tiles mất khoảng 15-30 phút
docker run -d --name valhalla -p 8002:8002 \
  -v "$PWD":/custom_files \
  ghcr.io/gis-ops/docker-valhalla/valhalla:latest

# Isochrone đi bộ 30 phút, trả về GeoJSON polygon
curl -s http://localhost:8002/isochrone --data '{
  "locations": [{"lat": 21.0245, "lon": 105.8480}],
  "costing": "pedestrian",
  "contours": [{"time": 30}],
  "polygons": true
}' | jq '.features[0].geometry' > walk30.json

Có polygon rồi thì ghép lại với PostGIS. Mình làm theo flow 2 bước để vẫn tận dụng được index:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant API as API Server
    participant V as Valhalla
    participant DB as PostGIS
    C->>API: GET /nearby?lat=..&lng=..
    API->>V: POST /isochrone (pedestrian, 30 min)
    V-->>API: GeoJSON polygon
    API->>DB: ST_DWithin 2.5km AND ST_Intersects polygon
    DB-->>API: Danh sách địa điểm
    API-->>C: JSON kết quả
SELECT id, name
FROM places
WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, ST_MakePoint(105.8480, 21.0245)::geography, 2500)
  AND ST_Intersects(
        geom::geometry,
        ST_SetSRID(ST_GeomFromGeoJSON($1), 4326)
      );

Điều kiện ST_DWithin ở đây đóng vai "lưới an toàn": nó dùng index để cắt nhanh tập ứng viên, rồi ST_Intersects với polygon chỉ phải chạy trên vài trăm dòng thay vì cả bảng. Gọi isochrone tốn khoảng 50–200ms, nên hãy cache polygon theo H3 cell của người dùng (ví dụ resolution 9, TTL vài ngày). Đường sá không thay đổi mỗi phút.

Vài cái bẫy production

  • Độ chính xác GPS trên điện thoại trong nhà hoặc giữa các tòa cao tầng có thể lệch 50–200m. Đừng hứa "cách bạn 37m". Làm tròn hiển thị tới 50m hoặc 100m.
  • Privacy: tọa độ người dùng là dữ liệu nhạy cảm. Nếu chỉ cần query thì làm tròn hoặc snap về H3 cell trước khi log. Đừng bao giờ ghi lat/lng chính xác vào access log.
  • Dữ liệu OSM ở Việt Nam khá đầy đủ ở các thành phố lớn, nhưng nhiều hẻm nhỏ còn thiếu. Isochrone vùng ven có thể bị "hụt" so với thực tế.
  • Đừng tính khoảng cách ở frontend cho hàng nghìn marker. Để database làm, client chỉ render.

Kết luận

Những việc bạn làm được ngay tuần này:

  1. Bỏ kiểu lat FLOAT, lng FLOAT + loop trong code. Chuyển sang GEOGRAPHY(Point, 4326) + index GiST, dùng ST_DWithin để lọc và <-> để sắp xếp.
  2. Kiểm tra thứ tự (lng, lat) ở mọi chỗ gọi ST_MakePoint. Đây là bug phổ biến nhất, và hay chạy "có vẻ đúng" ở những khu vực gần xích đạo.
  3. Không có PostGIS thì dùng H3: lưu cell ID như một cột thường, lọc thô bằng grid_disk, lọc tinh bằng Haversine. Tận dụng luôn cell ID làm cache key.
  4. Nếu UX nói "đi bộ X phút" thì dùng isochrone (Valhalla hoặc OSRM tự host với dữ liệu Geofabrik), kết hợp với ST_DWithin làm bộ lọc trước để giữ query nhanh.
  5. Luôn EXPLAIN ANALYZE để chắc query thật sự dùng index. Một geo query không dùng index là quả bom hẹn giờ khi data tăng lên.

"Gần tôi có gì?" nghe có vẻ là một feature nhỏ, nhưng làm đúng thì nó là ranh giới giữa một app lag và một app khiến người dùng thấy "ồ, nhanh thật".

title: Syntax Comparison of ES5 vs ES6
description:
Basically, I was revising JavaScript fundamentals. While doing that, I had a curious thought that led me to write content on it. And this is a common topic roaming all over the internet.

## Demo Data
const users = [
{ id: 1, name: "Rafi", age: 22, role: "intern" },
{ id: 2, name: "Nila", age: 17, role: "student" },
{ id: 3, name: "Sami", age: 28, role: "developer" },
{ id: 4, name: "Tina", age: 31, role: "developer" },
];

## ES6 functional expression using template literals

// Option A: Print each user using .forEach()
users.forEach(u => console.log(`${u.name} (${u.age})`));

// Option B: Create a new array of strings using .map()
const names = users.map(u => `${u.name} (${u.age})`);
console.log(names);

## ES5 functional expression

// Option A: Print each user using .forEach()
users.forEach(function(u) {
  console.log(u.name + " (" + u.age + ")");
});

// Option B: Create a new array of strings using .map()
var names = users.map(function(u) {
  return u.name + " (" + u.age + ")";
});
console.log(names);

This Code could be a responsible way to set a vision of understanding ES5 & ES6.
