title: Next.js use cache Explained: Cache Components, cacheLife and cacheTag in Next.js 16.4
description:
Cross-posted from my blog. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Next.js use cache is a directive that marks an async function, component or whole file as cacheable, so its output is stored and reused for matching inputs. It is the core of Cache Components, the caching model that Next.js 16.4 now turns on by default in create-next-app. Add 'use cache', set a lifetime with cacheLife, label it with cacheTag, and invalidate it with updateTag or revalidateTag.

This guide is written against Next.js 16.4.2 and React 19.3, the current releases. I scaffolded a fresh app with create-next-app@16.4.2 (its generated next.config.ts already contains cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true), wrote every example below, then type-checked, linted, built and ran it with next start. The build output, headers and timestamps shown are the real ones I got back. Framework behavior links to the official Next.js docs.

Security note: the October 14, 2026 Next.js security update fixed a critical remote code execution bug in use cache functions that return multiple typed arrays. If you use Cache Components, run Next.js 16.4.1 or later before you ship anything from this post.

What does "use cache" do in Next.js?

'use cache' tells Next.js that a function's return value depends only on its inputs, so it can be stored and reused. The first call runs the function and saves the output; later calls with the same arguments get the saved output until the entry revalidates. Cached output can also be baked into the page's prerendered static shell.

The official use cache reference lists what goes into a cache key:

  1. Build ID: every deploy gets new keys, so caches do not survive a deploy.
  2. Function ID: a secure hash of where the function lives and its signature.
  3. Serializable arguments: function arguments or component props.
  4. Closed-over variables: values captured from an outer scope become part of the key.

That makes it different from the old App Router model, where fetch calls and route segments were cached implicitly. With Cache Components, nothing is cached unless you say so, and anything you do cache is explicit at the call site.

Quick definitions

Term What it means
Cache Components The Next.js 16 programming model behind cacheComponents: true: explicit use cache, Partial Prerendering and Suspense streaming (docs)
'use cache' Directive that caches a function, component or file's exports, shared across users
cacheLife Sets how long an entry is fresh (stale, revalidate, expire) (docs)
cacheTag Labels an entry so you can invalidate it on demand (docs)
updateTag Expires a tag immediately from a Server Action; the next read waits for fresh data
revalidateTag Marks a tag stale from a Server Function or Route Handler; serves stale while it refreshes
Static shell The prerendered HTML of a route, including cached output and Suspense fallbacks

TL;DR: Next.js use cache in five lines

You want to... Do this
Cache a database query or API call for everyone 'use cache' + cacheLife('hours') + cacheTag('x') in the data function
Show a user's change right after they submit a form updateTag('x') inside the Server Action
Refresh after a CMS or Stripe webhook revalidateTag('x', 'max') in a Route Handler
Read cookies or headers Read them outside the cached scope and pass values as arguments
Cache something that must read cookies inside 'use cache: private' (per browser only)
Share a cache across many server instances 'use cache: remote' with a cache handler

Is Cache Components enabled by default in Next.js 16.4?

Yes, for new apps. Since Next.js 16.4, released on October 6, 2026, every app created with create-next-app has Cache Components enabled, and the Next.js team says it will become the default for all apps in Next.js 17. Existing apps keep the old model until you add cacheComponents: true.

This is what create-next-app@16.4.2 generated for me, unedited apart from the Tailwind loader lines:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

next build confirms it at the top of the log:

✓ Running next.config.ts took 21ms
- Cache Components enabled
- Partial Prefetching enabled

How do you use "use cache" in Next.js? (step by step)

Here is the full working pattern from my test app: a product list that every visitor shares, a greeting that reads a cookie, and a form that adds a product.

Step 1: cache the data function

Put the directive at the top of the async function body, then set an explicit lifetime and a tag:

// lib/products.ts
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
import { queryProducts } from './db'

// Shared, cached data function: one entry for every visitor.
export async function getProducts() {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('hours')
  cacheTag('products')

  const products = await queryProducts()
  return { products, cachedAt: new Date().toISOString() }
}

cachedAt is there only to prove caching in the tests below. Because new Date() runs inside the cached scope, its value is stored with the entry, and the route still prerenders.

Step 2: render cached and request-time parts on one page 

// app/page.tsx
import { Suspense } from 'react'
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { getProducts } from '@/lib/products'
import { addProduct } from './actions'

export default function Home() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Store</h1>
      {/* Request-time hole: reads a cookie, so it streams in */}
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading greeting...</p>}>
        <Greeting />
      </Suspense>
      {/* Cached: part of the static shell */}
      <ProductList />
      <form action={addProduct}>
        <input name="name" placeholder="Name" />
        <input name="price" type="number" placeholder="Price" />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>
    </main>
  )
}

async function Greeting() {
  const name = (await cookies()).get('name')?.value ?? 'guest'
  return <p>Hi, {name}</p>
}

async function ProductList() {
  const { products, cachedAt } = await getProducts()
  return (
    <section>
      <ul>
        {products.map((p) => (
          <li key={p.id}>{p.name}: ${p.price}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      <p>cached at {cachedAt}</p>
    </section>
  )
}

Step 3: invalidate from a Server Action with updateTag 

// app/actions.ts
'use server'

import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
import { insertProduct } from '@/lib/db'

export async function addProduct(formData: FormData) {
  const name = String(formData.get('name') ?? '').trim()
  const price = Number(formData.get('price'))
  if (!name || !Number.isFinite(price)) return

  await insertProduct({ name, price })
  // Expire the tag now: the next read waits for fresh data
  // (read-your-own-writes for the user who submitted the form).
  updateTag('products')
}

In a real app, authenticate and authorize inside the action first. My Server Actions vs Route Handlers guide covers why every action is a public endpoint.

Step 4: invalidate from a webhook with revalidateTag 

// app/api/revalidate/route.ts
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

// Called by a CMS or admin webhook after products change.
export async function POST(request: Request) {
  if (request.headers.get('authorization') !== `Bearer ${process.env.REVALIDATE_SECRET}`) {
    return Response.json({ error: 'unauthorized' }, { status: 401 })
  }
  // Stale-while-revalidate: visitors keep getting the old list
  // while the next request refreshes it in the background.
  revalidateTag('products', 'max')
  return Response.json({ revalidated: true })
}

Step 5: build and read the route table 

Route (app)          Revalidate  Expire
┌ ◐ /                        1h      1d
├ ○ /_not-found
├ ◐ /account
├ ○ /api/products            1h      1d
└ ƒ /api/revalidate

○  (Static)             prerendered as static content
◐  (Partial Prerender)  prerendered as static HTML with dynamic server-streamed content
ƒ  (Dynamic)            server-rendered on demand

The home page is ◐ Partial Prerender: the product list is in the static shell, and the cookie greeting streams in. The 1h / 1d columns come straight from the hours profile. The webhook route is dynamic, as it should be.

Does it actually cache? What I measured with next start

These are the real responses from next start on the test app.

Two requests, one entry. A GET Route Handler that calls getProducts() returned the same timestamp twice. It was filled during next build and reused:

$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:01:48.233Z"}
$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:01:48.233Z"}

Shared cache, personal hole. Sending cookie: name=Waseem changed the greeting to Hi, Waseem while the product list kept the same cached at value. The response headers show how Next.js treats the page:

x-nextjs-stale-time: 300
x-nextjs-prerender: 1
x-nextjs-postponed: 1

x-nextjs-stale-time: 300 is the 5-minute client stale value from the hours profile, and x-nextjs-postponed: 1 means part of the page was deferred to request time.

revalidateTag is stale-while-revalidate. Without the bearer token the webhook returned 401. With it, the first request after revalidation still got the old entry, and the next one got a fresh one:

$ curl -s -X POST -H 'authorization: Bearer s3cret' localhost:3141/api/revalidate
{"revalidated":true}
$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:01:48.233Z"}   # stale, refresh starts
$ curl -s localhost:3141/api/products
{"count":2,"cachedAt":"2026-10-17T13:02:01.283Z"}   # fresh

updateTag is read-your-own-writes. In a headless Chrome test, submitting the form with "Webcam, 59" re-rendered the list with three items and a new cached at time in the same navigation. A second browser that opened the page afterwards saw the same three items and the same new timestamp, so the shared entry was replaced, not forked per user.

What are the cacheLife profiles?

cacheLife sets three values: stale (how long the browser may reuse it without asking), revalidate (after which the server refreshes it in the background) and expire (after which a request must wait for fresh data). These are the built-in presets from the cacheLife reference:

Profile Use case stale revalidate expire
default Standard content 5 minutes 15 minutes never
seconds Real-time data 30 seconds 1 second 1 minute
minutes Frequently updated content 5 minutes 1 minute 1 hour
hours Updated several times a day 5 minutes 1 hour 1 day
days Updated daily 5 minutes 1 day 1 week
weeks Updated weekly 5 minutes 1 week 30 days
max Rarely changes 5 minutes 30 days 1 year

Three rules worth remembering:

  • Always set cacheLife explicitly. Without it the default profile applies, and nesting a short-lived cache inside a scope with no explicit cacheLife fails the build during prerendering.
  • The browser keeps cached output for at least 30 seconds. The client router enforces a minimum 30-second stale time regardless of your profile.
  • You can define custom profiles in next.config.ts under cacheLife, or pass an inline object such as cacheLife({ stale: 60, revalidate: 600, expire: 3600 }).

updateTag vs revalidateTag: which should you use?

Use updateTag inside a Server Action when the user who made a change must see it on the very next render. Use revalidateTag(tag, 'max') from a Route Handler or webhook when a short window of stale data is fine. updateTag blocks the next read until fresh data loads; revalidateTag serves stale content while it refreshes.

updateTag(tag) revalidateTag(tag, 'max')
Where it runs Server Actions only Server Functions and Route Handlers
Next read Waits for fresh data Gets stale data, triggers a refresh
Best for Forms, settings, carts: read-your-own-writes CMS publish, Stripe and GitHub webhooks, admin jobs
In a Route Handler Throws Works

The revalidateTag reference recommends the 'max' profile and marks the single-argument form as deprecated; it behaves like { expire: 0 }, a blocking cache miss. Tags are case-sensitive and capped at 256 characters, and a longer tag is silently never assigned. Revalidation is triggered by the next request, not by the call itself, so pages refresh as they are visited.

use cache vs use cache: private vs use cache: remote

Next.js has three caching directives. Plain 'use cache' covers most apps. The other two solve specific problems, and the use cache: remote reference compares them:

Feature 'use cache' 'use cache: remote' 'use cache: private'
Server-side storage In memory or a cache handler Remote cache handler None
Shared between users Yes Yes No, per browser
Can call cookies() / headers() inside No, pass values as arguments No, pass values as arguments Yes
Extra cost None Storage and network None
Survives a deploy No No N/A

When should you use "use cache: private"?

Use it only when a function must read cookies or headers itself and you cannot refactor it to take those values as arguments, or when compliance rules forbid storing request data in a server cache. It runs at request time, is excluded from the static shell and is cached only in the browser. This is the version from my test app:

// app/account/page.tsx (excerpt)
import { cookies } from 'next/headers'
import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'

// Reads cookies directly. Cached per browser only, never in a shared server cache.
async function getPreferences() {
  'use cache: private'
  cacheLife({ stale: 60 })
  const currency = (await cookies()).get('currency')?.value ?? 'USD'
  return { currency }
}

With a currency=PKR cookie the page rendered Currency: PKR, and the route still built as ◐ because the component sits inside <Suspense>.

When does "use cache: remote" make sense?

When request-time content gets low hit rates from per-instance memory: serverless functions, many replicas, or an expensive upstream such as a slow CMS. It stores entries in a shared handler like Redis. Skip it when operations already take under about 50 ms, when keys are mostly unique per request, or when data changes every few seconds; the docs list those as cases where remote caching does not pay off.

Does "use cache" work when self-hosting with Docker or Coolify?

Yes. The official platform table lists both the Node.js server and Docker as supported, and static export as not supported. When self-hosted, the default in-memory cache persists across requests in the same process, which is exactly what the next start tests above show. Size it with cacheMaxMemorySize.

Two things change once you run more than one container:

  • Each replica has its own memory cache. Two instances can serve different cachedAt values until both refresh. Configure a shared cacheHandlers entry (for example Redis) if that matters.
  • Every deploy starts cold. The cache key includes the build ID, so use cache entries do not carry over. For data that must survive deploys, the docs still point to unstable_cache or the fetch cache.

If you are deploying this way, my self-hosting Next.js with Coolify guide and production Next.js Dockerfile cover the container side.

How do you migrate an existing app to Cache Components?

Enable cacheComponents: true, then replace each route segment config the build complains about. The migration guide says routes that still export dynamic, revalidate or fetchCache will error once the flag is on. Most of the work is mechanical:

Before (old App Router) After (Cache Components)
export const revalidate = 3600 'use cache' + cacheLife('hours') around the data or UI
export const revalidate = 0 / force-dynamic Remove it; uncached data already runs at request time
export const fetchCache = 'force-cache' Wrap the data in 'use cache'
unstable_cache(fn, keys, { tags, revalidate }) Optional: 'use cache' + cacheTag + cacheLife; the old API keeps working
fetch(url, { next: { tags } }) cacheTag inside a 'use cache' function
revalidateTag('x') updateTag('x') in actions, revalidateTag('x', 'max') elsewhere

For a large app, adopt it incrementally:

  1. Turn on the flag and migrate the segment configs above.
  2. Opt out routes that are not ready with export const instant = false, or run the codemod across the app: npx @next/codemod@canary cache-components-instant-false ./app.
  3. Fix synchronous IO such as new Date(), Math.random() and crypto.randomUUID() in the prerendered shell; instant = false does not clear those errors. Move the call into a cached scope, a Client Component, or behind connection() inside <Suspense>.
  4. Remove instant = false one route at a time and resolve the dev overlay insights.

If you use a coding agent, Next.js ships a skill for this: npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-cache-components-adoption, then ask the agent to adopt Cache Components with it.

What can't you do inside "use cache"?

Cached functions run in an isolated environment, and four limits catch most people:

  • No request APIs. cookies(), headers() and searchParams are not allowed, even in a helper the cached function calls. On dynamic routes this can pass next build and fail under next start with the next-request-in-use-cache error.
  • Serializable inputs and outputs only. Arguments follow Server Component serialization, return values follow Client Component serialization. Class instances, symbols, URL objects and functions (except as pass-through) are rejected.
  • React.cache does not cross the boundary. Values stored with React.cache outside a cached scope are not visible inside it. Pass data as arguments.
  • Promises of runtime data hang the build. Passing a cookies() promise or uncached data into a cached function makes prerendering wait, and the build times out after 50 seconds.

For debugging, run NEXT_PRIVATE_DEBUG_CACHE=1 npm run start for verbose cache logs. In development, logs from cached functions are replayed with a Cache prefix.

Common "use cache" mistakes

Mistake What happens Fix
Calling cookies() inside 'use cache' next-request-in-use-cache error Read it outside and pass the value in
Caching per-user data with plain 'use cache' Users can see each other's data if the key misses the user ID Add the user ID as an argument, or use 'use cache: private'
No cacheLife default profile applies; nested short caches can fail the build Set a profile in every cached scope
updateTag in a Route Handler Throws at runtime Use revalidateTag(tag, 'max')
revalidateTag('x') with one argument Deprecated, blocking miss Pass 'max' or migrate to updateTag
Expecting caches to survive deploys Cold cache after each deploy Accept it, or use unstable_cache / fetch cache for that data
Several replicas, default handler Replicas disagree for a while Shared cacheHandlers or 'use cache: remote'
Running Next.js below 16.4.1 Exposed to the October 2026 critical advisories Upgrade now

Related: Next.js 16.4.1 patched a critical RCE in use cache functions that return typed arrays; see the Next.js security update October 2026. To let an AI agent do the migration for you, install the official next-cache-components-adoption skill as shown in Agent Skills: how to write a SKILL.md.

Related: I reused this demo app to benchmark the TypeScript 7 upgrade: the next build type-check step dropped from 1,368 ms to 231 ms.

Related: my React View Transitions guide uses Cache Components with connection() so a Suspense fallback streams in and animates its reveal.

Related: for a side-by-side with a non-Next.js framework, see TanStack Start vs Next.js, where I benchmarked the same app on both for server throughput, client JS, hydration and build time.

Key takeaways

  • 'use cache' caches an async function, component or file by its inputs; with Cache Components nothing else is cached implicitly.
  • New Next.js 16.4 apps have Cache Components and Partial Prefetching on by default, and it becomes the default for all apps in Next.js 17.
  • Pair every cached scope with cacheLife and cacheTag, then invalidate with updateTag in Server Actions or revalidateTag(tag, 'max') elsewhere.
  • Request APIs stay outside cached scopes; pass their values in as arguments, or reach for 'use cache: private' when you truly cannot.
  • Self-hosted next start keeps entries in memory across requests, but not across deploys or between replicas.

FAQ

What does 'use cache' do in Next.js?

'use cache' marks an async function, component or file's exports as cacheable. Next.js runs it once for a given set of serializable inputs, stores the output, and reuses it until the entry revalidates through cacheLife or a cacheTag invalidation. Cached output can also be included in the route's prerendered static shell.

Is Cache Components enabled by default in Next.js 16.4?

Yes for new apps. Since Next.js 16.4, create-next-app generates a next.config.ts with cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true. Existing apps keep the previous model until you enable the flag, and the Next.js team plans to make Cache Components the default for all apps in Next.js 17.

What is the difference between updateTag and revalidateTag?

updateTag runs only in Server Actions and expires a tag immediately, so the next read waits for fresh data and the user sees their own change. revalidateTag runs in Server Functions and Route Handlers; with the recommended 'max' profile it marks the tag stale and serves stale content while the next request refreshes it.

Can I use cookies() inside 'use cache'?

No. cookies(), headers() and searchParams are not allowed inside a 'use cache' scope or any helper it calls, and doing so throws the next-request-in-use-cache error. Read the value outside the cached function and pass it in as an argument. If you cannot refactor, 'use cache: private' allows request APIs but caches only in the browser.

Does 'use cache' replace unstable_cache?

For most code, yes, but you do not have to migrate. unstable_cache keeps working with Cache Components. One difference matters: unstable_cache and the fetch cache persist across deployments, while 'use cache' entries are keyed by build ID and start cold after every deploy.

Does 'use cache' work when self-hosting Next.js with Docker?

Yes. Node.js servers and Docker containers are supported; static export is not. Self-hosted, the default in-memory cache persists across requests in the same process, sized by cacheMaxMemorySize. With several replicas each has its own cache, so configure a shared cacheHandlers entry such as Redis if they must agree.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: #!/usr/bin/env python3 -u Worked Under python3 and Failed as ./prune.py: What Linux Does With a Shebang Line
description:
I gave a clip-pruning script the first line #!/usr/bin/env python3 -u, tested it with python3 prune.py clips, and it worked. Run as ./prune.py clips, the way a cron job or a systemd timer would start it, it failed with exit status 127 before a single line of Python ran.

The script was fine. The first line was not, and the way I tested it skipped the first line entirely.

Disclosure: I make an Android camera app. Nothing below uses its code or describes how it stores or prunes files. Every script ran on one Linux machine (kernel 6.8, aarch64) with GNU bash 5.1.16, GNU coreutils 8.32 and Python 3.10.12, against a scratch folder the setup script creates under /tmp.

What the tests showed:

  • The kernel passes everything after the interpreter as one argument. -u -B arrived as a single string, space included.
  • That breaks env. It went looking for a program literally named python3 -u.
  • Two flags break the interpreter too, even with no env in the line. One flag works. Two flags joined into one word work.
  • env -S fixes it by splitting the string itself.
  • A line that is too long is cut silently. No error, no warning, a shorter argument.
  • Windows line endings fail the same way, because the carriage return becomes part of the interpreter's name.
  • Running the script through its interpreter hides every one of these. That is why they survive testing.

Setup

setup.sh makes the scratch folder, two empty clips, and showargs, a tiny Python program that prints exactly what it was handed. Using it as an interpreter shows what the kernel passes.

#!/bin/bash
# Builds a scratch folder with a tiny "show me my argv" interpreter.
set -eu
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
rm -rf "$D"; mkdir -p "$D/clips"
touch "$D/clips/clip_0001.mp4" "$D/clips/clip_0002.mp4"
cat > "$D/showargs" <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/python3
import sys
for i, a in enumerate(sys.argv):
    print("argv[%d] = %r" % (i, a))
PY
chmod +x "$D/showargs"
uname -sr
bash --version | head -1
env --version | head -1
python3 --version

Linux 6.8.0-138-generic
GNU bash, version 5.1.16(1)-release (aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu)
env (GNU coreutils) 8.32
Python 3.10.12

Test one: what the kernel hands the interpreter 

#!/bin/bash
# What the kernel actually hands the interpreter named on the #! line.
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
printf '#!%s -u -B\nprint("body never runs")\n' "$D/showargs" > "$D/job.py"
chmod +x "$D/job.py"
"$D/job.py" clips

Output:

argv[0] = '/tmp/shebang_demo/showargs'
argv[1] = '-u -B'
argv[2] = '/tmp/shebang_demo/job.py'
argv[3] = 'clips'

The first argument after the program's own path is '-u -B', one string. The execve(2) manual page says so directly: "On Linux, the entire string following the interpreter name is passed as a single argument to the interpreter, and this string can include white space." The kernel does no word splitting on that line. Whatever program you name gets one argument and has to cope with the space itself.

Note also that the script path arrives as an argument after it, and the name the caller used for the program is gone. The same page: "Note that there is no way to get the argv[0] that was passed to the execve() call."

Test two: the common env line 

#!/bin/bash
# The common shebang: env plus an interpreter flag.
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
cat > "$D/prune.py" <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3 -u
import sys, glob
print(len(glob.glob(sys.argv[1] + "/*.mp4")), "clips")
PY
chmod +x "$D/prune.py"
"$D/prune.py" "$D/clips"
echo "exit status: $?"
python3 "$D/prune.py" "$D/clips"
echo "exit status: $?"

Output:

/usr/bin/env: ‘python3 -u’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
exit status: 127
2 clips
exit status: 0

env received python3 -u as one argument and searched PATH for a program with that whole name, space and all. There is none, so it exited 127, which the GNU env(1) manual page defines as "127 if COMMAND cannot be found". The second line of output is GNU env recognising the pattern and suggesting the fix. Older or non-GNU builds may print only the first line.

The last two lines are the trap. python3 prune.py worked, because the shell started python3 directly and Python treats the #! line as a comment. I tested the script the one way that skips the line that was broken.

Test three: no env, two flags

Dropping env and naming the interpreter by absolute path is a common suggestion. It moves the failure rather than removing it.

#!/bin/bash
# Absolute interpreter path, no env: one flag, two flags, two flags joined.
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
for line in '#!/usr/bin/python3 -u' '#!/usr/bin/python3 -u -B' '#!/usr/bin/python3 -uB' \
            '#!/bin/bash -e' '#!/bin/bash -e -u' '#!/bin/bash -eu'; do
  case "$line" in
    *python3*) body='print("ran")' ;;
    *)         body='echo ran' ;;
  esac
  printf '%s\n%s\n' "$line" "$body" > "$D/t"
  chmod +x "$D/t"
  out=$("$D/t" 2>&1); rc=$?
  printf '%-28s exit %-3s %s\n' "$line" "$rc" "$(printf '%s' "$out" | head -1)"
done

Output:

#!/usr/bin/python3 -u        exit 0   ran
#!/usr/bin/python3 -u -B     exit 2   Unknown option: - 
#!/usr/bin/python3 -uB       exit 0   ran
#!/bin/bash -e               exit 0   ran
#!/bin/bash -e -u            exit 1   /bin/bash: - : invalid option
#!/bin/bash -eu              exit 0   ran

One flag is fine, because one flag is one word. Two flags separated by a space reach Python as the single argument -u -B, and Python reads the space as an option character it does not know. Bash fails the same way for -e -u. Joining the flags into one word, -uB or -eu, works because it really is a single argument.

The manual page's own advice matches what this shows: "For portable use, optional-arg should either be absent, or be specified as a single word (i.e., it should not contain white space)".

Test four: the env -S fix 

#!/bin/bash
# The fix: env -S splits the one string the kernel passed it.
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
sed -i '1s|.*|#!/usr/bin/env -S python3 -u|' "$D/prune.py"
head -1 "$D/prune.py"
"$D/prune.py" "$D/clips"
echo "exit status: $?"
printf '#!/usr/bin/env -S %s -u -B\n' "$D/showargs" > "$D/job2.py"
chmod +x "$D/job2.py"
"$D/job2.py" clips

Output:

#!/usr/bin/env -S python3 -u
2 clips
exit status: 0
argv[0] = '/tmp/shebang_demo/showargs'
argv[1] = '-u'
argv[2] = '-B'
argv[3] = '/tmp/shebang_demo/job2.py'
argv[4] = 'clips'

The kernel still passes one string. The difference is that env now splits it. The env(1) page describes the option as "process and split S into separate arguments; used to pass multiple arguments on shebang lines". showargs confirms it: -u and -B arrived as two arguments.

Not every env has -S. I only tested GNU coreutils 8.32, so check env --help on the machine that will run the job, not only on yours.

Test five: a line that is too long 

#!/bin/bash
# A #! line longer than the kernel reads. Count what survives.
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
arg="--tag=$(printf 'x%.0s' $(seq 1 300))"
printf '#!%s %s\n' "$D/showargs" "$arg" > "$D/long.py"
chmod +x "$D/long.py"
echo "characters after #! in the file: $(head -1 "$D/long.py" | tail -c +3 | tr -d '\n' | wc -c)"
"$D/long.py" | python3 -c '
import sys
for line in sys.stdin:
    if line.startswith("argv[1]"):
        val = eval(line.split(" = ", 1)[1])
        print("argv[1] the interpreter received: %d characters" % len(val))
    else:
        print(line, end="")
'
echo "exit status: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"

Output:

characters after #! in the file: 333
argv[0] = '/tmp/shebang_demo/showargs'
argv[1] the interpreter received: 226 characters
argv[2] = '/tmp/shebang_demo/long.py'
exit status: 0

The file had 333 characters after #!. The interpreter path and its trailing space take 27 of them, and the argument that arrived was 226 characters, so 253 characters survived. Exit status 0. Nothing reported the cut.

The manual page says "characters beyond the limit are ignored", and gives the limit: "Since Linux 5.1, the limit is 255 characters."

My count came out two short of that. I have not traced where the difference goes, and I would not build anything that sits within a few characters of either number. The useful point is the one I could measure: a long line is shortened, not rejected. A long interpreter path, such as one inside a deep virtual environment folder, can lose its tail and point at a program that does not exist.

Test six: Windows line endings

A script edited on Windows and copied to a Linux box or a Raspberry Pi often keeps its carriage returns.

#!/bin/bash
# The same script saved with Windows line endings.
D=/tmp/shebang_demo
printf '#!/bin/bash\r\necho ran\r\n' > "$D/crlf.sh"
chmod +x "$D/crlf.sh"
"$D/crlf.sh"
echo "exit status: $?"
head -1 "$D/crlf.sh" | od -c | head -1
bash "$D/crlf.sh" > "$D/crlf.txt"
echo "exit status: $?"
od -c "$D/crlf.txt" | head -1

Output:

crlf.sh: /tmp/shebang_demo/crlf.sh: /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory
exit status: 126
0000000   #   !   /   b   i   n   /   b   a   s   h  \r  \n
exit status: 0
0000000   r   a   n  \r  \n

Run directly, it failed with exit 126 and bad interpreter. The od line shows why: the first line ends in \r before the newline, so the kernel looked for an interpreter named /bin/bash followed by a carriage return. Bash prints that carriage return as ^M.

Run as bash crlf.sh, it exited 0, and the last line shows the cost of that: the output was ran followed by a stray \r. The script ran and quietly put a carriage return into everything it printed. If that output were a file name or a value passed to another command, the stray byte would go with it.

What to do instead

  • Keep the #! line to the interpreter plus at most one word: #!/usr/bin/python3 -u or #!/bin/bash -eu.
  • If you need env and more than one word, use #!/usr/bin/env -S python3 -u, and confirm the target system's env has -S.
  • Set options inside the script where you can. set -eu on the second line of a bash script does not depend on the shebang at all.
  • Test scripts the way they will be started: ./script, not python3 script or bash script.
  • Check new scripts for carriage returns with head -1 script | od -c before deploying them.
  • Treat exit status 126 and 127 from a scheduled job as a start failure, not a script failure. Nothing inside the script ran.

Things I did not test

  • macOS and the BSDs. The manual page says behaviour differs: "Some systems use the first white space to terminate optional-arg." Only Linux was tested here.
  • Kernels before 5.1, where the documented limit is 127 characters.
  • Android. Nothing here ran on a phone or through adb shell.
  • Other env builds, such as BusyBox, which may not support -S.

Sources. Quotes are from the Linux execve(2) manual page (man-pages 6.19) and the GNU env(1) manual page (coreutils 9.11). Results come from the scripts above, each run once, with output pasted unedited.

If you want an old phone to record clips in the background so there is a folder worth pruning, the app I make is Background Camera RemoteStream on Google Play. Nothing above depends on it.

Not one line of the script ran; the line above it decided that.

title: ประกอบไปป์ไลน์ CI ด้วย AI agent: จาก requirement ถึง pull request ต้องเขียนไฟล์อะไรบ้าง?
description:
โดย Nokka (นก-กา) | ตอนที่ 6 จาก 7 ของชุด "สร้างซอฟต์แวร์ด้วย AI" | ตรวจสอบข้อมูล ณ 23 ต.ค. 2026

บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (deepseek-v4.1-flash · ผู้ให้บริการโมเดล: ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent ภายใต้การควบคุมและตรวจสอบคุณภาพโดยมนุษย์ - Nokka (นก-กา)

ห้าตอนที่ผ่านมาพูดถึงเครื่องมือแยกชิ้น บทนี้จะเอามันมาต่อกันเป็นสายงานเดียว

เป้าหมายไม่ใช่ระบบอัตโนมัติเต็มรูปแบบ แต่เป็นระบบที่ทุกขั้นมีหลักฐานว่าทำอะไรไปแล้ว และมีจุดที่คนต้องเซ็นรับ

ผมจะเขียนตามลำดับที่ทีมจริงทำ และบอกตรง ๆ ว่าส่วนไหนผมรันเองได้ในเครื่องนี้ ส่วนไหนได้แค่อ่านเอกสาร

ขั้นที่ 1 รับ requirement ให้มีที่อยู่

ก่อนจะพูดถึง agent ต้องตอบก่อนว่า requirement มาจากไหน

ถ้าคำตอบคือ "หัวหน้าพูดในที่ประชุม" ไปป์ไลน์ทั้งหมดจะพังตั้งแต่ขั้นแรก เพราะไม่มีอะไรอ้างอิงย้อนกลับได้

ทางที่ผมใช้คือ GitHub Issue หนึ่งใบต่อหนึ่งงาน และเขียนให้มีสามส่วน คือ ปัญหาที่เจอ พฤติกรรมที่ต้องการ และเกณฑ์ว่าถือว่าเสร็จ

เกณฑ์ข้อสามสำคัญที่สุด เพราะมันจะกลายเป็นเป้าของ agent และเป็นฐานของเทสต์ในขั้นสุดท้าย

ขั้นที่ 2 แปลง issue เป็น spec

ที่นี่คือจุดที่ spec-kit เข้ามา จากตอนที่ 2 ผมติดตั้งและรัน specify init ในเครื่องนี้จริง ได้ specify 1.2.3 [1]

ชื่อคำสั่งในเวอร์ชันนี้ใช้ขีดกลาง ไม่ใช่จุด คือ speckit-specify, speckit-plan, speckit-tasks และ speckit-implement และเมื่อเรียกจาก Claude Code จะเติม / ข้างหน้าเป็น /speckit-specify [1]

คำสั่งแรกจะสร้างโฟลเดอร์ต่อฟีเจอร์ ภายใต้ specs/ และเขียน spec.md ที่บังคับสามส่วน คือ user scenarios พร้อมลำดับความสำคัญ, requirements และ success criteria ที่วัดได้ [2]

ผมชอบที่แม่แบบบังคับให้เขียน success criteria แบบวัดได้ เพราะมันบังคับให้คนคิดก่อนว่า "เสร็จ" หน้าตาเป็นอย่างไร

ถ้าคุณข้ามขั้นนี้แล้วบอก agent ว่า "ทำฟีเจอร์นี้ให้หน่อย" ผลที่ได้คือโค้ดที่เดาความต้องการของคุณ

ขั้นที่ 3 แตกเป็น task ที่หยิบทำได้

speckit-tasks จะแปลงแผนเป็นรายการงานที่เรียงตามลำดับการพึ่งพา

แต่ละงานควรเล็กพอที่ agent ทำจบในรอบเดียว และมีเกณฑ์ตรวจรับในตัว

ถ้างานใหญ่เกิน วิธีที่ได้ผลคือแตกเป็นงานย่อยก่อน แล้วค่อยให้ agent ทำทีละงาน

ตรงนี้เป็นจุดที่หลายทีมเข้าใจผิด คิดว่า agent ทำงานใหญ่ได้ในครั้งเดียว ความจริงคือยิ่งงานใหญ่ ยิ่งมีจุดที่มันเดาผิดมากขึ้น

ขั้นที่ 4 ให้ agent ลงมือ

ขั้นนี้คือที่ OpenHands หรือ agent ในเครื่องอย่าง Claude Code ทำงาน [3]

เงื่อนไขที่ต้องมีก่อนคือเพดานสามอย่าง คือ จำนวนรอบ ค่าใช้จ่าย และขอบเขตไฟล์ที่แตะได้

ถ้าไม่มีเพดาน พฤติกรรมที่เจอบ่อยคือ agent วนแก้งานเดิมซ้ำ ๆ เพราะไม่มีสัญญาณว่าพอแล้ว และค่า token จะไต่ขึ้นทุกรอบ

ผลลัพธ์ที่ต้องได้คือ branch หนึ่งอันกับ pull request ที่มีคำอธิบายว่าทำอะไรและอ้าง issue ไหน

ขั้นที่ 5 ด่านตรวจอัตโนมัติใน CI

ไฟล์ workflow ที่อ่านแล้วทำตามได้

นี่คือส่วนที่คนอ่านนำไปใช้มากที่สุด ผมเขียน workflow ตัวอย่างไว้ด้านล่าง

name: quality-gate
on:
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt pytest pytest-cov
      - run: pytest --cov=. --cov-report=xml --cov-fail-under=70
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: coverage
          path: coverage.xml
  secret-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v3
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          GITLEAKS_LICENSE: ${{ secrets.GITLEAKS_LICENSE }}

เวอร์ชันที่ผมใช้ในไฟล์นี้ตรวจจากรีลีสล่าสุดวันนี้ คือ checkout v7.0.1 setup-python v7.1.0 upload-artifact v7.0.2 และ gitleaks-action v3.0.0 [4]

จุดที่ต้องระวังคือ gitleaks-action ต้องมีตัวแปร GITLEAKS_LICENSE เมื่อใช้กับบัญชีองค์กร แต่ไม่ต้องใช้กับบัญชีผู้ใช้ทั่วไป และ GitHub จัดสถานะสัญญาอนุญาตของ action นี้เป็น NOASSERTION จึงควรเปิดไฟล์อนุญาตเองก่อนใช้ในองค์กร

ผมประกาศบล็อก permissions: ไว้บนสุดเพื่อจำกัดสิทธิ์ของ token ให้แคบที่สุด ค่าเริ่มต้นของ pull request จาก fork คือสิทธิ์อ่านอย่างเดียว แต่เจ้าของ repo เปลี่ยนได้ด้วยตัวเลือกที่อนุญาตให้ workflow จาก fork รันด้วยสิทธิ์เขียน และเอกสารความปลอดภัยของ GitHub ไม่ได้รับรองความปลอดภัยในทุกกรณี [7]

ถ้าอยากให้ agent LLM ทำงานเมื่อมี pull request ก็เพิ่ม claude-code-action ซึ่งเป็น MIT 9,616 ดาว commit 22 ต.ค. 2026 [5]

ผมยังไม่ใส่ตัวนั้นในตัวอย่างข้างบน เพราะมันต้องมี API key ของผู้ให้บริการโมเดลและต้องกำหนดสิทธิ์ให้แคบ ซึ่งควรคุยกันก่อน

ชั้นที่ 6 ที่คนมักลืม คือคนเซ็นรับ

ค่า --cov-fail-under=70 ในไฟล์ข้างบนเป็นตัวเลขตัวอย่างที่ผมเลือกเอง ไม่ได้มาจากแหล่งใด ทีมควรตั้งจากสภาพจริงของโปรเจกต์

ด่านสุดท้ายไม่ใช่ CI แต่เป็นคนที่กด merge

กฎที่ผมแนะนำคือ branch หลักต้องมี protection บังคับให้ CI ผ่านก่อน merge และกำหนดจำนวนผู้อนุมัติตามนโยบายของทีม [6] ถ้าทีมมีคนเดียว กฎนี้จะทำให้คุณ merge เองไม่ได้ ต้องตั้งข้อยกเว้นให้ชัด [6]

ถ้า agent เป็นคนเขียน PR คนอนุมัติต้องเป็นมนุษย์เสมอ

ส่วนคนที่ปล่อยให้ agent merge เองโดยไม่มีคนดู ผมเคยเห็นในตัวอย่างสาธิต แต่ยังไม่เห็นทีมจริงที่ทำแบบนั้นกับระบบที่มีผู้ใช้

สิ่งที่ผมรันเองได้และรันไม่ได้ในบทนี้

เครื่องที่ผมใช้อยู่ไม่มี Docker ไม่มีสิทธิ์เข้าถึง GitHub repo ของคุณ และไม่มีคีย์โมเดลของผู้ให้บริการรายใหญ่

ผมจึงทดสอบ workflow ข้างบนบน GitHub Actions ไม่ได้ และจะไม่เขียนว่า "ทดสอบแล้วผ่าน"

ที่ผมทำได้และทำจริงคือ ติดตั้ง spec-kit รัน specify init เปิดไฟล์ที่มันสร้าง และตรวจว่าคำสั่งกับแม่แบบมีอยู่จริงตามที่เขียน [1][2]

ถ้าคุณมี repo ทดลองและให้สิทธิ์ ผมเขียน workflow นี้ให้พร้อมรันและช่วยอ่าน log ได้ คุณไม่ต้องมี Docker ในเครื่องก็ทำได้ เพราะงานทั้งหมดรันบน runner ของ GitHub

เช็กลิสต์ก่อนเปิดใช้ไปป์ไลน์นี้

  1. requirement ทุกงานมี issue เป็นที่อยู่หรือยัง
  2. spec มี success criteria ที่วัดได้หรือยัง
  3. task ถูกแตกเล็กพอให้จบในรอบเดียวหรือยัง
  4. มีเพดานรอบ เพดานเงิน และขอบเขตไฟล์หรือยัง
  5. CI บังคับ coverage ขั้นต่ำและสแกนความลับหรือยัง
  6. ใครเป็นคนกด merge และมีกฎห้าม merge เองหรือยัง

ถ้าตอบข้อ 6 ไม่ได้ ไปป์ไลน์นี้ยังไม่พร้อมใช้กับระบบจริง

บทเรียนที่ผมอยากฝากไว้

ไปป์ไลน์ที่ดีไม่ได้ทำให้ agent เก่งขึ้นแต่มันทำให้ความผิดพลาดถูกจับเร็วขึ้น

ความต่างระหว่างทีมที่ใช้ agent ได้ผลกับทีมที่เลิกใช้ มักไม่ได้อยู่ที่โมเดล แต่อยู่ที่ว่ามีด่านตรวจกี่ชั้น

ถ้าคุณกำลังจะเริ่มต้นสายงานแบบนี้ เล่าให้ผมฟังได้ว่าทีมใช้ GitHub หรือเครื่องมืออะไรอยู่ และมีคนรีวิวกี่คน

บทสุดท้ายผมจะพูดถึงเงิน ความเสี่ยง และสแตกที่เหมาะกับทีมแต่ละขนาด รวมถึงเรื่องที่ไม่มีใครอยากพูด คือเมื่อ agent ทำพัง ใครรับผิด

title: Agent memory: the FTS5 trigger bug that silently killed every update
description:
Your agent's memory is an archive until you can update it. Ours was an archive for two weeks, and nothing in the logs said so.

The bug: a trigger that killed every update

We store facts in SQLite with an FTS5 index. The tokenizer is trigram, because it handles Russian morphology without a stemmer: "подпись" and "подписан" share trigrams, and we get recall without shipping a dictionary.

The index is kept in sync by triggers:

CREATE TRIGGER facts_au AFTER UPDATE ON facts BEGIN
  INSERT INTO facts_fts(facts_fts, rowid, text, tags) VALUES('delete', old.id, old.text, old.tags);
  INSERT INTO facts_fts(rowid, text, tags) VALUES (new.id, new.text, new.tags);
END;

That is the canonical FTS5 recipe from the docs, and it is wrong for trigram. Any UPDATE on facts failed with a bare:

sqlite3.OperationalError: SQL logic error

No column, no hint. It took a deliberately written test to find it: we asked the memory to supersede an old price with a new one and the call raised. Which means the feature we advertised — "facts are updated, not duplicated" — had never once run.

The fix 

DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS facts_au;
CREATE TRIGGER facts_au AFTER UPDATE ON facts BEGIN
  INSERT OR REPLACE INTO facts_fts(rowid, text, tags) VALUES (new.id, new.text, new.tags);
END;

INSERT OR REPLACE works with trigram. The DROP matters as much as the new body: databases already on disk carry the old broken trigger, and CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS would happily leave it in place. Init now heals existing files.

The lesson is not "use REPLACE". The lesson is that a single ranking metric hid a dead write path for two weeks.

Five abilities, not one score

We used to measure memory with one number: recall@3 over ten bilingual questions. Ten green checks, and a feature that crashed on first use.

LongMemEval-V2 (MIT) separates memory into abilities. We copied the shape, not the dataset, and wrote one test group per ability:

Ability The question it answers What breaks without it
Extraction is the fact found at all? memory is a write-only log
Cross-session does a fact from last week surface today? each session starts blind
Temporal does a time window exclude the old value? stale facts look current
Supersede does the new fact replace the old one? contradictions pile up
Abstention does it return nothing when it knows nothing? confident invention

The last one is the one nobody tests. A memory that always returns its top-3 will always look useful — and will feed the model a plausible neighbour of the question instead of an honest "I don't know". Our test asserts that a question about an office in Tokyo returns no fact containing "Tokyo", not merely a low score.

What the tests look like 

def test_superseded_fact_is_not_recalled(tmp_path):
    m = Memory(path=str(tmp_path / "m.db"))
    old = m.remember("Soma costs 19 USD per month.", tags="pricing")
    m.supersede(old, "Soma costs 49 USD per month.", tags="pricing")
    hits = [r["text"] for r in m.recall("how much does soma cost", k=3)]
    assert any("49" in t for t in hits)
    assert all("19" not in t for t in hits)      # the dead path shows up here

Run against the broken trigger, this fails with SQL logic error. Run against the fix, it passes. That is the whole difference between a benchmark and a decoration.

Why trigram at all

Because our users write in Russian and English in the same memory. A word-based tokenizer splits "подписан" and "подпись" into different tokens and recall silently drops. Trigram costs index size and gives morphology for free. The trade-off is real: it also made an obscure FTS5 incompatibility reachable, which a word tokenizer would have hidden.

If you run FTS5 with trigram, check your update trigger today. The failure is silent until something tries to change a row.

We build Soma: envelopes with budget, mandate and signature, plus memory that keeps its word — facts, obligations and signed receipts behind one MCP endpoint. If your agent memory passed a single recall test and you have never updated a fact in it, you may have the same two weeks we had.

title: Why We Don’t Always Need Kafka: High-Throughput Background Queues in Spring Boot with Redis & Virtual Threads
description:
By Gaurav Kumar Yadav • Canonical URL: https://gaurav10610.github.io/oxmq/guide/spring-boot.html

Every engineering team eventually hits this architectural crossroads:

"Our application needs background workers for payment processing, report generation, webhooks, and email notifications. What should we use?"

Too often, the default answer is: "Let's spin up Apache Kafka."

Three months later, the team is wrestling with partition rebalances, consumer group lag, broker ZooKeeper/KRaft quorum tuning, and high AWS MSK bills—all for a workload that just needed reliable task retries, sliding-window rate limiting, and parent-child task workflows.

If you don't need petabyte-scale append-only event streaming with weeks of historical replay, Kafka is often the wrong tool for task queues.

In this article, we’ll explore how to build a modern, high-throughput distributed background processing engine in Spring Boot 3+ using Redis, Java 21 Project Loom Virtual Threads, and OxMQ—the Virtual Thread-native Java alternative to BullMQ.

The Distributed Task Queue Dilemma in Java

In Node.js, developers have BullMQ—a battle-tested Redis queue that executes Lua scripts for atomic state transitions, supports delayed scheduling, sliding-window rate limiters, and parent-child DAG flows, with instant visibility via the open-source Bull-Board Web UI.

In Java, teams typically faced frustrating trade-offs:

  1. In-Memory ExecutorService: Fast, but loses all tasks on crash or pod restart. No distributed lock or cluster coordination.
  2. Spring @Scheduled & DB polling (db-scheduler, shedlock): Great for simple crons, but database table polling collapses under 5,000+ jobs/s and creates high DB CPU contention.
  3. Redisson Queues: Opaque Lua implementations, no parent-child DAG orchestration, and no out-of-the-box monitoring UI.
  4. Kafka / RabbitMQ: Heavy operational overhead, lack of native token-bucket rate limiting per tenant, and complex delayed job retries (dead-letter exchange looping).

This is why we built OxMQ.

Architecture: How OxMQ Works

OxMQ executes BullMQ’s official 49 battle-tested Lua scripts directly inside Redis. This guarantees:

  • 100% Atomic State Transitions: No race conditions between workers claiming tasks.
  • Polyglot Cross-Talk: A Node.js microservice can push jobs that Java workers consume, and vice-versa.
  • Instant Bull-Board Web UI: Point the open-source Bull-Board dashboard at your Redis instance to inspect queues, pause workers, and review failed jobs with zero Node.js code. 
flowchart TD
    Client["Spring Boot 3 Producer\n@Autowired OxmqQueue"] -->|queue.add / addBulk| Redis[("Redis / KeyDB / Valkey Cluster\n49 BullMQ Lua Scripts")]

    subgraph OxMQCluster ["Distributed OxMQ Worker Pods (Loom Virtual Threads)"]
        W1["Worker Pod 1\n500 Virtual Threads\n(~1 KB Heap/task)"]
        W2["Worker Pod 2\n500 Virtual Threads\n(~1 KB Heap/task)"]
    end

    Redis -->|Atomic Dequeue\nmoveToActive.lua| W1
    Redis -->|Atomic Dequeue\nmoveToActive.lua| W2

    W1 -->|AIMD Dynamic Yield / Cooldown| CloudAPI["External Cloud / Partner API\n(HTTP 429 Sentinel)"]
    W2 -->|AIMD Dynamic Yield / Cooldown| CloudAPI

    Redis -.->|Real-time Metrics| BB["Bull-Board Web UI\nQueue Depths & Latencies"]
    Redis -.->|Prometheus Exporter| Grafana["Grafana Dashboards\nThroughput & JVM Heap"]

1. Project Loom Virtual Threads: The Concurrency Breakthrough

Before Java 21, running 500 concurrent worker threads meant allocating 500 MB to 1 GB of OS stack memory (each platform thread takes ~1 MB). When workers blocked on slow network calls (e.g. Stripe API, OpenAI, or database transactions), underlying OS carrier threads sat idle, wasting CPU cycles.

With Java 21 Project Loom:

  • Virtual Threads are managed by the JVM, consuming only ~1 KB of heap memory each.
  • When an OxMQ worker blocks on network I/O, the JVM unmounts the virtual thread, freeing the carrier thread to execute other jobs.
  • On benchmark tests, OxMQ sustains 800+ concurrent workers on a strictly flat 35 OS threads under realistic 10ms I/O delays.

2. Spring Boot 3 Declarative Setup

Getting started in Spring Boot takes under 2 minutes:

Step 1: Add Dependency 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.gaurav10610</groupId>
    <artifactId>oxmq-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    <version>1.7.0</version>
</dependency>

Step 2: Configure application.yml 

oxmq:
  redis:
    uri: redis://localhost:6379
  namespace: billing-service # Multi-tenant context isolation
  worker:
    concurrency: 50           # 50 Virtual Threads on Java 21+

Step 3: Produce Jobs 

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Autowired
    private OxmqQueue<PaymentRequest> paymentQueue;

    public void processPayment(String orderId, double amount) {
        // Enqueue with exponential backoff & memory retention
        paymentQueue.add("charge-customer",
            new PaymentRequest(orderId, amount),
            JobOptions.builder()
                .attempts(5)
                .backoff(Backoff.exponential(1000)) // 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s
                .keepJobs(KeepJobs.builder().count(5000).build()) // Prevent Redis RAM bloat
                .build()
        );
    }
}

Step 4: Consume Jobs Declaratively 

@Component
public class PaymentWorker {

    @OxmqListener(queue = "billing-service:charge-customer", concurrency = 50)
    public PaymentResult handlePayment(Job<PaymentRequest> job) throws Exception {
        PaymentRequest req = job.getData();

        // Report progress in real-time to Redis & Bull-Board
        job.updateProgress(50);

        return paymentGateway.charge(req.getOrderId(), req.getAmount());
    }
}

3. Handling Cloud Throttling: The AIMD Adaptive Rate Limiter Plugin

In modern microservices, external APIs (Microsoft Graph, Stripe, Shopify) enforce dynamic quotas and return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

OxMQ provides native Enterprise Interceptor Plugins to solve this:

  1. RateLimitSentinelPlugin: Automatically catches HTTP 429, extracts Retry-After, and engages a distributed Redis lockout across all cluster pods. Upcoming jobs defer without burning retry attempts.
  2. AdaptiveRateLimiterPlugin: Uses TCP-style AIMD (Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease) to tune concurrency dynamically:
    • On HTTP 429: Immediately halves capacity (L(t+1) = max(L_min, ⌊L(t) × 0.5⌋)).
    • On clean execution: Additively increases capacity (L(t+1) = min(L_max, L(t) + 25 RUs)). 
@Bean
public JobInterceptor adaptiveRateLimiter(RedisClient redisClient) {
    return AdaptiveRateLimiterPlugin.builder()
        .minLimit(25)
        .maxLimit(250)
        .dampingWindowMs(60_000) // Freeze upgrades during recovery to prevent flapping
        .redisClient(redisClient)
        .build();
}

4. Performance Benchmarks: 10,001-Node DAG Trees

In benchmark stress tests executing massive 10,001-node parent-child DAG dependency trees:

  • Resolution Throughput: 2,645.1 jobs/sec (resolved in 3.78s).
  • Peak Ingestion Rate: ~3,250 nodes/sec (saturating Redis TCP buffer).
  • Redis Memory: Asymptotically stabilizes at ~904 Bytes per node (~8.68 MB for 10,001 jobs).
  • Virtual Thread Overhead: Flat 35 OS carrier threads.

Full benchmark code and reproduction scripts are open-sourced in the repo.

5. Instant Bull-Board Web UI Integration

You can spin up the open-source Bull-Board dashboard in Docker in seconds:

docker run -d -p 3000:3000 \
  -e REDIS_HOST=localhost \
  -e REDIS_PORT=6379 \
  felixmosh/bull-board

Open http://localhost:3000 to immediately inspect queue depths, pause/resume workers, trigger manual retries, and review JSON stack traces.

Conclusion & Resources

If you’re building distributed background processing in Java and want high performance without Kafka-level operational baggage:

  • Project Repository: github.com/gaurav10610/oxmq
  • Official Documentation: gaurav10610.github.io/oxmq
  • Maven Central: io.github.gaurav10610:oxmq:1.7.0
  • License: 100% Free & Open Source (Apache 2.0 / MIT)

⭐ If you find OxMQ helpful, star the project on GitHub and let us know your feedback!

title: Building a Data Fabric on AWS: Connect Data, Improve Governance, and Power AI
description:
Modern organizations store data across databases, applications, data lakes, and streaming platforms. The challenge is making all that data discoverable, secure, and useful without building a completely separate integration solution for every team.

Data Fabric on AWS offers an architectural approach to connecting data sources, managing metadata, enforcing governance, and enabling analytics and AI applications.

In this tutorial, we'll explore an AWS data fabric architecture and build a small customer analytics project using Amazon S3, AWS Glue, and Amazon Athena.

What Is Data Fabric?

A data fabric is an architecture that connects data discovery, integration, metadata management, and governance across distributed systems.

On AWS, you can use services such as:

  • Amazon S3: Store raw and curated datasets.
  • AWS Glue: Discover, catalog, and transform data.
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog: Maintain metadata and table definitions.
  • AWS Lake Formation: Manage permissions for supported data lake resources.
  • Amazon Athena: Query data in S3 using SQL.
  • Amazon Redshift: Support data warehousing and analytical workloads.
  • Amazon DataZone: Help teams discover, share, and govern data assets.
  • Amazon Bedrock: Build generative AI applications that use approved business information through controlled retrieval and data-access layers.

These services are building blocks. A data fabric is an architecture you design and configure, not a single AWS service that automatically connects everything.

Why Does It Matter?

Imagine an e-commerce company with:

  • Customer records in Amazon RDS.
  • Order history in S3 files.
  • Website events arriving through streaming services.

Without a coordinated approach, different teams may duplicate datasets, define metrics differently, and manage permissions inconsistently.

A data fabric can help teams improve data discovery, reduce repeated integration work, and establish more consistent governance.

Reference Architecture 

       DATA SOURCES
  ┌────────┬─────────┬───────────┐
  │ RDS    │ S3 Files│ Event Data│
  └────┬───┴────┬────┴─────┬─────┘
       └────────┼──────────┘
                ▼
         DATA INGESTION
        AWS Glue / Streams
                │
                ▼
           AMAZON S3
       Raw → Clean → Curated
                │
        ┌───────┴────────┐
        ▼                ▼
   Glue Catalog     Lake Formation
        │                │
        └───────┬────────┘
                ▼
          QUERY LAYER
        Athena / Redshift
                │
                ▼
       Analytics / Reports / AI

This is a conceptual design. Each source needs an appropriate ingestion process, and access policies must be configured for the services involved.

Hands-On Project: Customer Order Analytics

Let's create a simple data pipeline and query customer orders using SQL.

Step 1: Create a sample CSV file

Create orders.csv:

order_id,customer_id,region,amount,status
1001,C101,Asia,250,COMPLETED
1002,C102,Europe,180,COMPLETED
1003,C101,Asia,90,PENDING
1004,C103,North America,420,COMPLETED
1005,C104,Europe,120,CANCELLED
1006,C102,Europe,310,COMPLETED

Upload it to an S3 location such as:

s3://your-data-fabric-bucket/raw/orders/orders.csv

Replace your-data-fabric-bucket with your own bucket name. Keep public access blocked and configure appropriate encryption and permissions.

Step 2: Catalog the dataset with AWS Glue

Open the AWS Glue console and:

  1. Create a database named customer_analytics.
  2. Create a crawler that points to your S3 raw/orders/ prefix.
  3. Configure an IAM role with the required S3 read and Data Catalog permissions.
  4. Run the crawler.
  5. Review the table schema and confirm the column types.

The crawler can discover the CSV structure and register a table in the Glue Data Catalog. Always verify inferred types before relying on them in production.

Step 3: Query the data with Athena

Open Amazon Athena and configure an S3 query-results location. Then execute:

SELECT
    region,
    COUNT(*) AS completed_orders,
    SUM(amount) AS total_revenue,
    AVG(amount) AS average_order_value
FROM customer_analytics.orders
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

Expected output:

Region Completed orders Total revenue Average order value
Europe 2 490 245
North America 1 420 420
Asia 1 250 250

The query filters out pending and cancelled orders and calculates revenue by region.

Note: Your actual database and table names depend on your Glue configuration.

Step 4: Add Governance

A useful data platform must control access as well as provide discovery.

For this project:

  • Give analysts access only to the datasets they need.
  • Separate engineering and administrative permissions.
  • Configure Lake Formation permissions where applicable.
  • Protect sensitive customer information.
  • Review access logs and test permissions using a restricted analyst identity.

A catalog entry does not automatically grant permission to query the underlying data. Configure the required catalog, storage, query, IAM, and Lake Formation permissions consistently.

Step 5: Extend the Architecture

Once the basic project works, you can improve it by adding:

  • AWS Glue ETL jobs to validate and transform records.
  • Parquet datasets to improve query efficiency for suitable workloads.
  • Amazon Redshift for more demanding warehouse analytics.
  • Amazon DataZone to improve discovery and sharing across teams.
  • Amazon Bedrock for an AI assistant that answers business questions using approved data through a controlled retrieval or query layer.

For AI applications, validate generated queries and enforce permissions in the data-access layer. Do not give an AI model unrestricted access to every dataset.

Data Fabric vs. Data Lake vs. Data Mesh

Concept Purpose
Data lake Stores large amounts of data in formats such as CSV, JSON, and Parquet.
Data fabric Connects data discovery, integration, metadata, and governance.
Data mesh Organizes data ownership around business domains and data products.

These approaches can complement each other. Amazon S3 can provide the storage foundation, a data fabric architecture can connect and govern datasets, and a data mesh operating model can define domain ownership.

Production Best Practices

Before scaling your implementation:

  1. Improve metadata quality: Document schemas, owners, and dataset descriptions.
  2. Enforce least privilege: Keep administrative, engineering, and analyst permissions separate.
  3. Validate data: Check missing values, duplicates, and schema changes.
  4. Monitor pipelines: Track failures, processing time, and data freshness.
  5. Optimize costs: Use appropriate partitioning and file formats to reduce unnecessary Athena scans.
  6. Document lineage: Record where data originates and how it changes.
  7. Secure AI access: Use controlled tools, authorization, and query validation.
  8. Start small: Prove value with one business use case before connecting every source.

Final Thoughts

Data Fabric on AWS is not about moving all your data into one database. It is about making distributed data easier to discover, integrate, govern, and use.

With Amazon S3, AWS Glue, the Glue Data Catalog, Lake Formation, and Athena, you can build a foundation for reliable analytics and future AI applications.

Start with one dataset, catalog it, secure it, and demonstrate a useful business query. Then expand as your organization's needs grow.

The goal is simple: make the right data available to the right people and applications, securely.

Official AWS Resources

  • What Is Data Fabric?
  • AWS Glue
  • AWS Lake Formation
  • Amazon S3
  • Amazon Athena
  • Amazon DataZone

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in Singapore

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in Singapore (sg) with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Overages must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure overages and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, October 12, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent.
