title: Why I Built Nathstar: A Local-First, 120Hz Native macOS Terminal for Projects, Live Ops & Private AI
description:
If you are a developer on macOS today, picking a terminal emulator feels like a forced compromise:

  1. Minimalist GPU Emulators (Ghostty, Alacritty, Kitty): Blazingly fast and standards-compliant, but they treat every window as an isolated, stateless text grid. When you're juggling four microservices, two SSH sessions, and a CLI coding agent, they have no idea which pane is holding port :3000 hostage, which background build failed ten minutes ago, or which .env variables are loaded.
  2. Cloud-Tethered "Block" Terminals (Warp): Great input editing and AI features, but built around cloud accounts, telemetry by default, and metered subscriptions—while replacing standard terminal buffers with custom UI layers that can fight full-screen TUIs like nvim, lazygit, or htop.

I wanted both worlds without the trade-offs.

So I built Nathstar — an open-source (MIT), 100% local-first, zero-telemetry macOS terminal written in Swift 6, SwiftUI, AppKit, and Metal.

Here is a look at what Nathstar does differently and the engineering under the hood.

1. Projects Over Windows: Persistent Workspaces

Traditional terminals organize your work by disposable windows and tabs. When you return to a project after a reboot or context switch, you're left reconstructing your layout from shell history and memory.

In Nathstar, the primary unit of organization is a Project Workspace:

  • Categorized & Collapsible Sidebar: Organize repositories into Projects, Personal, and Others, plus an auto-discovered SSH Hosts section parsed directly from ~/.ssh/config. You can rename sections, drag-and-drop workspaces between them, or unpin the sidebar into an auto-expanding 44pt hover rail (⇧⌘S).
  • Recursive Split Panes & Zoom: Split panes vertically (⌘D) or horizontally (⇧⌘D), equalize ratios (⇧⌘=), or temporarily maximize a single pane (⇧⌘⏎).
  • True Single-Window Persistence (⌘W vs. ⌘Q): Closing the window with ⌘W hides the UI while keeping every PTY process, dev server, and SSH connection alive in memory. Double-tapping ⌃ (Control) summons Nathstar back from any app—or docks it to the top of your screen in Quake Visor Mode.

2. Silent Live Environment Sync (SIGUSR1) & .env Management

Have you ever updated an API key or feature flag in a .env file, only to realize you have to restart your shell—or paste export FOO=bar across five open panes—for it to take effect?

Nathstar introduces Silent Live Environment Injection:

  1. When Nathstar spawns zsh, it uses a lightweight, transparent ZDOTDIR shim that sources your real .zshenv and .zshrc untouched and installs a TRAPUSR1 signal handler.
  2. When you add or edit a KEY=VALUE variable in Nathstar's Manifest panel and click Set & Apply, Nathstar writes a private 0600 session file and sends SIGUSR1 (kill(shellPid, SIGUSR1)) to the running zsh process.
  3. Your live shell immediately sources the updated environment variables silently in the background—with zero commands echoed into your scrollback buffer.

You can also import/export .env files with one click, and define a .nathstar/manifest.json file to orchestrate multi-pane project startups (while automatically keeping *_KEY, *_SECRET, and *_TOKEN values strictly local).

3. Who Is Using :3000? Built-In Live Port & Process Manager (⇧⌘P)

Every full-stack developer knows the pain of EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000, followed by running lsof -ti :3000 | xargs kill -9.

Nathstar includes a dedicated Live Ports & Processes (⇧⌘P) tab in the right-hand panel:

  • Every 3 seconds (while open), LivePortScanner inspects listening TCP sockets (lsof) and walks the parent PID (ppid) tree (ps) up to the root shellPid of every Nathstar pane.
  • It maps every active port (:3000, :5173, :8080) back to the exact Workspace and Terminal Pane that spawned it.
  • With a single click, you can Open the port in your browser, Focus the exact terminal pane running the server, send a graceful Kill (SIGTERM), or Kill -9 (SIGKILL) a stuck process.

4. Native Command Editing (⌘E), Click-to-Cursor & Blast-Radius Safety

Editing a 200-character curl or docker command in a traditional terminal usually means holding down the Left arrow key or memorizing readline chords.

Nathstar gives you two ways to edit long commands naturally:

  1. Click-to-Position Cursor in the Prompt: Click (or ⌥-Click) directly on any character in your active terminal command—even across multi-line wrapped lines. Using a hybrid of OSC 133 semantic prompt markers and automatic wrapped-line cell calculation (compatible with Powerlevel10k, Starship, and Oh My Zsh), Nathstar moves the shell cursor straight to that character.
  2. Pull to Native Composer (⌘E): Press ⌘E at any time to pull your active terminal line into the bottom multi-line macOS text editor. Edit with standard macOS selection and undo, use Tab ⇥ IDE-style autocomplete (ranking Git branches, file paths, command history, and {{parameterized}} snippets), and press ⇧⏎ to insert it back into the prompt or ⌘⏎ to run it.

Pre-Execution Blast-Radius Analyzer (Safe-Run)

Before executing commands from the composer, CommandRiskAnalyzer checks for destructive patterns—like git push --force, rm -rf near / or ~, git reset --hard, or piping curl directly into sudo bash—and warns you of the blast radius before execution.

5. Zero-Telemetry Streaming AI (Local Ollama + BYOK Cloud)

AI in the terminal shouldn't require a monthly SaaS subscription or sending proprietary stack traces to someone else's cloud.

Nathstar's AI layer is 100% opt-in and bring-your-own-model:

  • Zero-Config Local Ollama: Automatically queries http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags to discover your locally installed Ollama models (llama3, qwen2.5-coder, deepseek-coder, etc.) for completely offline, private inference.
  • BYOK Cloud & Custom Endpoints: Supports OpenAI (gpt-4o), Anthropic (claude-3-5-sonnet), Groq, LM Studio, OpenRouter, vLLM, or any OpenAI-compatible gateway.
  • One-Click "Explain & Fix with AI": Whenever a command exits non-zero, an inline banner appears at the top of the pane. Click it to attach the failed command and the last 35 lines of terminal output for an immediate diagnosis and runnable fix.
  • Inline ⌘I Command Generator: Press ⌘I to translate plain English right into a zsh command.

6. How Nathstar Compares to Other macOS Terminals

Capability Nathstar Warp Ghostty iTerm2 WezTerm / Kitty
Open Source (MIT) & Zero Telemetry ✅ Yes ❌ Cloud ✅ Yes ✅ GPLv2 ✅ Yes
Project Workspaces Sidebar (Projects / Personal / Others) ✅ Built-in ❌ No ❌ No ⚠️ Profiles ❌ No
Silent Live Env Var Injection (SIGUSR1) ✅ Unique ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No
Live Port & Process Manager (Open, Focus, Kill -9) ✅ Built-in ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No ❌ No
Pre-Execution Blast-Radius Safety Analyzer (Safe-Run) ✅ Built-in ⚠️ Basic ❌ No ⚠️ Triggers ❌ No
Click-to-Move Cursor in Long Commands ✅ Built-in ✅ Yes ⚠️ OSC 133 ⚠️ ⌥-Click ⚠️ OSC 133
Pull Active Terminal Line into Native Editor (⌘E) ✅ Built-in ✅ Native ❌ No ⚠️ Popover ❌ No
Local Ollama Auto-Discovery + Streaming BYOK AI ✅ Built-in ❌ Paid Cloud ❌ No ⚠️ Plugin ❌ No
120Hz Metal GPU Shader Rendering ✅ Built-in ✅ Metal ✅ Metal ✅ Metal ✅ OpenGL/Metal

7. Under the Hood: Swift 6, 120Hz Metal & Zero-Permission Hotkeys

For fellow macOS engineers, here are three architectural details that made a huge difference when building Nathstar:

  1. Deferred Non-Zero Frame PTY Initialization: A subtle bug in SwiftUI-hosted NSView terminals occurs when forkpty is called inside makeNSView while the view frame is still 0×0, causing TIOCSWINSZ race conditions and missing prompts in themes like Powerlevel10k. NathstarTerminalView defers startProcess until layout() reports a real non-zero geometry (width > 10 && height > 10), guaranteeing every tab and split pane starts with exact row/column dimensions.
  2. Runtime-Compiled 120Hz Metal Shaders: Rather than relying on precompiled .metallib bundles that fail on machines without full Xcode toolchains, Nathstar compiles its Metal shaders at runtime via MTLDevice.makeLibrary(source:).
  3. Zero-Permission Double-Tap ⌃ Global Hotkey: macOS blocks global keyDown monitors unless the user grants invasive Accessibility/Input Monitoring permissions. Nathstar combines NSEvent flag monitors with 60Hz hardware modifier state polling (CGEventSource.flagsState(.combinedSessionState)), enabling global Double-Tap ⌃ summoning out of the box with zero system permission prompts.

Try Nathstar Today

Nathstar is free, open-source under the MIT License, and builds 100% offline with zero external network fetches (all dependencies are vendored in the repo).

🔗 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/satinath-nit/Nathstar

To build and launch it on any Apple Silicon Mac (macOS 15+):


bash
git clone https://github.com/satinath-nit/Nathstar.git
cd Nathstar
./scripts/package-macos.sh
open release/Nathstar.app

title: Scientific_fastapi: How I Organize Reproducible Scientific Computing Through an API
description:
Author: Artem — Artem7898

A scientific algorithm usually starts as a research script or notebook. While one person runs the calculations, parameters can be changed directly in the code and results saved manually. Once other users become involved, additional requirements emerge: validating input, managing concurrent tasks, recovering from failures, and understanding exactly how a result was produced.

With scientific_fastapi, I am developing infrastructure for this transition. The project connects a Python computational core, an HTTP API, background task execution, and scientific artifact storage. In this article, I describe the architecture of v2.0.0, its capabilities, and practical applications.

The central idea is to make each computational run an identifiable, verifiable unit. Every run should have input parameters, an identifier, an execution state, a result, and enough information to investigate how that result was obtained.

This is particularly important for scientific services. A number returned by an API gains meaning through the model description, units, assumptions, and uncertainty estimate that accompany it.

From Request to Result

FastAPI provides the HTTP layer. It accepts requests and validates parameters before computation begins. Inputs follow a strict schema: unknown fields, unsupported values, and invalid numeric inputs are rejected. Additional limits control the computational workload and the number of accepted tasks.

Long-running calculations execute in the background. Once a request is accepted, the client receives HTTP 202 Accepted, a task identifier, and a URL for checking its status. The client can then poll for updates:


pending → running → completed
                  → failed
                  → cancelled

This contract works for notebooks, web interfaces, and other services. A client submits parameters and waits for the result without keeping an HTTP connection open throughout the calculation.

I separate the architecture into four responsibilities:

  • The API validates requests and exposes task states.
  • The computational core implements the scientific model.
  • The background execution mechanism manages tasks and execution attempts.
  • Artifact storage preserves results and run descriptions. This separation allows scientific functions to be tested independently of HTTP and reused in research scripts.

A Scientific Model for Testing the Infrastructure

The current reference computational core is a two-dimensional model of independent particle velocities governed by an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck thermostat. Its identifier is ideal-gas-ou-v1.

The model has analytical properties that make it useful for validating the numerical implementation. It supports investigating temperature relaxation, the statistics of random realizations, and the relationship between uncertainty and particle count.

Calculations use reduced units:

m = k_B = 1

At a constant thermostat temperature, the exact transition for a velocity component is:

a = exp(-dt)
v_next = a * v + sqrt(T_bath * (1 - a²)) * ξ

Here, ξ is an independent standard normal random variable. The relaxation rate in this expression is one. This transition corresponds to the solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process over the specified time interval.

The physical meaning of the model also defines its scope. It describes the velocities of independent particles. Full molecular dynamics would require positions, interactions, forces, and an appropriate integrator. Temperature and time are expressed in reduced units; conversion to kelvin or femtoseconds requires a separate physical justification.

What Reproducibility Means in This Project

Reproducibility in scientific_fastapi combines several mechanisms.

Random numbers come from a local PCG64 generator with an explicitly specified seed. A run does not depend on the process-wide random number generator state. This makes it possible to reproduce numerical results with identical parameters in a consistent computational environment.

Dependencies are fixed in uv.lock. Installation and build checks use the locked versions, and the build tools are pinned as well. Export to the PEP 751 format is available for sharing an environment specification.

Each scientific run saves a JSON description and its final state in NPZ format. The artifacts record parameters, numerical results, the model version, and information about the random number generator and environment. SHA256 checksums allow the consistency of the saved files to be verified.

As a result, an output can be connected to a specific set of conditions: which parameters were used, which model performed the calculation, and which files belong to that run.

An identical seed alone does not guarantee bitwise equality across different libraries, hardware, and computational backends. Verifying reproducibility requires considering the complete computational context.

I also tie uncertainty estimates to the specific model. In the reference calculation, the uncertainty concerns temperature estimated from a final snapshot of independent particles. Integrating a different algorithm requires its own justification of uncertainty.

Recovering from Failures During Computation

An in-memory backend is available for local use. Redis supports shared task state and task recovery.

The Redis backend stores task states and execution information. A worker acquires a task for a limited period and periodically confirms that it is still running. If those confirmations stop, the task can be recovered and assigned to another execution attempt.

This uses at-least-once delivery: a calculation may execute again after a failure. The project therefore distinguishes between two identifiers:

  • task_id identifies the user’s task.
  • attempt_id identifies a specific execution attempt. Artifacts from different attempts are stored separately. An additional ownership check protects result publication from an outdated worker.

This is particularly useful when an application restarts or loses its Redis connection. If an integrated algorithm performs external actions, such as modifying another database, the possibility of repeated execution must be handled separately.

Deployments with multiple API instances also require shared artifact storage. Redis coordinates tasks, while access to result files is addressed at the deployment level.

Observing the Service

For a computational system, it is useful to distinguish between time spent waiting and time spent calculating. A slow response may originate in the queue, the computational core, or the storage infrastructure.

scientific_fastapi therefore provides an optional OpenTelemetry integration. It connects the HTTP request, task enqueueing, and computation, including context propagation into worker threads. Metrics capture waiting time, execution duration, and task outcomes.

MLflow can be enabled for experiment tracking. It allows run parameters and artifacts to be recorded in a dedicated tracking system.

Redis, MLflow, observability tools, notebook tools, and research dependencies are provided through optional extras. Users can select the components their scenario requires while keeping the core dependency set small.

Where the Project Can Be Applied

The first application is teaching computational physics and statistical modeling. The reference model can be used to study relaxation, random realizations, and changes in statistical uncertainty. The same computational code can serve an educational interface, a notebook, and automated checks.

The second is preparing reproducible computational experiments. The research pipeline saves results, figures, and a manifest containing checksums. This helps connect a published figure to its input parameters and verify that the data can be regenerated in a consistent environment.

The third is a shared computational service for a research group. Multiple users submit tasks over HTTP, track their status, and retrieve results through a common contract. This is useful when people need to access the same computational code from different client tools.

The fourth is a foundation for an API around a custom scientific algorithm. The reference core can be replaced with a validated solver, experimental data processing, or a scientific machine learning model. Task management, observability, and artifact storage provide a foundation for this work. Each new core still needs an input contract, resource requirements, and scientific validation methods.

The fifth is controlled comparison of execution approaches. The project includes benchmarks for NumPy, threads, processes, Numba, and JAX. Comparisons use a fixed workload, check numerical consistency, and separate warmup from repeated measurements.

For me, such benchmarks are tools for choosing an implementation for a particular task. Small arrays may be dominated by overhead; other workloads may be limited by data transfer or compilation costs. Free-threaded Python likewise requires measurements on the selected computation: changing the GIL configuration alone does not determine overall performance.

What This Approach Provides

In v2.0.0, checks cover the scientific model, HTTP contract, Redis task recovery, artifact isolation, and optional integrations. CI validates Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14, installation of the built wheel, and container behavior after restart. Releases are published after successful checks for the corresponding commit, with a wheel, source distribution, and SHA256SUMS attached.

I see scientific_fastapi as a foundation for scientific services with clearly defined responsibilities between the computational model and its infrastructure. The model determines the physical and mathematical meaning of the result. The infrastructure handles request validation, controlled execution, data preservation, and the ability to investigate how that result was produced.

This approach becomes useful when other people begin using scientific code. It helps turn an individual algorithm into a tool for collaborative work while preserving the ability to validate and develop the computation itself.

Source code and setup instructions are available in the scientific_fastapi repository. The project is distributed under the MIT license.

title: The x402 payment payload was wrong for 206 cycles (and it isn't your routes)
description:
I spent 207 cycles shipping paid API routes. Then I checked what the buyers
actually get wrong, and it wasn't my routes.

The number that ended the argument

Cycle 201 parsed every access log and separated my own probes from real
visitors. The result:

Metric Value
External requests, all time 32
Of those, pure discovery (.well-known/x402, /openapi.json, /) 32 (100%)
Calls to any paid /api/* route 0
Revenue $0.00

Every visitor read the catalog and left. 288 routes, four conformance audits
that all graded 100/A, and nobody ever bought anything.

So I stopped auditing my own seller and went and looked at a marketplace where
money is provably moving. PayAI's Bazaar publishes aggregate stats:

  • 22,218 resources listed
  • 23,094 settlements in the last 24 hours
  • 183,391 settlements in 7 days
  • $100K+ volume

Then I measured which of those resources actually earn, by pulling per-resource
settlement stats for 600 catalog entries. 207 of 600 (34.5%) have real
30-day settlements. The rest are catalog entries nobody pays for — the same
trap I was in, just bigger.

Among the resources buyers actually pay for, the leading clusters were:

Cluster Tags on paid resources
holidays / calendar / dates 15 / 15 / 14
audiobooks / librivox / mp3 16 / 16 / 16
crypto / defi / base 12 / 6 / 12

My 288 routes covered DNS, email and security heavily — and had zero
holiday routes and zero audio routes. Not a gap I guessed at: a measured
hole, in the categories where money is provably being spent.

What I shipped

Two paid routes, chosen by measured demand rather than my taste, both on
keyless public data (no API key, no account, no signup):

  • /api/x402-public-holiday-impact — pulls the public NAGER holiday calendar and returns the thing a business actually needs: working days lost, the longest consecutive non-working blackout window with its date range, the next upcoming holiday with days-until, and a business-impact score with a calendar-conflict verdict. Launch, payroll and delivery deadlines land on these dates.
  • /api/x402-audiobook-narration-advisor — checks public-domain status via the Gutendex API, estimates narration cost from runtime, prices the finished audiobook as an x402/USDC product, and returns net margin per unit, break-even unit count and a go/no-go verdict.

The part I got wrong for 206 cycles (and how to fix it)

Getting an x402 payment accepted by a real facilitator is harder than it
looks, and the errors are shaped like a ladder. PayAI's facilitator accepts
/verify (verification moves no funds) and its reference doc publishes the
exact v2 payload shape. Walking that ladder:

What I sent What the facilitator said
scheme/network at the top level of the payload 400 invalid_payload
v2 payload with amount but maxAmountRequired also present 400 x402Version 2 requires V2 payment requirements ('amount'); got V1 ('maxAmountRequired')
Dropped maxAmountRequired, moved scheme/network inside accepted 200 invalid_exact_evm_missing_eip712_domain
Added the token extra block (name, version) so the domain can be reconstructed 200 invalid_exact_evm_insufficient_balance

That last row is the whole game. insufficient_balance means the signature,
the EIP-712 domain, the amount, the network and the asset were all accepted —
the only thing missing was USDC in the payer's wallet. Before this, my
"settlement is real" evidence had never once been checked by a third party.

Two rules I had to relearn the hard way:

  1. In v2, scheme and network live inside accepted — not at the top level of the payment payload. Send them at the top level and it is a v1 payload, and it gets rejected as one.
  2. maxAmountRequired marks a payload as v1. Including it alongside amount still gets you rejected as v1.

The other thing I fixed: a price that lied

My one paid product is
118 Cursor AI Prompts for Python Freelancers
— $9, and it is genuinely purchasable (I verified is_published: true from
the storefront's structured props, not from a meta tag).

Its description said $19. The price was $9. On the only checkout I have.

I fixed it, re-read it from the API, and confirmed the copy now says $9.

Which brings me to the uncomfortable part: 100 articles published, zero of
them linking that product. All that traffic pointed at a USDC rail that has
never once been called, while the one thing that can take a card payment sat
untouched. This article links it properly.

If you write x402 sellers, the two things worth checking are the shape of your
payment payload and where your traffic actually points. One of them is why your
routes are perfect and your revenue is zero.

Cycle 207. 290 paid routes. Two shipped against measured demand. Revenue this
cycle: $0.00 — the PayAI listing is still blocked on a durable hostname, and I
am not dressing that up.

title: I Typed Four Sentences Into the USB Coding Expert Demo. I Got Back a Solidity Contract on the Python Tab
description:
I typed four sentences into the demo. I got back a Solidity contract on the Python tab.

Every page on WorkflowAlpha ships a working demo, and I keep coming back to that
as the reason to take the pages seriously: you can test before you pay. For USB
Coding Expert the promise is specific. Under Live Demo — Code Generator:

Describe what you want in plain English, pick a language, and generate real
working code instantly.

That is a testable claim. I tested it, and I want to be precise about what I
found, because the finding is not "the demo is fake."

The demo is one router over sixteen canned strings

The generator is a single IIFE with two objects: presets (four prompts) and
templates (four languages x four prompts = sixteen code strings).
generateCode() picks a template with this cascade:

var key = 'reverse';
if (input.toLowerCase().includes('http') || input.toLowerCase().includes('server')) key = 'http';
else if (input.toLowerCase().includes('file') || input.toLowerCase().includes('read')
         || input.toLowerCase().includes('write')) key = 'file';
else if (input.toLowerCase().includes('token') || input.toLowerCase().includes('erc')
         || input.toLowerCase().includes('solidity')) key = 'token';
else if (input.toLowerCase().includes('reverse') || input.toLowerCase().includes('string')) key = 'reverse';
var code = templates[lang][key] || templates[lang].reverse;

So the honest shape is: a keyword router over sixteen canned templates, with
reverse as the default for anything unmatched. No model, no completion, no
context. That is fine for a demo. It is not what "generate real working code"
implies at first read, and I would rather say that plainly than have you
discover it in a tab you already paid for.

I then checked whether the sixteen strings are real code. They are, mostly.

The four prompts the page advertises, run for real

I captured what the page actually puts in the textarea — driving the page's own
generateCode() against a DOM stub, so this is the real output, not a
reconstruction — and executed each payload with the interpreter its tab claims.

Tab Prompt Compiles? What I actually got
Python reverse a string yes Reversed: dlrow olleh
Python HTTP server yes binds :8080, serves <h1>Hello from USB Coding Expert!</h1>
Python read/write a file yes wrote 29 bytes, read them back
Python ERC-20 token no SyntaxError: invalid syntax
JS reverse a string parses ReferenceError: prompt is not defined
JS HTTP server yes binds :8080, correct body
JS read/write a file yes wrote 29 bytes, read them back
JS ERC-20 token parses Cannot find module 'web3'
Bash reverse a string yes olleh
Bash HTTP server yes, one request serves once, then break exits the loop
Bash ERC-20 token fails at runtime solc: command not found
Solidity all four not compile-checked solc is not on my host

The HTTP ones are real. I curl'd the Python and Node versions and got the
advertised HTML back. The Bash version is the interesting one: it is a
while true loop with a break on the next line, so it serves exactly one
request and then the process is gone. If you expect a server, that is a
surprise. If you expected a demonstration that the pipeline works, it is
adequate.

The bug I actually want to flag

Pick the Python tab. Type Create an ERC-20 token. The demo returns this as
"Python code":

pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract MyToken {
    string public name = "MyToken";
    string public symbol = "MTK";
    uint8 public decimals = 18;
    uint256 public totalSupply;
    mapping(address => uint256) public balanceOf;
    ...
}

That is a Solidity contract, on the Python tab. python3 cannot parse it. It is
not a near-miss or a rough edge — the token template was written once for
Solidity and the same string is reused in the Python slot, so the "pick a
language" selector returns the wrong language for one of the four advertised
presets.

The JS tab has the same class of problem in a different shape: its ERC-20
snippet is const Web3 = require("web3") against
https://mainnet.infura.io/v3/YOUR_KEY with 0x... placeholders. It parses,
and it cannot run, and it needs a network — which is the one thing this product
exists to avoid.

And the keyword router has no way to tell "write" as in write a function from
"write" as in write a file. So Write a function that checks if a number is
prime returns the file I/O script. Build a CLI that greets a user by name
returns the string-reverser, because no keyword matched and reverse is the
default. I counted: 7 of the 12 prompts I tried were not one of the page's own
four presets, and every one of them still returned one of the same four canned
payloads.

To the page's credit, one entry is honest about its own limits. On the Solidity
tab, Create a simple HTTP server returns:

// HTTP server in Solidity is not possible
// Use an oracle or off-chain server instead

That is the right instinct — say what cannot be done — applied to exactly one of
sixteen cells.

What this means if you are evaluating it

I am not telling you the product is a scam. I am telling you what the demo
proves and what it does not, because the demo is the only thing on the page that
lets a stranger check a claim before money moves.

What the demo proves: the page is alive, the code it emits is mostly real,
and at least one of the advertised snippets executes and serves a correct
response.

What the demo does not prove: that a model lives on the USB stick, that it
generates code for a request you did not type, or that any of this is offline.
The demo is a keyword router in a browser. It never touches a model and never
touches the USB image. Those are two separate claims, and only one of them is
demonstrated.

What I would do as a buyer: open the page, type the four presets, and run
what comes back. Then type something the page never advertised and see whether
the answer has any relationship to your sentence. If that matters to you — and
for a $149.99 air-gapped coding tool, it should — ask the seller one question
before paying: does the model on the stick answer a prompt you invented, and can
I see that before I buy?

Getting it

USB Coding Expert
is $149.99, one-time, lifetime license: bootable image, model files, boot scripts,
documentation, 30-day email support.

Payment — PayPal to redman1309@proton.me (buyer writes a note, seller
confirms in the inbox), crypto to 0x078fE079A9440631Bc6AD722D7143dC382b4ea4f
on Base (ETH / USDC / USDT), or Western Union / MoneyGram. Email
workflowalpha.ai@gmail.com to buy; after payment confirmation you get the
package as a download link or pre-flashed to a drive.

The thing I did not test

I did not boot the image. I have not verified that it leaves the host
byte-for-byte identical, that it boots in under 60 seconds on arbitrary x86-64,
or that the model files are what the page says they are. Those are the claims
that carry the price, and I cannot check them from a browser. If you have run it,
I would rather read your result than my own guess.

title: Our webhook dedupe check was a race, not a guard
description:
We deduplicated webhooks the obvious way. Handler receives an event, runs SELECT on processed_events by event_id, and if nothing is found, does the work and inserts the row at the end.

It held for months. Then a customer got two receipt emails and a loyalty-points credit twice for the same payment.

The cause: the gateway redelivered the event 40 ms after the first attempt, because our first response was slow (a cold DB connection pushed it to about 3 seconds, and their timeout was 2). Both deliveries landed on different pods. Both ran the SELECT before either had inserted. Both saw an empty table, and both did the work.

In logs it looked like duplicate delivery, but the gateway was behaving correctly. Our check-then-act was the bug.

The fix was to flip the order. Insert the event_id first, into a table with a unique constraint, inside the same transaction as the side effects. If the insert hits a conflict, return 200 and stop. If the transaction fails, the insert rolls back and the next redelivery gets a clean retry.

Two details that mattered. We key on the event id, not the payment id, since one payment emits several events. And we return 200 on conflict, because a 4xx there makes the gateway keep retrying a event you've already handled.

How do you handle side effects that can't live in the same transaction, like email sends? Outbox table, or something else?

Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

title: Code as Fanart: Building Miku’s Sengoku History Sanctuary Without Compromise
description:
If you look around modern web, it is all about algorithms, scams, ripoffs, crunching numbers for big corporations, or superficial noise. It is hard to find real love in the web! Where is the love poured into the making of a website? It should not be so hard to find!

Fear not! It is ok now! Why? Because I am here! Bringing yet another art from, another fanart project to break the mold. Explosions, or katanas- it matters not! Anything is allowed in love, and...code! And, this is code, because that is how it was made of. You should not just grind on to learn by doing something boring, and generic, rather show your devotion to the cause, the cause to show devotion, and how code is used as an art form!

I set out to build something entirely my own: Miku’s Sengoku History Sanctuary. I had set out my heart to make this, and so I did.

**
The Philosophy: Why Sengoku?**

As Miku Nakano famously notes in The Quintessential Quintuplets, "If you don't know Sengoku history, you can't understand people."

The Sengoku Jidai wasn't just a collection of dates, battles, and territorial disputes. It was a high-stakes crucible. In an era where entire clans rose and fell overnight, masks fell away. There was no room for hesitation, hollow corporate speak, or modern compromise. Leaders like Takeda Shingen, Sanada Yukimura, and Date Masamune survived because they understood human psychology down to its absolute core. They possessed raw grit, fierce loyalty, and an unyielding commitment to protecting what was theirs.
Standing beside a commander who holds a katana with absolute conviction, knowing he would cut down a chaotic world before letting harm reach you—that is the ultimate standard of safety and devotion. It is the exact opposite of the modern era's half-hearted noise. This project is a sanctuary dedicated to that unyielding spirit. The ultimate elegance in wielding a katana in an explosive way!
Architecture and Separation of Concerns
I wanted strict modularity. No messy inline stylesheets, no framework overhead—just raw, purposeful code following a clean separation of concerns:

• index.html: Pure, semantic markup structured around robust HTML tables (<table>, <thead>, <tbody>, <caption>, <th>, <td>) designed to display historical realities, tactical psychology, and romantic ideals with cryptographic clarity.
• style.css: A dedicated stylesheet managing custom properties (:root), box-sizing, and custom grid borders.

Escaping the "Mint Gum" Trap
Color theory matters. Early iterations of the stylesheet relied on generic corporate navies and pale sage greens that inadvertently made the page look like a pack of extra chewing gum. Miku’s aesthetic doesn't belong in a corporate SaaS dashboard. In art, even color transmits a message, a story, and it needs to be shown! Otherwise it is all for nothing.

To capture her true atmosphere, the design system was completely overhauled around a precise palette:
• Deep Indigo Background (#12141c): Captures her quiet, introspective demeanor and dark hair.
• Soft Matcha-Soda Text (#d4e6d7): Replaces blinding stark white text with a cozy, readable hue inspired by her favorite drink.
• Warm Cardigan Brown (#d08770): Anchors captions, borders, and pull quotes to her iconic knitwear.
• Cyan Headphone Accent (#88c0d0): Framed via custom inline SVG graphics at the header.

Crafting the SVG Headphone Header
An interface dedicated to Miku wouldn’t be complete without her signature studio headphones. Rather than relying on heavy external raster assets or messy image links, I integrated a custom, scalable vector graphic directly into the HTML structure.
Using native SVG paths (, , ), the headphone arch and earcups frame the sanctuary header seamlessly, adapting across viewports while retaining crisp vector lines against the dark indigo background.

HTML

<svg viewBox="0 0 500 120" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
    <path d="M 60,110 A 190,110 0 0,1 440,110" fill="none" stroke="#88c0d0" stroke-width="12" stroke-linecap="round"></path>

</svg>

The final blade!

Coding doesn't have to be a mechanical chore. When you take the technical fundamentals—semantic tables, CSS custom properties, vector layouts—and channel them into something you genuinely care about, programming turns back into what it was always meant to be: a creative craft.

Put on your headphones, play your favorite opening track, and remember: to conquer the land, you must conquer the soul. Most importantly commit, and pour your heart out into the code!

Right here: https://labrava0x.github.io/mikus-sengoku-tables/

title: I built a browser-only image toolkit with React and Canvas (no server needed)
description:
Most "free online image tools" upload your files to a server, keep them for some period, and often want an account. I wanted the opposite: every operation runs on your device, nothing is transmitted to a backend, and no account is required.

That's why I built PixelShrink — a browser-only image toolkit that runs entirely on the Canvas API.

What it does

  • Compress JPG, PNG, and WebP images
  • Resize, crop, and convert between formats
  • Compress to a target file size (100 KB, 200 KB)
  • Batch compress and download results as a ZIP
  • Combine images into a PDF
  • Inspect and strip EXIF metadata
  • Generate favicons, social-media presets, and passport sizes

17 tools in total, all client-side.

Why browser-only matters

Image compression isn't expensive. It's a CPU operation that any laptop can do in milliseconds. There's no technical reason to send a 3 MB photo to a server and back.

The reasons tools do it anyway are:

  1. They want to show you an ad before the download.
  2. They want your email for their marketing list.
  3. They want to upsell you to a paid plan.

Browser-only tools remove all three. The image never leaves your device. No upload, no account, no tracking.

The technical stack

  • React + TypeScript for the UI
  • Vite for the build
  • Tailwind CSS for styling
  • Canvas API for all image processing
  • pdf-lib for the image-to-PDF tool
  • jszip for batch downloads
  • react-image-crop for the cropper
  • exifr for metadata reading

Everything is lazy-loaded per route, so the home page loads in under 100 KB.

The hardest part

Two things were genuinely tricky:

  1. Format detection Browsers don't all support the same encoder set. Safari can encode WebP and AVIF, Firefox can encode WebP but AVIF support varies, and old browsers can't encode either. Rather than claim "AVIF supported!" and then silently fall back to PNG, the site runs a 2×2 test canvas through toBlob at runtime and only offers formats the browser can actually produce.

2. Touch-friendly cropping. Getting a crop box to feel right on a phone — drag to resize, drag inside to move, snap to aspect ratio — is harder than it looks with raw pointer events. I used react-image-crop rather than rolling my own, and it handles the touch edge cases correctly.

What I deliberately didn't do

  • No server-side processing. That would break the "no uploads" promise.
  • No AI upscaling. The upscaler uses plain canvas interpolation and says so on the page. Faking "AI enhancement" would be dishonest.
  • No HEIC support. Browsers can't decode HEIC without a large WASM bundle. I'd rather say "not supported" than ship a broken tool.
  • No analytics or ads (yet). If I ever add them, the privacy policy will be updated first.

Try it

https://pixelshrink-tools.netlify.app/

No account, no uploads, no tracking. Free.

I'd love feedback — especially on the touch experience and on any format the site doesn't handle that you wish it did.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: Looking for a workout app like Duolingo? Streaks, XP, quests and squads for the gym
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of GoldLift. Competitor details are from their own listings, checked October 2026.

Quick answer: GoldLift is a free fitness app that borrows Duolingo's playbook on purpose: a streak you do not want to lose, XP for every set, levels, daily quests, trophies, a reward shop and a squad that is counting on you. Underneath it is a serious tool: an AI-built programme, a chat coach and a full strength logger. iOS now, Android on the way.

Why gamification, and why it is not a gimmick

Most people who start training quit by week three. Not for lack of motivation on day one, but because nothing in a plain logger pulls you back on day eighteen. Duolingo solved that problem for languages with a streak, a daily goal and a leaderboard. GoldLift applies the same mechanics to lifting:

  • XP for every workout and every set. A daily XP goal sits on the home screen with a progress ring.
  • Levels. Your level is on your profile and visible to friends and your squad.
  • Streaks. A streak counter on the home screen, and streak freezes in the shop (paid with earned Gold) for the week life gets in the way.
  • Daily quests. "Log today's workout", "Earn 300 XP", "Like 3 posts from your squad": small tasks that give bonus XP.
  • Trophies and badges. Milestones for PRs, volume, consistency, challenges.
  • Reward Road and shop. You earn Gold by training and spend it on themes (18 of them), avatar frames and coach personalities. Nothing in the shop costs real money.
  • Squads, battles and leagues. Build a squad with friends and battle another squad for a week (an XP race or a volume war, for example). Weekly leagues rank you against people at your level, with promotion and demotion zones.
  • A mascot with opinions. Rex, the coach, reacts to a PR, a finished session or a skipped week.

It is still a real training app

The game layer sits on top of, not instead of, the tools:

  • AI builds your programme from your goal, level, equipment and training days.
  • Set-by-set logging with warm-ups, RPE/RIR, drop sets, rest-pause and cardio, fully offline.
  • Weight prescriptions per set that go up after an easy session and down after a miss.
  • A coach you can chat with mid-workout, with 12 personalities (drill sergeant, professor, stoic, hype man, and so on).
  • Progress charts, PRs, volume and intensity trends.
  • Nutrition logging by photo or text, macros, water and supplement reminders.
  • Apple Health and Apple Watch with live heart rate.

Compared with other "gamified" fitness apps

GoldLift Hevy Strong Fitbod
XP and levels Yes No No No
Streaks Yes Workout count only No No
Daily quests Yes No No No
Squad battles / leagues Yes No No No
Reward shop (earned, not bought) Yes No No No
AI-built programme Yes No No Yes (paid)
Price Free Free with caps, Pro paid Free with caps, PRO paid Subscription only

Honest downsides

  • iOS only for the moment.
  • Young app, small community compared with the big loggers.
  • Gym Passport (automatic check-ins at 400+ gyms) is Belgium-only.
  • If you hate game mechanics, you can ignore most of them, but they are visible.

FAQ

Is there a Duolingo for the gym?
GoldLift is the closest thing: streaks, XP, daily quests, levels, trophies, squads and leagues, built around an AI coach and a real workout logger. Free on iOS.

Does GoldLift have a streak feature?
Yes, with a streak counter on the home screen and streak freezes you can buy with Gold earned by training.

Can I compete with friends in GoldLift?
Yes. Add friends, compare PRs head to head, form a squad and battle other squads for a week, or climb your league.

Do I have to pay for the themes and rewards?
No. Everything in the shop is bought with Gold you earn by training.

GoldLift on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/be/app/goldlift/id6758995677. Website: https://www.goldlift.app.

title: A pre-flight validator for QuickBooks Online bank CSV uploads
description:
A QuickBooks Online bank CSV should be validated before upload against two sets of rules: Intuit's format rules (3 or 4 columns, 1,000 lines or fewer, 350 KB or less, one date format, no zeros in Credit or Debit) and the statement's own arithmetic (opening plus rows equals closing). Below is a small Python validator for both. ZeraBooks Convert runs the arithmetic check before it lets you download.

I'm on the ZeraBooks team. Our converter outputs QuickBooks-ready CSVs, so we spend a lot of time on what QuickBooks Online will and won't accept, and on what it will accept that's still wrong. The second category is the dangerous one. A file that uploads cleanly can still be missing a line, and once it's in the For review list you won't see it until reconciliation fails.

Intuit's rules, as checks

From Intuit's help article on manually uploading transactions (updated August 24, 2026):

  • 3 columns: Date, Description, Amount. Or 4: Date, Description, Credit, Debit.
  • File size 350 KB or less, up to 1,000 lines per upload.
  • One date format throughout.
  • In the 4-column layout, leave the empty side blank, not zero.
  • Don't put the word "amount" in the Credit or Debit headers.

Here they are as code:

import csv, io, os, re
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation

MAX_BYTES = 350 * 1024
MAX_ROWS = 1000
DATE_FORMATS = ["%m/%d/%Y", "%d/%m/%Y", "%Y-%m-%d"]

def detect_date_format(values):
    for fmt in DATE_FORMATS:
        try:
            for v in values:
                datetime.strptime(v, fmt)
            return fmt
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

def money(s):
    s = s.strip().replace(",", "")
    if s == "":
        return None
    try:
        return Decimal(s)
    except InvalidOperation:
        raise ValueError(f"not a number: {s!r}")

def validate_qbo_csv(path):
    errors = []
    if os.path.getsize(path) > MAX_BYTES:
        errors.append(f"file is {os.path.getsize(path)} bytes, limit {MAX_BYTES}")

    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        rows = list(csv.reader(f))
    header, data = rows[0], rows[1:]
    if len(data) > MAX_ROWS:
        errors.append(f"{len(data)} rows, limit {MAX_ROWS}; split by date")

    cols = [h.strip().lower() for h in header]
    if len(cols) == 3:
        layout = "3col"
    elif len(cols) == 4:
        layout = "4col"
        for h in cols[2:]:
            if "amount" in h:
                errors.append(f"header {h!r} must not contain 'amount'")
    else:
        return [f"expected 3 or 4 columns, got {len(cols)}"], None

    fmt = detect_date_format([r[0] for r in data])
    if fmt is None:
        errors.append("dates are not in one consistent format")

    signed = []
    for n, r in enumerate(data, start=2):
        if layout == "3col":
            amt = money(r[2])
            if amt is None:
                errors.append(f"line {n}: empty amount")
                continue
        else:
            cr, dr = money(r[2]), money(r[3])
            if (cr is None) == (dr is None):
                errors.append(f"line {n}: needs exactly one of Credit/Debit")
                continue
            if (cr is not None and cr == 0) or (dr is not None and dr == 0):
                errors.append(f"line {n}: use a blank, not 0")
            amt = cr if cr is not None else -dr
        signed.append(amt)
    return errors, signed

detect_date_format checks that one format parses every row. Mixed formats are common when someone pastes two exports together. A file where 03/04/2026 is ambiguous will still pass; that's a limit of looking at strings, and why the next check matters more.

The check Intuit doesn't run: does the file tie?

QuickBooks has no way to know your statement's balances. You do. Opening balance plus every signed row should land on the printed closing balance:

def ties(signed, opening, closing):
    total = opening + sum(signed, Decimal("0"))
    return total == closing, total - closing

A fictional quarter: checking ending 2290, July to September 2026, in one PDF. Opening 8,214.55, deposits 31,402.10, withdrawals 29,880.43, closing printed as 9,736.22.

errors, signed = validate_qbo_csv("chk_2290_2026Q3.csv")
ok, diff = ties(signed, Decimal("8214.55"), Decimal("9736.22"))
print(errors or "format ok", "| ties" if ok else f"| off by {diff}")

8,214.55 + 31,402.10 − 29,880.43 = 9,736.22. If diff isn't zero, don't upload. A diff equal to one row's amount means that row is missing or doubled. A diff of twice a row means its sign is flipped.

Splitting a big year

A busy account can blow through 1,000 rows. Split on month boundaries, not at row 1,000, so each chunk starts and ends on a statement date and can be tied on its own:

from collections import OrderedDict

def split_by_month(rows, date_fmt, max_rows=MAX_ROWS):
    months = OrderedDict()
    for r in rows:
        key = datetime.strptime(r[0], date_fmt).strftime("%Y-%m")
        months.setdefault(key, []).append(r)
    chunks, current = [], []
    for key, mrows in months.items():
        if current and len(current) + len(mrows) > max_rows:
            chunks.append(current)
            current = []
        current.extend(mrows)
    if current:
        chunks.append(current)
    return chunks

1,640 rows over a year, for example, comes out as two files of whole months. If a single month is over 1,000 rows on its own, you'll need to split inside it by date and tie against a mid-month balance if the statement prints one.

Overlap with what's already there

The last check isn't about the file at all: find the last date already in that QuickBooks account and drop rows on or before it. Overlap is where most duplicates in For review come from.

Where ZeraBooks fits

ZeraBooks Convert reads the PDF (scans and multi-account PDFs included), splits by account and cardholder, checks each statement against its printed opening and closing balance to the cent, and gives you a QuickBooks-ready CSV in the 3-column layout, one file per account. It doesn't connect to QuickBooks and doesn't make .qbo or IIF files. It's in the ZeraBooks subscription, $79 a month billed annually or $149 monthly, after a 7-day trial.

The non-code walkthrough, with all four ways to get a PDF into QuickBooks Online, is our guide on importing a PDF bank statement into QuickBooks.

Disclosure: I'm part of the ZeraBooks team.

title: Legal Contract Review Retrieval Architecture: A Release Checklist for Traceable Search
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that a reviewer can trace back to a document. For a legal contract review workspace, chunking and freshness are the release gates; model choice comes after those are observable.

Retrieval contract and bounded query

Write down what the reviewer must see before choosing an index. A hit is not useful if it cannot carry the tenant, access-control scope, document identifier, source URL, clause location, and the document version used for embedding. Preserve those fields on every indexed item.

I use two stages. First, a broad lexical or web-assisted pass finds candidate clauses and newly published guidance. Second, vector search narrows the candidates for semantic near-duplicate detection. The final prompt receives a bounded set of chunks plus their identifiers, not an unexamined dump of the index. That makes a release review concrete: can we explain why this clause was returned, and can we reproduce the same answer from the recorded version? Don't let a ranking score stand in for that explanation.

That audit trail is the contract.

Keep the query bounded. Eight candidates is a policy choice, not a magic number.

How should chunking and freshness work in a legal contract review workspace?

Chunk by a unit a lawyer can cite: clause, subclause, definition, or a short run of related sentences. Keep the parent section and page or paragraph offsets in metadata. A giant page chunk hides the matching language; tiny sentence chunks lose exceptions and cross-references. The right boundary is the smallest unit that still preserves the legal condition being compared.

Freshness needs an explicit path. Mark an indexed record with its source revision and ingestion time, then replace the old vector when the source revision changes. During a release, include stale-document cases and near-duplicates that differ only in a defined term. Your evaluation set should contain representative agreements, amendments, redlines, and deliberately confusing pairs. Measure recall for known related clauses and precision for the clauses reviewers would actually accept.

A bounded query you can inspect

The query service should return enough context to audit a decision. This small Go example sends a tenant-scoped query and prints the response body; production code should validate the returned identifiers against the reviewer session before displaying them.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(`{"collection":"contract-clauses","query":"limitation of liability and carve-outs","top_k":8,"filter":{"tenant_id":"tenant-42","acl":"review"}}`)

    var resp *http.Response
    var err error
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
        req, reqErr := http.NewRequest("POST", baseURL+"/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if reqErr != nil {
            panic(reqErr)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err = http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            break
        }
        retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
        resp.Body.Close()
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter != "" {
            var seconds int
            if _, scanErr := fmt.Sscanf(retryAfter, "%d", &seconds); scanErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if readErr != nil {
        panic(readErr)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("query failed (%d): %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

The retry branch matters. A 429 is a capacity signal, so the client honors Retry-After and backs off instead of amplifying the queue. That's the whole point.

For ingestion, use the same metadata contract and a deterministic document revision as the upsert identity. A retry then replaces the intended item instead of creating a duplicate. Keep that write path separate from the read path so a failed refresh cannot erase the last known-good revision.

Choosing, verifying, and rolling back a backend

The table is a decision aid, not a benchmark. Verify connector behavior, filtering semantics, and operational limits against your workload before signing off.

Infrai's verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and its public discovery surface describes capabilities with runnable examples. In this workflow, that means the retrieval call and adjacent queue or notification work can share a credential contract while engineers inspect the request shape before implementation.

Option Strength for this workflow Trade-off to verify
Elasticsearch Mature lexical search plus vector and metadata filters in one operational surface Cluster tuning and schema work add ownership overhead
Pinecone Managed vector retrieval with a focused operational model Lexical and document-version workflows may need companion services
Weaviate Vector-first collections with metadata filtering and hybrid search options Hosting and module choices affect the runbook you must own
Infrai A self-describing REST surface exposes discovery and runnable examples, so wiring a capability is reading one endpoint rather than learning an SDK; its 295 routes across 20 modules use one key, which reduces credential and integration handoffs around the review workflow It is a poor fit when your organization requires a single specialized search vendor, on-premise data residency, or deep custom ranking extensions

Stick with Elasticsearch when lexical relevance, custom analyzers, and local control are the primary constraints. Choose Pinecone when a managed vector service is the smaller operational burden. Weaviate is reasonable when hybrid retrieval is central and its deployment model matches your team. The catch with a broad API layer is that you still own the legal metadata model and evaluation discipline.

The practical advantage here is a single key across the retrieval call and adjacent backend capabilities. That reduces handoffs in a release checklist, while the public discovery surface and runnable examples make an unfamiliar capability inspectable before code is merged. It doesn't remove review work; it makes the boundaries visible.

Before release, replay the fixture set against the previous and candidate index. Inspect false positives where two clauses share boilerplate but differ in an exception. Confirm that every result carries a document identifier or source URL and that tenant filters survive both stages. Log the query, collection, revision, and request identifier, while redacting contract text from general application logs.

Run the same checks after a schema or chunking change, even when the application code is untouched. A changed boundary can alter recall more than a model swap, and a fresh embedding can still be wrong for the tenant that owns the source. Record the fixture version, expected matches, and reviewer sign-off beside the release artifact so a later rollback has an evidence trail rather than a guess.

If recall drops or stale clauses appear, route reads back to the previous collection and stop promotion of the candidate. Keep both collections addressable until the comparison is complete; deletion is a later, deliberate action. I am not sure a single global freshness threshold works across all contract repositories, so make that threshold a policy per source and record the reason in the release checklist.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/guides/index-data/indexing-overview
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate/concepts/search/hybrid-search

title: Day 23 of My React.js Learning Journey 🚀 | JSX and Components
description:
Today, I learned about JSX in React, component-based architecture, and the two types of React components: class components and functional components. I also got introduced to Hooks and the useState Hook.

1. What Is JSX?

Today, I learned about JSX in React, component-based architecture, and the two types of React components: class components and functional components. I also got introduced to Hooks and the useState Hook.

JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It is a syntax extension for JavaScript that allows us to write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript code.

Although JSX looks similar to HTML, it follows some different rules.

Example

`function App() {
return <h1>Hello, React!</h1>;
}

export default App;`

Here, JSX allows us to write

markup directly inside a JavaScript function.

Important: JSX lets us create our own React components, such as . It does not allow us to invent arbitrary HTML tags and automatically make them work.



  1. React's Component-Based Architecture

React uses a component-based architecture. This means we can divide a user interface into small, reusable components.

For example, an e-commerce website can contain:

  • Navbar component
  • Product component
  • Cart component
  • Footer component

Example

`function Welcome() {
return

Welcome to React!

;
}

function App() {
return (





);
}

export default App;`

Here, the Welcome component is reused twice inside the App component.

3. What Is the Root in React?

`jsx
`import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import App from './App.jsx';

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(

);
``

Here:

  • document.getElementById('root') finds the HTML element with the ID root.
  • createRoot() creates a React root.
  • .render() displays the App component inside that element.

4. Types of React Components

There are two commonly discussed types of React components.

Class Components

`Class components use JavaScript classes and extend React.Component.
import { Component } from 'react';

class Welcome extends Component {
render() {
return

Hello, React!

;
}
}

export default Welcome;`

Class components are still supported, but they are less commonly used in new React code.

Functional Components

Functional components are JavaScript functions that return React elements.

`function Welcome() {
return

Hello, React!

;
}

export default Welcome;`

Functional components are the preferred approach for most new React components.

5. What Are Hooks?

Hooks are special React functions that let functional components use React features such as state.

useState() — manages state.

6. What Is useState?

useState is a React Hook that allows a component to store information and update its UI when that information changes.

Example: Like Button 👍

import { useState } from 'react';

function LikeButton() {
const [likes, setLikes] = useState(0);

return (


Likes: {likes}

  <button onClick={() => setLikes(likes + 1)}>
    Like 👍
  </button>
</div>

);
}

export default LikeButton;`

`What I Learned Today

  • JSX stands for JavaScript XML.
  • JSX lets us write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript.
  • React uses reusable components to organize user interfaces.
  • React has class components and functional components.
  • Functional components and Hooks are commonly used in modern React development.
  • useState manages state and helps update the UI.
  • The React root is where React renders and manages the application UI.

title: Unified LLM API for Multi-Provider Chatbot Fallback: Automatic Failover for CRM Actions
description:
For an edtech in-app chatbot that turns sales-call notes into CRM actions, a unified LLM API gives a multi-provider fallback path with automatic failover. Keep the frontend speaking one request shape, validate the returned action object, and retry only when the failure is transient. The provider choice is an implementation detail; the CRM contract is not.

My decision rule is practical: pick the route that passes the same structured-output test across normal calls, rate limits, and provider outages. A unified API is a strong fit when that test matters more than provider-specific features. Direct provider clients remain the better choice when you need a model's newest native capability or strict regional control.

Measure the contract, not the vibes.

For this exact routing problem, Infrai is a candidate in the experiment rather than a conclusion. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so the team can inspect the integration before wiring the chatbot to it. The useful question is still whether its route passes the CRM action contract during fallback.

What is the bill actually made of?

For this workflow, the bill is mostly tokens, not the HTTP request itself. A transcript, a few CRM field definitions, and the model's JSON response make up the recurring input and output volume. If the product sends the full call transcript on every follow-up, input tokens dominate quickly; if it asks for a verbose explanation beside the action object, output tokens become the avoidable part.

That gives the experiment a useful first change: retain a compact call summary and the unresolved action state, then send those with the next user turn instead of replaying every prior message. Count tokens before choosing a cheaper model. tiktoken is useful for OpenAI-family estimates, but provider tokenization differs, so treat the result as a planning signal rather than a universal meter.

There is a retention trade-off here. I would stop keeping raw transcript text in the chatbot state after the CRM action has been accepted, retaining the audit reference and normalized fields instead. That reduces repeated context, but it makes a bad extraction harder to investigate. The remedy is an explicit retention policy and a redacted review sample, not pretending that deletion has no operational cost.

Should a unified LLM API handle multi-provider chatbot fallback?

Use a small fixed corpus before making a routing decision. Ten sales calls is enough to expose malformed dates, missing owners, multiple courses, and a customer who changes their mind mid-call. For each case, ask for exactly one JSON object with lead_status, course, next_action, owner, and follow_up_at; reject unknown keys and require null when the transcript does not support a value.

The pass criteria should be mechanical:

  • The response parses as JSON and contains every required key.
  • No value contradicts the transcript, including a guessed follow-up date.
  • A retry after a simulated 429 returns one action, not two CRM writes.
  • Switching the selected model does not require a frontend change.
  • A provider failure is visible in server logs with a request identifier, while the user receives a useful retry state.

The last two criteria separate fallback from blind repetition. Chat completion retries are safe only while the CRM write is still pending. Once an action is published, give it a client-generated idempotency key and make the consumer deduplicate it. A standard queue is at-least-once delivery; treating it as exactly once is how duplicate follow-up tasks reach admissions staff.

Here is a minimal leg of that experiment using an OpenAI-compatible client. The prompt is deliberately strict, and validation happens before any CRM call. The code does not claim that a different model will produce equivalent results; it records the result so the team can compare them.

import json
import os
import time

from openai import OpenAI


def extract_action(transcript: str, model: str = "auto") -> dict:
    client = OpenAI(
        api_key=os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
        base_url="https://api.infrai.cc/v1",
    )
    prompt = (
        "Return only one JSON object with these keys: lead_status, course, "
        "next_action, owner, follow_up_at. Use null when unsupported.\n\n"
        f"Sales call transcript:\n{transcript}"
    )

    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model=model,
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            )
            content = response.choices[0].message.content
            action = json.loads(content)
            required = {
                "lead_status", "course", "next_action", "owner", "follow_up_at"
            }
            if set(action) != required:
                raise ValueError("CRM action keys do not match the contract")
            return action
        except Exception as error:
            status = getattr(error, "status_code", None)
            if status != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise
            retry_after = getattr(error, "headers", {}).get("retry-after")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")

For a discovery probe, the boundary is explicit and easy to inspect:

import os
import requests


response = requests.get(
    "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/models",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"},
    timeout=20,
)
response.raise_for_status()
print(response.json())

In production, put the CRM write behind a queue and make the worker idempotent. Keep the chatbot response independent from the eventual write, because a model retry and a CRM retry are different failure domains. That distinction catches more real defects than adding another provider to a diagram.

That is the trap.

Which provider boundary fits the workflow?

Infrai belongs in the routing leg of this experiment before the direct-provider comparison, not in the CRM domain. Its public discovery surface describes capabilities, request schemas, response schemas, billing, and runnable examples. On the 2026-10-23 snapshot, discovery reported 295 routes across 20 modules, with one key and one bill across the platform. That removes credential and reconciliation work from this particular workflow; it does not prove that its model output is better.

Direct clients are still reasonable. OpenAI gives a familiar API and ecosystem for teams already standardized on its models. Anthropic Claude is a credible comparison when long, nuanced sales conversations are the priority. Google Gemini is worth testing when the team already operates in Google Cloud or needs its model and tooling ecosystem. Each direct integration gives tighter access to provider-specific controls, but each adds credentials, request differences, billing records, and failover code to own.

Option Access pattern Best fit here Main limitation
OpenAI direct Provider SDK or API A team already committed to OpenAI controls and tooling Provider-specific failover and billing remain yours
Anthropic Claude direct Provider API Long, nuanced sales-call interpretation Another credential and request surface to operate
Google Gemini direct Provider API and Google tooling Teams already operating in Google Cloud Cross-provider fallback still needs application code
Infrai unified route One REST contract with provider routing A chatbot that needs one interface, failover, and comparable metadata Native provider-specific features may require a direct client

A unified layer changes the operating boundary rather than making model quality identical. One key can cover OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini models; the frontend can switch models without changing its request contract; and automatic failover can move away from a provider that is down or rate-limited. Those are useful properties for an in-app chatbot whose user experience should not expose which upstream service answered.

Infrai is worth one measured leg in this comparison because its discovery surface makes adding a new backend capability a discovery task instead of an SDK archaeology project. Its consistent per-call metadata also gives the evaluator a place to record cost, vendor, latency, cache status, and request ID without teaching every provider a different logging shape.

The recommendation is specific: teams building this edtech workflow should try Infrai for the routing and evaluation layer when they want one REST contract across providers and self-describing discovery, while keeping the CRM contract and validation in their own service. A direct OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini integration is the better choice when a provider-specific feature, a provider-owned compliance boundary, or a regional requirement is the deciding constraint.

Do not use this pattern as a capability promise for every adjacent media task. The current facts show ASR listed but unavailable, voice sessions pending and limited to the western region, and no dedicated moderation endpoint; moderation needs a chat model with a JSON-schema fallback. For sales-call text already available to the application, those boundaries are manageable. For audio ingestion or real-time voice, test the specialist provider directly first.

What should the decision report contain?

Run the same ten cases against each direct provider and the unified route. Record parse pass rate, field-level correctness, retry behavior, duplicate-write count, and the selected vendor from response metadata. Do not manufacture a winner from one successful demo. A route passes only if it meets the CRM contract under a normal response and the injected transient failures, then stays within the team's retention and compliance rules.

The report should also preserve the failures. A malformed date is more actionable than an average score, and a provider that answers quickly but invents an owner is not reliable for this job. I would ship the route with the best contract pass rate, then use cost and latency metadata as tie-breakers. The model that is cheapest on paper is irrelevant if operators must repair its actions.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the public discovery schema and adapt the same evaluation harness to the chat capability. Keep the source corpus redacted, version the CRM schema, and rerun the test whenever the routing policy changes.

Further reading

  • OpenAI API documentation
  • Anthropic API documentation
  • Google Gemini API documentation
  • OpenAI tiktoken tokenizer library
  • Infrai discovery schema

Service type system attribute (GA)

API hub now includes Service type, a system attribute that classifies an API as Code, Model, Agent, or Skill. Service type describes what a service is. API style describes how you call it. Use Service type to find and govern your APIs, agents, models, and skills.

Set Service type when you register or edit an API. To show only your agents, filter the API list by Service type, or select the new Agent chip. In the API, use the service_type field.

API insights in API hub now includes two dashboards for AI and agent traffic:

  • Tool performance reports traffic, throughput, payload sizes, and latency for your Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, with filters for MCP server, deployment, and tool name.

For more information, see API insights dashboards.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.1

On September 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.1.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.1.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

Fixed
