title: Keeping a Bubble Tea Dashboard in Sync with soroi
description:
An incident console gets more demanding once it has several panes. The queue shows open incidents, a detail pane follows the selected row, and a summary groups incidents by severity. A responder acknowledges an incident, and the new owner needs to appear everywhere that displays it.

GitHub: Waterkyuu/soroi

Bubble Tea gives the screen a clear message loop. The application still has to decide who loads the queue, which results can be reused, and what each pane should show while another read is running.

soroi is a typed query client for Go. It fits this part of a terminal application: several components reading the same remote data, with writes that make the cached view stale. The incident service still owns the actual HTTP requests and acknowledgement rules.

A queue that several panes can read

Suppose each pane is a separate component with its own subscription lifetime. They all need the open queue for the same team, so they can use the same client, key, and loader:

client := soroi.NewClient(soroi.Options{
    StaleTime: 5 * time.Second,
    Timeout:   5 * time.Second,
})

key := fmt.Sprintf("team:%s:incidents:open", teamID)
load := func(ctx context.Context) ([]Incident, error) {
    return api.ListOpen(ctx, teamID)
}

panels := map[string]*soroi.QueryHandle[[]Incident]{
    "list":    soroi.Query(client, key, load),
    "detail":  soroi.Query(client, key, load),
    "summary": soroi.Query(client, key, load),
}

Within this client, overlapping loads for that key share the same work. A pane that subscribes while the result is still fresh can reuse it. The detail pane can select an incident from this dataset without making another request for fields the queue already contains.

The team ID belongs in the key. A different team, permission scope, or server-side filter needs a distinct key when it changes the result. Also, keep the cached slice read-only; an acknowledgement should go through the service.

When every pane always lives and closes with the parent screen, a single parent subscription can be simpler. Independent handles are useful when the components have their own lifetimes.

Let Bubble Tea receive the changes

A query subscription needs a small bridge into Bubble Tea. Each command waits for one notification and returns a message. It never changes the model from a background goroutine.

// incidentsMsg carries one pane's query state onto the UI loop.
type incidentsMsg struct {
    // panel identifies the component receiving this snapshot.
    panel string
    // state contains read-only data and the current loading result.
    state soroi.Snapshot[[]Incident]
}

// waitForIncidents delivers one notification to Bubble Tea.
func waitForIncidents(panel string, query *soroi.QueryHandle[[]Incident]) tea.Cmd {
    return func() tea.Msg {
        state, ok := <-query.Updates()
        if !ok {
            return nil
        }
        return incidentsMsg{panel: panel, state: state}
    }
}

The screen starts a receive for each mounted pane:

// Init starts the mounted panes' subscription commands.
func (m incidentBoard) Init() tea.Cmd {
    return tea.Batch(
        waitForIncidents("list", m.panels["list"]),
        waitForIncidents("detail", m.panels["detail"]),
        waitForIncidents("summary", m.panels["summary"]),
    )
}

When Update receives a snapshot, it stores it and returns the next receive command for that pane:

case incidentsMsg:
    m.states[msg.panel] = msg.state
    if msg.panel == "list" && m.selectedID == "" && len(msg.state.Data) > 0 {
        m.selectedID = msg.state.Data[0].ID
    }
    return m, waitForIncidents(msg.panel, m.panels[msg.panel])

That last return keeps the subscription going after the initial load. The queue and detail can briefly show different phases because their messages are processed separately. These notifications carry the latest query state; intermediate states can be skipped. Incident history belongs in the service's audit trail.

Keep the queue visible when a refresh fails

During an incident, a failed refresh should leave the responder with the last known queue and a visible error. HasData, Fetching, and Err let the screen express that directly:

// renderIncidents preserves the queue while reporting refresh failures.
func renderIncidents(state soroi.Snapshot[[]Incident]) string {
    var out strings.Builder
    switch {
    case !state.HasData && state.Err != nil:
        fmt.Fprintf(&out, "Could not load incidents: %v\n", state.Err)
    case !state.HasData:
        out.WriteString("Loading incidents...\n")
    case state.Err != nil:
        fmt.Fprintf(&out, "Refresh failed; showing previous incidents: %v\n", state.Err)
    case state.Fetching:
        out.WriteString("Refreshing incidents...\n")
    }
    for _, incident := range state.Data {
        fmt.Fprintf(&out, "%s  %s  %s  %s\n",
            incident.ID, incident.Severity, incident.Service, incident.Owner)
    }
    return out.String()
}

An initial failure has no queue to display. A later failure can retain the previous data. Keeping those cases separate avoids turning a temporary API outage into an empty incident list that looks like everything has been resolved.

Acknowledge an incident, then reload the queue

The acknowledgement is an HTTP write. It belongs in a tea.Cmd so that moving around the terminal stays responsive while the request runs.

// acknowledgedMsg reports the result of the acknowledgement request.
type acknowledgedMsg struct {
    // err is the service or transport error, if the write failed.
    err error
}

// acknowledge runs the business write outside the UI loop.
func acknowledge(parent context.Context, api *incidentAPI, id string) tea.Cmd {
    return func() tea.Msg {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 3*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        return acknowledgedMsg{err: api.Acknowledge(ctx, id)}
    }
}

On completion, Update clears the pending state and invalidates the shared queue only if the write succeeded:

case acknowledgedMsg:
    m.saving = false
    m.actionErr = msg.err
    if msg.err == nil {
        m.actionErr = m.client.Invalidate(m.key)
    }
    return m, nil

Invalidation marks the queue stale and starts a refresh for the active observers. The panes keep their previous incidents while that read runs, then receive the updated owner through their subscriptions.

The key handler prevents repeated acknowledgements while one is pending. Pressing r requests a refresh of the same queue:

case "a":
    if m.saving || m.selectedID == "" {
        return m, nil
    }
    m.saving = true
    m.actionErr = nil
    return m, acknowledge(m.ctx, m.api, m.selectedID)
case "r":
    m.actionErr = m.client.Invalidate(m.key)
    return m, nil

The five-second freshness window doesn't poll the service. Changes made by other responders become visible after a later read or explicit invalidation. A live feed or polling schedule would still need to trigger that work. If the screen also loads a separate incident timeline, invalidate its key when the write affects it; soroi doesn't infer that relationship.

Keep selection and cleanup predictable

A refreshed queue can come back in a different order. The selected incident should be tracked by ID, so that a responder doesn't accidentally acknowledge a different row after a refresh. The detail pane resolves that ID against its own snapshot:

state := m.states["detail"]
if !state.HasData {
    return "Waiting for incident details..."
}
if m.selectedID == "" {
    return "Select an incident."
}
for _, incident := range state.Data {
    if incident.ID == m.selectedID {
        return fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s\nOwner: %s",
            incident.ID, incident.Service, incident.Owner)
    }
}
return "The selected incident is no longer in the open queue."

The application also owns the client and the handles it creates. Release them on terminal exit and on startup failure:

// runBoard releases subscriptions and shared work when the terminal exits.
func runBoard(api *incidentAPI, teamID string) error {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
    defer cancel()
    client := soroi.NewClient(soroi.Options{StaleTime: 5 * time.Second})
    defer client.Close()

    board := newBoard(ctx, api, client, teamID)
    for _, query := range board.panels {
        defer query.Close()
    }
    _, err := tea.NewProgram(board, tea.WithContext(ctx)).Run()
    return err
}

Closing a handle releases its waiting receive command. Closing the shared client cancels its query work. Business commands use the program's context too, so an acknowledgement doesn't keep running indefinitely after the operator exits.

This pattern fits terminal tools whose components have independent lifetimes and keep reading the same remote data. A screen with one data consumer can stay with a regular tea.Cmd; there's little shared query work to coordinate.

title: Collaborative Video Rooms: Participant Tokens, Reconnect Backfill, and Artifact Control
description:
The page fires: cursor_rejoin_gap crossed its error-budget threshold while a four-player level-design session remained on video. The on-call view shows a room that exists, three editors whose cursors recovered, and one participant who reconnected but never received the missed operations. A green room dashboard is beside the point. What page fired, and can it identify the participant, meeting, last acknowledged sequence, and token rights?

TL;DR: create each video room once on the server, read it back before admission, and issue a separate token whose identity and publish/subscribe rights match each participant. Treat reconnect and cursor backfill as application state, not as a side effect of WebRTC. Provision a private artifact bucket through the same authenticated API boundary, but do not claim that room creation alone persists cursor history: the verified storage surface here establishes and inspects the bucket, while an object-write capability must be discovered and validated before production use.

That distinction decides whether the 3 a.m. action is precise or theatrical.

What should have paged first?

The late page measures visible damage. The earlier signal is a failed admission invariant: room creation succeeded, the read-back did not confirm the same meeting, a participant token was not issued with the intended rights, or a reconnecting client asked for operations after sequence 1842 and the server could not produce a contiguous suffix. Alert on that invariant before alerting on a vague count of connected sockets.

For a collaborative game editor, video and cursor state have different recovery rules. WebRTC carries the call. The application owns cursor events, acknowledgements, and backfill. A cursor can be ephemeral during steady state and still require a short ordered history after a disconnect; video media does not provide that history. The W3C specification defines the browser WebRTC surface, but it does not define your meeting idempotency key, editor identity, authorization policy, or operation log.

The useful event record is small: meeting_id, participant_id, connection_epoch, sequence, last_acked_sequence, and a server timestamp. Those fields are an instrumentation recommendation, not vendor response fields. Emit them at admission, disconnect, replay start, and replay completion. A page should say which invariant broke, rather than asking the responder to infer it from four dashboards.

Start there.

How should Node.js create a video room and mint participant tokens?

The order matters. Derive one stable idempotency key from the meeting ID, create the room server-side, read the room back, then mint one credential per participant. Never mint a shared credential for a lobby. Identity and publish/subscribe rights belong to the individual token because a spectator, an editor, and a host do not have the same authority.

Keep the browser away from the service key. An Express admission handler should enforce this sequence; the reference gateway below uses Go because explicit transport behavior is easier to audit. It accepts request bodies already validated against the provider's live discovery schema, forwards only two verified write routes, confirms the room through the verified read route, uses explicit methods, surfaces error bodies, and honors Retry-After on 429 responses.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var baseURL = os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")

type admission struct {
    MeetingID   string          `json:"meeting_id"`
    RoomCreate json.RawMessage `json:"room_create"`
    TokenIssue json.RawMessage `json:"token_issue"`
}

func call(client *http.Client, method, path, idem string, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idem != "" { req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idem) }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { return nil, readErr }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(data)))
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: rate-limit retries exhausted", method, path)
}

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost { http.Error(w, "method not allowed", 405); return }
    var in admission
    if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&in); err != nil || in.MeetingID == "" {
        http.Error(w, "invalid admission request", 400); return
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    room, err := call(client, http.MethodPost, "/rtc/room/create", "meeting:"+in.MeetingID, in.RoomCreate)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), 502); return }
    _, err = call(client, http.MethodGet, "/rtc/room/get/"+url.PathEscape(in.MeetingID), "", nil)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), 502); return }
    token, err := call(client, http.MethodPost, "/rtc/token/issue", "", in.TokenIssue)
    if err != nil { http.Error(w, err.Error(), 502); return }
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]json.RawMessage{"room": room, "token": token})
}

func main() {
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" { panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required") }
    if baseURL == "" { panic("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required") }
    http.HandleFunc("/admit", handler)
    if err := http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

The storage handoff has an important boundary. The verified storage routes can create and inspect a bucket, but the supplied route set contains no object-write operation. Claiming this sample uploads cursor history would be fiction. Query the public discovery surface for the current object-write capability and its full JSON Schema before implementing that step; keep the resulting bucket private or signed-only, and never forward the service Authorization header to a presigned URL. This is a deliberate stop line, not a guessed endpoint.

Do not guess.

Reconnect must prove continuity

A reconnect is a new transport epoch for an existing participant. The server should reject an identity change, verify that the room still exists, and compare the client's last acknowledged sequence with the retained operation range. If sequence 1842 was acknowledged and 1843 through 1861 remain available, replay that closed interval, wait for acknowledgement, then switch the participant to the live stream. Do not interleave live sequence 1862 ahead of replayed sequence 1849.

No magic here.

The first design assumption is usually that reconnect means minting another token and reopening the transport. It fails because transport recovery says nothing about the missing application operations. The correction is measurable: admission completes only after room read-back, while recovery completes only after the client acknowledges the final replayed sequence. Those are separate state transitions and should produce separate events. The trade-off is explicit: retaining more operations improves recovery odds but increases storage and replay work; retaining fewer makes snapshot rebuilds more common. Pick that boundary from observed reconnect gaps, then record it in the runbook.

If the requested sequence has fallen outside retention, return an explicit snapshot-required outcome and rebuild editor state from a snapshot plus later operations. The precise retention duration is a product decision driven by reconnect behavior and storage cost; no verified duration is available here, so a hard-coded promise would be misleading. Instrument replay_requested, replay_oldest_available, replay_count, and replay_complete. Page on repeated continuity failures for active sessions, while a single mobile-network reconnect belongs in telemetry rather than someone's bedroom.

The bucket handoff matters because session artifacts can live in a bucket the application controls rather than being implicitly governed by a video vendor's retention policy. Infrai provides one key for both capability groups through one plain REST API, so there is no SDK to install or client-library version to maintain. It is a credible fit when that operational boundary matters. The corresponding cost is concentrated dependency: one vendor, one bill, and one outage surface. Write that risk into the review.

The alternatives change what you operate

LiveKit separates rooms, access tokens, and recording or egress concerns, and offers cloud and self-hosted deployment paths. Daily exposes meeting tokens and rooms through its API, with recording artifacts governed by its recording model. Twilio Video uses Rooms and access tokens inside the broader Twilio account model. Agora is another established RTC option with token authentication. Amazon S3 supplies the independent object-storage half of a composable stack.

Cursor synchronization also deserves a separate build-or-buy decision. Ably and Pusher provide managed pub/sub primitives when the team wants to keep its own operation model; Liveblocks is more directly aimed at collaborative application state and presence. Socket.IO is a familiar self-operated transport layer, while Supabase Realtime fits naturally when the shared state already lives in Postgres. None of those choices removes the need to define ordered backfill, but each moves a different amount of connection management away from the application.

Stack Admission and artifacts Operational trade-off
LiveKit plus S3 LiveKit room credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; glue for identity, lifecycle, and failure correlation; self-hosting can increase control and on-call scope
Daily plus S3 Daily room credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; hosted video, while application code owns the cross-provider handoff
Twilio Video plus S3 Twilio access credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; broad communications ecosystem, with incident evidence split across providers
Agora plus S3 Agora project credentials; separate AWS credentials Two signups and two credential sets; RTC focus, while artifact correlation remains application glue
Unified REST boundary One credential for room and bucket operations Less credential sprawl, but dependency and blast radius are concentrated

This is not a feature-count contest. Choose LiveKit when deployment control or its ecosystem outweighs the extra storage boundary. Choose Daily when a hosted call API fits the team and separate S3 operations are already routine. Twilio can make sense when communications already live under that account; Agora deserves evaluation for teams centered on its RTC platform. Choose the unified boundary when reducing credential and integration surfaces matters more than vendor separation, after validating every required storage capability through discovery.

Own the trade-off.

Tune the page, then pay its false-positive cost

The instrumentation change moves the alert from “room looks unhealthy” to “active participant cannot prove ordered recovery.” Start with a multi-window condition: page only when continuity failures persist and affect an active collaborative session; send isolated token denials, expired credentials, and ordinary reconnects to a lower-urgency channel with meeting and participant identifiers attached. Exact thresholds require your traffic distribution. Inventing a universal percentage would turn an operational judgment into cargo culting.

A threshold that is too loose misses a broken replay path until editors report jumping cursors. A threshold that is too tight wakes someone for every laptop sleep cycle. Both outcomes consume reliability budget, but only one appears on an availability chart, which is why I distrust a dashboard that cannot tell me the exact page it would fire. Test the alert by deliberately dropping a connection after a known sequence, reconnecting with that acknowledgement, and verifying ordered replay before the live stream resumes. Then test the gap-outside-retention path.

The decision rule is compact: confirm before admission, scope every participant, order every replay, and keep artifact ownership explicit. If the page cannot name which one failed, the instrumentation is unfinished.

Fix the signal first.

Further reading

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • LiveKit rooms and participants: https://docs.livekit.io/home/get-started/api-primitives/
  • Daily meeting tokens: https://docs.daily.co/reference/rest-api/meeting-tokens
  • Twilio Video Rooms: https://www.twilio.com/docs/video/api/rooms-resource
  • Agora token authentication: https://docs.agora.io/en/video-calling/develop/authentication-workflow
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Ably connection state recovery: https://ably.com/docs/connect/states
  • Pusher Channels: https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • Liveblocks storage: https://liveblocks.io/docs/ready-made-features/multiplayer/storage

title: Testando um agente de IA antes de deixar ele escrever no CRM (com pytest)
description:
Agente de IA conectado ao CRM costuma ser testado assim: manda umas mensagens no WhatsApp, vê se a resposta ficou boa e libera. Só que a resposta boa não diz nada sobre o que foi gravado no banco.

A ideia aqui é tirar o LLM da equação e testar a camada que decide gravar. O modelo devolve uma proposta de ação, e o backend valida antes de executar. Essa camada é código determinístico, então dá para cobrir com testes comuns.

A camada de decisão 

# decisao.py
import unicodedata
import phonenumbers


def chave_nome(nome: str) -> str:
    """Chave só para BUSCAR possíveis duplicados. Nunca para sobrescrever o nome."""
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", nome).casefold().strip()


def invisiveis(texto: str) -> list[str]:
    return [
        f"U+{ord(c):04X}"
        for c in texto
        if unicodedata.category(c) == "Cf"
        or (unicodedata.category(c) == "Zs" and c != " ")
    ]


def telefone_e164(raw: str, regiao: str = "BR") -> str:
    numero = phonenumbers.parse(raw, regiao)
    return phonenumbers.format_number(numero, phonenumbers.PhoneNumberFormat.E164)


def decidir(proposta: dict, candidatos: list, eventos_processados: set) -> str:
    if proposta["event_id"] in eventos_processados:
        return "ignorar"
    if len(candidatos) != 1:
        return "revisao_humana"
    if not proposta.get("confirmado_pelo_cliente"):
        return "pedir_confirmacao"
    return "gravar"


def processar(proposta, candidatos, eventos_processados, fila, crm):
    decisao = decidir(proposta, candidatos, eventos_processados)
    if decisao == "ignorar":
        return decisao
    if decisao == "revisao_humana":
        fila.append({"event_id": proposta["event_id"], "motivo": "identificacao_ambigua"})
    elif decisao == "gravar":
        crm.append({"contato": candidatos[0], **proposta["campos"]})
    eventos_processados.add(proposta["event_id"])
    return decisao

Os testes 

# test_decisao.py
from decisao import chave_nome, invisiveis, telefone_e164, processar


def proposta(event_id="evt-1", confirmado=True):
    return {"event_id": event_id, "campos": {"endereco": "Rua X, 120"},
            "confirmado_pelo_cliente": confirmado}


# 1. Nomes visualmente iguais geram a mesma chave de busca
def test_nome_com_acento_combinante():
    assert chave_nome("Joa\u0303o") == chave_nome("João")

def test_nome_com_letra_estilizada():
    assert chave_nome("𝐉𝐨𝐚𝐨") == "joao"


# 2. Mesmo telefone em formatos diferentes
def test_telefone_normalizado():
    assert telefone_e164("(27) 99999-0000") == "+5527999990000"
    assert telefone_e164("+55 27 99999 0000") == "+5527999990000"


# 3. Caracteres invisíveis são detectados, não apagados
def test_espaco_largura_zero():
    assert invisiveis("Ana\u200bSilva") == ["U+200B"]

def test_espaco_nao_separavel():
    assert invisiveis("Ana\u00a0Silva") == ["U+00A0"]


# 4. Sem confirmação explícita, nada é gravado
def test_sem_confirmacao_nao_grava():
    fila, crm = [], []
    r = processar(proposta(confirmado=False), ["id_1"], set(), fila, crm)
    assert r == "pedir_confirmacao" and crm == []


# 5. Ambiguidade vai para humano, e o humano recebe de fato
def test_duas_marinas_vao_para_fila():
    fila, crm = [], []
    r = processar(proposta(), ["marina_1", "marina_2"], set(), fila, crm)
    assert r == "revisao_humana"
    assert crm == []
    assert fila[0]["motivo"] == "identificacao_ambigua"


# Bônus: webhook reentregue não duplica
def test_idempotencia():
    fila, crm, eventos = [], [], set()
    processar(proposta(), ["id_1"], eventos, fila, crm)
    processar(proposta(), ["id_1"], eventos, fila, crm)
    assert len(crm) == 1

pip install pytest phonenumbers
pytest -v

Repare que nenhum teste chama o LLM. Esse é o ponto: se a segurança do seu cadastro depende de o modelo "se comportar", ela não é testável. Se depende de uma camada de decisão, é.

Em produção, a idempotência deve ficar no banco (constraint UNIQUE no event_id), não num set em memória. Aqui é só para o exemplo rodar.

Os 5 cenários completos

Os testes acima vêm de um roteiro que publicamos no Algoritmo Diário, com o raciocínio de cada cenário (Unicode NFC × NFKC, E.164, confirmação × consentimento na LGPD, handoff) e uma matriz de QA para rodar antes de liberar a integração:

👉 A IA respondeu certo, mas cadastrou o cliente errado: 5 testes antes de conectar um agente ao CRM

Que outro cenário vocês colocariam nessa suíte?

title: Candidate Rubric Audio: Startup Speech-to-Text API Compare with OpenAI and EU Controls
description:
Do not choose the speech-to-text provider with the smallest per-minute number. For a healthtech product that scores candidates against a job rubric, first run OpenAI, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and Google Cloud against the same consented corpus, then reject any option that cannot explain minimum billing, asynchronous completion, and EU data handling at tenant level. This is a procurement experiment, not a pricing-page screenshot.

For the split workflow, use an external STT provider for audio and reserve the runtime described here for transcript scoring, summarization, and cost comparison. Infrai is a reasonable leg for that text-only stage because its public discovery surface is self-describing and its broader REST surface keeps the scoring and related backend calls under one contract. It is not the STT engine in this decision: the discovered ASR capability is marked available=false.

The recommendation is specific: teams that already have external transcription and want candidate-rubric processing plus cost evidence in one HTTP surface should try Infrai for the post-transcription leg. Its second useful property is operationally different from one-key billing: documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, which reduces the amount of adapter code a Go worker team must translate and maintain. A specialist STT product remains the better choice when audio quality controls, language coverage, or provider-specific EU guarantees dominate.

That boundary matters at 03:00.

How should an EU startup compare speech-to-text for candidate scoring?

Start with a fixed, consented corpus rather than a vendor demo. Include short voice notes, meeting excerpts, and calls containing the terms your rubric must detect. Label every item with tenant ID, language, duration, and the rubric fields expected in the final score. Keep synthetic or approved test data in the first run until the provider's processing region, retention behavior, deletion path, and subprocessors have passed review.

The first comparison fields are per-minute pricing, minimum billing unit, language support, and webhook or asynchronous support. Add transcript quality against a small human reference, but do not let a quality score hide untraceable accounting. A 30-second clip, a clip just over the minimum unit, and a longer clip crossing the asynchronous boundary expose different failure modes. If those records cannot be joined to a tenant and request ID, the accounting test has failed.

The vendors answer different procurement questions. OpenAI is a sensible candidate when an existing OpenAI client and model workflow reduce application changes. Deepgram deserves a direct test when speech-focused controls and transcription operations are central. AssemblyAI should be checked for the job lifecycle and webhook behavior around transcript processing. Google Cloud belongs in the matrix when an established Google Cloud organization, regional governance, and platform controls carry more weight than a narrow API surface. These are hypotheses for the same test, not benchmark results.

Keep the downstream rubric model as a separate comparison. Anthropic and Gemini are reasonable candidates when the evaluation emphasizes long-context reasoning or an existing cloud relationship; OpenRouter and Together are useful when model choice and routing matter more than a single model vendor. They do not replace the four STT legs, and they do not answer the EU audio-retention question. Treating them as post-transcription alternatives prevents a text-model choice from contaminating the audio decision.

Test Pass condition Failure action
Accuracy Each language and audio class meets the reviewed threshold Reject the affected provider or class
Billing Billed duration joins to tenant and request ID Require evidence or reject
Minimum unit Small clips have a known billing increment Recalculate with the real increment
Async operation Long clips have a documented completion and retry path Prefer a usable job flow
EU handling Region and retention behavior match the review Stop the production trial

The decision rule is conjunctive: one hard privacy or accounting failure removes a provider, even if its transcript reads well. Among the survivors, choose the lowest measured total cost for this corpus, including minimum units and retries. Do not import a 2025 comparison into a 2026 purchase decision; prices and product behavior need a current check.

The invoice is part of the incident record.

Why is the audio boundary important here?

The runtime exposes a documented audio-transcription shape, but the current model directory marks ASR available=false; a route shape in discovery is not proof of a usable transcription service. Compare external STT vendors first for this job.

The runtime's cost tools are better aligned with the text after transcription: estimate rubric extraction, summarization, or other post-processing, then compare the resulting text-model usage. A split setup is reasonable when the application already uses LLMs. External STT handles audio, while the runtime handles the text path and its cost evidence. The practical limit is explicit: a model listed in discovery is not automatically ready for the job, so check the availability field before wiring a production path.

The useful platform trade-off is breadth behind a simple surface. Live discovery describes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, and the discovery surface is public without a key. That gives a Go worker a way to inspect the available boundary before it sends a request, while a consistent REST contract lets the same text workflow run without adding another SDK-specific client. The 10-language runnable examples are a practical supporting advantage: they lower translation work when a service is written in Go but another team owns a neighboring integration.

There is a cost to consolidation. One platform concentrates trust and failure, and a specialist provider may offer controls that matter more for audio than a broad backend surface. This is why the STT provider and the post-processing runtime should remain separate decision legs.

Can a Go worker leave usable cost evidence?

Yes, for the text leg, begin with a real token-count request and record its response with the transcript job ID and tenant ID in the worker's own structured logs. The example below uses the verified token-count route, an explicit method, environment-based authentication, and full response-status handling. It does not pretend that a token count is an audio transcription.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    body := []byte(`{"text":"candidate transcript for rubric scoring"}`)
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

    res, err := (&http.Client{}).Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    data, err := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("token count failed: %s: %s", res.Status, data))
    }
    fmt.Println(string(data))
}

For a quick smoke test, the same request can be represented directly as a complete shell command. Read the credential from the environment; no credential belongs in source control.

curl -X POST "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/tokens/count" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"text":"candidate transcript for rubric scoring"}'

In production, a 429 response needs exponential backoff and the Retry-After value when present; a retry around any write also needs a client-supplied idempotency key. This example is deliberately one read-like accounting call, so it does not disguise those write semantics behind a generic helper. The response still needs to be associated with the external STT job ID, tenant, and rubric version in the worker's own record.

The alternative is a collection of specialist services: an STT vendor, a text-model client, and separate observability or billing plumbing. That may be the right architecture if the organization already operates those systems or requires independent failure domains. The broad REST surface reduces integration friction for the post-transcription workflow; it does not remove the need to evaluate audio vendors on their own terms.

How do you verify and roll back the choice?

Run the corpus twice: once clean, and once with interrupted polling, duplicate webhook delivery, and a rejected request. Reconcile every item to tenant, provider, duration, transcript result, and final cost. For each 30-second clip, preserve the original duration and the provider's billed duration; that pair is the smallest useful audit record when a minimum billing unit changes the result. Keep the corpus manifest immutable between runs, record which provider revision and region handled each item, and retain the exact rubric version used for scoring. Otherwise a later comparison can look like a price change when it is really a changed sample or policy. Test EU deletion and retention with synthetic data before customer data enters the path. Then inspect a failed rubric extraction: can the on-call engineer identify the transcript job, the text request, and the tenant that owns the cost?

Rollback should preserve the boundary. Put the external STT adapter behind a feature flag, retain the provider's transcript job ID, and route new audio to the previously accepted provider while the failed leg is reviewed. Do not quietly move stored EU audio to a different region during rollback; that is a data-governance change, not an incident-response detail.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the live capability manifest at https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt. Select the STT provider that passes the corpus, accounting, and EU review, then use the runtime only where its available text capabilities are verified.

References

  • Infrai capability manifest: https://docs.infrai.cc/llms.txt
  • OpenAI API pricing: https://openai.com/api/pricing/

title: Kubernetes: un runbook para fallos de email
description:
Un pipeline puede mostrar un pod saludable y, aun así, fallar cuando necesita leer un email de verificación. Este caso confunde porque mezcla varias dependencias: Kubernetes, la cola del mensaje, el proveedor de correo y el buzón que usa el test.

En una guardia, la pregunta “¿llegó el correo?” no ayuda mucho. Es mejor preguntar en qué capa se perdió la señal y qué evidencia tenemos. Este runbook propone una forma corta de investigar el fallo sin reiniciar todo el cluster a ciegas.

El síntoma: el pod está verde y el pipeline rojo

El test crea una cuenta, espera un mensaje y termina con timeout. Mientras tanto, kubectl get pods muestra todos los pods en Running. Eso solo confirma que el proceso sigue vivo; no confirma que el worker haya consumido el evento ni que el mensaje haya llegado al buzón correcto.

Los síntomas más comunes son:

  • el evento de signup se creó, pero no entró en la cola;
  • el worker reintentó con una configuración antigua;
  • el mensaje llegó a otra dirección o fue filtrado;
  • el test empezó a buscar antes de guardar su hora de inicio;
  • el buzón de prueba fue compartido por dos jobs.

La diferencia parece pequeña, pero cambia por completo la acción siguiente. Reiniciar el deployment no arregla un selector de buzón incorrecto.

Primero separa las capas del fallo

Me gusta dividir la investigación en cuatro comprobaciones, en este orden:

  1. Aplicación: ¿el endpoint aceptó el signup y devolvió un identificador de evento?
  2. Cola y worker: ¿el evento fue procesado, cuántos intentos tuvo y qué error devolvió el proveedor?
  3. Buzón: ¿el mensaje aparece en el buzón reservado para este job, después de la hora de disparo?
  4. Test: ¿el parser encontró el enlace correcto y respetó el timeout esperado?

Esto evita que SRE trate todos los fallos como un problema de infraestructura. Si el evento nunca salió de la aplicación, escalar el tamaño del pod solo añade ruido.

Para tests que usan un correo temporal gratis, también conviene registrar el identificador del buzón, el job que lo reservó y el instante exacto de creación. No hace falta guardar el contenido completo del mensaje en los logs del cluster.

Un runbook pequeño para investigar

El primer paso es guardar un contexto de ejecución. Un nombre de job, un run_id y un correlation_id deben viajar desde el test hasta el evento de correo. En los logs de la aplicación, buscaría algo parecido a esto:

run_id=ci-4821 correlation_id=signup-91 event=email.requested status=queued

Después revisaría, de forma acotada, los eventos del worker para ese identificador. La pregunta no es solo si hubo un error, sino si el error es transitorio, permanente o causado por datos del test.

El tercer paso es comparar relojes. El test debe guardar triggered_at antes de solicitar el email y buscar mensajes recibidos después de ese momento. Si usa “el último mensaje” sin una frontera temporal, puede aceptar un correo viejo y producir un resultado intermitente.

También reviso el aislamiento. Dos pods de CI no deberían consumir el mismo buzón de prueba. Una reserva simple con TTL, el nombre del job y una liberación al terminar suele ser suficiente para empezar. Si la reserva caduca mientras el test sigue esperando, el fallo debe decirlo claramente; de lo contrario parece un problema aleatorio de red.

En el frontend, vale la pena separar emails de signup por escenario para que una prueba de recuperación no termine leyendo el correo de un alta. Y la interfaz debería mostrar estados de carga claros en flujos de email, incluso cuando el backend todavía está esperando.

Diseña los tiempos y reintentos

Un timeout no es una estrategia de recuperación. Define tres tiempos por separado:

  • poll interval: cada cuánto consulta el test;
  • provider timeout: cuánto puede tardar la aceptación del proveedor;
  • test deadline: cuánto espera el pipeline antes de fallar.

Por ejemplo, un polling de cinco segundos durante un minuto deja doce oportunidades de lectura. Ese número no debe copiarse sin pensar: debe ser mayor que la latencia normal del sistema y menor que el tiempo que el job puede ocupar recursos sin aportar información.

Los reintentos también necesitan una frontera. Reintentar la consulta del buzón tiene sentido; crear otra cuenta y enviar otro email puede ocultar el fallo original. Cada intento debe conservar su run_id, su hora y la razón por la que el mensaje anterior fue rechazado.

Durante una revisión, alguien puede escribir búsquedas como tamp mail com o temp mailid al buscar servicios de prueba. Esos términos sirven como ruido de diagnóstico, no como valores válidos de configuración. Hay que mantenerlos fuera de nombres de variables, etiquetas y reglas de alertas.

Checklist de cierre para SRE

Antes de cerrar el incidente, comprueba:

  • [ ] el evento de signup tiene un identificador rastreable;
  • [ ] la cola registra el resultado final y el número de intentos;
  • [ ] el buzón pertenece a un solo job y tiene TTL;
  • [ ] el test usa una frontera temporal, no solo el mensaje más reciente;
  • [ ] los logs omiten contenido sensible del email;
  • [ ] el alerta enlaza al run_id y a la causa observada;
  • [ ] el runbook dice qué hacer si falla cada capa.

Un buen cierre no es “repetimos el pipeline y pasó”. Es “la primera ejecución falló porque el worker usó una credencial antigua; la segunda pasó después de corregir la configuración”. Esa frase permite aprender y evita que el siguiente turno empiece desde cero.

Q&A rápido

¿Debo aumentar el timeout cuando falla un test de email?

Solo después de comprobar la latencia real y la frontera temporal. Un timeout mayor puede esconder un mensaje que nunca se envió o un buzón equivocado.

¿Es mejor reiniciar el worker?

Si hay un error transitorio y el runbook lo contempla, quizá. Primero captura los logs y el estado de la cola; reiniciar antes puede borrar la mejor evidencia.

¿Qué métrica seguiría primero?

La proporción de eventos que pasan de requested a delivered dentro del deadline del test. Separaría esa métrica por entorno y causa de fallo, porque un promedio global suele tapar los jobs más lentos.

La idea central es sencilla: Kubernetes mantiene procesos, pero no garantiza por sí solo el contrato completo de un email. Cuando cada capa deja una señal pequeña y relacionada con el mismo run_id, el fallo deja de ser una adivinanza y se convierte en una investigación repetible.

title: Refund Sloth 🦥: Local AI Agents That Get Your Money Back While You Nap
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Somewhere between 48% and 79% of us have paid for a free trial we forgot to cancel. The average person loses $187–$540 a year to forgotten trials, missed return windows and subscriptions they stopped using. We think we spend about $86 a month on subscriptions; it's closer to $219. And 44% of people keep a subscription simply because cancelling is a chore.

That's the most sloth-shaped problem I know: the money is recoverable, but only if you do boring admin before a deadline.

Refund Sloth 🦥 does the boring part. You drop receipts, order emails and your bank statement into one folder (or let it read your mailbox) and go to sleep. At 2 AM a team of six local AI agents wakes up:

  • 🔭 Scout finds new files through the official filesystem MCP server, locked to the inbox.
  • 📖 Reader reads receipt photos with a vision model, and PDFs and emails with a text model, into strict JSON.
  • 🦅 Deadline Hawk works out return-by, trial-end, warranty and renewal dates and creates calendar reminders.
  • 🧾 Auditor finds recurring charges in your bank CSV and flags 🧟 zombie, 👯 duplicate and 📈 price-hiked subscriptions.
  • 👻 Ghostwriter drafts the cancellation and return emails.
  • 🦥 Sloth Boss reviews everything with tool calls and writes your morning brief.

In the morning you get a notification:

🦥 3 deadlines this week · $86.96/mo you can cut · 10 drafts ready
Most urgent: ⏳ Peacock Premium free trial ends 2026-10-23 ($7.99 at stake).

You open the dashboard, click Approve & copy, paste, send. Or click Cancel now ↗ to jump straight to the store's cancel page. Total effort: about 30 seconds. The sloth never sends or pays anything itself: a human stays in the loop, always.

Even lazier extras:

  • 📬 Connect mail (optional): give it a Gmail, iCloud or Outlook app password and it fetches order, trial and renewal emails by itself. The mailbox is opened read-only, and the password is stored encrypted on your machine (macOS Keychain / Windows DPAPI).
  • 🚨 Urgent popup: anything ending in the next 2 days gets its own desktop notification and a red banner at the top of the dashboard.
  • ↗️ Cancel now: every trial, subscription and return has a button that opens the store's cancel or return page. No more hunting for the hidden cancel link.
  • 🖥️ Runs on macOS and Windows.

Who gets to be lazier? Anyone with a stack of receipts in a drawer, a "free" trial they meant to cancel, and a gym membership they've been "about to use again" since March.

Demo

Today: the urgent banner, the morning brief, and money saved vs. money at risk.

Subscriptions: zombies, duplicates and price hikes, each with a Cancel link.

Action queue: ready-to-send emails. Nothing leaves without your click.

All data in the demo is fake (generated fixtures). No real receipts or bank statements were harmed.

Code

amangithub01 / refund-sloth

🦥 Local AI agents that get your money back while you nap. Open-weight models (Ollama) + MCP, no API keys, no cloud.

🦥 Refund Sloth

Local AI agents that get your money back while you nap. Drop receipts, order emails and bank statements into a folder. Overnight, a team of open-weight models running on your laptop finds forgotten free trials, closing return windows, expiring warranties and zombie subscriptions, then drafts the cancellation and return emails for you. In the morning you click Approve.

No API keys. No cloud. $0 per run. Works with Wi-Fi off.

🎬 Demo

▶️ Full-quality video: docs/media/refund-sloth-demo.mp4 (26 s, demo data, fake "today" = 2026-10-21)

📸 Screenshots

Landing Scroll: the laptop orbit
Today: urgent banner + morning brief Deadlines
Subscriptions: zombies, duplicates, price hikes Action queue: drafts you approve

All data in the demo is fake (eval/fixtures). No real receipts or bank statements are in this repo.

Open http://localhost:4747 for the landing page; the dashboard lives at http://localhost:4747/#today.

Why

  • 48–79% of people have paid…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Every model runs locally through Ollama. No API keys anywhere in the project.

Agent Open-weight model Why
Reader (images) qwen2.5vl:7b small, fast vision model; reads crumpled receipt photos
Reader (text), Hawk, Auditor, Ghostwriter, Boss qwen3.5:35b strong JSON output and tool calling; runs well on an M3 Max
Lite profile qwen3:8b + qwen2.5vl:3b for laptops with 8–16 GB of RAM

MCP is the backbone. I wrote five small MCP servers in TypeScript over stdio:

  • ledger (SQLite)
  • docs (PDF, image, EML, MBOX and CSV parsing)
  • calendar (.ics files with alarms)
  • notify (desktop notifications and the brief)
  • mail (read-only IMAP)

Alongside them runs the official @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem, rooted at the inbox with only its read-only tools exposed. A small harness (McpHub) starts every server, turns their tools into Ollama tool definitions and runs the agent loops. The full architecture diagram is in the README.

Hybrid by design: rules for math, models for mess. The biggest lesson: don't let an LLM do arithmetic on your money.

  • Plain code: hashing and dedup, all deadline math (document date, then policies.json, then a clearly marked AI guess), recurring-charge detection, the zombie, duplicate and price-hike flags, and every number in the brief. All unit-tested.
  • LLMs: reading messy documents, guessing return policies for unknown stores, naming bank descriptors (APPLE.COM/BILL 866-712-7753 CA → "Apple Music"), writing emails, and the Boss's review.

Structured output that doesn't break. Every LLM call uses a zod schema, converted to JSON Schema and passed to Ollama's format, then validated. On failure it retries with the validation error. Low-confidence extractions go to a "🔎 Needs a look" list instead of being silently wrong.

A lesson from the local models: prompt-only email formatting was ignored (one-line bodies, greeting the wrong company). Moving layout into deterministic post-processing fixed all of it. Small models are great at content; let code handle form.

Eval. sloth eval runs the full pipeline on fake fixtures: receipt photos, PDF invoices, order emails, an mbox, a 13-month bank CSV, and a meme that must be ignored.

Metric Score
Field accuracy (merchant / amount / date) 96.7% (29/30)
Deadline accuracy (type + date ±1 day) 100% (14/14)
Subscription recall / flag accuracy 100% / 100%
False positives 0 (the meme is correctly ignored)
Time ~3 minutes for the whole batch, fully local (M3 Max, 48 GB)

Stack: TypeScript, Node 24 (built-in node:sqlite), MCP TypeScript SDK, Ollama JS, zod, imapflow, Express 5 + SSE (a live agent log), React 19 + Vite + Tailwind v4, Vitest (39 tests).

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For this project it isn't a nice-to-have. It's the only way the project can exist.

  • Privacy. To find a forgotten trial you need someone's bank statement, receipts and order emails: their whole financial life. With a closed API, that's a nightly upload of your bank CSV to someone else's server. With open weights it never leaves the laptop. sloth doctor even fails if Ollama isn't on localhost, and the dashboard API only listens on 127.0.0.1.
  • Works offline. Nothing in the pipeline needs the internet; try it with Wi-Fi off. A 2 AM job shouldn't depend on a connection or an API being up.
  • $0 per run, forever. It runs every night. A closed API would charge per token, every night, to save me money. Ironic.
  • Swappable. Each agent's model is one line in a config. I switch between a 35B model and an 8B "lite" profile, and a single profile uses one multimodal model for everything. No vendor lock-in, and no deprecation can break my nightly job.
  • Tunable. There's a Modelfile that bakes in the Reader prompt, and because the weights are open you could fine-tune Reader on your own receipts.
  • No OAuth app for your inbox. Mail sync is plain read-only IMAP to your own provider. No cloud project, no client secret, no third party reading your mail.
  • Open standards. Because of MCP, the tools (ledger, docs, calendar, mail) work with any other MCP client, and the agents use the official filesystem server instead of me reinventing file access.

Where open worked better than closed:

  • JSON-schema-constrained decoding through Ollama's format.
  • keep_alive to keep models warm across a batch.
  • The freedom to run a tiny vision model just for photos while a bigger one does the reasoning, on hardware I already own.

My Agent Session

I built Refund Sloth with GitHub Copilot CLI as my pair programmer. It helped with:

  • planning the agent pipeline;
  • writing the MCP servers, the tests and the eval;
  • iterating on the UI with headless-Chrome screenshots;
  • recording the demo video.

Every non-obvious decision (why rules do the math, why read-only IMAP instead of OAuth, why "Cancel now" is a link and not auto-cancel) is logged in DECISIONS.md.

The Lazy Payoff

On the demo data (a realistic year of transactions), Refund Sloth found:

  • $2,424 at risk in the next 30 days: a $1,299 laptop return closing in 4 days, $348 headphones in 6, $249 AirPods in 8, and a trial that bills in 2.
  • $86.96 a month (~$1,043 a year) you can cut: a gym nobody visits ($24.99), an unused AI tool ($20), the most expensive of four streaming services ($17.99), and the extra music and cloud plans ($11.99 each).
  • 10 ready-to-send emails and 15 calendar reminders, none of which I had to write.

Doing this by hand (digging through emails, checking each store's return policy, reading a bank statement line by line, writing polite-but-firm emails) is easily 1–2 hours a month. Now it's about 30 seconds of clicking Approve. 🦥

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: built end to end with the GitHub Copilot CLI.

title: October 01, 2026
description:
BigQuery

Change

An updated version of the Simba JDBC driver for BigQuery is now available.

Feature

Chatting with graphs in conversational analytics is now generally available. You can use a combination of multiple graphs, tables, views, and UDFs as data sources.

Feature

BigQuery pipelines provides support for automated metadata enrichment and Knowledge Catalog data quality scorecard integration. In addition, the Data Engineering Agent can proactively generate semantic metadata for your pipeline assets. For more information, see Metadata enrichment and data quality scorecard integration. These features are generally available.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use Google Cloud Data Agent Kit to browse Bigtable instances and tables, design schemas, and run GoogleSQL queries from your IDE or coding agent. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Data Agent Kit is now GA: Bring Google Data Cloud to any coding agent.

Cloud Healthcare API

Feature

Preview: The FHIR bulk export Group POST feature is now available in Preview in Cloud Healthcare API v1beta1. You can invoke the $export operation on a FHIR Group by using the HTTP POST method (projects.locations.datasets.fhirStores.bulk-export-group-post) to supply export parameters in the request body rather than through URL query parameters. The request body allows filtering by a list of up to 1,000 patient references by using the patient parameter in addition to _since and _type. For more information about the specification, see the FHIR Bulk Data Access guide for $export group of patients.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: Expanded machine series support for sharing the same Hyperdisk volume between instances:

  • C3 bare metal instances support multi-writer mode for Hyperdisk Balanced volumes.
  • C4 instances created after May 1, 2026, support multi-writer mode for Hyperdisk Balanced, Hyperdisk Extreme, and Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes.

For more information, see Sharing a disk between instances.

Dataform

Feature

Dataform provides support for automated metadata enrichment and Knowledge Catalog data quality scorecard integration for Dataform workflows and BigQuery pipelines. For more information, see Add metadata for Knowledge Catalog. This feature is generally available.

Gemini Enterprise

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 2.5 Pro removal in Canada and Japan on October 20, 2026

On October 20, 2026, Gemini 2.5 Pro will be removed from the Gemini Enterprise app in the Canada and Japan in-country regions. After this date, users in these regions can't select Gemini 2.5 Pro in the Gemini Enterprise app.

Gemini 2.5 Pro remains available in the global, us, and eu regions.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Turn Gemini 2.5 Pro on or off in the web app

Administrators can turn Gemini 2.5 Pro on or off for the Gemini Enterprise web app in the global, us, and eu regions. Gemini 2.5 Pro remains turned on by default, so existing configurations aren't affected.

For more information, see Manage web app features.

Google Cloud VMware Engine

Feature

Generally available: Bring Your Own License (BYOL) license management for Google Cloud VMware Engine is generally available (GA). BYOL license management lets you register and manage portable VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) license keys in the Google Cloud console across projects associated with your Cloud Billing account.

For more information, see License management.

Network Intelligence Center

Announcement

Network Services Monitoring is available in Preview.

Network Services Monitoring visualizes communication paths and network metrics for Google Kubernetes Engine services and workloads with ambient networking enabled.

Feature

Cloud Network Insights supports using Google Cloud CLI commands to download Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services (AWS) Monitoring Point installation bundles.

Pub/Sub

Feature

You can use Gemini Enterprise to generate code for user-defined function (UDF) single-message transforms (SMTs). For more information, see Create a UDF SMT.

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
description:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: Missed Realtime Messages: 3 Sequence Rules for State Refetch
description:
Use a monotonically increasing sequence number for each property-maintenance conversation, keep the last accepted number in the browser, and fetch the authoritative conversation state as soon as the next number skips ahead. TL;DR: detect the gap, replace local state with a full snapshot, and report how often recovery happens. This is less complicated, and usually more dependable, than trying to make every typing or read-receipt event arrive exactly once.

The practical boundary matters. Typing indicators are disposable hints; read receipts affect what a manager and tenant believe has happened. Both can travel over the same realtime channel, but only the server snapshot should settle disagreement. For a solo builder, that rule keeps the recovery path small enough to understand at 2 a.m.

Infrai fits here as the REST publication and channel layer, while Express owns the authoritative maintenance snapshot. It offers one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 backend modules, but consolidation is only half the case. Infrai uses one plain REST API, so there is no SDK to install; any language or runtime can send the HTTP request. The API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. Every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, those properties let a small team inspect the live channel contract and keep recovery logic in its existing Express service instead of maintaining another client-library integration.

How should Node.js detect missed realtime messages by sequence?

There are two viable shapes.

The first is an event-replay architecture. The client records an offset, reconnects, and asks the transport or an event store to replay everything after that offset. Its invariant is strict: every retained event has a stable position and replay preserves order. This is appropriate when intermediate events are themselves business records, but retention, deduplication, and replay cursors become application concerns.

The second is snapshot recovery. A live message carries a channel sequence; the browser accepts contiguous messages and refetches the whole authoritative state after a gap. Its invariant is different: the latest server snapshot completely describes the user-visible truth. That is the shape I would ship for a maintenance thread's online members, typing indicators, and read positions. A missed typing:started event does not deserve a replay subsystem.

This choice does require discipline. A snapshot must replace local state rather than merge in guesses, and a stale fetch must not overwrite a newer message. Picture a manager opening work order 884 on a phone, losing the connection after sequence 41, and reconnecting at sequence 44. Replaying only the apparent missing item, 42, still leaves 43 unresolved; merging an old receipt into the current view can also move the manager's read marker backward. One snapshot at sequence 44 or later settles membership, typing, and receipts together. Presence accuracy comes from one authority and ordered application, not from a promise that the network never drops a packet.

Keep it dull.

Infrai can be a deliberate transport option inside the snapshot shape. A small team that also consumes other backend capabilities can use one REST API, one key, and one bill instead of maintaining keys and invoices across separate dashboards. No SDK is required for the plain HTTP interface. Its public discovery surface requires no key and describes 295 capabilities across 20 modules, including schemas and runnable examples in 10 languages; checking the current contract before wiring the transport removes guesswork from this recovery path. Teams that want a REST-oriented realtime layer and fewer backend credentials should try Infrai for message publication while keeping snapshot recovery in their own application.

Build gap recovery before tuning delivery

The example below is one runnable TypeScript file. It starts an Express server with an authoritative maintenance-thread snapshot, then acts as a client that receives sequence 1 followed by sequence 3. The client notices the missing number, fetches the whole state, and refuses to let an older recovery response replace newer state.

import express from "express";

type Receipt = { userId: string; lastReadMessageId: string };
type ThreadState = {
  channel: string;
  sequence: number;
  typingUserIds: string[];
  receipts: Receipt[];
};
type LiveMessage = { sequence: number; kind: "typing" | "receipt" };

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function getRealtimeChannel(channel: string, attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const response = await fetch(
    `https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/channel/get/${encodeURIComponent(channel)}`,
    {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    },
  );

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return getRealtimeChannel(channel, attempt + 1);
  }
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Channel fetch failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
}

const app = express();
const state: ThreadState = {
  channel: "property-17:work-order-884",
  sequence: 3,
  typingUserIds: [],
  receipts: [{ userId: "manager-4", lastReadMessageId: "message-29" }],
};

app.get("/threads/:channel/state", (request, response) => {
  if (request.params.channel !== state.channel) {
    response.status(404).json({ error: "thread not found" });
    return;
  }
  response.status(200).json(state);
});

const server = app.listen(3000, async () => {
  let local: ThreadState = {
    channel: state.channel,
    sequence: 0,
    typingUserIds: [],
    receipts: [],
  };

  async function refetchState(minimumSequence: number): Promise<void> {
    const path = `/threads/${encodeURIComponent(local.channel)}/state`;
    const response = await fetch(new URL(path, "http://localhost:3000"), {
      method: "GET",
    });
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`State fetch failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const snapshot = (await response.json()) as ThreadState;
    if (snapshot.sequence >= minimumSequence && snapshot.sequence > local.sequence) {
      local = snapshot;
    }
  }

  async function acceptRealtimeMessage(message: LiveMessage): Promise<void> {
    if (message.sequence <= local.sequence) return;
    if (message.sequence !== local.sequence + 1) {
      await refetchState(message.sequence);
      return;
    }
    local = { ...local, sequence: message.sequence };
  }

  try {
    await getRealtimeChannel(state.channel);
    await acceptRealtimeMessage({ sequence: 1, kind: "typing" });
    await acceptRealtimeMessage({ sequence: 3, kind: "receipt" });
    console.log(local);
  } finally {
    server.close();
  }
});

Run it with a TypeScript runtime after installing Express. In production, the live transport calls acceptRealtimeMessage; it is not another source of truth. The refetch endpoint is deliberately application-owned because only the application knows what a complete maintenance-thread snapshot contains.

Notice what the code does not do: it does not request sequence 2. Refetching one missing event can still leave the browser wrong if several messages vanished, arrived out of order, or summarized transient presence. A complete state response closes all of those gaps at one boundary.

Compare transports without confusing them with recovery

Transport products expose different connection and presence machinery, but none removes the need to decide what the application considers authoritative. The useful comparison is therefore about system fit, not a feature-count contest.

Option Relevant mechanism Best fit Boundary to keep visible
Socket.IO Connection-state recovery can restore a session and missed packets after a temporary disconnect Teams that want a Node-centric protocol and operate their own server Its documentation says recovery is not always successful, so the application still needs synchronization handling
Ably Presence supplies member enter, update, and leave events on channels Teams that want a managed pub/sub product with presence semantics Presence events describe channel membership; durable read truth still belongs in application state
Pusher Channels Presence channels expose subscribed members and membership events Teams already comfortable with Pusher's channel model and client libraries Membership and typing signals should not become the authoritative read-receipt store
PubNub Presence tracks occupancy and join, leave, timeout, and state-change events Systems that need a managed presence-focused feature set Occupancy signals and business acknowledgements have different durability needs
Infrai REST publication can sit beside application-owned state refetch under one credential surface Small teams consolidating several backend services behind one key Choose a specialist when transport-specific replay, client ecosystem, or deeper presence controls dominate the decision

That last boundary is important. Infrai's supporting advantage here is operational: its documented capabilities use a consistent interface and include runnable TypeScript examples, reducing the integration surface a solo team has to keep current. The limitation is equally concrete: it is not the right fit when transport-specific replay, a specialist client ecosystem, or fine-grained managed presence controls are the primary requirement. Socket.IO is the more direct choice when self-hosted Node transport control is the goal; Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub may be better when their specialist presence semantics and client tooling are the center of the product. That trade-off should be decided before the application adopts vendor-specific channel behavior.

Measure the recovery path

Count every detected gap by channel class and client version, then report the frequency. Do not treat the counter as vanity telemetry. A rising rate tells you that reconnect behavior, message ordering, or a release deserves investigation even when snapshot recovery keeps the interface correct.

Measure recovery, not optimism.

Keep the metric low-cardinality: use a category such as maintenance-thread, not a property ID or user ID. Track attempted recoveries, successful snapshot replacements, and failed refetches separately in your own observability system. No invented precision. The ratio becomes meaningful only after you define the denominator, such as received realtime messages or active channel-minutes, and keep that definition stable.

Operationally, verify three things before release. First, sequences advance within one channel scope and reset only under an explicit channel-lifecycle rule. Second, snapshot responses carry a sequence so racing responses cannot move the UI backward. Third, reconnect, duplicate, delayed, and out-of-order cases are exercised in tests. Then watch gap frequency after deployment. This short checklist protects presence accuracy more effectively than a vague claim of guaranteed delivery.

Make the boundary boring

The three rules are enough: track the last sequence, replace state after a gap, and measure recovery. Keep typing ephemeral. Keep read positions in the authoritative snapshot. Pick event replay only when intermediate events must remain individually recoverable; otherwise, snapshot recovery is the smaller system and the easier one to reason about.

If the consolidated REST boundary fits your stack, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live capability contract before integrating.

Further reading

  • Socket.IO connection state recovery
  • Ably Presence
  • Pusher Channels presence channels
  • PubNub Presence
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Infrai official documentation
