title: Case Study: Making My Portfolio Loud (Without Making It Slow)
description:
My portfolio worked fine. That was the problem.

It was a tidy neubrutalist site: yellow, cyan and green cards, thick black borders, hard drop shadows, a dark-mode toggle. And it did its job: it helped me land Oatopia, Rev6 and Digital Trek (Rodentia Pest Products) as clients.

But it looked like a lot of other neubrutalist portfolios, and a UX audit I'd been working through kept pointing out the same thing. It was clean and it was forgettable.

So I tried something I'd normally talk myself out of. I went maximalist. Kinetic type, colours that clash, stickers you can throw around, marquees that react to your scroll. Internally I called it the loud redesign.

This post covers what I built, the rules that kept it usable, and the bugs that caught me out.

Live site: vicentereyes.org

The brief I gave myself

  1. Loud, but still a portfolio. Every animation had to sit on top of real content: projects, services, testimonials, blog posts. Nothing decorative could block reading or contacting me.
  2. No new backend. Everything still comes from my existing Django REST API. The redesign was frontend only.
  3. Respect the user. prefers-reduced-motion and touch devices get a proper experience, not a broken one.
  4. Don't tax every page for the homepage's party tricks. Animation code ships in its own chunk.

Step 1: Prototype on a hidden route

I didn't touch the live homepage at first. I built the whole thing on a hidden /loud route so I could compare it with the real site side by side and throw it away if it didn't work.

That first commit added a set of reusable motion primitives under components/motion/:

Primitive What it does
KineticText Splits a headline into letters with a staggered spring entrance; letters get pushed away from the cursor
Marquee Infinite ticker whose speed and skew follow scroll velocity
StickerWall Draggable, throwable skill stickers kept inside their section
HorizontalScroll A pinned section where vertical scrolling moves you sideways
MagneticButton, LiftCard, Parallax, Counter, CustomCursor, ScrollProgress, IntroLoader The supporting cast

All of them are built on Motion (the library formerly known as Framer Motion).

Once /loud felt right, I moved it onto the real homepage, wired it to the live API hooks I already had, and redirected /loud to /.

Step 2: A design system made of clashes

The new palette is deliberately louder than the old one:

@theme {
  --color-loud-lime: #a3e636;
  --color-loud-ink: #111903;
  --color-loud-cool: #e0e7f1;
  --color-loud-paper: #eeefe9;
  --color-loud-blue: #2d5bff;
  --color-loud-orange: #ff7a00;
  --color-loud-purple: #8b5cf6;

  --shadow-loud: 8px 8px 0 #111903;
  --shadow-loud-sm: 4px 4px 0 #111903;

  --font-anton: Anton, Impact, sans-serif;
  --font-jet: 'JetBrains Mono', ui-monospace, monospace;
}

Anton for the giant headlines, JetBrains Mono for the sticker labels, Space Grotesk for body copy, all on a grid-paper background.

The hard part was making API data look hand-placed. Projects, services and FAQs come from the backend in whatever order and quantity they come in, so I couldn't art-direct each card. Instead, each card gets a colour and a tilt based on its position in the list:

export const FACES = [
  'bg-loud-lime',
  'bg-loud-blue text-loud-paper',
  'bg-loud-orange',
  'bg-loud-purple text-loud-paper',
  'bg-loud-cool',
  'bg-loud-paper',
];

// Small fixed tilts so lists look hand-placed but stay stable between renders.
const TILTS = [-2, 2.5, -3, 3, -1.5, 2, -2.5, 1.5];
export const tilt = (i: number) => TILTS[i % TILTS.length];
export const face = (i: number) => FACES[i % FACES.length];

It looks random, but it's deterministic. Nothing reshuffles when the page re-renders, so you don't get layout jank or hydration surprises. The featured-work grid works the same way, with a repeating pattern of bento column and row spans.

Huge headlines that fill the width need some maths. Anton capitals are about 0.47em wide, so each line gets a font size that keeps it under roughly 92vw:

export const fitLine = (text: string, max = 17) => ({
  fontSize: `min(${max}vw, ${(92 / (Math.max(text.length, 1) * 0.47)).toFixed(2)}vw)`,
});

Step 3: Motion that doesn't fight the browser

Kinetic text without layout thrashing

The hero headline reacts to your cursor letter by letter. The obvious way to build that is to call getBoundingClientRect() on every letter on every pointermove, which is a great way to drop frames.

What I did instead:

  • One shared pointer listener feeds every component, through Motion values: 
  let pointer: { x: MotionValue<number>; y: MotionValue<number> } | null = null;

  export function usePointer() {
    if (!pointer) {
      pointer = { x: motionValue(-9999), y: motionValue(-9999) };
      window.addEventListener('pointermove', (e) => {
        pointer!.x.set(e.clientX);
        pointer!.y.set(e.clientY);
      }, { passive: true });
    }
    return pointer;
  }
  • Each letter measures its centre once (and again on resize and when fonts finish loading) by walking the offsetParent chain. That skips transforms, so the letter's own animation doesn't change the measurement.
  • The per-frame work is pure maths on cached numbers: the distance to the pointer becomes a force, and the force drives springs for x, y, rotation and scale. No DOM reads happen while the pointer moves.

On touch devices there's no hover, so tapping a letter makes it jump instead.

Marquees that speed up with your scroll

My first marquee set its speed as a percentage of the track. That meant a marquee with more items scrolled faster in pixels, and every band on the page moved at a different speed. The fix was to define speed in pixels per second and convert it to a percentage using a track width that only gets read on resize:

useAnimationFrame((_, delta) => {
  if (reduced || !inView || !trackWidth.current) return;
  // px/s → percent of the track, so speed doesn't depend on content length.
  let moveBy = direction.current * ((baseVelocity * (delta / 1000)) / trackWidth.current) * 100;
  const factor = velocityFactor.get();
  if (factor < 0) direction.current = -1;
  else if (factor > 0) direction.current = 1;
  moveBy += direction.current * moveBy * factor;
  baseX.set(baseX.get() + moveBy);
});

Scroll velocity also pushes a small skewX, so the bands lean as you scroll fast. Marquees that are off screen (!inView) skip their frame updates entirely.

Case studies that grow out of their card

Clicking a featured project opens a full-screen case study that expands from the card itself, using Motion's shared layoutId. The overlay is lazy-loaded, so react-markdown stays out of the homepage's first load. It handles focus, closes on Escape and locks page scrolling while it's open.

The intro plays once

The homepage has an intro loader. Seeing it every time you come back to the homepage would get old quickly, so it runs once per session behind a sessionStorage flag wrapped in try/catch (private windows can throw).

Step 4: Accessibility rules I didn't break

A maximalist site is where accessibility tends to get dropped. These were non-negotiable:

  • Reduced motion is a real mode. Marquee renders as static text with no skew. HorizontalScroll becomes a normal vertical stack. Letter entrances become a simple fade. Parallax layers stay still.
  • Cursor effects need a fine pointer and motion allowed: 
  export function usePointerEffects(): boolean {
    const isTouch = useIsTouch(); // (hover: none), (pointer: coarse)
    const reduced = useReducedMotion();
    return !isTouch && !reduced;
  }
  • Split text is still readable. KineticText puts aria-label with the full headline on the wrapper and hides the individual letter spans from screen readers.
  • Duplicated marquee copies (it renders four for a seamless loop) are aria-hidden after the first.
  • The case study overlay is a proper role="dialog" with aria-modal and aria-labelledby, and focus moves to the close button.

Step 5: Rebuild every page

A loud homepage next to a quiet inner site would have felt like two different websites, so I rebuilt every page in the new style:

  • About and its sub-pages (Now, Uses, Music, Certifications)
  • Blog list, posts, series and tag pages: grid-paper backgrounds, sticker metadata, article prose restyled to the new palette
  • Services list and detail, plus the Works hub, Professional, Personal, Audio, Tech and project pages
  • Contact, Guestbook (entries are now sticky notes), Privacy, Terms, 404 and Unsubscribe
  • The cookie banner, resume modal and loading/error fallbacks

Doing this many pages forced me to extract shared pieces: LoudLayout (the page shell), LoudPageHeader (kinetic title plus sub-page tabs), LoudPostGrid, LoudProjectBrowser (search, category filters, animated grid), LoudFaqList, and LoudBriefSection. That last one replaced three separate copies of the inline contact form.

The form logic moved into useContactForm and useNewsletterForm hooks, so the old and new UIs submitted the same way during the transition. That made the switch-over low-risk.

Step 6: Delete everything

This is the part I'm proudest of. After the rebuild, I removed:

  • Components: the old Navbar, Footer, Hero, Projects, Services, Stats, Testimonials, FAQs, Button, Card, DevIcon, the old project and service modals, and an AI assistant widget that wasn't earning its place
  • Packages: framer-motion (as a direct dependency), lucide-react, react-countup, react-intersection-observer and @google/genai
  • Dark mode. The loud design is light-only on purpose: the whole look depends on ink on paper. LoudLayout removes the dark class while it's mounted.

Across the redesign: 86 files changed, 5,423 lines added, 8,454 lines removed. The site does more than it did before, with about 3,000 fewer lines of code.

Bundle split

Motion gets its own chunk, so pages that don't animate much don't pay for it up front. Because motion depends on framer-motion internally, they have to go in the same chunk, or you end up with duplicated runtime code:

manualChunks(id) {
  if (['react', 'react-dom', 'react-router-dom', 'react-helmet-async'].some(pkg => id.includes(`/node_modules/${pkg}/`))) {
    return 'chunk-react';
  }
  // motion depends on framer-motion internally; keep the whole animation stack in one chunk.
  if (['motion', 'motion-dom', 'motion-utils', 'framer-motion'].some(pkg => id.includes(`/node_modules/${pkg}/`))) return 'chunk-motion';
  if (id.includes('/node_modules/@sentry/')) return 'chunk-sentry';
},

Current production build, gzipped:

Chunk Size (gzip)
App entry ~26 KB
React + router ~71 KB
Motion ~56 KB
Sentry ~54 KB
Each page 0.5–7.5 KB raw

Every page is lazy-loaded, so a visitor only downloads the page they're looking at.

Gotchas I hit

1. overflow-x: hidden broke position: sticky.
The pinned horizontal-scroll section wouldn't stick. The cause was a global overflow-x: hidden on html and body, which turns body into a scroll container and breaks sticky positioning for everything inside it. The fix is overflow-x: clip, which hides overflow without creating a scroll container:

// The global overflow-x: hidden on html/body makes body a scroll container,
// which breaks position: sticky (HorizontalScroll). clip hides overflow
// without that side effect.
els.forEach((el) => (el.style.overflowX = 'clip'));

2. A CommonJS-only package crashed the homepage under Vite 8.
During a dependency upgrade, react-countup (which only ships CommonJS) had its default import resolved to the entire exports object. React tried to render that object, threw error #130, and the homepage crashed as soon as the stats section scrolled into view. I unwrapped .default as a quick fix, then removed the package in the cleanup.

3. @vercel/og 0.11 and later wouldn't build on Edge.
The newer edge build imports Node's module (createRequire), which Vercel Edge Functions reject at build time. I pinned it to 0.11.1.

4. Social previews were quietly broken.
The fallback og:image pointed at a Twitter profile-photo URL that had started returning 404, so links to the homepage were shared with no image. It's now a self-hosted 1200×630 card with og:image:width and og:image:height declared, so Facebook renders it on the first share instead of processing it in the background. Detail pages (case studies, blog tags, series, tech) also get their own generated OG images from an edge function.

5. Phones needed their own layout.
The first version of the hero looked great on desktop and fell apart on phones. Phones now get one word per headline line, the stickers sit above the headline instead of scattered around it, the hero height is capped on tall tablets, and the bento grid only uses four columns at lg and up.

What I'd do differently

  • Plan for reduced motion from day one. I did this, and it's the only reason the reduced-motion version doesn't feel like an afterthought. Every primitive decides its fallback up front.
  • Prototype on a hidden route again. Being able to compare /loud with the live site was the most useful decision in the whole project.
  • Extract shared components sooner. I wrote the contact form three times before turning it into LoudBriefSection. I should have stopped at two.

Wrapping up

The redesign took four days, from the first /loud prototype to the final cleanup. The site is louder and lighter, and every page shares one set of components.

Go throw some stickers around at vicentereyes.org, and if you're planning a site that needs to stand out, let's talk.

Built with React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4 and Motion, on a Django REST backend.

title: Choosing a stack by proof of concept
description:
A technology choice defended with "it is what we know" is sometimes right and never checkable. A proof of concept makes it checkable — but only when it is run as a decision procedure, and not as an early version of the product.

00 / A proof of concept is a question with a deadline

Three things separate it from a prototype: a question whose answer is allowed to be no, a criterion agreed before anyone writes code, and a date on which it ends. Drop any one of them and the PoC quietly becomes the first version of the system — the demo ships, nobody re-reads the question, and the stack has been chosen by sunk cost.

The question has to be able to fail. "Can we build this in X?" cannot: the answer is always yes, given enough time. "What does X cost us on the part we are actually worried about, in two days?" can.

01 / Make the comparisons comparable

Same task, same timebox, same reviewer, and the criteria with their weights written down before the first commit. The task should be the thing you are afraid of — the query that worries you, the concurrency, the integration whose documentation looks thin — and not an endpoint every candidate
handles identically.

Three ways this goes wrong, all of them common:

  • each candidate is built by the person who already prefers it;
  • the candidates get different amounts of time, usually in favour of whoever started first;
  • the criteria are written after the results, and fit the winner remarkably well.

02 / Criteria that survive the meeting

On the consumer product behind this case study, the backend language was chosen after several proofs of concept rather than by preference, against four criteria: scalability, maintainability, speed, and how well the codebase would work with AI-assisted development. Go came out of that balance, and other parts of the stack were decided the
same way.

Three of those four are ordinary, and each is worth turning into a question with an answer rather than an adjective:

  • Scalability — what happens at ten and a hundred times the load you expect, and what does it cost there? Measure it; do not reason from the vendor's page.
  • Maintainability — how long does it take someone who did not write the code to make a small change safely? That is a number, and the PoC is the cheapest time to take it, while the codebase is still small enough for a newcomer to read in an hour.
  • Speed — of the system and of the team. A runtime that is fast and that nobody on the team writes fluently is slow.

03 / The criterion almost nobody tests for

The fourth criterion is the one worth being explicit about, because teams now take it on faith in one direction or the other: how well a codebase in this stack will hold up when much of it is written with an assistant.

It is testable, and the thing to measure is the review, not the output. Give the same feature to the assistant in each candidate and look at:

  • how much of what came back was correct, and how much was plausible and wrong;
  • what the compiler or the type system rejected before a human had to — a stack where wrong code fails to build is cheaper than one where it runs and fails later;
  • whether the standard library covered what the assistant would otherwise have pulled a dependency for, because dependencies chosen by autocomplete are a maintenance decision made by nobody;
  • whether formatting is settled by a tool, so that diffs are about logic instead of style;
  • how long the result took to review, which is the number that actually scales with the team.

A large public corpus helps. It is not the whole story: the wider a language's surface, the more there is to be confidently wrong about, and the more a reviewer has to hold in their head to catch it.

04 / Letting the answer be no

A PoC can also answer "do we keep what is already here?". On that engagement an earlier codebase existed, written by one developer more than a year earlier, and for the scope being started it offered little foundation. That is a legitimate result, and it needs the same written question and the same deadline as any other — otherwise the discussion drifts towards the previous author instead of the code.

When a question has been answered, the PoC should be deleted, or promoted deliberately with a plan for the parts that were never finished. Kept "just as a reference", it gets copied.

05 / The half a PoC does not cover

The language decision on that project anticipated AI-assisted development. The team's workflow for it was not standardised from the start, and output often did not meet shared expectations and had to be reworked, which lowered quality overall. It is the thing I would do differently, and it is
not a tooling problem.

A technology evaluation answers which tool. It does not answer how we work: what a task looks like before it is handed to an assistant, what review covers that it did not before, what gets written by hand, and what nobody merges without reading twice. That second question deserves the
same deliberate treatment as the first, and usually gets none — because it has no artefact to show at the end of the week.

Choose with evidence, then write down how the chosen thing is used. The first half is the easy one.

title: Your API Returned 202. Why Does the UI Say Done?
description:
Your export button turns green. The API returned 202. The worker has not produced a file.

That screen may be reporting a success your system has not observed yet.

Here is a hypothetical implementation:

const response = await fetch("/exports", { method: "POST" });
if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Export request rejected");
showToast("Your export is ready");

The last line silently changes the meaning of the response. HTTP 202 means the request was accepted for processing. Processing may be incomplete or may not have started, and it can still fail. A successful HTTP response is insufficient evidence that this particular file exists.

Give the button a job lifecycle

For this export feature, use distinct application states: submitting, queued, running, completed and failed. Add a state for losing the ability to observe the job. That last state matters when the browser loses its connection while a worker continues.

These are proposed product states, not extra meanings assigned to the HTTP status code. Your backend must define how the client observes them: a status resource, events, or another documented mechanism.

An illustrative response contract could be:

{
  "jobId": "export-demo-17",
  "state": "queued",
  "statusUrl": "/exports/export-demo-17"
}

Those field names are specific to the example. HTTP 202 does not automatically supply a status endpoint.

Make each claim depend on evidence

“Request received” can follow acceptance. “Preparing your file” needs a known active job. “Download ready” needs a completed result the user can access.

If a status request fails, keep the job identifier. Show that its state cannot currently be checked and let the user check again. Creating another export immediately can duplicate work and leave two jobs whose results are difficult to distinguish.

Refreshing the page is another useful rehearsal. Does the screen reconnect to the original job, forget it, or start over? Decide that behavior before shipping the optimistic toast.

Test the promise made by the interface

I would use a controlled service with these outcomes:

  • acceptance followed by completion;
  • acceptance followed by worker failure;
  • acceptance followed by a lost status response;
  • page reload while the job is queued;
  • a completed job whose download is no longer available.

For every case, compare the visible message with the state the application actually knows. Include a check that observation failure never becomes a “ready” badge.

The interesting review artifact is a short sequence of observations: accepted response, job state, final result, visible copy. A screenshot of the green toast by itself cannot establish that an export worked.

Which part of your product currently uses “success” for a request that only entered a queue?

title: Hardening Enterprise SSO with Keycloak: SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE, and Zero-Trust RBAC
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Free Website Speed Test & Core Web Vitals Checker, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

This guide presents a production-grade Keycloak deployment that hardens SAML, OAuth2 PKCE, and RBAC for zero-trust enterprises. It includes HA design, configuration snippets, and an operational runbook.

Scope and Design Premise

This guide details a production-grade Keycloak deployment that satisfies PCI-DSS, NIST-800-53, and internal zero-trust mandates. The architecture couples a multi-node Infinispan cache, strict SAML 2.0 assertion signature verification, OAuth2 PKCE with token rotation, and a federated RBAC model that maps external LDAP groups to fine-grained resource policies.

Clustered High Availability with Infinispan

Keycloak stores sessions, tokens, and client metadata in an Infinispan cache. For enterprise resilience we configure a three-node synchronous replication cluster behind a virtual IP managed by Keepalived. The following

standalone-ha.xml

excerpt shows the cache container definition:

Key parameters:

  • Lock timeout 60 s prevents deadlock under burst load.
  • Max-idle 30 min evicts idle sessions, limiting memory pressure.
  • Synchronous replication guarantees that a write succeeds only when all three nodes acknowledge.

Network latency must stay below 5 ms for the 99th percentile of cache writes; otherwise the lock timeout will trigger failover. Use jumbo frames (MTU 9000) on the intra-cluster VLAN and enable net.core.somaxconn=65535 on each host.

SAML 2.0 Assertion Signature Validation

Keycloak validates inbound SAML assertions against the IdP metadata. The security posture requires:

  • Enforced RSA-SHA256 or ECDSA-SHA384 signatures.
  • Rejecting assertions with NotOnOrAfter timestamps older than 5 seconds.
  • Strict audience restriction matching the service provider entity ID.

Configuration snippet for the IdP metadata provider:

{
 "entityId": "https://idp.example.com/saml2",
 "singleSignOnService": [{"binding": "POST", "location": "https://idp.example.com/SSO"}],
 "singleLogoutService": [{"binding": "POST", "location": "https://idp.example.com/SLO"}],
 "signature": {
 "algorithm": "RSA_SHA256",
 "certificate": "MIID..." 
 },
 "wantAssertionsSigned": true,
 "wantAuthnRequestsSigned": true
}

Keycloak must be started with -Dkeycloak.saml.forceSignatureAlgorithm=RSA_SHA256 to reject weaker hashes. The assertion validation code path runs inside the org.keycloak.saml.SAML2LoginProcessor class; enabling DEBUG logging for that package provides audit trails for rejected assertions.

OAuth2 PKCE with Token Rotation

Public clients (mobile, SPA) are required to use PKCE (RFC 7636) with rotating refresh tokens. The server enforces a maximum token lifetime of 15 minutes and a refresh token reuse limit of 1. The following JSON client definition encodes the policy:

{
 "clientId": "mobile-app",
 "protocol": "openid-connect",
 "publicClient": true,
 "standardFlowEnabled": true,
 "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false,
 "pkceCodeChallengeMethod": "S256",
 "accessTokenLifespan": 900,
 "refreshTokenLifespan": 3600,
 "reuseRefreshToken": false,
 "rotateRefreshToken": true
}

Keycloak’s TokenManager rotates the refresh token after each use and stores the previous token hash in the user session. A failed reuse attempt increments the failedRefreshTokenAttempts counter; exceeding three attempts locks the user for 10 minutes. This behavior is configurable via the realm settings revokeRefreshToken and maxRefreshTokenReuse.

Zero-Trust RBAC Federation

The enterprise policy engine lives in an external OPA (Open Policy Agent) service. Keycloak forwards the authenticated principal’s attributes to OPA over a signed JWT. The policy decision point (PDP) evaluates group membership against a hierarchical RBAC matrix stored in PostgreSQL. Example policy fragment:

{
 "input": {
 "user": "{{.sub}}",
 "groups": {{.groups}},
 "resource": "{{.resource}}",
 "action": "{{.action}}"
 },
 "policy": "allow if input.groups contains \"finance:admin\" and input.action == \"write\""
}

Keycloak’s AuthorizationProvider is configured with a remote policy provider:

Network latency to the OPA endpoint must stay below 2 ms for 99 % of requests; otherwise the request timeout (set to 500 ms) will trigger a fallback deny. Deploy OPA as a sidecar on each Keycloak node to meet latency targets.

Operational Runbook

Startup Sequence

  • Provision three VMs with identical kernel parameters: vm.max_map_count=262144, net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1, fs.file-max=200000.
  • Install JDK 17, set JAVA_OPTS="-Xms8g -Xmx8g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200".
  • Deploy Infinispan container, verify cluster health via curl http://localhost:11222/rest/v2/cache-manager.
  • Start Keycloak with systemd unit that includes ExecStart=/opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh start --optimized and Restart=on-failure.
  • Run kc.sh export --realm master --output realm-export.json to capture baseline configuration.

Failure Detection

Prometheus scrapes /metrics on each node. Alert rules:

ALERT KeycloakNodeDown {
 expr: up{job="keycloak"} == 0
 for: 2m
 labels: {severity="critical"}
 annotations: {summary="Keycloak node unreachable", description="Check Keepalived and JVM logs"}
}

ALERT InfinispanReplicationLag {
 expr: infinispan_cache_replication_lag_seconds > 5
 for: 1m
 labels: {severity="warning"}
 annotations: {summary="Cache replication lag", description="Investigate network jitter"}
}

Patch Cycle

Apply quarterly Keycloak patches using rolling updates. Drain a node with kubectl cordon (if deployed on K8s) or disable the virtual IP on the node. After the node is out of service, replace the JARs, run kc.sh build, and bring the node back online. Verify session continuity by checking infinispan_cache_hits_total does not drop below 95 % of baseline.

Monitoring, Auditing, and Observability

Log aggregation uses Elastic Stack. Keycloak logs are emitted in JSON format with fields event_type, client_id, user_id, and duration_ms. A Kibana dashboard tracks:

  • Successful SAML assertion validations per IdP.
  • PKCE token exchange latency (target
  • OPA deny ratio (target

Kernel audit rules capture privileged system calls made by the JVM process:

-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F uid=0 -k keycloak-audit

Retention policy: 90 days for audit logs, 180 days for authentication logs, complying with GDPR retention schedules.

Architectural Trade-offs

Dimension Choice Impact
Cache Replication Mode Synchronous (SYNC) Higher write latency (≈3 ms) but guarantees strong consistency across nodes.
Token Lifetime 15 min access, 1 h refresh Reduces exposure window; increases token refresh traffic (~12 % of auth volume).
OPA Deployment Sidecar per node Meets sub-2 ms latency; raises pod count and resource fragmentation.
Signature Algorithm RSA-SHA256 only Eliminates weaker hashes; requires IdPs to support RSA-2048 minimum key size.

The design favors deterministic security guarantees over raw throughput. In environments where peak login bursts exceed 10 k req/s, consider scaling the Infinispan cluster to five nodes and enabling client-side load balancing.

Final Remarks

The configuration presented delivers a repeatable, auditable SSO platform that satisfies zero-trust mandates while preserving high availability. Operators should embed the runbook steps into CI/CD pipelines to enforce drift-free deployments.

Production Verification Checklist & Operational Runbook: Hardening Enterprise Single Sign-On: Keycloak SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE & Zero-Trust RBAC

Before promoting any Hardening Enterprise Single Sign-On: Keycloak SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE & Zero-Trust RBAC deployment into production traffic, senior platform and SRE teams validate deterministic failure handling, kernel resource ceilings, and observability telemetry across keycloak high availability infinispan, oauth2 pkce token rotation, saml 2.0 assertion signature validation, enterprise rbac identity federation. Unlike lab prototypes, production clusters must survive upstream network partitions, sudden concurrency bursts, and rolling node maintenance without dropping in-flight client transactions.

Pre-Cutover Acceptance Gates 

- **Synthetic Load & Tail-Latency Benchmarking:** Execute sustained concurrency tests against staging endpoints for Hardening Enterprise Single Sign-On: Keycloak SAML 2.0, OAuth2 PKCE & Zero-Trust RBAC, verifying that p95 and p99 response latencies remain within contractual SLO boundaries under 3x peak projected load.

- **Fault Injection & Chaos Verification:** Simulate primary worker termination, AZ link degradation, and storage IOPS saturation to confirm automated failover and circuit-breaker recovery complete within sub-second thresholds.

- **Telemetry & Alert Routing Validation:** Confirm Prometheus scrape targets, structured JSON log pipelines, and OpenTelemetry trace propagation emit actionable metrics for hardening-enterprise-sso-keycloak-saml-oauth2-pkce-rbac before live traffic cutover.

- **Immutable Rollback Readiness:** Verify that declarative GitOps manifests, database migration snapshots, and previous container image digests can restore the prior production state in under 120 seconds.

sysctl net.core.somaxconn net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse vm.swappiness

" http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz

title: The Cloud Is Now Optional: Inside the Offline AI Stack You Can Actually Run Today
description:
Offline AI is genuinely usable today for chat, coding and voice — here is the stack, the hardware tiers, and the honest limits.

For three years, the assumption was simple: serious AI lives in someone else's data center, and you rent it by the token. This week that assumption cracked. A voice stack that runs entirely on cheap Android phones, a 428B open-weights model you can download, a PIN lock on ChatGPT, and a new encrypted assistant all landed within about 48 hours — different products, same direction. The cloud did not disappear. It became a choice. We researched the announcements, the specs and the reporting to work out what you can actually run today, where the limits still bite, and who should bother.

How we put this together: We reviewed vendor announcements and launch-week coverage for VoxNexus VoxEdge and VoxSense, OpenAI's ChatGPT PIN lock and Dark.ai, plus Nasscom's India Voice AI Readiness 2026 report and MiniMax's M3.1 Flash release. Specs and figures are quoted from those sources; where a vendor makes a performance claim we have not seen independently reproduced, we label it as a vendor claim. We have not hands-on tested these systems — this is researched analysis based on specs and reporting, not a lab test.

Verdict: Offline AI is genuinely usable today for chat, coding assistance and voice — not as a stunt, but as a daily driver for a lot of work. Small and mid-size open-weights models run well on a normal laptop, voice recognition and synthesis can now live entirely on a phone, and the tooling has gone from hobbyist to install-and-go. The limits are real at the frontier end: the smartest models, the longest contexts and the hardest reasoning still live in the cloud, and at the extreme a single downloadable model can need 220GB just to sit on disk. Start local for privacy, cost and speed on routine tasks. Keep the cloud for the jobs that actually need it.

What changed this week

Start in Madrid. On October 23, 2026, VoxNexus unveiled VoxEdge: a full voice AI stack designed to run entirely offline on cheap Android phones. Speech recognition in 36 languages, translation in 103 languages, speech synthesis in 45 languages — with no connection required and, in the pitch that matters to businesses, zero per-token cloud bills.

The detail that got engineers' attention was size. VoxEdge's speech recognition model is just 65 million parameters, and VoxNexus claims — vendor claim, not independently verified — that it beats open models ten times its size. Whether that claim survives independent testing matters, but the direction does not: models are getting small enough that "phone-grade" no longer means "toy-grade."

Alongside it came VoxSense, an always-on listening layer. VoxNexus says it can listen for 12 hours on 2.49% battery — again, a vendor figure — with audio never uploaded. That last part is the product. Always-on listening is only acceptable to most people if the recording never leaves the device.

The unveiling landed in the slipstream of MediaTek's Dimensity 9600 launch on October 19, which is not a coincidence. Better on-device silicon is what makes a stack like this plausible on inexpensive hardware, not just on a flagship.

And the framing from VoxNexus's CEO is worth quoting in full, because it explains why this is not just a cost story: "Under-resourced languages aren't small languages." A language can have tens of millions of speakers and still be underserved by cloud AI built around English-first data centers. An offline stack that ships recognition and translation on the phone itself serves people the cloud roadmap keeps postponing.

There is outside evidence that this demand is real, not just a launch-week narrative. Nasscom's India Voice AI Readiness 2026 report found 31% of organisations have voice AI in limited production and 13% have scaled it. India's BHASHINI programme even ran a dedicated offline and low-connectivity voice AI challenge — a signal that "works without reliable internet" is a procurement requirement, not a nice-to-have. The same report says 61% of organisations report a reduction of more than 20% in cost per interaction from voice AI. Take the cloud bill out of that interaction entirely and the maths gets more interesting still.

The privacy side of the week told a more complicated story. Also on October 23, OpenAI began rolling out a conversation PIN lock for ChatGPT, available on the free tier too. It is a useful feature. It stops a colleague or family member who picks up your unlocked phone from scrolling your chats.

It is not, however, privacy in the strong sense — and it is worth being precise. A PIN lock is a lock on the app, not end-to-end encryption. Your conversations still travel to and live on cloud infrastructure under the provider's normal policies. A lock protects you from people in the room. It does not change who runs the servers.

That distinction is exactly what Dark.ai, announced October 22, is pitching against. It positions itself as an encrypted AI assistant running on infrastructure it controls, rather than as a feature added to a mainstream cloud product. We have not tested its claims, and encryption pitches deserve the same scepticism as benchmark pitches. But its existence, in the same week as a PIN lock, shows the market splitting: mainstream tools adding surface-level locks, challengers selling architecture-level privacy, and offline tools removing the server from the equation altogether.

Three different answers to the same question — who else can see what I say to this thing?

The offline stack, layer by layer

"Run AI offline" sounds like one decision. It is actually four: a runtime to load the model, a model to run, a voice layer if you need one, and — if you are serving other people — a serving engine. Here is each layer in plain English.

Runtimes: where most people should start. Ollama is the simplest on-ramp for developers: install it, pull a model by name, and you have a local API that feels familiar if you have ever called a cloud one. LM Studio is the friendlier desktop option, with a graphical interface for finding, downloading and chatting with models — better for non-developers and for anyone who wants to see memory use before they commit. llama.cpp is the low-level engine underneath much of this ecosystem: efficient, portable, runs almost anywhere, and rewards people comfortable with the command line. Jan and GPT4All round out the desktop choices, both aiming at a private, local-first chat experience without much setup.

The honest drawbacks at this layer are not performance. They are housekeeping. You manage model downloads, updates and disk space. When something breaks, there is no support desk — there is a GitHub issue and a community forum. For an individual that is a fair trade. For a business, price in the support burden before you celebrate the saved API bill.

Models: open weights are the fuel. None of this works without models whose weights you are allowed to download and run. That catalogue is now deep: small models for phones, capable 7B to 14B-class models for laptops, and much larger mixture-of-experts releases at the top end. The trade-off is consistent — a model small enough to run locally is, today, less capable than the best cloud model. Quantization, which compresses a model to fit less memory, narrows the hardware gap and widens the quality gap a little more. More on that below.

Voice: the layer that changed most this week. Until recently, good speech recognition usually meant sending audio to the cloud. VoxEdge is a sign that on-device automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech are now credible on cheap hardware, in many languages, without that round trip. If your use case is a kiosk, a field worker's phone, a clinic in a low-connectivity area, or simply a user who does not want their voice uploaded, this is the layer to watch.

Serving: for teams, not laptops. If you want one machine to serve a model to many users, vLLM is the name you will meet most often. It is built for high-throughput inference on GPU servers — your own cloud bill, in effect, except you own the machine and the data never leaves it. It is overkill for personal use and essential context for the biggest models, including the one in the next section.

What you can actually run today

Forget parameter counts for a second. What matters is your hardware tier. Work through ours with the Can I Run It? calculator on Pick a Tools before you download anything — it will save you a 40GB mistake.

  • Phone. Small chat models and, increasingly, real voice. VoxEdge is designed for exactly this tier: recognition, translation and synthesis on inexpensive Android hardware. Expect quick, useful answers and excellent voice — not deep research.
  • Laptop with 16GB of RAM. The sweet spot for most readers. 7B to 14B-class open-weights models at quantized quality run comfortably here through Ollama or LM Studio: drafting, summarising, code completion, private document chat. This is where offline AI stops being a hobby.
  • Gaming GPU with 24GB of VRAM. Larger models, faster responses, longer contexts, better coding assistance. If you already own the GPU for games, your marginal cost of a serious local setup is close to zero.
  • Workstation and server. Multi-GPU rigs running vLLM, serving bigger models to a team — or attempting the ceiling. Which brings us to the extreme.

At the far end sits MiniMax M3.1 Flash, whose weights dropped on October 23: a 428B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with an FP8 checkpoint of roughly 220GB. It is downloadable. It is, in the literal sense, "local AI." It is also a multi-GPU commitment that we broke down in full on Pick a Tools. Keep it in mind as the ceiling of the category, not the entry point.

Not sure which tier you are really in? Run your exact RAM and VRAM through Can I Run It? — the calculator matches your hardware to model sizes before you spend an evening downloading. And for the full map of tools, models and guides, start at the Offline AI hub on Pick a Tools.

The honest limits

Four limits, stated plainly, because the offline conversation attracts hype from both directions.

Frontier capability still lives in the cloud. The best reasoning, the hardest coding, the longest and most reliable contexts — as of October 2026, the top of every serious capability ladder is still a cloud model you cannot download. Local models are good, and improving fast. "Good enough for most tasks" and "best available" are different claims.

Quantization costs quality. The model that fits your laptop is usually a compressed version of the original. Compression is clever and the losses are smaller than they used to be, but they concentrate exactly where you notice them: precise, multi-step, edge-case work. If a quantized local model disappoints you on hard tasks, that may be why.

Offline does not automatically mean private. A local model cannot send your prompt to a model provider. The app wrapped around it still might sync, log or upload, depending on how it was built. Privacy comes from checking network behaviour, settings and policies — not from the word "offline" on a landing page. This is also why the ChatGPT PIN example matters: a feature can improve one kind of privacy while leaving the architecture untouched.

The support burden is yours. Updates, model management, storage, troubleshooting, keeping a team's machines consistent — the cloud bill you stop paying is partly replaced by time. For individuals that trade is often excellent. For organisations, it is a real line item, which is one reason Nasscom's numbers show far more limited production (31%) than scaled deployment (13%).

What we'd actually do

If you are a curious individual: install LM Studio or Ollama tonight, pull a mid-size model, and turn your Wi-Fi off. Summarise a document, draft something, ask it about a file you would never paste into a cloud chatbot. That hour will teach you more than any benchmark chart — including where it falls short.

If you are a developer: build against a local runtime for development and routine tasks — code completion, test drafting, log summarising — and keep a cloud API for the hardest jobs. That hybrid is where most sensible stacks will land: local by default, cloud by exception, with the bill and the privacy exposure shrinking together.

If you work with voice, or in low-connectivity settings: watch the VoxEdge class of tools closely and test the language coverage for your actual users. The CEO's line bears repeating here — under-resourced languages are not small languages. For millions of users, offline voice is not a privacy luxury. It is the first version that works at all.

If you run a business: do the full accounting. Saved per-token costs and the interaction savings Nasscom describes are real, but so are hardware, maintenance and support. Pilot with one team, on one workflow, and measure — the same discipline you would apply to any cloud migration, in reverse.

The bottom line: a year ago, "offline AI" meant compromises most people would not accept. Today it means a real stack — runtimes that install in minutes, models worth running, voice that lives on a cheap phone — with clear, honest limits at the top end. The cloud is still there, and for the hardest work it is still the answer. It is just, finally, optional.

FAQ

Can AI really work without internet?
Yes, for a lot of everyday work. Once you have downloaded a model and a runtime like Ollama or LM Studio, chat, summarising, coding assistance and on-device voice recognition can all run with Wi-Fi off. What you lose offline is live web access, cloud sync and the very largest frontier models — not the core ability to generate and understand language.

What is the best way to run an LLM offline?
For most people, start with Ollama or LM Studio on a laptop. Both install in minutes, manage model downloads for you and run popular open-weights models locally. If you want maximum control or the smallest footprint, llama.cpp is the engine underneath much of the ecosystem. For serving a model to a team, look at vLLM on your own server.

Is offline AI more private?
It can be, but offline does not automatically mean private. A model running locally cannot send your prompt to a model provider, which is a real gain. But the app around it can still collect telemetry, sync history or upload files if it is built that way. Check the app's network behaviour and settings — the model being local is only one layer.

What hardware do I need to run AI offline?
A modern phone can run small voice and chat models. A laptop with 16GB of RAM handles 7B to 14B-class models comfortably at quantized quality. A gaming GPU with 24GB of VRAM opens up larger, faster models. At the extreme end, a model like MiniMax M3.1 Flash has a roughly 220GB FP8 checkpoint and needs multi-GPU workstation or server hardware. Use a VRAM calculator before you download anything large.

What can't offline AI do yet?
Offline AI cannot match the best frontier cloud models on the hardest reasoning, coding and long-context tasks, and it cannot browse the web, check live prices or sync across devices while disconnected. Quantized local models also lose some quality compared with the full-precision originals, especially on precise, multi-step work.

Does offline AI cost anything to run?
The software in this guide is mostly free and open source, and there are no per-token cloud bills once a model is on your device. Your costs are hardware, electricity and your own time for updates and troubleshooting. Paid apps and support plans exist, but they are optional.

title: Muse AI Invite Code (Oct 2026): How to Redeem and Get 1 Billion Free Tokens
description:
Meta's Muse is invite-gated right now, but there's an official referral program built right into Settings: redeem someone's invite code within 48 hours of joining and you get 1 billion Muse tokens — the person who shared it gets 1 billion too. I claimed mine and it showed up as 'Additional tokens' on top of the free weekly allowance.

My code: H8MB3S (disclosure: it's my personal code — we both get the 1B bonus when you redeem it; it costs you nothing)

How to redeem it, step by step:

  1. Sign up at muse.ai/join or download the Muse app (US, Canada, and Japan)
  2. Open Settings right away — on mobile: Settings → Redeem token; on web: Settings → General → Usage → Redeem invite code
  3. Enter H8MB3S and confirm
  4. Check your token balance — the bonus appears separately from your weekly allowance

The 48-hour rule is the part people miss: the redeem option disappears 48 hours after you join. Miss it and the bonus is gone — no late claims. Do it in your first session.

A few honest notes: each code has limited uses (around 30) — if H8MB3S ever shows as used up, find another fresh code. The tokens never expire and stack on top of your free weekly allowance. Redeeming never asks for your password or card — if anyone asks for those, walk away.

title: เครื่องมือเขียนเทสต์ที่หยุดพัฒนาไปแล้ว: Qodo Cover และกับดักของ coverage ที่สูงแต่จับบั๊กไม่ได้?
description:
โดย Nokka (นก-กา) | ตอนที่ 5 จาก 7 ของชุด "สร้างซอฟต์แวร์ด้วย AI" | ตรวจสอบข้อมูล ณ 23 ต.ค. 2026

บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (deepseek-v4.1-flash · ผู้ให้บริการโมเดล: ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent ภายใต้การควบคุมและตรวจสอบคุณภาพโดยมนุษย์ - Nokka (นก-กา)

สมมติว่าตัวเลข coverage เพิ่มจาก 62 เปอร์เซ็นต์เป็น 84 เปอร์เซ็นต์ เรื่องแบบนี้ฟังดูเหมือนความสำเร็จ

แต่ถ้าเทสต์ที่เพิ่มเข้ามาไม่มี assertion สักบรรทัด ตัวเลขนั้นก็ไม่ได้บอกอะไรเกี่ยวกับคุณภาพของโค้ดเลย

บทนี้ผมจะเล่าเรื่องเครื่องมือที่เคยถูกแนะนำว่าเป็นคำตอบของปัญหานี้ว่าตอนนี้เป็นอย่างไร แล้วชี้ว่ากับดักที่แท้จริงอยู่ตรงไหน

Qodo Cover คืออะไร และทำไมมันหยุดพัฒนา

Qodo Cover หรือชื่อเดิม Codium Cover Agent เป็นเครื่องมือที่ทำงานต่างจาก agent ตัวอื่นในซีรี่ส์นี้

มันไม่ได้เขียนฟีเจอร์ แต่รับโค้ดที่มีอยู่แล้ว ดูว่า coverage ส่วนไหนยังขาด แล้วเขียนเทสต์เพิ่มให้

ตัวเลข ณ วันที่ผมตรวจคือ 5,670 ดาว สัญญาอนุญาต AGPL-3.0 commit ล่าสุด 24 มิ.ย. 2025 และมีการ push ครั้งหลังสุด 5 เม.ย. 2026 [1]

แต่จุดที่สำคัญกว่าตัวเลขคือบรรทัดใน README ที่เขียนไว้เมื่อ 15 มิ.ย. 2025 ว่า repo นี้ไม่ได้รับการดูแลต่อแล้ว และแนะนำให้ fork ไปทำต่อเองถ้าต้องการ [1]

แปลว่าโค้ดไม่ถูกแตะมากว่าสิบหกเดือน รีลีสสุดท้ายคือ 0.3.10 เมื่อ 21 พ.ค. 2025 [5] และไม่มีใครรับประกันว่ามันจะยังทำงานกับ API ของโมเดลรุ่นใหม่ได้

ในมุมมองของผม การที่มันยังมีดาวเยอะและยังถูกพูดถึง เป็นตัวอย่างที่ดีของปัญหาในวงการนี้ คือข้อมูลเก่าไหลเวียนนานกว่าอายุของเครื่องมือ

สิ่งที่มันต้องการก่อนเริ่มทำงาน

README ระบุเงื่อนไขสองข้อที่คนอ่านข้ามบ่อย [1]

ข้อแรกคือต้องมีคีย์ของโมเดล ตัวแปรที่มันอ่านคือ OPENAI_API_KEY

ข้อสองคือต้องมีไฟล์ coverage รูปแบบ Cobertura XML อยู่แล้ว

ข้อสองนี้สำคัญมาก เพราะมันหมายความว่าเครื่องมือนี้ไม่สามารถเริ่มจากศูนย์ได้ คุณต้องมี test runner ที่ออกรายงาน XML ได้ก่อน

ถ้าโปรเจกต์ของคุณยังไม่มีอะไรแบบนั้น Qodo Cover จะไม่มีข้อมูลว่าโค้ดส่วนไหนยังไม่ถูกทดสอบ

หน้าตาของคำสั่งที่ต้องรัน

ผมเขียนตัวอย่างสมมติด้านล่างเพื่อให้เห็นลำดับงาน ไม่ได้คัดลอกจาก repo ตรง ๆ

1. รัน pytest --cov --cov-report=xml  ->  ได้ coverage.xml
2. ตั้งค่า OPENAI_API_KEY ใน environment
3. เรียก cover-agent ผ่าน CLI พร้อมระบุ path ของ coverage.xml
4. ตรวจ diff ของเทสต์ที่มันเขียน แล้วตัดสินใจว่าจะรับหรือไม่

ขั้นที่ 4 คือขั้นที่คนมักข้าม และเป็นขั้นที่ทำให้ coverage สูงขึ้นโดยที่คุณภาพไม่ขยับ

กับดักที่แท้จริงไม่ใช่ตัวเครื่องมือ

สมมติว่าคุณมีฟังก์ชันหาราคาสินค้าที่มีส่วนลดหลายชั้น และ agent เขียนเทสต์ให้ออกมาแบบนี้ (ตัวอย่างสมมติที่ผมแต่งขึ้น)

def test_calculate_price():
    result = calculate_price(100, 10)
    assert result is not None

เทสต์นี้ทำให้บรรทัดในฟังก์ชันถูกเรียกครบ และ coverage เพิ่มขึ้นจริง

แต่ถ้าฟังก์ชันคืนค่า 9999 มา มันก็ยังผ่าน เพราะสิ่งที่ตรวจมีแค่ว่าไม่ใช่ค่าว่าง

นี่คือความหมายของคำว่า coverage วัดว่าโค้ดถูกเรียกหรือไม่ ไม่ได้วัดว่าโค้ดให้คำตอบถูกหรือไม่

เครื่องมือที่ optimize ตัวเลข coverage จึงมีแรงจูงใจให้เขียนเทสต์ที่เรียกโค้ดให้ครบ มากกว่าเขียนเทสต์ที่จับบั๊กได้

ผมคิดว่า นี่เป็นเหตุผลที่ทีมจำนวนหนึ่งเลิกใช้เครื่องมือประเภทนี้หลังสองสามเดือน แม้ตัวเลขจะสวยขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ

ทางเลือกที่ยังมีคนดูแลอยู่

ถ้าเป้าหมายคือเทสต์ที่จับบั๊กได้จริง วิธีวัดที่ตรงกว่าคือ mutation testing

แนวคิดคือให้เครื่องมือแก้โค้ดของคุณทีละจุด เช่น เปลี่ยนเครื่องหมายบวกเป็นลบ แล้วดูว่าเทสต์จับได้ไหม

ถ้าเทสต์ยังผ่านทั้งที่โค้ดถูกทำให้ผิด แปลว่าเทสต์ชุดนั้นอ่อน

เครื่องมือที่ผมตรวจสถานะแล้วว่ายังเดินอยู่มีสองตัว

  • mutmut สำหรับ Python · BSD-3-Clause · 1,501 ดาว · commit 19 ต.ค. 2026 [2]
  • Stryker สำหรับ JavaScript และ TypeScript · Apache-2.0 · 3,269 ดาว · commit 10 ต.ค. 2026 [3]

ทั้งสองตัวไม่ได้เขียนเทสต์ให้คุณ แต่บอกว่าคุณภาพเทสต์ที่คุณมีอยู่ในระดับไหน

ส่วนคนที่ยังอยากได้พฤติกรรมเดิม คือให้ AI เขียนเทสต์เพิ่ม มีทางที่ Qodo เองลิงก์ไว้ คือ GitHub Action ชื่อ qodo-cover [4]

สถานะของมันคือยังอยู่ในช่วง preview ไม่มีไฟล์สัญญาอนุญาตในรีโป และ commit ล่าสุด 13 มี.ค. 2025 [4]

ตัวเลข 27 ดาวน้อยมากเมื่อเทียบกับตัวหลัก ผมจึงอ่านว่า ที่นี่ไม่ใช่ทางที่คนใช้งานจริงเลือก

วิธีออกแบบไปป์ไลน์ที่ไม่หลงตัวเลข

สิ่งที่ผมจะทำถ้าต้องตั้งระบบนี้จริง มีสามชั้น

ชั้นแรก รันเทสต์เดิมและบังคับ coverage ขั้นต่ำใน CI เพื่อกันไม่ให้แย่ลง

ชั้นที่สอง รัน mutation testing แบบจำกัดขอบเขต เฉพาะไฟล์ที่ถูกแก้ใน pull request เพื่อไม่ให้กินเวลาเกิน

ชั้นที่สาม ให้ agent ช่วยเขียนเทสต์ แต่ต้องผ่านการตรวจสองอย่าง คือ mutation score ต้องดีขึ้น และต้องมีคนอ่าน diff

ชั้นที่สามนี้คือจุดที่ Qodo Cover เคยช่วยได้ แต่ตอนนี้ผมต้องบอกตรง ๆ ว่ามันไม่มีคนดูแลแล้ว

ถ้าคุณยังต้องการความสามารถนี้ ทางที่เป็นไปได้คือ fork ไปดูแลเอง หรือใช้ความสามารถเขียนเทสต์ของ agent ที่ยังมีคนดูแลอยู่ แล้วกำหนดเงื่อนไขตรวจรับเอง

สิ่งที่ผมไม่ได้ทดลอง

ผมไม่ได้รัน Qodo Cover ในเครื่องนี้ เพราะต้องมีคีย์ OpenAI และเครื่องที่ผมใช้มีเพียงคีย์ของผู้ให้บริการผ่านทาง OpenRouter

ผมจึงไม่เขียนว่ามันเขียนเทสต์เก่งแค่ไหน และไม่ยกตัวอย่างผลลัพธ์ที่ผมไม่ได้เห็นด้วยตา

ที่ผมยืนยันได้คือสถานะของ repo ถ้อยใน README ตัวเลขจาก GitHub API และเงื่อนไขการใช้งานที่ README ระบุ

เช็กลิสต์ก่อนเลือกเครื่องมือเขียนเทสต์

  1. โปรเจกต์ออกรายงาน coverage แบบ XML ได้แล้วหรือยัง
  2. coverage ขั้นต่ำที่คุณตั้งไว้ วัดจากอะไร
  3. มีเทสต์ที่ assertion ชัดเจนกี่เปอร์เซ็นต์
  4. เครื่องมือที่คุณจะใช้ commit ล่าสุดเมื่อไร
  5. ถ้ามันหยุดพัฒนา พอร์ตไปตัวอื่นใช้เวลากี่วัน

ข้อ 5 ทำให้ผมเลี่ยงเครื่องมือที่ผูกกับรูปแบบไฟล์เฉพาะตัวมากเกินไป เพราะวันหนึ่งคุณต้องย้ายออก

บทเรียนที่ผมอยากฝากไว้

Coverage เป็นตัวเลขที่วัดความพยายามได้ดี แต่วัดคุณภาพได้ไม่ดี

ความมั่นใจว่าเทสต์จะจับบั๊กได้ ต้องมาจากตัววัดที่จับบั๊กเป็น ไม่ใช่ตัววัดว่าโค้ดถูกเรียกหรือยัง

title: Error Messages Are Writing, Too
description:
Error messages are some of the most carefully read sentences in any piece of software. They appear at the exact moment the reader is stuck, often a little frustrated, and looking for help. Yet they are frequently written last, in a hurry, by someone thinking about the code rather than the person on the other side of it.

The good news is that a useful error message follows a simple pattern, and it can be learned like any other kind of editing.

The three parts of a useful message

A clear error message answers three questions:

  1. What happened?
  2. Why did it happen, if that is known?
  3. What can the reader do now?

Most weak messages answer only the first question, and sometimes not even that.

Before:

Error: invalid input.

After:

The date "31.02.2026" could not be read. February has no 31st day. Please enter a date in the format DD.MM.YYYY.

The second version is longer, but every word earns its place. The reader knows which value was wrong, why it was rejected and what a correct value looks like.

Name the thing, not the category

"Invalid input", "operation failed" and "something went wrong" describe a category of problem. The reader needs the specific case.

Whenever the program knows which file, field, value or setting caused the problem, include it in the message. "Could not open config.yaml" is immediately useful. "Could not open file" sends the reader searching.

This also helps when people copy the message into a search engine or a support request. A specific message leads to specific answers.

Speak to the reader, not about the code

Internal terms leak easily into error text: exception names, function names, abbreviations that only the team uses. They make sense to the author and to nobody else.

Before:

NullReferenceException in UserProfileLoader.

After:

Your profile could not be loaded because no account is linked to this email address.

Technical details still have a place. Developers debugging the problem may need the exception and the stack trace. Put those in logs, or below the human-readable message, clearly separated. The first line should be readable by the person who actually sees it.

Do not blame, do not joke

Tone matters more than usual here, because the reader is already having a bad moment.

  • Avoid blame. "You entered an invalid password" sounds like an accusation. "The password does not match this account" states the same fact neutrally.
  • Avoid jokes. A playful "Oops!" can feel friendly the first time and irritating the tenth time, especially when work has been lost.
  • Avoid false certainty. If the cause is only a guess, say "This may be caused by..." rather than presenting it as fact.

Calm, plain language works best. The aim is to sound like a helpful colleague, not a machine and not a comedian.

Offer a way forward

The most important part of an error message is the last one: what the reader can do next. Even when the program cannot fix the problem, it can usually point somewhere.

  • Retry later, if the problem is temporary.
  • Correct a specific value, and show the expected format.
  • Check a specific setting, and name where it is.
  • Contact support, and say what information to include.

A message without a next step leaves the reader at a dead end. A message with one turns a failure into a short detour.

Review your errors like any other text

Collect the error messages in your project in one list and read them in a row. This simple exercise reveals a lot: inconsistent wording, messages that say the same thing in five different ways, and messages that say nothing at all.

Edit them as you would edit any other text. Check that each one names the problem, explains it where possible and offers a next step. They are short, but for the reader in that moment, they may be the most important words in the whole product.

title: Agent Skills Moves to the Agentic AI Foundation: What Developers Need to Know
description:
Short answer: Anthropic donated the Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation on October 22, 2026. This transfer places the skill specification under neutral Linux Foundation governance alongside the Model Context Protocol. Developers can build skills using simple local directories, Markdown instructions, and executable scripts, then run them across dozens of supported agent clients and model backends without encountering platform lock-in.

What did Anthropic donate on October 22?

On October 22, 2026, Anthropic transferred the Agent Skills standard and all related assets to the Agentic AI Foundation. The donation includes the core specification, the Agent Skills name and logo, the official GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. Anthropic stated that it is committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral.

The Agentic AI Foundation operates as a project under the Linux Foundation to host vendor-neutral agent standards. Anthropic, Block, and OpenAI co-founded the foundation in 2025 to create a shared home for open agent infrastructure. The foundation already hosts the Model Context Protocol, which Anthropic donated in an earlier governance transfer.

Anthropic first launched Agent Skills inside its Claude products in October 2025. Two months later, in December 2025, Anthropic published the underlying format as an open standard for the developer community. Donating the assets to the Agentic AI Foundation completes the transition from a single-vendor feature to a neutral industry specification.

Who maintains Agent Skills now?

Two Lead Maintainers, David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag, now guide the Agent Skills project. Individual software engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other technology companies maintain the specification on their own behalf rather than through corporate representation.

Development teams do not need to join the Agentic AI Foundation to use the standard or contribute code to the repository.

Anyone who wants to suggest changes to the specification can send feedback through the project's Discord server.

How widely is the standard used?

More than 70 agent platforms have integrated the Agent Skills specification across their production tools. That adoption footprint includes major coding agents and developer environments such as ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code.

According to Anthropic, developers have published 1 million skills and end users have installed nearly 280 million skills across those integrated platforms. These are Anthropic's own figures and are not independently audited.

For skill authors, that means one package format across competing platforms. Developers who author a skill can deploy that package directly to multiple editors and command-line agents without rewriting instructions for each client.

What is inside a skill?

A skill is a directory containing at minimum a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter followed by standard Markdown instructions. The directory can also house optional subdirectories by convention, including scripts for executable code, references for documentation loaded on demand, and assets for templates, images, or data files.

api-cost-check/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   └── estimate.py
└── references/
    └── prices.md

File references inside SKILL.md should be relative paths from the skill root, kept one level deep. The specification advises against long chains of nested references.

The YAML frontmatter defines two required fields: name and description. The name field takes a string between 1 and 64 characters containing only lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens. It must match the parent directory name exactly, with no leading hyphens, trailing hyphens, or double hyphens.

The description field accepts 1 to 1,024 characters explaining what the skill accomplishes and when the agent should select it. Authors should write clear descriptions with relevant keywords, because the agent runtime inspects this text to decide which skill fits a given user prompt.

Frontmatter also supports four optional fields. The license field names the distribution license, while compatibility accepts up to 500 characters outlining environment requirements. Authors can provide arbitrary string key-value pairs through the metadata map, or specify an experimental allowed-tools list containing space-separated pre-approved tools.

---
name: api-cost-check
description: "Estimates the API cost of a prompt or batch job before it runs. Use when the user asks what a request, batch or agent run will cost on a given model."
license: Apache-2.0
metadata:
  author: example-org
  version: "1.0"
---

# API cost check

1. Count input tokens and estimate output tokens.
2. Read per-1M-token prices from references/prices.md.
3. Run scripts/estimate.py and report the cost per request and per 1,000 requests.

Developers can verify their directory structure and schema formatting before distributing a package. Running skills-ref validate ./my-skill through the skills-ref reference library checks that the frontmatter is valid and follows the naming rules.

How does progressive disclosure keep context small?

Roughly 100 tokens of metadata per skill enter the context window when an agent session initializes. The runtime loads only the name and description fields at startup, allowing an agent to index dozens of capabilities without consuming substantial context space.

The agent defers reading the rest of the package until the user prompt triggers that specific skill. The full body of SKILL.md loads into the active prompt only upon activation, and the specification recommends keeping that body under 5,000 tokens and under 500 lines of text.

Files located inside the scripts, references, and assets subdirectories remain unloaded until the activated instructions specifically call for them. This phased approach prevents large documentation files and scripts from bloating context during unrelated prompts.

Fifty installed skills add about 5,000 tokens of metadata at session start. At an input price of $2 per 1M tokens before prompt caching, loading metadata for all 50 skills costs roughly $0.01 per session.

How are skills different from MCP?

The Model Context Protocol connects an agent to external tools and live data stores through client-server connections. In contrast, an Agent Skill packages procedural instructions, executable scripts, and static reference files that an agent runtime reads directly from disk.

MCP relies on active server processes that expose tool definitions, resources, and prompt templates over standard communication protocols. A skill functions as a static file bundle that informs the model how to complete a specific task using tools already available on the host.

Both standards now operate under the Agentic AI Foundation as complementary building blocks. A skill can direct an agent on when and how to call an MCP server, while the MCP server handles the protocol communication with remote systems.

What is on the roadmap, and why does security matter?

The proposed starting roadmap for Agent Skills focuses on three areas: versioned releases, a formal specification proposal process, and security guidance for authors and users. A structured release cycle will help tool builders maintain compatibility as the format matures under foundation governance.

Security guidance represents an immediate priority because a skill can include arbitrary code in its scripts directory. When a skill's instructions tell the agent to run those scripts, they run with whatever access the agent has on that machine.

Installing a skill therefore means trusting the author who packaged it. Malicious or poorly tested scripts can modify local files, execute dangerous shell commands, or expose sensitive project data. Developers should always review the contents of the scripts directory before installing third-party skills into their environments.

How do you use skills with any model through one API key?

Claude Code reads personal skills from ~/.claude/skills//SKILL.md and project-level skills from .claude/skills//SKILL.md inside the root of a repository.

Skills are plain text files evaluated by the agent client rather than the upstream model provider. Because the client parses the frontmatter and passes the instructions to the model, the same skill files work whichever model the client calls, although results still depend on the model.

Developers can run Claude Code through the Tokely API gateway by setting two environment variables. The skill directories stay exactly as they are.

skills-ref validate ./api-cost-check
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.tokely.me ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN='<YOUR_TOKELY_API_KEY>' claude

A single Tokely API key and unified balance grants access to Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Kimi models, including Kimi K3.1 Pro. The gateway exposes an Anthropic-compatible endpoint for Claude Code and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for other agent clients, so a team can test the same skill on several models from one account. You can view all supported options on the Tokely models page or read our guide on using Claude Code with a cheaper API.

Sources

Read the announcement details at Anthropic's announcement and explore technical definitions in the Agent Skills specification. Further context appears in Simon Willison's note and our setup tutorial for Claude Code with a cheaper API.

Originally published at tokely.me.
