title: One Load per Key: Collapsing Duplicate Lookups with Spring Boot's Cache and Caffeine
description:
Rule engines, aggregators and validation pipelines share a hidden cost. Many independent components ask the same downstream question, with the same key, at the same moment. Each component is correct on its own; together they multiply the load on whatever sits behind them.

This article shows how to collapse those calls into a single load using Spring's cache abstraction backed by Caffeine. It also covers what tends to bite afterwards: cached empty results, metrics that change meaning, and tests that pass for the wrong reason.

The scenario

Take a promotion eligibility service. To decide whether a product qualifies for a promotion, it evaluates about 20 rules in parallel: in stock, price above a threshold, seller in good standing, category not excluded, and so on.

List<CompletableFuture<Boolean>> results = rules.stream()
        .map(rule -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> rule.test(productId), executor))
        .toList();

Each rule depends on a small, focused service:

@Component
class InStockRule implements Rule {

    private final StockService stockService;

    @Override
    public boolean test(String productId) {
        return stockService.isInStock(productId);
    }
}

@Service
class StockService {

    private final ProductCatalogue catalogue;

    boolean isInStock(String productId) {
        return catalogue.findProduct(productId)
                .map(product -> product.stock() > 0)
                .orElse(false);
    }
}

PricingService, SellerService and CategoryService look the same: each one reads a different field from the same Product, which comes from one place:

@Service
public class ProductCatalogue {

    // Reads from a shared cache (Redis, DynamoDB, ...), falls back to the catalogue API on a miss.
    public Optional<Product> findProduct(String productId) {
        return store.get(productId).or(() -> fetchAndStore(productId));
    }
}

The design is clean: every rule is small, testable and independent. But one evaluation of one product calls findProduct about 20 times:

  • Warm path: 20 reads from the shared cache, plus 20 deserialisations of the same object.
  • Cold path: all 20 calls miss at the same time, so the catalogue API gets 20 concurrent requests for the same product. That's a cache stampede, and it hits hardest when the downstream system is already struggling.

The calls don't need 20 answers. They need one.

Why not request scope?

The first idea is usually a request-scoped cache: memoise the response for the lifetime of the HTTP request. That works less well than it sounds:

  • Thread hopping. The rules run on executor threads. Request attributes are bound to the request thread, so request-scoped beans only work if you propagate the context to every executor (for example with a TaskDecorator).
  • No request at all. Queue consumers, Kafka listeners and scheduled jobs have no HTTP request. A @RequestScope bean there fails with No thread-bound request found.

A short-lived, in-process cache gives the same effect on every entry point. The price is bounded staleness, and with a short enough TTL that price is negligible.

Setup

Dependencies

spring-boot-starter-cache brings Spring's cache abstraction, but not Caffeine. Add both. Spring Boot manages the Caffeine version.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.github.ben-manes.caffeine</groupId>
    <artifactId>caffeine</artifactId>
</dependency>

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-cache")
implementation("com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine")

Enable caching 

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableCaching
public class Application { }

Configure the cache 

spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine
    cache-names: products
    caffeine:
      spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=30s,recordStats

Each line matters:

  • type: caffeine makes the application fail at startup if Caffeine is missing. Without it, Spring Boot silently falls back to ConcurrentMapCacheManager. That cache ignores caffeine.spec, so it has no size limit and entries never expire: unbounded memory and unbounded staleness, a worse problem than the one you set out to fix. Dependencies move around, so don't rely on Caffeine always being on the classpath.
  • cache-names creates the listed caches at startup and turns off dynamic creation: a @Cacheable that uses an unlisted name fails at runtime. It's also what lets Spring Boot register Micrometer metrics for the cache, because only caches that exist at startup are bound.
  • spec: maximumSize caps memory, expireAfterWrite caps staleness, and recordStats turns on the hit/miss statistics behind the metrics.

The annotation 

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId", sync = true)
public Optional<Product> findProduct(String productId) {
    return store.get(productId).or(() -> fetchAndStore(productId));
}

Two attributes do most of the work here.

sync = true is the difference between caching and collapsing. Without it, Spring checks the cache, misses, calls the method and stores the result. When 20 threads miss at the same moment, all 20 call the method. With sync = true, Spring hands the load to Caffeine's atomic get(key, loader): the first thread runs the method, and the other 19 wait for its result.

key = "#productId" makes the key explicit. The default key generator uses the bare argument for single-argument methods, but the moment someone adds a second parameter, the key changes shape and any matching @CacheEvict silently stops working. Referring to parameters by name needs the -parameters compiler flag (Spring Boot's build plugins enable it); otherwise use #p0.

Evicting works the same way:

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
public void evict(String productId) { }

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", allEntries = true)
public void evictAll() { }

A classic mistake: @CacheEvict("products") on a method with no arguments evicts the key SimpleKey.EMPTY, which clears nothing. Use allEntries = true to clear the whole cache.

What will surprise you

1. Empty results are cached too

Spring unwraps Optional: present values are stored as the value, and empty ones are stored as null. CaffeineCacheManager allows null values by default, so "product not found" is memoised for the full TTL.

This is often what you want: without it, a missing product is looked up again by every one of the 20 callers. But decide it deliberately. The usual escape hatch, unless = "#result == null", isn't allowed together with sync = true. If you can't accept caching empty results, you'll need a different shape, for example throwing a not-found exception (exceptions are never cached) or using the Cache API directly.

2. Failures are not shared

Exceptions aren't cached. That's good: a transient failure doesn't stick for the next 30 seconds. But it also means that when the load fails, the waiting callers don't get the error. They retry the load one after another. Under a sustained outage, put a circuit breaker or a stale-fallback strategy inside the loaded method. Don't count on the cache to absorb the failures.

3. Every caller gets the same instance

Before the cache, each caller got its own freshly deserialised copy. Now all callers within the TTL share one object, across threads. If anything modifies it, you have a data race between components that don't know about each other. Prefer immutable types (records, or immutable generated classes). If you can't, say so in a comment on the cached method.

4. Self-invocation bypasses the cache

@Cacheable works through a Spring proxy. A call from inside the same class (this.findProduct(...)) skips the proxy and the cache. Check that every hot caller goes through the bean.

5. The cache is per instance

Each pod or instance has its own cache. An eviction endpoint only clears the instance that received the request; the others keep serving the old value until the TTL expires. That's acceptable when the TTL is short. Write it down for whoever operates the endpoint.

6. Your existing metrics change meaning

Any counter incremented inside the cached method (misses on the shared cache, remote calls, fallbacks) now only fires on in-memory misses. On the day you deploy, dashboards show a sudden drop that looks like an outage or a miracle. It's neither. Warn people before the deploy, and add the cache's own metrics, which recordStats exposes:

  • cache.gets{cache="products", result="hit"|"miss"}
  • cache.puts
  • cache.evictions
  • cache.size

7. Pick the TTL for the unit of work

The goal is to collapse the calls within one unit of work, not to build a long-lived performance cache. So the TTL needs to be long enough to cover one evaluation including slow paths (retries and their backoff), and short enough that the extra staleness is negligible compared with how fresh the data behind it is anyway. Seconds to tens of seconds is usually right. If you want a longer TTL, that's a different cache, and it needs its own invalidation design.

8. Virtual threads on JDK 21–23

With sync = true, the load runs inside Caffeine's atomic compute, which holds a synchronized lock. On JDK 21–23, a virtual thread that blocks on I/O inside synchronized pins its carrier thread. Since carrier threads are few (one per core by default), many concurrent cold loads can starve the scheduler. JDK 24 fixed this (JEP 491). On older JDKs, load-test the cold path with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full.

Testing it

Prove that concurrent misses collapse

A naive test fires 20 calls and checks that the loader ran once. It usually passes even without sync = true: the stubbed load returns instantly, so the calls run one after another and the first one fills the cache before the second arrives. The test has to keep callers inside the loader until all of them have arrived:

@SpringJUnitConfig(ProductCatalogueCachingTest.Config.class)
class ProductCatalogueCachingTest {

    private static final int CALLERS = 20;

    @Autowired
    ProductCatalogue catalogue;
    @MockitoBean
    ProductStore store;

    @Test
    void concurrentMissesLoadOnce() throws Exception {
        var allCallersLoading = new CountDownLatch(CALLERS);
        var release = new CountDownLatch(1);
        // Every caller that reaches the loader waits here, so without sync = true all of them would load.
        when(store.get("p-1")).thenAnswer(invocation -> {
            allCallersLoading.countDown();
            release.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            return Optional.of(new Product("p-1", 3));
        });

        try (var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(CALLERS)) {
            var futures = IntStream.range(0, CALLERS)
                    .mapToObj(i -> executor.submit(() -> catalogue.findProduct("p-1")))
                    .toList();
            allCallersLoading.await(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
            release.countDown();
            for (var future : futures) {
                assertThat(future.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isPresent();
            }
        }
        verify(store, times(1)).get("p-1");
    }

    @Configuration
    @EnableCaching
    static class Config {

        @Bean
        CacheManager cacheManager() {
            return new CaffeineCacheManager("products");
        }

        @Bean
        ProductCatalogue catalogue(ProductStore store) {
            return new ProductCatalogue(store);
        }
    }
}

With sync = true, the first caller enters the loader and the other 19 wait in Caffeine, so get runs once. Without it, all 20 enter the loader and the test fails with Wanted 1 time, but was 20 times. Remove sync = true once to see that failure: a test you've never seen fail hasn't proven anything.

Prove that the shipped configuration is the one you think

The test above builds its own CaffeineCacheManager, so it never touches application.yml. A typo in cache-names, or a missing type, would only show up in production. ApplicationContextRunner can load the real configuration file with only the cache auto-configuration:

@Test
void applicationConfigurationCreatesBoundedCaffeineCache() {
    new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withInitializer(new ConfigDataApplicationContextInitializer())
            .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(CacheAutoConfiguration.class))
            .withUserConfiguration(CachingEnabled.class)
            .run(context -> {
                var manager = context.getBean(CacheManager.class);
                assertThat(manager).isInstanceOf(CaffeineCacheManager.class);

                var cache = (com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.Cache<?, ?>)
                        manager.getCache("products").getNativeCache();
                assertThat(cache.policy().eviction().orElseThrow().getMaximum()).isEqualTo(10_000);
                assertThat(cache.policy().expireAfterWrite().orElseThrow().getExpiresAfter())
                        .isEqualTo(Duration.ofSeconds(30));
            });
}

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
static class CachingEnabled { }

CacheAutoConfiguration lives in org.springframework.boot.cache.autoconfigure in Spring Boot 4, and in org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.cache in Spring Boot 3.

Also add one test each for eviction (evict, call again, check the loader ran twice) and for whichever empty-result behaviour you chose.

Checklist

  • [ ] spring-boot-starter-cache and caffeine declared, @EnableCaching on
  • [ ] spring.cache.type: caffeine so a missing Caffeine fails at startup
  • [ ] cache-names declared (and new names added there)
  • [ ] maximumSize, expireAfterWrite and recordStats in the spec
  • [ ] @Cacheable(sync = true) with an explicit key
  • [ ] @CacheEvict uses the same key; clear-all uses allEntries = true
  • [ ] Empty-result caching decided and tested
  • [ ] Cached return type immutable, or documented as shared
  • [ ] No self-invocation on hot paths
  • [ ] Dashboard owners warned about counters inside the cached method
  • [ ] Concurrency test that fails without sync = true
  • [ ] Configuration test against the real application.yml
  • [ ] On JDK 21–23 with virtual threads: cold path load-tested for pinning

Wrapping up

The change itself is a dependency, a few lines of YAML and one annotation. Most of the value is in the rest: deciding what gets cached (including "not found"), making the configuration fail loudly instead of degrading silently, warning the people who read the metrics, and writing tests that actually fail when the behaviour breaks. Get those right, and twenty components asking the same question cost the same as one.

title: SlothSync: A Gentler Way to Get Things Done with Gemini
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

SlothSync turns a messy list of errands and obligations into a few small next steps, plus a list of tasks that can wait. It’s for anyone who has a full mind and could use help deciding where to start.

Demo

https://slothsync1.vercel.app/

Code

Repository: https://github.com/rohini-ray/SlothSync.git

How I Built It

SlothSync is a small Python web server with a browser interface. The backend reads the Gemini API key from .env and sends the task list to Gemini for a structured plan. The browser keeps the draft and latest plan in local storage.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The app and its planning prompt are open source, so people can inspect and change how the planner behaves. I chose Gemini for hosted inference to keep setup simple and avoid requiring a local model runtime.

There’s a tradeoff: task lists are sent to Google’s Gemini API, and the app requires an API key and an internet connection. This version does not use an open-weight model or run inference offline, so it doesn’t meet that part of the challenge brief. The API key stays in the backend .env file rather than being exposed to the browser.

The Lazy Payoff

SlothSync is designed to reduce the effort of sorting and prioritizing a task pile. I haven’t measured time saved yet, so I’m not claiming a specific number.

title: Laravel API for Mobile Apps: Backend Design Guide (2026)
description:
Laravel works well as the backend for iOS, Android, Flutter, and React Native apps if the API is designed around one fact: you cannot force users to update. Version every route, return one predictable JSON shape, issue revocable per-device tokens, paginate with cursors, and ship a minimum-supported-build check in the first release.

A web frontend and its API deploy together, so a breaking change is fixed in one release. A mobile client is different. Once a build is approved and installed, it keeps calling your API exactly as it was compiled to, sometimes for years. Every decision below follows from that constraint. This guide covers the design side; for hardening the same API, pair it with the Laravel API security checklist.

Is Laravel a good backend for a mobile app?

For most product apps, yes. Laravel gives a mobile team authentication, queues, scheduled jobs, notifications, file storage, validation, and an ORM out of the box, so a small team can ship a complete API without assembling a framework from parts. It is a weaker fit for workloads dominated by long-lived connections or heavy computation.

Where it fits well:

  • Transactional product apps: accounts, orders, bookings, content feeds, subscriptions, admin workflows. This is the bulk of what mobile apps need from a server.
  • Small teams who want one conventional codebase that a new hire can read on day one.
  • Apps with background work (push notifications, upload processing, syncing with third-party systems), because queues and the scheduler are first-party.

Where I would look elsewhere, or add a separate service:

  • Real-time systems where WebSocket fan-out is the core product rather than a feature.
  • CPU-heavy pipelines such as media transcoding or model inference, which belong in dedicated workers.
  • Teams whose entire skill set is in another ecosystem. The best backend is one your team can operate at 2 a.m.

How should a Laravel API shape JSON for mobile clients?

Return every resource through an API Resource class and every error through one envelope. Mobile decoders are strict: Swift’s Codable and Kotlin serializers fail on unexpected types, so a field that is sometimes a string and sometimes null, or an error that is sometimes HTML, becomes a crash or a blank screen in production.

Laravel API Resources decouple the response from the database schema, which is exactly what an API serving old app builds needs. Rename a column and the resource keeps emitting the old key.

class OrderResource extends JsonResource
{
    public function toArray(Request $request): array
    {
        return [
            'id' => $this->public_id,          // never the auto-increment key
            'status' => $this->status->value,  // backed enum, stable strings
            'total' => [
                'amount' => $this->total_minor, // integer minor units, not floats
                'currency' => $this->currency,
            ],
            'updated_at' => $this->updated_at->toIso8601String(),
        ];
    }
}

Rules that keep decoders working across releases:

  • Only additive changes within a version. Adding a field is safe; removing, renaming, or changing a type is a new version.
  • Money as integer minor units with a currency code. Dates as ISO 8601 with an offset.
  • Enums as strings, and clients that map unknown values to a fallback case instead of failing the whole decode. Swift: give the enum a raw value and a custom init(from:) that falls back to .unknown.
  • JSON for every error, including 401, 404, 422, 429, and 500. A mobile client cannot do anything useful with an HTML error page.

Laravel decides whether to render an exception as JSON from the Accept header, and mobile HTTP clients do not always send one. Force it for API routes in bootstrap/app.php and render your envelope from the same place:

// bootstrap/app.php
return Application::configure(basePath: dirname(__DIR__))
    // ...routing and middleware...
    ->withExceptions(function (Exceptions $exceptions) {
        $exceptions->shouldRenderJsonWhen(fn (Request $request) => $request->is('api/*'));

        $exceptions->render(function (ApiException $e, Request $request) {
            return response()->json([
                'error' => [
                    'code' => $e->code(),          // stable, machine-readable
                    'message' => $e->getMessage(), // display text, safe to change server-side
                    'fields' => [],
                ],
            ], $e->status());
        });
    })->create();

The code is what the app branches on, so it never changes once shipped. The message is copy you can reword without a release. fields carries per-field validation messages for 422 responses and is otherwise empty, so the client always has one decoder and one error-handling path.

Which authentication should a mobile app use with Laravel?

For a first-party app, use Laravel Sanctum API tokens: one token per device, named after the device, scoped with abilities, and revocable by deleting a row. Reach for Passport only when you need an OAuth2 server for third-party clients. Self-contained JWTs make revocation harder than it needs to be.

Sanctum vs Passport vs JWT for mobile apps

Factor Sanctum tokens Passport (OAuth2) JWT package
Token type Opaque, stored hashed in the database OAuth2 access and refresh tokens Signed, self-contained token
Revoke one device Delete the token row Revoke the token and its refresh token Needs a denylist until expiry
Refresh flow Not built in; use expiry plus re-login or a custom rotate endpoint Built in Provided by the package
Third-party clients Not designed for it Yes, including authorization code with PKCE Not designed for it
Setup and upkeep Low, first-party Higher: clients, grants, keys Moderate, community-maintained
Best fit Your own iOS, Android, Flutter, or React Native app Platforms where partners need delegated access Stateless verification across several services

Issue the token from a login endpoint that takes a device_name, so users can see and sign out individual devices, and a lost phone can be revoked without logging out everything else:

$token = $user->createToken(
    $request->input('device_name'),    // e.g. "iPhone 16 - iOS"
    ['orders:read', 'orders:write'],   // abilities checked per route
    now()->addDays(30),                // per-token expiry
);

return ['token' => $token->plainTextToken];

On both sides of the token lifecycle:

  • Store the token in the platform keystore: the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore-backed storage. Never in UserDefaults, plain shared preferences, or AsyncStorage.
  • Set an expiry. Sanctum tokens never expire unless expiration in config/sanctum.php is set (minutes) or createToken() gets a date. Pair it with a scheduled sanctum:prune-expired so the table does not grow forever.
  • Revoke on risk events. A password change, account recovery, or “sign out all devices” should delete the relevant token rows immediately.
  • Treat a 401 as a state, not an error. The client clears the stored token and returns to sign-in once, rather than retrying in a loop.

For the client side of the same problem, the mobile banking security checklist covers token storage, session handling, and the controls a security review expects in the app.

How do you version a Laravel API so old app builds keep working?

Put the version in the URL, starting at /api/v1 on day one, and only make additive changes inside a version. Ship a public configuration endpoint that returns the minimum supported build, so you can prompt or force an update before you remove anything an old build depends on.

// routes/api.php
Route::prefix('v1')->group(function () {
    Route::get('/app-config', AppConfigController::class);   // public, cacheable
    Route::post('/auth/token', [AuthController::class, 'store'])
        ->middleware('throttle:auth');

    Route::middleware(['auth:sanctum', 'throttle:api'])->group(function () {
        Route::get('/orders', [OrderController::class, 'index']);
        Route::delete('/auth/token', [AuthController::class, 'destroy']);
    });
});

The client sends its platform and build number on every request and checks the configuration endpoint at launch. A Swift version using URLSession:

struct AppConfig: Decodable {
    let minimumSupportedBuild: Int
    let latestBuild: Int
    let updateUrl: URL
}

func fetchAppConfig() async throws -> AppConfig {
    var request = URLRequest(url: URL(string: "https://api.example.com/api/v1/app-config")!)
    request.setValue("ios", forHTTPHeaderField: "X-Client-Platform")
    request.setValue(Bundle.main.object(forInfoDictionaryKey: "CFBundleVersion") as? String,
                     forHTTPHeaderField: "X-Client-Build")

    let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(for: request)
    guard (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 200 else {
        throw URLError(.badServerResponse)
    }

    let decoder = JSONDecoder()
    decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase
    return try decoder.decode(AppConfig.self, from: data)
}

A deprecation policy that holds up:

  • Log the client build on every request. You cannot retire a version without knowing which builds still call it.
  • Run versions side by side. v2 controllers reuse the same services and models; only the resources and request validation differ.
  • Soft prompt, then hard block. Raise a “recommended update” first, and only raise minimum_supported_build once usage of the old build is negligible by your own numbers, not by the calendar.
  • Return a specific error code, such as client_update_required, from retired endpoints so even a build that predates the update prompt shows something sensible.

Header-based versioning (Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json) is tidier in theory. In practice a URL prefix is easier to grep in logs, route in a load balancer, and explain to the person writing the Android client.

How should pagination and sync work for offline-first apps?

Use cursor pagination for lists and an updated_since parameter for sync. Offset pagination skips or duplicates rows when data changes between page requests, which happens constantly on a phone with a flaky connection. Cursors are stable, and delta sync means the app downloads only what changed.

$orders = $request->user()->orders()
    ->withTrashed()   // include soft-deleted rows as tombstones
    ->when($request->filled('updated_since'), fn ($query) =>
        $query->where('updated_at', '>', $request->date('updated_since')))
    ->orderBy('updated_at')
    ->orderBy('id')   // tie-breaker: cursor columns must be unique together
    ->cursorPaginate(min($request->integer('per_page', 50), 100));

return OrderResource::collection($orders);

Details that decide whether sync is reliable:

  • Deletions must sync too. Soft deletes with a deleted_at in the resource let the client remove local rows it would otherwise keep forever.
  • The client stores the server’s timestamp, not the device clock, as its next updated_since value. Return it in the response; device clocks drift.
  • Writes are idempotent. Accept a client-generated UUID or Idempotency-Key header on create requests, store it with the row, and return the existing record on a repeat, so a retry after a dropped response does not create a duplicate.
  • Conflicts have a rule decided up front: last write wins, server wins, or a 409 with both versions that the app resolves. Undefined behaviour here turns into data loss.

How do you send push notifications from Laravel?

Send them from queued jobs, never inside the request. Store each device’s push token against the user and platform, dispatch a queued notification, and deliver through APNs for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android. For APNs, use token-based authentication with a .p8 signing key rather than a certificate; the key does not expire and works across all your apps. For FCM, use the HTTP v1 API; the legacy API was shut down in 2024 and some older packages still target it.

  • Register tokens on every launch with an upsert endpoint. Push tokens change, and the app is the only party that knows when.
  • Prune invalid tokens when APNs returns 410 or FCM reports UNREGISTERED, otherwise the queue spends its time on devices that no longer exist.
  • Keep payloads small and non-sensitive. Send an identifier and let the app fetch the detail over the authenticated API; lock screens are not private.
  • Separate queues by priority so a bulk marketing send cannot delay a time-sensitive transactional alert.

How should mobile apps upload files to a Laravel backend?

Let the app upload directly to object storage with a short-lived presigned URL, then tell the API the upload finished. Streaming large photos or videos through PHP ties up workers on slow mobile connections. Laravel generates presigned S3 upload URLs, so the API only authorizes and records the file.

['url' => $url, 'headers' => $headers] = Storage::disk('s3')
    ->temporaryUploadUrl(
        'uploads/'.$request->user()->id.'/'.Str::uuid().'.jpg',
        now()->addMinutes(5)
    );

return ['upload_url' => $url, 'headers' => $headers];

A presigned PUT cannot enforce a size limit, so after the app confirms the upload, check the object server-side: Storage::size() against your cap, the real content type from the bytes rather than the extension, and that the key belongs to the caller. Push any processing such as thumbnails onto a queue. Never trust the file type the client claims.

What rate limits does a mobile API need?

At minimum, a general per-user limit for authenticated routes and much stricter limits on login, one-time codes, and password reset. Key limits by user ID when authenticated and by IP otherwise. Mobile carriers put many users behind shared IP addresses, so IP-only limits punish legitimate users.

Laravel’s named rate limiters express this in a few lines. The numbers below are starting points; tune them from your own traffic:

// AppServiceProvider::boot()
RateLimiter::for('api', function (Request $request) {
    return Limit::perMinute(60)->by($request->user()?->id ?: $request->ip());
});

RateLimiter::for('auth', function (Request $request) {
    return [
        Limit::perMinute(5)->by(strtolower((string) $request->input('email')).'|'.$request->ip()),
        Limit::perMinute(20)->by($request->ip()),
    ];
});

The throttle middleware adds Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers to the 429 for you; make sure the body is still your error envelope, and make the client honour Retry-After with jittered backoff. A client that retries instantly on failure turns a brief incident into a self-inflicted outage. The OWASP API Security Top 10 lists unrestricted resource consumption and broken authorization among the most common API risks, and both apply directly to mobile backends.

What should you monitor on a mobile backend?

Error rates and latency per endpoint, broken down by app version and platform. A backend change that looks healthy overall can break one older build entirely, and you will only see it if requests carry the client build and your dashboards can filter by it.

  • Request context: client platform, build, and a request ID. Generate the ID in middleware, put it in Log::withContext(), and return it in a response header so support can match an app report to a server log.
  • Error tracking on both sides, with the same request ID visible in app crash reports and server exceptions.
  • Queue health: backlog depth, failed jobs, and job duration. Laravel Pulse or a hosted APM covers the basics; Horizon adds detail if you run Redis queues.
  • Version adoption: requests per build over time, which is the number you need before retiring an API version.

Where does Next.js fit next to a Laravel mobile backend?

Beside Laravel, not in front of the mobile app. Next.js works well for an admin dashboard, marketing site, or web version of the product, consuming the same Laravel API or a separate web backend-for-frontend (see Next.js web development). The mobile app should call Laravel directly through its versioned API.

Adding a Next.js layer between the app and Laravel means two services that must both stay compatible with every installed build. Keep the mobile contract in one place. If you are planning the stack as a whole, my Laravel API backend development service covers the API, admin tooling, and infrastructure together.

What should you build first?

Before the first app release, get the decisions that are expensive to reverse in place: the /api/v1 prefix, the response and error envelope, per-device Sanctum tokens with an expiry, the app-config endpoint with a minimum build, and client build logging. Everything else in this guide can be added later without breaking installed apps. Cursor pagination is the one I would move up the list if the app has any list that grows, because switching from offset to cursor later changes the response shape.

If you are still scoping the product, the mobile MVP playbook covers what to include in a first release, and mobile app development covers the client side. When you want the backend designed and built alongside the app, I offer Laravel backend and API development for mobile apps.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should a mobile app use Laravel Sanctum or Passport?

Use Sanctum when your own first-party app is the only client. It issues revocable per-device tokens with very little setup. Choose Passport only when you need a real OAuth2 server, for example when third-party developers or partner apps must obtain delegated access to your users' data.

How long should a Laravel API keep supporting an old version?

Long enough that almost no active installs still depend on it. Set the window from your own analytics on build adoption rather than the calendar, announce it in-app before removal, and use a minimum-supported-build check so the last stragglers see an update prompt instead of broken screens.

Can Laravel handle real-time features for a mobile app?

Yes. Laravel broadcasting with Laravel Reverb, or a hosted WebSocket service, covers live updates while the app is in the foreground. Push notifications through APNs and FCM still handle the background case, because mobile operating systems suspend open sockets when the app is not active.

Should a mobile app call Laravel directly or go through Next.js?

Call Laravel directly. A mobile client gains little from an extra hop, and every layer is another thing that has to stay backward compatible with old app builds. Next.js earns its place for the admin panel, marketing site, or a web client, not as a proxy in front of the mobile API.

title: Your AI-Built App Broke After Launch: The 30-Minute Post-Mortem
description:
The break never happens at the demo

The demo always works. Stakes are zero, the input is clean, one user, one pass down the happy path. The break arrives after launch — when the export has a blank row, when two people use the tool at once, when the number on screen has to agree with the number on the invoice.

Nate B Jones gave the pattern a name in a video this month that hit with a lot of people: vibe-coded apps can "look right and fall apart after launch." The screen was convincing. The plumbing under it was never built — because it was never in the conversation.

The instinctive fix — go back to the chat and prompt harder — fails for a structural reason. The missing pieces weren't omitted by the model; they were omitted by the description. Error handling, state that survives a restart, what happens when the input is wrong — production software carries a layer of behavior nobody asks for, because nobody demos it. As the write-up that accompanied the video put it: a convincing screen tells you very little about what should happen next, what needs to be remembered, or which numbers have to agree.

The new lever: your agent can look inside real software

What changed this month is that the missing reference material is now reachable. REA — "Reverse Engineer Anything," an open-source project that has passed 200,000 GitHub stars — gives coding agents like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex a set of tools to inspect installed software and explain how a feature actually works. The flagship example from the REA team's published work: a developer pointed the agent at QuickBooks Desktop, investigated how the real thing handles transactions and reports, and then built a local accounting app — Ledger Reborn — with its own transaction engine.

The point of that story isn't "clone QuickBooks." The point is that the investigation turned years of taken-for-granted behavior into a visible list of decisions: which records to keep, how a result is calculated, what happens when something changes. That's exactly the layer your AI-built app is missing — and now there's a repeatable way to go look at it.

Here's the drill for the day the break arrives.

The 30-minute post-mortem

Step 1 — Reproduce the break (5 minutes)

Write down the exact steps that trigger it: which screen, which input, what you expected, what happened instead. Not "the invoicing tool is broken" — the specific row of input that breaks it. If it can't be reproduced, it can't be fixed, and there is nothing precise to hand an agent. The reproduction is your spec for the repair and your acceptance test after it.

Step 2 — Diff against a real one (10 minutes)

Ask the agent what an app that does this job for a living has that yours doesn't. If you run Claude Code or Codex, REA can point the agent at a real installed program and ask how that feature survives the situation that broke yours. If that's past your line, say so plainly in the chat: "Here is the broken path. What does production software typically have on this path that a generated app might be missing?" The answer is usually a short list: input validation, error handling instead of a crash, state that persists, defined behavior for empty or duplicated input. The goal is learning what production apps carry, not copying one — behavior ideas are fair game; lifting proprietary code or assets is not.

Step 3 — Rebuild the one path (10 minutes)

Not the whole app. The short list from step 2 becomes a mini-spec for the single path that broke: what goes in, what comes out, what happens when the input is wrong. Rebuild that path, then run the exact reproduction from step 1 as the acceptance test. One path, one fix, one test — a whole-app rewrite in this moment is how a 30-minute post-mortem becomes a bad weekend.

Step 4 — Make the keep-or-retire call (5 minutes)

This is the step everyone skips, and it's the entire point. If the fix holds and the failure was one path: keep the app, and write down the fix while it's fresh. But if this is the third week in a row the app breaks somewhere new, that's not bad luck — that's a tool doing production work it was never scoped for. The honest options are retire (buy the boring, supported tool that absorbs this class of failure) or promote (write the real spec — inputs, outputs, edge cases, rollback — and rebuild deliberately, treating the first version as the prototype it always was).

The honest boundaries

  • The deep inspection is a developer tool. If you don't already run Claude Code or Codex, step 2's full version is a one-afternoon job for whoever built the app or a freelancer, not a DIY evening. The post-mortem structure still works with the plain conversation version — you lose depth, not the drill.
  • One repair is data; two is a pattern. Don't let the keep-or-retire question drift just because the fix worked tonight. A tool that needs a post-mortem every week is a subscription you're paying in hours.
  • The post-mortem is the floor, not the ceiling. It exists so a single break costs you 30 minutes instead of a rebuild. It is not a substitute for writing the spec before the next build — the cheapest post-mortem is the one you never need.

Tonight's version

Pick the broken thing — you know the one. Write the reproduction steps. Run the diff conversation, even if it's the plain-chat version. Rebuild one path and test it against the reproduction. Then make the call out loud: keep, or retire.

If the app survives the night, write down what it does and who owns it — so the next post-mortem isn't the only documentation the tool has.

Want the frameworks that prevent this repair loop? The Boring Automation Pack includes the spec templates, acceptance-test prompts, and guardrail checklists that keep AI-built tools useful without becoming a liability.

title: Valid JSON Is Only Half the Output Contract
description:
A response can be valid JSON and still give a downstream consumer the wrong shape. A Markdown handoff can read fluently while omitting the one section the next engineer needs.

Those are concrete interface failures. They deserve checks that say which field or section broke the agreement.

Output Contracts is a small Python validator for explicit Markdown and JSON requirements. It does not call a model, score the writing, or silently repair the output.

Write down the consumer requirement

Imagine a work handoff that must contain these sections in order:

  1. Summary
  2. Evidence
  3. Unresolved questions
  4. Next steps

A handoff that omits unresolved questions and moves evidence below the next steps might be readable, but it no longer follows the agreed interface. The bundled Markdown contract declares required headings, ordering, and a forbidden completion phrase.

The last rule has a narrow meaning. Banning Everything is complete. can enforce a wording constraint. It cannot determine whether the work is actually complete or whether another phrase makes an equally unsupported claim.

Validate the bad handoff

Use Python 3.11 or newer. There are no third-party runtime dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/asadani/output-contracts.git
cd output-contracts
out_dir="$(mktemp -d)"

python -m output_contracts validate \
  fixtures/handoff-contract.json fixtures/handoff-bad.md \
  --format markdown --out "$out_dir/handoff-review.md"

python -m output_contracts inspect fixtures/handoff-contract.json

Validation exits with status 1 because the fixture violates the contract. The report identifies the missing section, the ordering problem, and the forbidden phrase. inspect validates the contract itself and prints its normalized summary.

A clean validation returns 0. Invalid contracts, unreadable input, and command errors return 2, so a calling script can distinguish a rejected output from a broken validation operation.

Check values as well as syntax

The JSON example requires an identifier, a constrained status, an integer count, and a non-empty items array. The bad fixture includes:

{
  "id": "case-18",
  "status": "accepted",
  "count": true,
  "items": []
}

This parses as JSON. It still violates two declared requirements: true does not satisfy the integer type, and an empty array does not satisfy the minimum item count.

Run both versions:

python -m output_contracts validate \
  fixtures/result-contract.json fixtures/result-bad.json \
  --format json --out "$out_dir/bad-result-review.json"

python -m output_contracts validate \
  fixtures/result-contract.json fixtures/result-good.json \
  --format markdown --out "$out_dir/good-result-review.md"

The adverse example exits with 1; the good example exits with 0. Fields use JSON pointers, and null remains distinct from a missing field.

Keep the contract proportionate

The current implementation is deliberately small. Markdown heading checks recognize ATX headings outside fenced code; they do not treat bold text or HTML as headings. Forbidden patterns scan the full output, including code blocks.

That detail can create false positives. A tutorial quoting a forbidden phrase in an example may need a different contract from a handoff that must never contain it. Patterns come from trusted contract authors, and complex regular expressions are not sandboxed or guaranteed to run in linear time.

For general JSON Schema validation, an established validator may fit better. This project is a compact option for a bounded workflow that needs both report-oriented Markdown checks and a small set of JSON field constraints.

Validate before the next operation

Put structural validation at the point where another person or program consumes the output. Save the report and route violations for correction. Keep content review separate: a required Evidence section can still contain a false statement, and a correctly typed count can still be wrong.

Start with one recurring failure that costs someone time. Add a rule for it, check useful and adverse examples, and watch for false positives before adding more constraints.

The MIT-licensed repository includes the fixture contracts, format reference, and validator. Its useful promise is precise feedback about declared rules.

AI disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance using the project's code and fixtures. Passing these checks establishes structural conformance, not factual correctness.

title: OpenAI Decisions API now available on AI Gateway
description:
OpenAI’s Decisions API is now available through AI Gateway at /v1/decisions. It uses the same request and response format as OpenAI, so existing OpenAI SDK integrations can switch by changing the base URL, credentials, and model ID.

Decision models answer typed questions about shared input and return structured answers rather than generated text. In one request, you can ask a model to:

  • Estimate the probability that a condition is true with a predicate question

  • Select from supplied options with a choice question

  • Rate the input against an ordered rubric with a score question

The endpoint works with any decision model on AI Gateway, including Jev, Liquid d1, and Laya. Use openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions model. This is separate from openai/gpt-6-luna, which generates text.

With OpenAI SDK 7.30.0 or later for JavaScript or 3.26.0 or later for Python, point the client at AI Gateway and call decisions.create:

The response returns answers in question order, each with the corresponding question’s name.

See the OpenAI Decisions API documentation for Python and cURL examples. To use decision models with the AI SDK or /v1/evaluate, see the decision documentation.

title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
description:
By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform Team

At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.

The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.

Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.

Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:

  • Does any consumer still call this method?
  • Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?
  • Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?
  • Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?

At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.

Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.

We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:

  1. What changed in the library’s public API?
  2. Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?

The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.

From API Changes to Consumer Impact

Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.

Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.

On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.

During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.

Consider this simplified API change:

public interface Client {
- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);
+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);
}

For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:

SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind,
       r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_path
FROM requested_changes c
JOIN quasar.symbol_refs r
  ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonical

requested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.

For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.

Bringing the Analysis Before Release

Version-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.

For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.

An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.

Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.

Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:

{
  "change": "REMOVED",
  "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)",
  "affectedRepositories": 137,
  "versionDistribution": [
    { "version": "4.2.1", "repositories": 86 },
    { "version": "4.1.7", "repositories": 38 },
    { "version": "3.9.4", "repositories": 13 }
  ],
  "sampleConsumerLocations": [
    {
      "repository": "checkout-service",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/checkout/CheckoutClient.java",
      "lines": [84, 129]
    },
    {
      "repository": "client-wrapper",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java",
      "lines": [57]
    }
  ],
  "libraryCriticality": {
    "tier": 1,
    "basis": "highest-tier downstream application"
  },
  "comparison": {
    "baseShaFound": true,
    "headShaFound": true
  }
}

The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.

Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.

A Polyglot Foundation with SCIP

The shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.

Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.

Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.

SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.

Moving Risk Assessment Earlier

Today, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.

We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.

Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”

Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.

What We Learned

Building this workflow led us to four practical lessons.

  • Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.
  • Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.
  • Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.
  • Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.

Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.

Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.

A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possible

Related Talks

  • From Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.
  • Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.

Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Where can I get free credits to test LLM inference
description:
DigitalOcean gives new customers a free \$5 credit, with no credit card required, through its Managed Agents free trial. The credit covers inference on DigitalOcean-hosted models plus the agent runtime and tools around them. It's sized for testing, and Managed Agents is in Public Preview.

Key takeaways:

  • New DigitalOcean customers get \$5 in free credit, no credit card required, to test inference through Managed Agents.
  • Trial inference runs on DigitalOcean-hosted models such as Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, and DeepSeek V4 Flash. Frontier models like Claude and GPT bill at list price.
  • Credit drains as you use compute, storage, and tools, so pause idle sessions and watch your balance.

What the free credit covers

Managed Agents pairs Harness Runtime, which runs agent sessions in isolated Firecracker microVMs, with Action Gateway, which gives agents governed access to 16,000+ tools through one MCP endpoint. It integrates natively with the Inference Engine, so inference tokens, agent execution, and tool use come together in one place.

Refer to the Agent Droplets pricing page for more details about the trial offer, as well as details for paid Pro (\$50 per month) and Team (\$200 per month) plans.

Which models you can test

The trial's inference is built around models DigitalOcean hosts, including Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3. For scale, as of October 2026, the DigitalOcean-hosted GLM-5.3 Flash lists at \$0.15 per million input tokens and \$0.50 per million output tokens on the Inference pricing page. Frontier models like Claude and GPT are also available through DigitalOcean without a provider key of your own, billed at list price and outside the Agent Droplets plan discounts. If you bring your own provider key, that provider bills you directly.

DigitalOcean's Agent Droplets announcement estimates the free trial at roughly 4.5M tokens of inference.

How to start

Sign up as a new customer, open Managed Agents in the control panel, and start the trial. The Harness Runtime docs include a quickstart that launches an agent with one doctl command, and the launch post reports supported harnesses like OpenCode and Codex CLI.

What to watch while you test

Usage draws down your balance as agents run, and Harness Runtime has no per-session or per-product spend limit. Some Action Gateway tools, like Exa web search and web fetch, are prepaid and metered per call. Serverless inference is prepaid too, so access is suspended when credits and balances run out.

To save credits, pause sessions you aren't using. Pausing stops CPU and memory charges, though retained checkpoints still accrue storage fees. Current rates are on the Harness Runtime pricing page.

LLM inference free credits FAQ

Is there an inference provider with a free tier?

DigitalOcean offers new customers a free trial with \$5 in credit through Managed Agents, no credit card required. It's a starter credit for new customers rather than an ongoing free tier, and it covers inference on DigitalOcean-hosted models, runtime, storage, and tools.

Where can I run inference for an AI app and bill it all through one invoice?

Managed Agents integrates with the DigitalOcean Inference Engine, so inference on DigitalOcean-hosted models, agent compute, storage, and tool calls bill together. Models you reach with your own provider key are billed by that provider.

How do I cap inference billing to avoid surprise costs from runaway agents?

Harness Runtime has no per-session or per-product spend limit, and usage draws down your prepaid balance. Pausing a session stops CPU and memory charges, and auto-pause handles idle sessions, though retained checkpoints still accrue storage fees. Monitor usage closely on autonomous workflows.

References & further reading

  • Start with the Managed Agents product page for trial terms.
  • The launch post and the Agent Droplets announcement explain the architecture and the trial.
  • Worth bookmarking: the Agent Droplets pricing page for plan comparisons.
  • The Harness Runtime pricing page lists compute and storage rates. Worth checking directly before you build.
  • The Inference pricing docs have per-model token rates and prepaid billing rules.
  • Learn more about Harness Runtime and the Inference Engine.

Announcement

Apigee Emulator

Apigee Emulator v2.0.2

On October 21, 2026, we released Apigee Emulator version 2.0.2.

This release upgrades the Apigee Emulator runtime to Java 21 (Eclipse Temurin JRE 21) to align local proxy development and policy execution with the production Apigee runtime, while keeping the embedded Apache Cassandra datastore pinned to Java 8. It also addresses 46 security vulnerabilities across Netty, Jackson, Apache Log4j, BouncyCastle, Apache CXF, Eclipse Jetty, and the embedded Cassandra Go standard library health-check binary.

The emulator image is available at Artifact Registry.

To upgrade, update the emulator version in your Cloud Code for VS Code settings to 2.0.2. See Manage the Apigee Emulator for details.

Feature

Apigee Emulator

  • Upgraded Netty to 4.1.137.Final (from 4.1.135.Final) and updated netty-tcnative-boringssl-static and netty-tcnative-classes to 2.0.81.Final (from 2.0.77.Final).
  • Upgraded Jackson (jackson-core, jackson-databind, and jackson-dataformat-yaml) to 2.21.7 (from 2.18.6 and 2.19.2) and jackson-annotations to 2.21.
