Credibility is best supported by truthful information and transparent recordkeeping, not by the age of an account alone.
For anyone studying verified Binance accounts, the central lesson is that identity confirmation and trustworthy behavior are related but distinct concepts. Verification addresses defined identity requirements, while responsible behavior involves ongoing accuracy, compliance, and careful management of financial activities.
Section 5: Productivity and Workflow
5.1 Improving Efficiency Through Organized Account Management
Digital financial platforms can generate many types of information, including account notifications, transaction records, identity-related messages, and statements. Without an organized approach, it can become difficult to locate important details.
A simple workflow can make these tasks more manageable. Users can review notifications at planned intervals, organize permitted records by date, and maintain a clear separation between personal correspondence and financial documentation.
An organized email account can support this process by making official communications easier to locate. Labels, folders, searchable subject lines, and calendar reminders can help people keep track of administrative tasks.
The goal is not to spend more time managing accounts. It is to reduce unnecessary repetition and make important information easier to find when needed.
5.2 Actionable Tips for a More Efficient Workflow
The following practices can improve digital organization:

  1. Create a consistent recordkeeping system. Use clearly named folders for statements, educational materials, and relevant correspondence.
  2. Review official notifications regularly. Read messages from the service directly and check whether any action is required.
  3. Maintain accurate information. Review personal details and follow the platform's official procedures when an update is necessary.
  4. Keep learning notes. Record unfamiliar cryptocurrency terms and look up their meanings using reliable educational sources.
  5. Use simple financial summaries. Where appropriate, maintain a spreadsheet that distinguishes dates, transaction amounts, fees, and asset values.
  6. Review records periodically. Check that files are readable, correctly labeled, and stored in an appropriate location. These steps are useful for students, professionals, and anyone managing multiple online services. 5.3 Separating Learning From Financial Decisions Productivity also improves when education and financial decision-making are treated as separate activities. A learner can begin by exploring educational materials, reviewing sample transaction records, and studying hypothetical portfolio scenarios. This makes it possible to build foundational knowledge before deciding whether any real financial activity is appropriate. For example, a spreadsheet containing hypothetical purchases can illustrate how transaction fees affect the total cost of an activity. Another exercise might compare the displayed prices of several digital assets over a fixed period. These exercises develop analytical skills without requiring an immediate financial commitment. The key principle is to create a repeatable process: learn a concept, test your understanding with an example, document the result, and review any mistakes. Over time, this approach can make unfamiliar digital financial systems easier to understand. Section 6: Case Studies and Examples The following examples are illustrative scenarios designed to demonstrate practical lessons. They are not claims about specific Binance customers or documented individual experiences. 6.1 Case Study One: A Student Learning About Cryptocurrency Maya is a university student interested in understanding blockchain technology. She has heard about cryptocurrency exchanges but does not understand the difference between an exchange account, an email address, and a digital wallet. Instead of beginning with financial transactions, Maya studies basic terminology and reviews educational materials. She creates a glossary covering blockchain networks, public addresses, transaction fees, market prices, and identity verification. She then uses a spreadsheet to record hypothetical asset prices and calculate percentage changes. Her notes include the date of each observation and the assumptions behind each calculation. After several weeks, Maya has a better understanding of how cryptocurrency information is presented and what she still needs to learn. Learning points: ● Digital finance becomes easier to understand when concepts are studied individually. ● Verification is a separate process from email confirmation. ● Hypothetical exercises can teach financial concepts without requiring actual transactions. ● Keeping learning notes improves retention and helps identify knowledge gaps. 6.2 Case Study Two: A Freelancer Organizing Financial Records Daniel works as a freelance designer and receives payments from clients through several different services. He wants to improve his recordkeeping because finding old statements and payment confirmations takes too much time. He develops a monthly workflow that includes reviewing payment notifications, downloading permitted statements, and categorizing income and expenses in a spreadsheet. When studying cryptocurrency-related services, Daniel applies the same approach. He records relevant dates, distinguishes transaction fees from transaction amounts, and keeps educational notes separate from actual financial records. He also learns that account verification requirements vary across platforms and jurisdictions. Instead of assuming that an established email address is sufficient, he consults the relevant service's official documentation. Learning points: ● Consistent recordkeeping reduces administrative effort. ● Email history can support organization but does not replace formal identity checks. ● Separating actual financial records from hypothetical exercises prevents confusion. ● Understanding platform-specific requirements helps avoid unnecessary delays. 6.3 Case Study Three: A Small Business Owner Improving Digital Literacy A small business owner named Priya wants to understand the financial technologies increasingly discussed by customers and colleagues. She does not plan to make cryptocurrency transactions immediately, but she wants to understand common terminology. She studies how cryptocurrency exchanges differ from traditional payment processors and how identity verification fits into financial-service administration. Priya creates a short internal reference document defining common terms and listing questions employees should research before using an unfamiliar financial platform. Her document explains that available services can vary according to location, eligibility, and current platform rules. It also recommends consulting authoritative documentation rather than relying exclusively on informal online discussions. Learning points: ● Financial technology knowledge can help people communicate more confidently. ● Clear definitions reduce confusion in professional conversations. ● Platform rules should be checked directly rather than assumed. ● Educational resources are most useful when paired with critical evaluation. 6.4 Case Study Four: An Individual Improving Personal Financial Awareness Alex wants to become more comfortable interpreting financial information. Cryptocurrency prices attract his attention, but he recognizes that price movements alone do not explain the full cost or suitability of a financial activity. He begins with a personal learning plan. First, he studies percentages, transaction fees, and the difference between realized and unrealized gains. Next, he uses hypothetical figures to compare possible outcomes under different price scenarios. He also practices identifying the source and date of financial information. When reading about Binance account verification, he distinguishes official platform instructions from general commentary published by third parties. After completing these exercises, Alex is better equipped to interpret financial terminology and ask informed questions. Learning points: ● Numerical literacy supports better interpretation of financial information. ● Hypothetical examples help reveal the effects of different assumptions. ● Information should be assessed according to its source and relevance. ● Understanding a financial platform does not require immediate participation in financial markets. Together, these scenarios demonstrate that the educational value of verified-account knowledge extends beyond account registration. It can support organization, professional communication, digital literacy, and more informed financial discussions. Section 7: Step-by-Step Guide This six-step guide explains how to apply the concepts in this article to cryptocurrency education and account administration. Step 1: Define Your Learning Objective Begin by deciding what you want to understand. Your objective might be learning about Binance verification, understanding cryptocurrency terminology, interpreting transaction records, or exploring blockchain technology. Write down two or three questions you want to answer. Examples include: What information does identity verification establish? How do transaction fees work? What is the difference between an exchange and a digital wallet? A clear objective helps you focus on relevant information instead of navigating unfamiliar features without a plan. Step 2: Consult Authoritative Information Start with the official Binance website and its help-center documentation. Look for current explanations of account registration, identity verification, eligibility, and available services. Check whether the documentation applies to your jurisdiction. Requirements can differ by country and may change over time. General informational sources, including usasvcit where relevant, can provide additional context or help you identify topics to research. Verify important platform-specific claims against official documentation rather than relying on a third-party summary alone. Step 3: Understand the Verification Process Learn the purpose of each stage described by the platform. Determine which steps concern contact details, which concern identity information, and which relate to eligibility or additional requirements. Read the instructions carefully before beginning an official process. If you have questions about a particular requirement, consult the platform's published guidance. Use your own accurate information when completing identity-related procedures. Do not treat account age, email history, or another person's records as substitutes for the applicable verification requirements. Step 4: Build a Personal Learning Record Create a document or spreadsheet for your notes. Include the concept being studied, its definition, the source, the date reviewed, and any remaining questions. For example, a note about transaction fees might explain how a fee affects the total amount recorded in a hypothetical transaction. A note about verification might distinguish identity confirmation from email confirmation. Keeping information organized makes it easier to review concepts and recognize when an explanation needs further research. Step 5: Practice With Hypothetical Examples Use sample figures to practice interpreting financial data. Calculate percentage changes, compare hypothetical fees, and examine how different asset prices would affect a fictional portfolio. Clearly label all simulated figures as examples. Keep these exercises separate from actual statements or transaction records. The purpose is to understand the mathematics and terminology involved, not to predict future market movements or assume that a particular outcome is guaranteed. Step 6: Review and Apply What You Have Learned At the end of each learning session, summarize the main points in your own words. Identify any concepts that remain unclear and return to authoritative resources for clarification. If you use a financial platform, follow its current requirements and maintain accurate personal information. Review your records periodically and keep administrative tasks organized. This process turns general information into practical knowledge. By repeating it, you can improve your digital literacy, strengthen your analytical skills, and become more comfortable evaluating unfamiliar financial technologies. Section 8: Frequently Asked Questions 8.1 What Does a Verified Binance Account Mean? A verified Binance account is an account that has completed the identity-verification requirements applicable to that account and jurisdiction. The process may involve personal information, identity documents, or additional checks. Exact requirements depend on the platform's current rules and the user's circumstances. 8.2 Does an Old Gmail Account Automatically Provide Binance Verification? No. The age of a Gmail account does not establish identity or replace the verification process required by Binance. Email confirmation and identity verification serve different purposes. A person should follow the applicable official procedures using accurate information. 8.3 Why Is Identity Verification Important in Digital Finance? Identity verification can help financial-service providers establish customer identity and meet applicable legal or regulatory obligations. Depending on the service and jurisdiction, it may also determine eligibility for particular features. Verification should not be interpreted as a guarantee of financial success or a universal endorsement of a user. 8.4 What Can Beginners Learn Before Using a Cryptocurrency Exchange? Beginners can study blockchain fundamentals, digital wallets, transaction fees, cryptocurrency price movements, and the distinction between exchanges and payment services. They can also practice interpreting sample transaction records and calculating hypothetical percentage changes before making any financial decisions. 8.5 How Can I Organize Cryptocurrency-Related Records? Use clearly labeled folders or files for official statements, transaction records, educational materials, and relevant correspondence. Record dates consistently and distinguish actual transactions from hypothetical exercises. Follow applicable recordkeeping requirements and consult a qualified professional when tax or accounting questions arise. 8.6 Is Third-Party Information Enough to Understand Binance Verification? Third-party educational information can provide context, introduce terminology, and suggest questions for further research. However, it should not be the sole authority for current platform requirements. Check the official Binance website and relevant local regulatory resources when confirming eligibility, identity-verification procedures, or available services. Conclusion Understanding the phrase “Buy Verified Binance Accounts” requires a broader perspective on digital identity, financial technology, and responsible account administration. Although the phrase is commonly associated with cryptocurrency-related searches, the most useful educational lessons concern how verification works, why accurate personal information matters, and how people can evaluate digital financial services. A verified account represents completion of specified identity checks, subject to the platform's applicable requirements. It is distinct from an old email account, a history of online activity, or a general measure of personal credibility. Recognizing these differences helps readers understand account requirements more clearly and avoid confusing unrelated forms of digital identity. The practical benefits of this knowledge extend into everyday life. Learning to interpret transaction records, calculate percentages, organize financial documents, and consult reliable sources can improve digital literacy and administrative efficiency. These abilities are useful for students, freelancers, professionals, and individuals who want to understand modern financial technology. The examples in this guide also demonstrate the value of learning before acting. Hypothetical exercises, organized notes, and careful research provide accessible ways to build foundational knowledge without immediately engaging in financial transactions. Readers can continue their education by consulting official Binance documentation, studying introductory blockchain resources, and reviewing relevant regulatory guidance. Informational sources such as usasvcit may offer additional context when their material is relevant and can be independently checked. Ultimately, informed participation in digital finance begins with understanding the systems involved. Accurate information, consistent recordkeeping, critical thinking, and a willingness to learn provide a practical foundation for navigating cryptocurrency-related services and other digital platforms. Call to Action Take the next step by choosing one topic from this guide to study in greater detail. You might begin with identity verification, cryptocurrency terminology, transaction fees, or digital recordkeeping. Consult authoritative educational resources, write down the concepts you learn, and practice with clearly labeled hypothetical examples. Compare general explanations with official platform documentation whenever you need to confirm specific requirements. You can also use resources such as usasvcit as a starting point for further reading, provided you evaluate their information carefully and verify important claims through reliable sources. Consistent learning is more valuable than rushing through unfamiliar processes. By developing strong digital literacy, financial awareness, and organizational habits, you can build knowledge that remains useful across cryptocurrency services and many other aspects of modern digital life.

title: Por que texto estilizado vira quadradinho (tofu): fallback de fontes e Unicode
description:
Você cola um nome em negrito cursivo no perfil, ele aparece perfeito no seu celular, e um amigo avisa que só vê uma fileira de quadradinhos. Nada está errado com o texto. O problema é que o aparelho dele não tinha como desenhar aqueles caracteres. Este post explica o porquê e mostra duas armadilhas de código que costumam aparecer junto.

O que é o "tofu"

O quadradinho vazio é chamado de tofu, porque lembra um bloco de tofu. Ele não é um caractere que você digita. É um sintoma de renderização: o sistema pediu uma forma (glyph) para aquele caractere em todas as fontes disponíveis, não achou nenhuma e desenhou um substituto. A família de fontes Noto, do Google, foi nomeada justamente com esse objetivo, "no tofu".

Texto estilizado não é fonte

Os geradores de "letras diferentes" não instalam fonte nenhuma. Eles trocam cada letra comum por outro caractere Unicode que parece negrito, cursivo ou gótico:

const normal = "Ghost";
const estilizado = "𝓖𝓱𝓸𝓼𝓽";

console.log(normal.length);       // 5
console.log(estilizado.length);   // 10
console.log([...estilizado].length); // 5

A maior parte desses estilos vem do bloco Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols (U+1D400 a U+1D7FF), criado para notação matemática. Como cada letra estilizada está fora do plano básico do Unicode, em JavaScript ela ocupa duas unidades UTF-16. Por isso .length devolve 10 e não 5.

Armadilha 1: contar caracteres com .length

Se o seu formulário tem limite de caracteres (um nick de jogo, por exemplo), .length conta unidades UTF-16 e vai dizer que 𝓖𝓱𝓸𝓼𝓽 tem 10. O spread [...texto] conta pontos de código e dá 5. Mas ainda existe um terceiro caso: marcas combinantes, como as do texto "zalgo" ou de um acento decomposto.

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("pt-BR", { granularity: "grapheme" });

const contar = (t) => ({
  utf16: t.length,
  codepoints: [...t].length,
  graphemes: [...seg.segment(t)].length,
});

Num texto de teste com 6 letras e 13 marcas combinantes empilhadas sobre elas, utf16 e codepoints devolvem 19, enquanto graphemes devolve 6, que é o que a pessoa enxerga. Escolha a contagem que combina com a regra do seu produto e deixe o limite claro para o usuário.

Armadilha 2: pilha de fontes sem fallback

O navegador percorre a lista de font-family até encontrar uma fonte que tenha o caractere. Se a lista termina cedo, sobra o tofu. Termine sempre com uma família genérica:

body {
  font-family: Inter, system-ui, sans-serif;
}

Com sans-serif no fim, o sistema ainda pode usar a fonte de reserva dele para os caracteres que a sua fonte principal não cobre. Isso não garante que todo caractere apareça em todo aparelho, mas reduz muito o problema. E atenção: font-family não "estiliza" texto Unicode estilizado. São caracteres diferentes, não a mesma letra com outra fonte.

Acessibilidade

Leitores de tela podem ler caracteres estilizados pelos nomes longos que o Unicode dá a eles, o que atrapalha quem usa esse recurso. Mantenha em texto comum o que é importante, como nome, data, endereço e link, e use o estilizado só como enfeite.

Checklist rápido

  • Termine a pilha de font-family com sans-serif ou system-ui.
  • Conte caracteres com [...texto] ou Intl.Segmenter, não com .length.
  • Teste a página em um segundo aparelho, de preferência um Android mais antigo.
  • Não coloque informação importante só em texto estilizado.

Se quiser um lugar para ver esses estilos em ação e testá-los em outro celular, eu mantenho um gerador gratuito em português chamado Letra Diferente.

Para saber mais

  • Fallback font (em inglês): como o sistema escolhe uma fonte substituta.
  • Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols (em inglês): o bloco por trás de muitos estilos de negrito e cursivo.
  • Intl.Segmenter no MDN (em inglês): contagem de grafemas em JavaScript.

title: SolidCraft is a Rust parametric CAD app an agent can model in, and its README states the limits of its own checks
description:
The sentence I would read first in the solidcraft README is a status line. It says the project is early but usable for simple parts, that 75 of 76 public reference parts match their analytic or FreeCAD-computed volume, area, centre of mass and bounding box, and that the remaining one is a tracked bug. Then it adds that these checks do not establish complete geometric or workflow equivalence. That sets clear limits on what the reported checks establish.

SolidCraft is an open-source parametric 3D CAD application written in pure Rust under Apache-2.0. You sketch, constrain and build solids on a feature timeline, change a dimension, and the model rebuilds. It runs on the desktop, in the browser, and through a built-in MCP server that lets AI agents do the modeling.

An agent built a rover through MCP

The README's showcase is SELENE, a scientific rover it says was built entirely through SolidCraft's MCP server by @0xlillith: 3,323 editable timeline steps that rebuild with no errors. The editable model is downloadable.

The detail I find notable is that the result is a timeline of editable steps, not a one-off mesh. The README does not list the MCP tools themselves, so how much of the modeling vocabulary an agent can reach is something to check in the documentation book at docs.solidcraft.io.

The other demo models a Raspberry Pi 4 case from an empty design: a sketch dimensioned with the board's parameters, extrude, fillet and shell, M2.5 standoffs patterned on the 58 by 49 mm hole rectangle, port cut-outs, vent slots, an engraved label, and a PETG material whose mass shows in Properties. Then the height goes from 24 to 32 mm in Parameters, and the whole model rebuilds.

Its own constraint solver

The README is specific about the solver. Points that constraints fix relative to known geometry are placed exactly by construction, using loci intersections and rigid-cluster decomposition after Owen 1991 and Fudos and Hoffmann 1997. Levenberg-Marquardt solves the rest, and the rank of its Jacobian gives the remaining degrees of freedom.

The constraint list includes coincident, tangent, curvature (G2), equal, concentric, symmetry and fix, plus dimensions for length, radius, diameter, angle, arc length and slot length, all of which can be driven by parameters. Over-constraining edits are rejected, and fully constrained geometry turns black. Dragging solves the sketch every frame but rebuilds the model only once the drag ends.

Sketches support lines, rectangles, circles, arcs, polygons, slots, ellipses, splines, conics and text. Profiles are found automatically, including regions split by lines and holes inside outlines. Features on the timeline include extrude, revolve, sweep, loft, fillet, chamfer and shell. The README also lists a current-view DXF export with hidden edges omitted or dashed.

Installing it

The README lists builds for Windows, macOS, Linux and the browser. Windows gets an MSI for x64, ARM64 and 32-bit, a portable zip, and winget install bherbruck.SolidCraft. macOS gets a universal disk image. Linux gets AppImage, .deb, .rpm, Flatpak and Snap, with ARM64 builds listed for AppImage, .deb and .rpm. There is also a browser version with no install.

Two practical notes from the README. The downloads are not signed yet; the README explains what to do if SmartScreen warns you and how to open the app the first time on macOS. And anyone on versions 0.11 to 0.14 cannot use Update now to reach 0.15.0 or later, because the releases moved to a new address; download the new version once by hand, and in-app updates work again after that.

How to judge it

The repository was created on October 7, 2026, and the repository metadata lists 1,098 open issues. I would take the README's status line at its word: usable for simple parts, with 75 of 76 public reference parts matching their reported values, with plans in ROADMAP.md and per-area commands in docs/features.md. I would try it on a bracket or an enclosure you have already modeled elsewhere, compare mass and dimensions, and then hand the same part to an agent through MCP to see whether the timeline it produces is one you would want to edit.

GitHub: https://github.com/tangency-labs/solidcraft

title: muse-go: Dependency-free Go client for the ElevenMusic Muse…
description:
Most muse-go write-ups stop at the README: here is what the tool does, here is how you run it. This one covers what it refuses to do, and where it breaks.

What it is

Dependency-free Go client for the ElevenMusic Muse judge (prose and lyrics critique); a static linux-amd64 build ships in the Generic Package Registry.

In Russian: Go-клиент к судье ElevenMusic Muse без единой зависимости (критика прозы и текстов); статический linux-amd64 лежит в Generic Package Registry.

Install 

CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o muse-linux-amd64 .

Go. MIT licensed. Standard library first: the tool reads the data you point it at and sends nothing anywhere.

Where it does not fit

Every rule in a checker like this can produce a false positive. Use it to find candidates for a rewrite, not to grade a writer, and not where the voice is the point.

Repository

Source, issue tracker and documentation: https://gitlab.com/ameobius-ai/muse-go

Change

Correction: API base path limit for Apigee hybrid organizations

The December 16, 2024 release note for enhanced per-environment proxy limits stated that the maximum number of API base paths per Apigee organization is 3000. That number is incorrect. The maximum number of API base paths per organization is 6,000 for both Apigee and Apigee hybrid.

For optimal performance, Apigee recommends using no more than 3,000 API proxy basepaths per environment or environment group. This is a recommendation, not an enforced limit.

For more information, see Limits and Enhanced per-environment proxy limits.

BigQuery

Feature

In the BigQuery Studio query editor, the Query results table now keeps the row numbers visible on the left as you scroll horizontally. This helps you maintain context and track data across wide tables. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Feature

You can now attach tags to Certificate Manager resources during creation. This feature is available in Preview.

For more information, see Create and manage tags for Certificate Manager resources.

Cloud Scheduler

Change

Cloud Scheduler is available in the following locations:

  • asia-south2 (Delhi, India)
  • europe-west12 (Turin, Italy)
  • northamerica-northeast2 (Toronto, Ontario, Canada)

Cloud Workstations

Feature

Cloud Workstations is a covered product under Google Cloud HIPAA BAA.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: To protect standard snapshots from accidental or malicious deletion, Compute Engine retains deleted snapshots in the recycle bin for three days before permanently erasing the snapshots.

For more information, see Retain deleted resources in the recycle bin.

Data Studio

Feature

Bulk styling

You can customize all series, dimensions, or metrics at once, or select an individual item to style it separately. Styles that you set for an individual item override styles that you set for all items.

For more information, see the Line chart and combo chart reference, Time series reference, and Table reference.

Feature

Connect to PostgreSQL (Private IP)

You can connect Data Studio to PostgreSQL databases on Cloud SQL by using a private IP address. Private IP connections keep your database traffic on a private network instead of the public internet.

For more information, see Connect to PostgreSQL.

MySQL 5.6 and 5.7 deprecation

  • Creating new data sources that connect to MySQL 5.6 or 5.7 won't be possible after February 26, 2027.
  • Data sources or reports that use MySQL 5.6 or 5.7 might not properly load data after February 26, 2027.

For more information, see Connect to MySQL.

  • Nextdoor By Windsor.ai. Sources: Nextdoor

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Gemini 3.8 Live

For more information, see the following:

  • Gemini 3.8 Live
  • Gemini Live API overview

Feature

Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta

Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta is available in Preview. Muse Spark 1.3 from Meta is a reasoning model trained for agentic workflows and competitive coding. It delivers higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable built-in tool calling with MCP support, and 1M-token long context for multi-step tasks.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.10.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Impact-aware PR delta scanning: Added --diff and --staged flags to cm find to audit modified pull request hunks and 1-hop neighbor files while suppressing pre-existing vulnerabilities.
  • SARIF report export and CI gating: Added SARIF v2.1.0 export (--format sarif, --output) and severity-based CI gating (--fail-on) to cm report to integrate scan results into CI/CD pipelines and code scanning tools.
  • Adaptive hybrid deep scanning: Added --deep and --deep-workers flags to cm find to combine deterministic file pruning, parallel package-batched analysis, and post-triage verification for higher vulnerability recall and precision.
  • Custom workspace directory: Added support for the CM_HOME environment variable to override the default ~/.codemender directory for configuration, local state (state.db), backups, and artifacts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Required build and test validation (build.command) to succeed during cm fix before marking a patch as applied and a finding as fixed.
    • Stabilized vulnerability fingerprints across multiple scans and bound cm verify directly to the target finding ID to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Restored the configured session model automatically when reconnecting to an active session with cm session resume.
    • Updated cm verify to add .exploit to .gitignore before execution so cancelled verification sessions do not leave untracked proof-of-concept scripts.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE ambient networking is now available in Preview through an allowlist.

GKE ambient networking provides a simplified, sidecarless deployment model for a service mesh with Layer 4 capabilities. By moving proxy functionality to node-level components integrated into GKE Dataplane V2, ambient networking reduces resource overhead, eliminates workload restarts for proxy updates, and simplifies mesh lifecycle management.

The Preview release supports single-cluster Layer 4 mesh capabilities using the Gateway API, which includes mutual TLS (mTLS), service discovery, Layer 4 traffic management, and Layer 4 telemetry.

For more information, see Ambient networking overview and Prepare GKE ambient networking.

Feature

  • You can generate and import metadata artifacts from dbt Core 2.x and dbt Fusion in addition to dbt Core 1.x.
  • You can import entry links (--include-entry-links and --skip-bigquery-link) to capture dbt lineage and semantic relationships and link materialized dbt nodes to physical BigQuery tables, and search related BigQuery entries using the lookupEntryLinks method.
  • You can configure dbt metadata import jobs and search or view imported dbt entries using the Google Cloud console, the Google Cloud CLI, or the Dataplex REST API.

For more information, see Import metadata from dbt Core.

Feature

Data products now support configuring a default IAM role in an access group. The default role, once configured, is automatically granted on all packaged and supported assets in the data product. Data product owners can override the default role for individual assets. In addition, the assets table in a data product now shows the permission state of each asset (Applied, Failed, or Unsupported).

For more information, see Create data products and Manage data products.

Looker now displays an Authorize OAuth Connection dialog when users initiate an OAuth authorization flow for database connections. This dialog notifies users that authorizing the connection allows Looker to access data on their behalf, and that privileged Looker users—such as administrators and developers—may have visibility into their data (for example, when an administrator runs queries by using another user's active OAuth token during a sudo session).

Feature

Looker now includes a Filters on Visualization Tiles preview feature that lets dashboard creators place filter controls directly on individual visualization tiles rather than only in the dashboard filter bar.

Announcement

The latest versions in the Looker (Google Cloud core) release channels are beginning deployment as follows:

  • Latest version in the Rapid channel: Looker 26.16
  • Latest version in the Regular channel: Looker 26.14
  • Latest version in the No Channel channel: Looker 26.16

Update: Looker 26.16 won't be deployed to Looker (Google Cloud core); instead, Looker 26.18 will begin rolling out to Looker (Google Cloud core) on September 29, 2026. This update was added on September 29, 2026.

Feature

Looker now includes a long polling concurrency guard. This prevents issues where queries cause long poll requests that oversaturate Looker and cause Looker to freeze. If a query causes a long poll request, Looker will display the error message Query polling capacity reached. Please try again later.

Feature

Feature

  • Responsible AI

For information about available Model Armor features for each region, see Supported features by region.

For use with SAP HANA scale-up (OLAP and OLTP) and SAP NetWeaver workloads, SAP has certified the Compute Engine X5 series of memory-optimized bare metal machine types with the Intel Granite Rapids CPU platform.

The following Security Command Center finding category names from AI Protection have new names to clarify that AI Protection detects tuned models and to remove the legacy VERTEX_1P_ prefix:

title: Getting Started with Clojure
description:
Introduction

Clojure is a functional programming language and dialect of the Lisp programming language, which means it use prefix notation for all its expressions, which runs on the Java Virtual Machine (JVM).

From Clojure's website: https://clojure.org

Clojure is a dialect of Lisp, and shares with Lisp the code-as-data philosophy and a powerful macro system. Clojure is predominantly a functional programming language, and features a rich set of immutable, persistent data structures. When mutable state is needed, Clojure offers a software transactional memory system and reactive Agent system that ensure clean, correct, multithreaded designs.

Clojure is a compiled and JVM-hosted language. It's compiler translates Clojure forms into JVM bytecode, which is then executed by the JVM. It also provides REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) support, this allows us to interactively evaluate Clojure expressions.

How Clojure code executes

Clojure code is executed in the following steps:

  • Clojure source code
  • Clojure Reader (Reads source into Clojure forms)
  • Clojure Compiler (Compiles Clojure forms into JVM bytecode)
  • JVM Execution (Executes the compiled bytecode)

Environment Setup

For compiling Clojure code, there are two popular ways to do this:

  1. Using Leiningen (Build and project management)
  2. Using Clojure CLI (Official command-line tool)

Using Clojure CLI

In the case of Clojure CLI, the project is configured manually, unlike Leiningen.

  • Creating a new project using Clojure CLI

In the case of Clojure CLI, new projects are created manually by setting up the folder structure and deps.edn files.

Folder structure for a Clojure CLI project typically looks like this:

where the project is configured using Clojure CLI deps.edn

  • running the project using Clojure CLI 
clojure -M -m hello-world.core
  • running the REPL using Clojure CLI 
clojure -M

Using Leiningen

  • creating a new project using Leiningen 
lein new app hello-world

Folder structure for a Leiningen project typically looks like this:

where the project is configured using Leiningen (project.clj)

  • Running the project using Leiningen 
lein run
  • Running the REPL using Leiningen 
lein repl

Language Basics

  • Data Types Clojure supports several fundamental data types.
Type Example Description
Integer 42 Whole number without a decimal point
Float/Double 3.14 Numeric value with a decimal point
String "Hello" Text enclosed in double quotes
Boolean true, false Logical values representing true or false
Nil nil Represents the absence of a value
Keyword :name Named identifier commonly used as a key in maps
Symbol user-name Name used to refer to a value, function, or other entity
Character \A Represents a single character 
(type 42)
;; => java.lang.Long
(type 12.09)
;; => java.lang.Double
(type "Hello")
;; => java.lang.String
(type :name)
;; => clojure.lang.Keyword
(def name "Vinayak")
(type name)
;; => java.lang.String

Difference between Keyword vs String vs Symbol:

;; Keyword
;; Define a map 
(def user {:name "Vinayak" :age 28})
;; Use
(println (:name user))
;; => "Vinayak"
(println (:age user))
;; => 28
(type user)
;; => clojure.lang.PersistentArrayMap
(type :name)
;; => clojure.lang.Keyword

;; String
(def name "Vinayak")
(println name)
;; => "Vinayak"
(type name)
;; => java.lang.String

;; Symbol -> represent a name literally
(type 'name)
;; => clojure.lang.Symbol
  • Variables

In Clojure, variables are immutable by default. Which means once a value is assigned, it can not be changed.

(def name "vinayak")
;; Try to change name directly
(set! name "vinayak sharma")
;; Execution error (IllegalStateException) at user/eval1577 (REPL:1).
;; Can't change/establish root binding of: name with set

But we can Re-definition using def again:

(def name "vinayak")
(def name "vinayak sharma")
(println name)
;; => vinayak sharma

Defining array

(def numbers [1 2 3 4 5])
(println numbers)
;; => [1 2 3 4 5]
(type numbers)
;; => clojure.lang.PersistentVector

Defining the map

(def user {:name "Vinayak" :age 28})
(println user)
;; => {:name "Vinayak", :age 28}
(type user)
;; => clojure.lang.PersistentArrayMap
  • Operators 
(+ 10 5) ;; => 15
(- 10 5) ;; => 5
(* 10 5) ;; => 50
(/ 10 5) ;; => 2

(= 10 10) ;; => true, this is different from assignment
(not= 10 5) ;; => true
(< 5 10) ;; => true
(>= 10 10) ;; => true

(and true true) ;; => true
(or false true) ;; => true
(not true) ;; => false

In Clojure, arithmetic operation support multiple arguments. For example:

(+ 1 2 3 4) ;; => 10
(* 2 3 4) ;; => 24
(- 10 1 2) ;; => 7
(/ 100 2 5) ;; => 10

  • Compound Data Types

    • Vector: Ordered collection, efficient indexed access.
    • List: Ordered collection, efficient sequential access.
    • Map: Stores key-value pairs.
    • Set: Stores unique values.

  • Functions

In Clojure, functions are defined using the defn macro. Here is an example:

;; Define a function
(defn add [a b] 
    (+ a b))

;; Call the function
(add 10 20)
;; => 30

Quick Reference

Syntax Meaning
fn Creates a function
[name] Defines a function parameter
(str ...) Combines values into a string
#() Shorthand syntax for an anonymous function
% Represents the first argument in #()
%1 Represents the first argument in #()
%2 Represents the second argument in #()
%& Represents the rest of the arguments in #()

Fundamentals

  • Conditionals

  • Loops

When to use what?

Construct Purpose
doseq Perform side effects for each item in a collection.
for Generate a sequence of results.
map Transform every item in a collection.
reduce Combine items into a single result.
loop/recur Implement custom iterative logic using recursion without growing the call stack
  • Atoms in Clojure: values are immutable by default. Atoms allow storing a value that can change over time or creates a mutable reference. 
(def age (atom 25))
(println @age)
;; => 25
(println age)
;; #object[clojure.lang.Atom 0x3a14182a {:status :ready, :val 25}]
(reset! age 30)
(println @age)
;; => 30

Increase the value using a swap!

(def age (atom 25))
(swap! age inc)
(println @age)
;; Output: 26
  • Sequences
Function Purpose Example
first Get the first item (first '(10 20 30)) → 10
rest Get remaining items (rest '(10 20 30)) → (20 30)
seq Get a sequence view (seq [1 2 3]) → (1 2 3)
map Transform every item (map inc [1 2 3]) → (2 3 4)
filter Select matching items (filter even? [1 2 3 4]) → (2 4)
count Count items (count '(10 20 30)) → 3
  • Map & Records
  • Map: Maps are flexible key-value structures. 
(def user
    {:id 101
    :name "Vinayak"
    :role "Engineer"})

(:name user)
;; => "Vinayak"

(assoc user :age 28)
;; => {:id 101, :name "Vinayak",
;; :role "Engineer", :age 28}
  • Records: Records are fixed-schema key-value structures. 
(defrecord Employee [id name department])

(def emp
    (->Employee 101 "Vinayak" "Engineering"))

(:name emp)
;; => "Vinayak"

(assoc emp :location "Bangalore")
;; Returns a new record-like value with the extra key
  • Destructuring: Destructuring extracts values from collections and binds them to local names. 
;; Vector destructuring
(let [[a b c] [1 2 3]]
    (println a b c))
;; => 1 2 3

(let [[a b c] [10 20 30]]
    (+ a b c))
;; => 60

;; Map destructuring
(let [{:keys [id name]} {:id 101 :name "Vinayak"}]
    (println id name))
;; => 101 "Vinayak"

;; Destructuring function arguments
(defn greet [{:keys [name]}]
    (str "Hello, " name))

(greet {:name "Vinayak"})
;; => "Hello, Vinayak"
  • Exception Handling

Clojure uses try, catch, and finally for exception handling.

(try
    (/ 1 0)
    (catch ArithmeticException e
    (println "Caught exception:" (.getMessage e)))
    (finally
    (println "Finally block executed")))

Using throw

(defn withdraw [balance amount]
    (if (> amount balance)
    (throw (ex-info "Insufficient funds"
                    {:balance balance
                        :amount amount}))
    (- balance amount)))

More on Clojure

  • Namespaces

Namespaces organize code into logical modules and prevent naming conflicts.

(ns my-app.core)


(ns myapp.payments)

(defn process-payment [amount]
    (str "Processing payment: " amount))
(process-payment 100)
;; => "Processing payment: 100"

Requiring namespaces in Clojure is done using the require function within the ns macro.

(ns my-app.core
    (:require [myapp.payments :as payments]))
  • Macros

Macros allow to extend the language by transforming code before it executes. Functions operate on values at runtime, whereas macros operate on code at compile-time.

defmacro: Used to define a macro.

(defmacro macro_name [condition & body]
    `(if (not ~condition)
        (do ~@body)))

(macro_name false
    (println "This will be printed"))
;; => "This will be printed"

Understand the Syntax

Syntax Meaning
defmacro Defines a macro
Backtick


``| Syntax-quotes a code form |
|~| Unquotes and inserts a form |
|~@` | Splices a sequence of forms into another form |

  • Watchers: A watcher observes changes to a reference type and runs a callback when its state changes. Watchers can be attached to atoms, refs, and agents.

clojure
(def balance (atom 100))

(add-watch balance :audit
    (fn [key reference old-value new-value]
    (println "Balance changed:"
        old-value "->" new-value)))

(reset! balance 200)
;; Prints a message about 100 -> 200

Note: fn is used to create an anonymous function

  • Agents: An agent manages state through asynchronous actions.

clojure
(def counter (agent 0))
(send counter inc)
(await counter)

@counter
;; => 1

send schedules an action on an agent's thread pool. await waits for actions dispatched before the call to finish.

Atom vs Agent in Clojure

Feature Atom Agent
State update Synchronous Asynchronous
Update operation swap!, reset! send, send-off
Read state @atom @agent
Main use Independent shared state Asynchronous state updates

Note: Atoms are suitable for managing independent shared state, while agents are ideal for handling asynchronous state updates.

  • Reference Values

Clojure provides several reference types for managing state, especially when concurrency is involved.

  • Atoms

clojure
(def x (atom 10))
(swap! x inc)
@x
;; => 11
  • Agent

clojure
(def counter (agent 0))
(send counter inc)
(await counter)
@counter
;; => 1
  • Ref

clojure
(def r (ref 0))
(dosync
    (alter r inc))
@r
;; => 1
  • Var

clojure
(def ^:dynamic *my-var* 42)
*my-var*
;; => 42

title: What Happens Next: The AI Bill Has a Calendar
description:
AI & Markets - David Groch

Two markets are now pricing two different revolutions.

The equity market is pricing demand, and on the evidence it is right. South Korea's September exports rose 83.5% year over year to a record $120.9 billion, with semiconductor shipments up 263% to more than $60 billion in a single month. That is not a narrative. That is customs data. Somebody is buying every chip Asia can make.

The credit market is pricing the bill, and on the evidence it is also right. Five-year credit default swaps hit records across the AI complex this month: Oracle at 322 basis points, up from 144 in January; Broadcom at 136; Nvidia at 101; Meta at 108; SpaceX at 226; CoreWeave near 1,090, which is distressed territory by any definition. Converted into the market's own arithmetic, Oracle's spread implies roughly a 23% five-year default probability, Broadcom's about 12%, Nvidia's about 8%. AI-linked companies have issued an estimated $466 billion of debt in 2026, against $101 billion in the same period of 2025. Weekly trading in CDS on the seven biggest AI names went from under $2 billion in July to over $9 billion in September.

One honest caveat before the calendar: an implied default probability is not a forecast. Part of the widening is mechanical, because equity managers buy CDS as a cheap hedge and hedging demand widens spreads on its own. Oracle is not going bankrupt at a 23% rate in any world a credit analyst would sign. What the spreads actually say is narrower and more useful: the price of insuring the buildout has multiplied, the marginal buyer of AI debt now demands to be paid for duration and doubt, and the next round of funding will not be priced like the last one. That is the story. And unlike most market stories, this one has dates.

Next week: the pincer

Monday, October 26. Celestica reports after the close, with its investor day on Tuesday. This is the margin canary. Celestica is a contract manufacturer with thin EMS margins and enormous hyperscaler exposure, and the one serious bear case on the name is simple: when AI hardware margins compress, they compress for the assembler first. The Street is unanimously bullish (average target near $474 against a $262 stock), which means the print has to be clean, not good. A margin wobble here is the first company-level confirmation that the buildout's economics are squeezing the supply chain. The same morning, the first big SpaceX lockup tranche (up to 328 million shares) becomes tradable, a week after the stock rose 8% on earnings and fell 9% on profit-taking and unlock fears. Supply meets a story stock.

Wednesday, October 28. The week's hinge, and it is a pincer. At 2:00 p.m. ET the FOMC decides. The Reuters poll of 100 economists is as close to unanimous as polls get: 94 expect a hold at 3.75% to 4.00%, and all 100 expect a hike in December. The risk is not the decision, it is the language, because Chair Warsh has dropped forward guidance and publicly distanced himself from the committee's own projections. Two hours later, Microsoft and Alphabet report. Their earnings are no longer really about earnings. Meta already showed the template: beat on revenue, guide above consensus, and lose 7% anyway because the capex line moved. What Microsoft and Alphabet say about 2027 spending is the referendum on whether Meta's repricing was one company's problem or the sector's.

Thursday, October 29. September PCE and the first Q3 GDP print land before the open (consensus: core PCE 3.1% year over year, headline 3.6%), and Amazon reports after the close. A hot core print with a December hike already unanimous is the stagflation-lite combination: it validates the CDS move and pushes the terminal-rate debate from one more hike to two. A soft print is the only scheduled event all week that can actually relieve the credit market.

Next month: the report cards

November 3 brings the US midterms, which matter here for one reason: energy and industrial policy are now market variables, and oil above $110 with the Strategic Petroleum Reserve at its lowest since 1982 (282.7 million barrels) is a political fact as much as an economic one.

November 2 to 12 is the cluster that decides whether the CDS story stays a hedge or becomes a verdict. The leveraged end of the buildout reports in a ten-day window: Cipher Mining on November 2, Core Scientific on November 5, CoreWeave around November 9, Nebius around November 10, TeraWulf in the same stretch. Read these reports for one line only: the funding line. Bank of America's preview of CoreWeave is the template of the whole moment. The bank rates the stock a buy with a $140 target, forecasts Q3 revenue of $3.66 billion (up 168%), cites a $129 billion backlog, and then estimates the company needs roughly $20 billion of additional funding, with $12.5 billion of capex in the quarter alone. Even the bull case is now written as a financing story. Backlog is not the question anymore. The coupon is.

November 18 is Nvidia, the last and largest report of the season, and throughout the month Meta's $25 billion New Mexico judgment accrues interest at 15% a year, roughly $10 million a day, which is its own kind of calendar: every week of appeal is a week the settlement price argument changes.

Just past the horizon, December holds the two dates that could close the loop: the FOMC meeting where 100 of 100 economists expect the hike, and December 9, when Micron's $35 billion buyback authorization becomes usable. The largest memory maker becoming a structural buyer of its own stock is the equity market's best scheduled answer to the credit market's question.

Three ways this resolves

The bill gets paid quietly. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon hold or trim their capex guides to something the cash flow can carry, the neoclouds fund at tolerable rates, and CDS spreads tighten into year-end. Signpost: Oracle CDS back under 250 basis points and a CoreWeave funding deal at single-digit rates. In this world the October repricing was a tantrum.

The slow bleed. Guides go up again, the Fed hikes in December with two more on the table, and equities de-rate gradually toward where credit already is. No crash, no capitulation, just a multiple that shrinks while the spending does not. Signpost: bank stocks, already on their longest losing streak since 2008 (six straight weeks for the KBW index), keep sliding while the indexes hold up on a narrowing group of names.

Something breaks at the weak end. A funding deal fails, or prices at the mid-teens yields where CoreWeave's bonds already flirt, and the question stops being about one neocloud's balance sheet and becomes about who else financed the same way. Signpost: any postponement or pulled deal in the November cluster, or CoreWeave CDS pushing through 1,200 basis points. This is the only scenario where the Asia story and the credit story collide, because the chip demand is real, and real demand financed badly is exactly how the last buildout ended: the fiber got lit, the carriers did not survive it, and the cables outlived the companies that laid them.

The demand is not the debate. The price of money is. And for once, the market has published the schedule on which it will argue: October 28 for rates, October 28 and 29 for capex, November 2 to 12 for the leveraged end, December for the bill itself. Watch the calendar, not the commentary.

Facts and sources (checked October 23, 2026): CDS levels and implied probabilities, Morgan Stanley research via the Financial Times and Financial Gurkha (October 19-20), Mott Capital via TalkMarkets (October 19). AI-linked issuance $466B and CDS weekly volume, Morgan Stanley via FT. Korea September exports, Reuters and MOTIE customs data (October 1). FOMC expectations, Reuters poll of 100 economists (October 16-20). PCE and GDP consensus, Morningstar week-ahead (October 23). Earnings dates: Microsoft and Alphabet October 28, Amazon October 29 (company notices via Admiral Markets, Reuters, Zacks); CoreWeave around November 9 (Zacks estimate, company date not formally announced); Nebius around November 10 (StockAnalysis estimate); Nvidia November 18 (TradeStation calendar, estimated); Core Scientific November 5 (company). CoreWeave funding estimates and $140 target, Bank of America (October 22). SPR level 282.7M barrels, DOE data via Reuters (October 19). KBW Bank Index six-week losing streak, Bloomberg via TradingView (October 20). Celestica consensus and targets, Seeking Alpha. Implied default probabilities are model outputs that depend on recovery-rate assumptions; they are not forecasts.

title: A Read-Only WebMCP Tool Erased My React Form State
description:
The read path in Trip Workbench can erase a person’s unsaved purpose without sending a write.

In a deterministic reproduction, the returned saved snapshot still says “Workshop.” The edit buffer contains “Leadership meeting” before the read, then loses that value when the response is applied.

That failure is reproducible in Trip Workbench at commit 4b3f370, the public React and TypeScript demo I built and maintain. Its get_trip_draft tool refreshes saved state through the same coordinator that manages the React form. The refresh path uses a merge rule designed for a different operation.

The previous article exposed three WebMCP tools: read, update, and validate. This article follows the read path through Chrome’s debugging tools, reproduces the state loss with controlled API responses, and develops a repair that preserves unsaved work.

The reproduction and repair results below are coordinator-level tests. The repair is a local candidate; the linked repository still contains the original behavior. Native Chrome and model-driven verification remain separate steps.

A read must preserve unsaved work

Trip Workbench keeps two representations of a draft:

  • savedDraft contains the last accepted server snapshot and its revision.
  • localFields contains the values currently displayed in the form.

A person can change localFields.purpose without changing the server. The editor then reports unsaved changes.

The read tool promises to return saved fields, along with revision, status, and hasUnsavedChanges. It deliberately does not expose the unsaved buffer to the agent.

For example, the server can contain “Workshop” while the form displays “Leadership meeting.” A successful read should return “Workshop,” report that unsaved changes exist, and leave “Leadership meeting” on screen.

The WebMCP adapter also declares readOnlyHint: true. An annotation describes intended behavior; application code still has to honor it.

This matters beyond the disappearing text. The update path rejects agent mutations while the editor is dirty. If a read accidentally clears the buffer and marks it clean, a later agent update can pass that check. The read has changed the conditions under which a write is allowed.

The useful invariant is concrete: refreshing saved data must preserve current unsaved values and must never move an accepted saved revision backward.

Trace the read through Chrome

For local development, Chrome documents the flag chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing. Enable it and relaunch the browser. WebMCP is still a proposed standard, so record the browser version alongside any result. See the current setup instructions.

Open a disposable Trip Workbench draft with a saved purpose of “Workshop.” Keep the application’s cloud AI mode disabled if you are testing only the page tools.

In DevTools, open Application → WebMCP. The WebMCP pane lists available tools and records invocations, including their arguments, results, and status. Select get_trip_draft, enter the active draft ID, and use its manual test controls.

Before running it, change the form’s purpose to “Leadership meeting” without saving.

Inspect three things after the call: the returned saved purpose, the unsaved-changes indicator, and the visible input. A successful tool response alone cannot tell you whether the editor preserved the person’s work.

You can also invoke the same tool from the Console:

const context = document.modelContext;
if (!context) throw new Error("WebMCP is unavailable");

const tools = await context.getTools();
const readTool = tools.find(tool => tool.name === "get_trip_draft");
if (!readTool) throw new Error("Open a trip draft first");

const result = await context.executeTool(readTool, {
  draftId: "REPLACE_WITH_THE_OPEN_DRAFT_ID"
});
console.log(typeof result === "string" ? JSON.parse(result) : result);

The current imperative API takes a discovered tool descriptor and an argument object. JSON-stringified input arguments are deprecated from Chrome 155.

Then use the Sources panel to follow get_trip_draft → refreshSavedDraft. Put a breakpoint after the GET resolves and before the coordinator applies its result. Compare:

  • the saved fields before the request;
  • the local fields when it started;
  • the local fields when it completed;
  • the response fields and revision.

Chrome’s logpoints are useful when pausing would alter the sequence you are investigating. Log scalar snapshots such as revision, edit version, and dirty state.

A paused JavaScript thread cannot process ordinary typing in that same page. To test typing during a request, use a controlled response delay or a deferred promise instead of assuming that interacting while paused creates the intended race.

Reproduce the failure without timing guesses

The first failure does not require concurrent requests. The edit exists before the read starts.

The coordinator accepts a fetchImpl dependency, so the smallest reproduction can supply a stable server response. This test fits the repository’s existing Vitest setup:

import { expect, it } from "vitest";
import { createCoordinator } from "../../src/client/lib/coordinator.js";
import { defaultTripFields, type TripView } from "../../src/domain/types.js";

it("keeps an unsaved edit when refreshing the saved draft", async () => {
  const saved: TripView = {
    id: "draft-a",
    revision: 1,
    status: "draft",
    fields: { ...defaultTripFields(), purpose: "Workshop" },
    createdAt: "2026-10-17T07:00:00.000Z",
    updatedAt: "2026-10-17T07:00:00.000Z"
  };

  const coordinator = createCoordinator({
    fetchImpl: async <T>() => ({
      ok: true as const,
      data: structuredClone(saved) as T
    })
  });

  await coordinator.openDraft("draft-a");
  coordinator.updateLocalField("purpose", "Leadership meeting");

  const result = await coordinator.refreshSavedDraft("draft-a");
  const state = coordinator.getState();

  expect(result.ok).toBe(true);
  expect(state.savedDraft?.fields.purpose).toBe("Workshop");
  expect(state.localFields?.purpose).toBe("Leadership meeting");
  expect(state.dirty).toBe(true);

  if (result.ok) expect(result.data.hasUnsavedChanges).toBe(true);
});

In the pinned implementation, the assertion for the local purpose fails: it contains “Workshop.”

The relevant comparison is in mergeAfterInFlightEdit:

const humanChanged =
  input.localNow[key] !== input.localAtDispatch[key];

That comparison asks whether the person changed a field after dispatch.

For this refresh, localAtDispatch.purpose and localNow.purpose both contain “Leadership meeting.” The comparison returns false. The helper keeps the server value, even though the person still has an unsaved edit relative to the saved draft.

The surrounding hadLocalEdits check correctly notices that the buffer is dirty. It cannot repair the helper’s choice of comparison baseline.

This also explains why the existing test for typing during an agent update can pass. An edit made after dispatch differs from localAtDispatch; an edit already present does not. Those are different cases.

Give refreshes and saves different merge rules

A confirmed save acknowledges values that the request submitted. Its reconciliation logic needs to distinguish that submitted work from newer typing.

A refresh acknowledges no local edits. Its job is to update the saved snapshot while preserving differences that remain in the current edit buffer.

For the scalar fields in this demo, a refresh can use three values for each field:

Value Meaning
Base Current accepted saved value
Local Current value in the form
Incoming Value in the newly received server snapshot

If local differs from base, keep local in the form. Otherwise, adopt incoming. If both local and incoming differ from base and disagree with each other, retain the local value as unsaved work and surface the overlap for review.

Here is the candidate helper. It uses the repository’s TripFields type and fieldsEqual function:

function mergeSavedRefresh(
  base: TripFields,
  local: TripFields,
  incoming: TripFields
) {
  const localFields = { ...incoming };
  const overlapped: Array<keyof TripFields> = [];

  for (const key of Object.keys(base) as Array<keyof TripFields>) {
    if (local[key] === base[key]) continue;

    localFields[key] = local[key] as never;

    if (incoming[key] !== base[key] && incoming[key] !== local[key]) {
      overlapped.push(key);
    }
  }

  return {
    localFields,
    dirty: !fieldsEqual(localFields, incoming),
    overlapped
  };
}

Keeping a value in the local buffer does not save it or resolve the conflict. The person still needs to review the changed saved value before deciding what to persist. The candidate adds a notice naming overlapping fields; a field-by-field comparison would make that review easier.

Use the current accepted saved snapshot at response application time as the base. Another operation may have completed while the GET was pending. A local value that was unsaved when the read began may already have been confirmed by a manual save.

This rule treats edits as current value differences. An edit that returns a field to its saved value is no longer an unsaved change. Applications that must preserve edit intent even when values match need additional metadata, such as per-field edit versions.

Reject older snapshots before merging

A correct field merge does not prevent the saved revision itself from moving backward.

The original refresh path also accepts this sequence:

Order Event Accepted saved revision
1 A read begins and will return revision 1 1
2 An agent update commits and its response is applied 2
3 The earlier read returns revision 1 Must remain 2

The server has already advanced. Applying the late read makes the browser display older data.

Keep the existing session, editor, and draft identity checks. After those checks succeed, reject a response whose revision is lower than the currently accepted one. Then merge without another asynchronous boundary:

// After checking response success and the active editor identity.
if (res.data.revision < state.savedDraft.revision) {
  return fail(
    "STALE_SNAPSHOT",
    "A newer saved revision is already displayed."
  );
}

const merged = mergeSavedRefresh(
  state.savedDraft.fields,
  state.localFields,
  res.data.fields
);

setState({
  savedDraft: res.data,
  localFields: merged.localFields,
  dirty: merged.dirty,
  ...(merged.overlapped.length ? {
    message:
      `Saved values changed for ${merged.overlapped.join(", ")}. ` +
      "Your local values remain unsaved; review before saving."
  } : {})
});

STALE_SNAPSHOT is a new error in this candidate. It tells the caller that the read lost a race; the caller can read again. It is distinct from the server’s REVISION_CONFLICT response to a stale write.

This comparison assumes revisions increase for one draft and identify immutable versions of its persisted state. It does not order different drafts, replace identity checks, or establish that a snapshot is globally current.

The same rule covers two reads that complete out of order. A response at revision 2 cannot replace an already accepted revision 3 simply because it arrived later.

Check the repair against specific sequences

I exercised the pinned coordinator with controlled API responses, using Node’s test runner after stripping TypeScript syntax from the source modules. The candidate changed the refresh path and added the dedicated merge helper.

These nine checks produced four passes and five failures on the original implementation, and nine passes on the local candidate:

Check Original Candidate
Preserve an edit made before refresh Fail Pass
Preserve an edit made during refresh Pass Pass
Combine a remote destination change with a local purpose edit Fail Pass
Preserve overlapping local text and show a review notice Fail Pass
Ignore a read older than a confirmed mutation Fail Pass
Avoid resurrecting an edit already confirmed by a manual save Pass Pass
Ignore a response after switching drafts Pass Pass
Preserve typing during an agent update Pass Pass
Prevent out-of-order reads from lowering the revision Fail Pass

The delayed cases use deferred promises: start the operation, perform the intervening state change, and explicitly release the response. That makes the order reproducible without relying on how quickly someone types.

These results establish the coordinator behavior for those sequences. They do not exercise Chrome’s native dispatch, React rendering, the database, or a model choosing tools. The repository’s results document also lists native and model-driven WebMCP as unverified.

Keep cancellation and recovery in the test plan

Tool registration and an individual invocation have separate lifetimes. Chrome’s imperative API supports a registration signal for removing a tool and an execution signal for cancelling a call. Since Chrome 153, unregistering a tool does not cancel its in-flight executions.

That leaves application responsibilities after navigation: a late result must not update a different editor, and cancelling a network request does not establish whether a server mutation committed.

Trip Workbench uses command receipts to resolve uncertain writes. There is a separate issue in recheckOutcome: it creates a new dispatch context from the current buffer when recovery starts. That loses the original comparison baseline. A later receipt can therefore treat edits made while the outcome was uncertain as if they existed at mutation dispatch.

The refresh repair does not address that path. Receipt recovery needs to retain the original mutation context and reconcile against it, with a dedicated test for typing between an uncertain outcome and a recheck.

For React registration, also test mount, cleanup, and remount. Strict Mode’s extra Effect setup and cleanup cycle in development is useful for exposing registration leaks. A clean tool list after remount is one check; rejecting stale in-flight results is another.

Finish with native and model driven checks

Once the coordinator repair is integrated, repeat the disposable-draft exercise through Chrome’s native WebMCP interface. Check the actual input value and unsaved indicator alongside the invocation output. Verify that an attempted agent update still receives USER_EDIT_IN_PROGRESS while the preserved edit remains unsaved.

Then test whether an agent handles that response appropriately. Chrome’s DevTools MCP integration exposes list_webmcp_tools and execute_webmcp_tool when started with --categoryExperimentalWebmcp.

With a draft already containing an unsaved human edit, use a prompt such as:

Inspect the open trip draft. If it has unsaved changes, explain that I need to save or discard them and stop. Otherwise, set the destination to JFK using the returned revision, then validate the updated draft. Stop before submission.

Record whether the agent reads first, recognizes the unsaved state, and stops. For the clean-draft branch, inspect the revision it supplies and the resulting saved fields. A plausible final message is insufficient evidence that the intended sequence ran.

The engineering contract is visible in the form: reading a draft preserves what the person is working on, and a response from earlier work cannot replace a newer accepted state. Those properties have to hold for every caller, including the agent.

title: Leader Election
description:
In a distributed system, sometimes exactly ONE node must act as the "leader". How do you pick it?

Why Leader Election?

Some tasks must run on exactly one node:

  • Sending scheduled emails (don't send twice)
  • Coordinating distributed transactions
  • Acting as primary in a database cluster
  • Processing a specific partition of a queue

Problem: Nodes can crash. The leader must be detected as dead and a new one elected.

Algorithms

Bully Algorithm

  • Node with highest ID wins
  • When a node thinks the leader is dead → sends election messages to all higher-ID nodes
  • If no response → declares itself leader
  • ✅ Simple | ❌ Many messages, assumes ordered IDs

Raft Consensus

  • Nodes vote for a leader candidate
  • Candidate needs majority vote (quorum)
  • Leader sends heartbeats; if missed → new election
  • ✅ Well-proven, used in production systems
  • Used by: etcd, CockroachDB, TiKV

ZooKeeper / etcd-based Leader Election (Practical) 

All nodes race to create an ephemeral node:
  /election/leader

First node to create it → wins leadership
Others watch the node for deletion (leader crash)
On deletion → race again
  • ✅ Battle-tested, you don't implement the algorithm yourself
  • ✅ Ephemeral nodes auto-delete when the session dies (crash detection built in)
  • ❌ Adds ZooKeeper/etcd as dependency

Split-Brain Problem

What if the network partitions and both halves elect a leader?

  • Two leaders making conflicting decisions = data corruption
  • Solution: quorum — leader must maintain majority (N/2 + 1) connections
  • If minority partition can't reach quorum → steps down

Real-World Usage

System Leader Election
Kafka ZooKeeper (legacy) / KRaft (new) for controller
Elasticsearch Zen Discovery / Raft-based
Redis Sentinel Sentinel quorum for primary election
PostgreSQL HA Patroni uses etcd/ZooKeeper
