title: Reliable User Reminder Retries with Node.js Queues — Expiring Stale Reservations
description:
Short answer: Handle failed user reminders in Node.js by using queues with bounded retries, message expiration, a dead-letter queue, and an idempotent worker; that combination protects a reminder from transient failures without allowing a corrupt message to loop forever.

At 09:00, the page says the reminder queue is empty. At 09:07, support reports that a customer still holds a reservation that should have expired after its fixed hold window. The worker did not crash. It acknowledged a message after a transient delivery failure, and the reservation stayed in the wrong state.

The practical answer is to retry failed reminders through a queue with bounded retry policy, message expiration, and a dead-letter queue (DLQ). Make the worker idempotent because a standard queue is at-least-once: the same reminder can arrive twice. A retry policy without that last property is an incident generator with better telemetry.

How should I handle retries for failed user reminders using queues?

The useful alert is not “worker failed.” It is a traceable lifecycle: reservation ID, reminder ID, attempt number, failure class, next eligible time, and final disposition. I want to know whether a message is waiting, being retried, or parked for review before I open a terminal.

Start by logging the enqueue event. Log every negative acknowledgement and every successful send with the same reminder ID. Include a bounded attempt count. Do not log the full message body if it contains customer data; a stable identifier and a reason code are enough to connect the queue record to application logs.

The threshold needs judgment. Alerting on one retry creates noise during a short provider hiccup. Alerting only after the DLQ grows means a customer-facing promise has already been missed. For a fixed hold window, page on an approaching expiry with no successful reminder, and use DLQ depth plus age as the operational signal for unresolvable failures.

That distinction is easy to miss.

The false-positive cost matters. A low threshold trains the on-call to ignore the page; a high threshold leaves support discovering the problem first.

How do bounded retries prevent a queue loop?

Separate transient errors from poison messages. A timeout, connection reset, or temporary upstream refusal can be requeued with a delay. Invalid payloads, missing reservation IDs, and permanent authorization failures should not circulate forever. Set a maximum attempt count, then route the message to the DLQ for inspection or manual intervention.

Message expiration provides another boundary. A reminder for a reservation that is already expired has no useful work left, even if the queue eventually becomes healthy. The worker should check the reservation state before sending and treat an obsolete reminder as a handled outcome, with a log entry that explains why it was dropped.

This is the decision rule I use:

  • Requeue a classified transient failure with exponential backoff.
  • Stop after a small, explicit attempt limit rather than retrying indefinitely.
  • Expire work that can no longer meet its business deadline.
  • Dead-letter everything that needs a human or code change.
  • Redrive only after the cause is understood, and preserve the original reminder ID.

The exact delay is application policy, not a magic queue setting. Backoff should fit inside the reservation hold window, and the final attempt should happen while a successful reminder can still change the customer outcome. The platform limit here is 604800 seconds for delayed messages, so longer workflows need a different coordinator or a scheduled trigger that enqueues fresh work.

The worker contract matters more than the queue brand

Retries create duplicates by design. A worker that sends a reminder and then loses its acknowledgement can receive the message again. Store a send decision keyed by reminder ID, or use an idempotency key supported by the downstream notification service. Marking the queue message as “processed” before the send reverses the failure mode: it prevents duplicates by accepting missed reminders.

No shortcuts here.

The ordering deserves a concrete test. Let attempt 1 send the reminder, then simulate a worker timeout before acknowledgement. Attempt 2 must find the same reminder ID and return “already sent” without delivering a second notification. If the reservation has changed state in the meantime, the worker should record that decision and acknowledge the queue message as well. If the send provider is unavailable, the worker should leave the message eligible for the next bounded retry. These are different outcomes, even though all three occur around the same network timeout, and the log needs to distinguish them so an operator can redrive only the messages that still have useful work.

The following Go example uses the queue list endpoint to verify the REST connection before a worker starts. It uses an environment variable for the key, an explicit method, bounded exponential backoff, and real response handling. The actual Node.js service can implement the same startup check and state machine; the important part is the ordering around the side effect.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Reminder struct {
    ID            string
    ReservationID string
    Attempt       int
    ExpiresAt     time.Time
}

func process(ctx context.Context, r Reminder, send func(context.Context, Reminder, string) error) error {
    if r.ID == "" || r.ReservationID == "" {
        return errors.New("permanent: missing reminder or reservation ID")
    }
    if time.Now().After(r.ExpiresAt) {
        log.Printf("reminder=%s outcome=expired", r.ID)
        return nil
    }

    const maxAttempts = 4
    if r.Attempt >= maxAttempts {
        return errors.New("permanent: retry limit reached")
    }

    // The downstream service must deduplicate this key if the worker is retried.
    idempotencyKey := fmt.Sprintf("reservation-reminder:%s", r.ID)
    err := send(ctx, r, idempotencyKey)
    if err != nil {
        log.Printf("reminder=%s attempt=%d outcome=retryable_error error=%v", r.ID, r.Attempt, err)
        return err
    }
    log.Printf("reminder=%s attempt=%d outcome=sent", r.ID, r.Attempt)
    return nil
}

func checkQueueAPI(ctx context.Context) error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/v1/queue/list", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if retryAfter, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && retryAfter > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(retryAfter) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("queue API returned HTTP %d", resp.StatusCode)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return errors.New("queue API rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    if err := checkQueueAPI(context.Background()); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented API base before running this check. Keeping the base URL in configuration also avoids scattering an endpoint through worker code. A write path would additionally carry a client-generated idempotency key; this read-only health check does not need one.

In production, the queue adapter should make the corresponding negative acknowledgement explicit, apply the retry delay, and acknowledge only after the idempotent send has returned success or a deliberate “already sent” result. A 256 KB message limit also argues for putting identifiers in the message and fetching the current reservation record in the worker, rather than copying a customer conversation into every retry.

Which queue fits this delivery guarantee?

RabbitMQ is a strong fit when you need explicit acknowledgements, dead-letter exchanges, and queue-level routing controls in an environment you operate. Its DLX model is powerful, but it adds broker topology and operational ownership. The team must understand how rejected messages, expiration, and dead-letter permissions interact.

Amazon SQS is attractive when the requirement is a managed queue with visibility timeouts and a redrive policy. Its delivery model still requires idempotent consumers, and the worker has to extend visibility for work that takes longer than the initial timeout. It is a good boundary around a simple consumer fleet, less so when you need RabbitMQ-style routing semantics.

BullMQ is a practical Node.js choice when Redis is already part of the service. It gives JavaScript teams familiar job and retry abstractions, but Redis becomes part of the durability and operational story. That is a meaningful dependency, not a footnote.

An HTTP queue API such as Infrai is useful when the worker should depend on plain REST rather than install and version a queue SDK. Any language that can make an HTTP request can publish or consume through that boundary. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, which can reduce the friction of checking request and response contracts before wiring a Node.js worker. It remains the wrong tool for DAG orchestration, fan-out joins, or replay through multiple Kafka-style consumer groups; those requirements deserve a system designed for them.

Here is the trade-off in one view:

Option Integration Fits this reminder workflow when Main limitation
RabbitMQ Broker protocol and client libraries You need explicit acknowledgements, DLX routing, and broker control You own topology and broker operations
Amazon SQS Managed cloud API and SDKs You want a managed queue with visibility timeouts and redrive policy Routing semantics are narrower, and idempotency is still the consumer's job
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Redis is already a durable part of the service Redis becomes part of the queue reliability story
Temporal Workflow SDKs The process needs durable orchestration, timers, and multi-step state It is a larger workflow platform than a reminder queue
Infrai Plain REST A language-neutral API avoids another SDK and the surrounding backend already uses its single key It has no DAG or join primitive, no Kafka-style replay, and delayed messages are limited to 7 days

The REST option also concentrates integration on one credential and one billing relationship across a broader backend surface. That can remove operational paperwork when a team needs queues alongside other backend capabilities, but it is not a reason to force every workflow into one queue abstraction.

The choice follows the failure boundary, not the feature checklist. Pick RabbitMQ for routing control, SQS for a managed cloud queue, BullMQ for a Redis-backed Node.js application, or a REST queue when a language-neutral integration surface removes real deployment friction. In every case, preserve the same consumer contract.

The instrumentation change that closes the loop

Track three timestamps: scheduled, first attempted, and completed or dead-lettered. Track attempt count and a reason category, not just an exception string. A useful dashboard can then answer two different questions: “Are transient failures recovering?” and “Are reminders aging past their business deadline?”

Keep retention long enough for an investigation, but do not confuse retention with replay. Messages are removed after acknowledgement, and this queue model does not provide Kafka-like replay or multiple consumer groups. If an audit trail is required, write an application event separately before acknowledging the message.

For a longer operation, let a cron task trigger queue work and let workers consume it. A cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, so it should not hold a reservation cleanup loop open while waiting for downstream notifications. Also remember that a paused cron does not backfill missed triggers; a separate reconciliation check is needed if missed schedules affect the business deadline.

The runbook should end with a controlled redrive: inspect the DLQ, correct the payload or dependency, redrive a bounded batch, and watch successful and duplicate-send metrics. Never turn a DLQ into an automatic infinite retry lane. That only moves the page.

Reliable reminder retries are a small state machine: pending, retrying, sent, expired, or dead-lettered. The queue supplies delivery mechanics. The worker supplies the business guarantee. Once those responsibilities are explicit, the on-call signal points to a decision instead of a symptom.

Further reading

  • RabbitMQ dead letter exchanges
  • BullMQ retrying failing jobs
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • Amazon SQS message deduplication and exactly-once processing
  • Temporal durable execution

title: Text Grab: Fast, Frictionless Offline Windows OCR Powered by Native APIs
description:
Text Grab: Fast, Frictionless Offline Windows OCR Powered by Native APIs

Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is often over-engineered with bloated cloud APIs, heavy Python dependencies, or massive Docker containers. Text Grab takes the opposite approach: a lightweight, lightning-fast C# utility that brings native Windows OCR directly to your desktop workflow with zero inference cost and zero cloud latency.

TL;DR

Text Grab eliminates the cost and latency of cloud-based vision APIs by leveraging the native Windows.Media.Ocr engine directly on your local device. It turns any visual screen region—videos, paused streams, PDFs, or legacy UIs—into clean, structured text in milliseconds without spinning up hefty local LLMs or external pipelines. For developers and AI practitioners, it bridges the gap between multimodal inputs and programmatic desktop automation with zero runtime overhead.

Key Features & Benchmarks

  • Zero-Latency Native Inference: Utilizes the built-in Windows OCR API (Windows.Media.Ocr), removing the need for Tesseract builds, PyTorch runtimes, or CUDA dependencies for simple text extraction tasks.
  • Multiple Capture Modes:
    • Fullscreen Grab: Instant OCR on arbitrary screen areas with automatic clipboard copy.
    • Grab Frame: An interactive, floating transparent window that monitors and captures dynamic text in real time.
    • Edit Text Window: Quick post-processing scratchpad equipped with regex replacement, case formatting, and table parsing.
  • Zero Telemetry / 100% Offline: Completely air-gapped and local-first. Confidential datasets, enterprise dashboards, and private credentials never touch third-party servers.
  • Background Hotkeys & Automation: Global shortcut support (Win + Shift + F or custom keybinds) to trigger captures, pipe directly into clipboards, or feed downstream CLI tools.
  • Multi-Language Support: Automatically binds to installed Windows language packs for high-accuracy multilingual recognition.

Quick Start

Install Text Grab via WinGet directly from your terminal:

# Install Text Grab via Windows Package Manager
winget install TheJoeFin.Text-Grab

Alternatively, install via Chocolatey:

choco install text-grab

Workflow Example: Piping Captured Text

  1. Press Win + Shift + F (or launch Fullscreen Grab from the system tray).
  2. Select the screen region containing data (e.g., an unselectable terminal log, error trace, or locked spreadsheet).
  3. The text is immediately copied to your clipboard, sanitized, and ready for your prompt context or code editor: 
# Instantly pipe your clipboard OCR output to a local LLM prompt via CLI
Get-Clipboard | ollama run llama3 "Explain this stack trace:"

Why It Matters

Not every vision problem warrants an expensive multimodal model like GPT-4o or a 7B vision-language checkpoint running on high-wattage VRAM. When you simply need deterministic, fast text extraction from your desktop display—whether debugging unresponsive GUI software, reading text from screen recordings, or feeding context to a local agent—Text Grab delivers instant utility at zero cost.

It is an indispensable lightweight tool for developers, data engineers scraping locked interfaces, and local AI practitioners seeking fast visual data extraction without infrastructure overhead.

title: Hybrid Cloud Security: The Gaps Nobody Talks About Until It's Too Late
description:
Most organisations don’t move to the cloud in one clean jump. They end up with a foot in both worlds: some systems on-premises, some in Azure or AWS, and a lot of plumbing connecting the two. That in-between state is where most of the real security risk lives, and it rarely gets the attention it deserves.

I’ve spent years working in and around hybrid environments, and the same gaps come up again and again. None of them are exotic or unusual. They are just the kind of thing that gets missed when everyone assumes someone else is handling it.

What is the identity seam in a hybrid setup?

When you connect your on-premises Active Directory to a cloud identity provider, you create a seam. Accounts sync, permissions flow, and suddenly a compromise in one environment can walk straight into the other.

The mistake I see most often is treating the two directories as if they’re one trusted system. They are not. A service account with too much reach on-premises becomes a much bigger problem the moment it has a path into your cloud tenant. Privileged accounts especially need to be looked at end to end, not just within whichever environment you happened to be reviewing that day. It’s the same reason break-glass accounts should be cloud-only.

Map out exactly what can move between the two, and assume an attacker will find the shortest path. Usually they do.

Stale permissions that never get cleaned up

Hybrid setups accumulate permissions like a garage accumulates junk. Someone needs temporary access for a migration project, it gets granted, the project ends, and the access stays. Multiply that across a few years and a few hundred people and you’ve got a sprawl that nobody fully understands anymore.

The fix isn’t glamorous. It’s regular review, automated where possible, and a genuine willingness to remove access that isn’t being used. The hardest part is cultural. People hate having access taken away, even access they’ve never touched. But every unused permission is a door left unlocked.

Logging that looks fine until you actually need it

Plenty of organisations tick the “logging enabled” box and move on. Then an incident happens, they go to investigate, and they find the logs don’t cover the thing they actually care about, or they’re scattered across systems that don’t talk to each other.

Hybrid makes this worse because your visibility is split. On-premises logs live in one place, cloud logs in another, and the connection between them is exactly where you need clarity during an incident. It’s worth doing the boring work upfront. Decide what you’d need to see if something went wrong, then check you’re actually capturing it. Test it before you’re depending on it at 2am. If those logs land in Sentinel, a few lines of KQL is the quickest way to check what’s really there.

The shared responsibility confusion

Cloud providers are clear about where their responsibility ends and yours begins. The problem is that internally, teams often assume the provider handles more than it does. “It’s in the cloud, so it’s covered” is a sentence that has preceded a lot of incidents.

In a hybrid setup this gets muddier still, because responsibility shifts depending on which part of the stack you’re looking at. The only fix is to be explicit. Write down who owns what, for each system, and make sure the people running things have actually read it.

None of this is about buying more tools

Here’s the part that tends to surprise people. Most hybrid security gaps get solved by understanding your environment properly, removing what you don’t need, and being honest about who’s responsible for what, rather than by spending more money on products.

Tools do help, but a clear picture of your own estate, kept up to date, is worth more than any dashboard you bolt on top of confusion. Handling hybrid well has far less to do with the size of the security budget than with knowing what you’re actually running.

That’s the unglamorous truth of it. Good security in a hybrid world is mostly about paying attention to the joins, the places where two systems meet and everyone assumes the other side has it covered.

I write about security, Azure, data, and the practical side of running things. If this was useful, connect with me on LinkedIn.

Originally published at alanconlon.com, where I post practical security, Azure and data write-ups every other Tuesday.

title: One-Time Token passwordless Login in spring security
description:
The Password Paradox:

  • Create a password strong enough to protect state secrets.
  • Forget it instantly.
  • Click 'Forgot Password?'
  • Go through the 5-step authentication ritual.
  • Try to set a new password, only to hear: 'You cannot use a previous password.'

Meanwhile, Chrome is hoarding 47 saved passwords like a digital dragon, yet none of them unlock the one page you actually need right now. 😅"

And just when you think you’ve finally cracked it, the system hits you with:

Your new password must contain at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one number, one special character, one emoji of existential dread, and the blood of a virgin spreadsheet… and still not be the same as any of the 47 passwords Chrome already knows.

This is one of the reasons passwordless authentication is becoming an attractive approach to modern application security. Instead of asking users to remember yet another password, what if we could authenticate them using a short-lived, one-time token sent to a trusted channel, such as their registered email address?

Setting Up Spring Security

To get started with One-Time Token (OTT) passwordless authentication, we need to add the appropriate Spring Boot dependency to our project.

Depending on the application's requirements, we can use either of the following dependencies:

Option 1: Spring Boot OAuth2 Authorization Server

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server")

Option 2: Spring Boot Security

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-security")

For this implementation, we will use spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server, as it provides the Spring Authorization Server functionality built on top of Spring Security.

Note: The choice of dependency depends on the application's architecture. If you only need to implement OTT authentication in an existing Spring Security application, spring-boot-starter-security may be sufficient. The authorization server starter is more appropriate when you are building an OAuth 2.0 or OpenID Connect authorization server.

We invented passwords to protect our data, then made them so complicated that we need another password to recover the first one. Maybe the biggest security vulnerability was asking humans to remember everything! 😅

And here’s the best part: Spring Security makes implementing passwordless authentication much easier than remembering all those passwords! 😄

Instead of reinventing the authentication wheel, we can leverage Spring Security’s built-in One-Time Token (OTT) support and focus on integrating it into our application.

In other words, let Spring Security handle the authentication plumbing while we focus on building features users actually care about.

“Why make users jump through password-reset hoops when Spring Security can help them log in with a one-time token? Less password drama, more actual development!” 🚀

Configuration 

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) {
        http
        .oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());
        return http.build();
    }

}

How does it work?

When we enable oneTimeTokenLogin() with its default configuration, Spring Security automatically provides the necessary login pages:

One-Time Token Submission Page: The DefaultOneTimeTokenSubmitPageGeneratingFiltergenerates a default page where users can submit their one-time token to complete authentication.

You enable .oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults()), start your Spring Boot application, and expect passwordless authentication to work out of the box.

Instead, Spring greets you with a familiar Java experience: a long stack trace and an UnsatisfiedDependencyException. 😅

org.springframework.beans.factory.UnsatisfiedDependencyException: Error creating bean with name 'org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.WebSecurityConfiguration': Unsatisfied dependency expressed through method 'setFilterChains' parameter 0: Error creating bean with name 'defaultSecurityFilterChain' defined in class path resource [web/security/SecurityConfig.class]: Failed to instantiate [org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain]: Factory method 'defaultSecurityFilterChain' threw exception with message: A OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler is required to enable oneTimeTokenLogin().
Please provide it as a bean or pass it to the oneTimeTokenLogin() DSL.

Token Delivery
Usually a custom OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandlermust be implemented, responsible for delivering the token to the end user.

@Component
public class OneTimeTokenSenderHandler implements OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler {
    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, OneTimeToken oneTimeToken) throws IOException, ServletException {
         String tokenValue = oneTimeToken.getTokenValue();
        // Send the token to the user
        IO.println("One-Time Token generated: " + tokenValue);
    }
}

Customising the OTT Login Page with Angular

When we enable One-Time Token authentication using:

.oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

Spring Security generates default pages for initiating the OTT login process and submitting the token. This is convenient for getting started, but production applications often require a customised login experience that matches the application's branding and frontend architecture.

For example, if our frontend is built with Angular and Angular Material, we probably want users to see our own login component rather than a default Spring Security page.

Fortunately, Spring Security allows us to customise the login page through the loginPage() method in the OTT DSL.

** Configure Spring Security**
We can configure a custom login page and provide a OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler to handle successful token generation.

.oneTimeTokenLogin(ott ->
                        ott.loginPage("/login")                     .tokenGenerationSuccessHandler(oneTimeTokenSenderHandler)
                );

Here:

loginPage("/login") specifies the custom OTT login page.

tokenGenerationSuccessHandler(oneTimeTokenSenderHandler) defines what happens after Spring Security successfully generates a one-time token. For example, our handler can deliver the token to the user by email.

Important: The login page configuration and token delivery are separate concerns. Customising the login page does not automatically configure email delivery or redirect the user to the Angular application.

<form
      #loginForm="ngForm"
      class="mt-8"
      action="/ott/generate"
      method="POST"
      (ngSubmit)="onSubmit(loginForm)"
    >
      <input type="hidden" name="_csrf" [value]="csrfToken" />
      <div class="flex flex-col">
        <div class="flex flex-col space-y-2">
          <mat-label>Email</mat-label>
          <mat-form-field appearance="outline">
            <input
              name="username"
              type="email"
              matInput
              placeholder="Enter your email"
              required
              email
              #username="ngModel"
              [(ngModel)]="model.username"
              autofocus
            />
            <mat-icon matPrefix>mail</mat-icon>
            @if (username.invalid && (username.dirty || username.touched)) {
              <mat-error>
                @if (username.errors?.['required']) {
                  <span class="text-sm">Email is required</span>
                }
                @if (username.errors?.['email']) {
                  <span class="text-sm">Please enter a valid email</span>
                }
              </mat-error>
            }
          </mat-form-field>
        </div>
      </div>
      <button
        mat-flat-button
        type="submit"
        class="mt-5 w-full font-medium text-base text-white py-3 px-4"
        [disabled]="loginForm.invalid"
      >
        Sign in
      </button>
    </form>

The important detail is the form's endpoint:

action="/ott/generate"

Spring Security processes this request to generate a one-time token. The form submits the user's email address using the username parameter, which is the expected parameter name in the default OTT configuration.

Because this is a POST request, CSRF protection must also be handled correctly. The hidden CSRF field is one way to submit the token, provided the Angular application obtains a valid CSRF token from the backend.


public class SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler implements CsrfTokenRequestHandler {
    private final CsrfTokenRequestHandler plain = new CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler();
    private final CsrfTokenRequestHandler xor = new XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler();

    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, Supplier<CsrfToken> csrfToken) {
        /*
         * Always use XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler to provide BREACH protection of
         * the CsrfToken when it is rendered in the response body.
         */
        this.xor.handle(request, response, csrfToken);
        /*
         * Render the token value to a cookie by causing the deferred token to be loaded.
         */
        csrfToken.get();
    }

    @Override
    public @Nullable String resolveCsrfTokenValue(HttpServletRequest request, CsrfToken csrfToken) {
        String headerValue = request.getHeader(csrfToken.getHeaderName());
        if (StringUtils.hasText(headerValue)) {
            return (StringUtils.hasText(headerValue) ? this.plain : this.xor).resolveCsrfTokenValue(request, csrfToken);
        }

        // Fallback to form parameter
        String paramValue = request.getParameter(csrfToken.getParameterName());
        if (StringUtils.hasText(paramValue)) {
            return (StringUtils.hasText(paramValue) ? this.plain : this.xor).resolveCsrfTokenValue(request, csrfToken);
        }

        return null;
    }
}

Redirecting the User After Token Generation

Once Spring Security successfully generates the one-time token, the next step is to deliver it to the user and redirect them to a page where they can enter the code to complete authentication.

To achieve this, we can implement OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler and delegate the redirect to Spring Security's RedirectOneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler.

public class OneTimeTokenSenderHandler  implements OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler {
    private final OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler redirectHandler = new RedirectOneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler("/ott/validate");

    @Override
    public void handle(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response, OneTimeToken oneTimeToken) throws IOException, ServletException {
        String tokenValue = oneTimeToken.getTokenValue();
        // Send the token to the user
        IO.println("One-Time Token generated: " + tokenValue);
        this.redirectHandler.handle(request, response, oneTimeToken);
    }
}

Conclusion

One-Time Token passwordless authentication provides a practical alternative to traditional password-based login. By combining Spring Security's built-in OTT support with a custom Angular frontend, we can create a login experience that is straightforward for users while retaining the security controls provided by the Spring Security framework.

The implementation requires only a few key pieces: enabling oneTimeTokenLogin(), configuring a custom login page, implementing a token-generation success handler, delivering the token securely, and providing a page where users can submit it.

Of course, passwordless authentication is not automatically secure just because passwords are no longer involved. Token expiration, single-use enforcement, rate limiting, CSRF protection, and secure delivery remain essential.

The real advantage is that we can reduce password-related friction without having to build an authentication system from scratch.

And perhaps the best part? Users can finally stop asking, “Was my password Spring@123, Spring@1234, or Spring@12345?” 😄

Let Spring Security handle the authentication. Let Angular handle the experience. And let your users get on with what they came to do. 🚀

title: Per-block difficulty adjustment in a post-quantum Proof-of-Work chain (Rust, integer-only) published:
description:
I'm building Quantum-Lattice (QL), a Layer 1 Proof-of-Work chain written in Rust that signs every transaction with ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204), a post-quantum signature scheme. This post covers one piece of the latest hard fork: moving from a coarse every-10-blocks difficulty retarget to a per-block, fixed-point adjustment.

The old rule

Difficulty was an integer number of leading zero bits, recalculated every 10 blocks and clamped to ±2 bits per step. That is simple, but coarse: it only reacts at window boundaries, it moves in whole bits, and a window can land in a band where the rounded result is zero change.

The new rule

Three ideas:

  1. Fixed-point difficulty. 65,536 units = 1 bit. The target is 2^(256 - d) for fractional d, so difficulty can move in tiny steps.
  2. Integer-only math. Consensus code must give identical results on every machine, so no floats. The fractional power of two uses a cubic polynomial approximation (the same constants as Bitcoin Cash's aserti3 family). Whole-bit values give exactly the old leading-zero-bits result, so history stays valid.
  3. Per-block, relative update. Each block nudges difficulty according to how far its gap was from the 300 s target: 
pub fn next_fine(parent_baseline: u32, gap_secs: i64) -> u32 {
    let delta = ((TARGET_BLOCK_TIME_SECS - gap_secs) as i128 * FP_ONE as i128)
        / FORK2_TAU_SECS as i128;           // tau = 3600 s
    let v = parent_baseline as i128 + delta;
    v.clamp(FORK2_MIN_FP as i128, FORK2_MAX_FP as i128) as u32
}

A block that comes after 200 s raises difficulty by about 0.028 bits. One that takes 1,200 s lowers it by about 0.25 bits. Because the updates telescope, the result depends on the end points of a stretch of blocks, not on the order of the gaps in between.

A block is valid if hash < target(difficulty), compared as 256-bit big-endian integers.

Timestamps

Per-block rules lean on timestamps, so those get stricter too: a block's timestamp must be above the median of the previous 11 blocks, and no more than 15 minutes ahead of the node's clock.

Does it behave?

I simulated the controller before shipping it (steady hashrate with exponential block arrivals). With a 3,600 s time constant the steady-state wobble is about 0.25 bits, and it recovers from a 5× hashrate step in either direction within about 60 blocks, and from a 100× exodus in about 40.

On the live chain the switch at block 35,600 went through with no stall and no split. Difficulty now moves every block, and blocks have averaged close to the 5-minute target at roughly 330 MH/s.

What I'd flag

  • This does not stop an attacker with majority hashrate. It makes difficulty harder to disturb and smoother to track, nothing more.
  • A hard fork means every node operator has to run the new build. Nodes on the old rules stop following the chain at the activation height.
  • The hashrate is concentrated among a handful of operators, and the difficulty swings show it. That's a network-growth problem, not a code one.

Code and tests

The consensus code and its tests (known target values, monotonicity, a check that whole-bit values match the old rule exactly, timestamp rules) are in src/consensus.rs:

https://github.com/AlthaafM/Quantum-Lattice

Questions, review and criticism welcome. I'd especially like eyes on the integer approximation and the clamp bounds.

title: Edge Requests are now called CDN Requests
description:
CDN Requests is now the name for the usage metric previously called Edge Requests. This is a naming change only: pricing, limits, and how usage is measured are all unchanged.

The new name appears on the usage dashboard, the Observability Events chart, usage notifications, and invoice line items. It reflects that these are requests served by Vercel's CDN. Metric IDs and product aliases are unchanged, so saved queries keep working. In the billing charges API, ServiceName now returns the new name. Integrations that match charges on ServiceName should switch to the new SkuId field, which stays stable across renames.

See the CDN pricing and usage documentation for details.

Read more

title: RBAC Is Not Enough for Sensitive Investigation Workflows
description:
At first, an anonymous reporting system looks like a fairly ordinary CRUD application.

Someone submits a report.

An administrator receives it.

Evidence gets attached.

The case moves through a few statuses.

Eventually, someone closes it.

You can model that with roles:

reporter
investigator
admin

And permissions:

reporter      -> create report, read own case
investigator  -> read cases, add notes
admin         -> read everything, manage users

Simple.

Until the first sensitive case arrives.

Imagine an employee reports their own manager.

That manager happens to be an administrator.

Should admin still mean:

can_read_all_cases = true

Obviously not.

And that's where the authorization model starts getting much more interesting.

The problem is no longer:

What role does this user have?

It becomes:

What is this user's relationship with this specific case?

Role-based access is only the first layer

RBAC works well when permissions mostly follow organizational roles.

A billing employee sees billing information.

Support sees tickets.

Administrators configure the system.

Sensitive investigations introduce another dimension: context.

A user can be perfectly authorized to investigate reports in general and still be forbidden from accessing one particular report.

For example:

can_access_case =
    has_investigator_role
    && !is_subject_of_case
    && !has_conflict_of_interest

That is already different from standard RBAC.

Now imagine another situation.

An HR director is allowed to access investigations.

But the case mentions their spouse.

Or their direct report.

Or their own department.

The role didn't change.

The context did.

This is why systems that deal with sensitive cases often need some combination of:

  • role-based permissions;
  • case-level permissions;
  • explicit exclusions;
  • conflict-of-interest rules;
  • temporary assignments;
  • auditable overrides.

"Admin" stops being a sufficient security model very quickly.

Case access and identity access should not be the same permission

Another mistake is treating a report as one indivisible object.

Suppose the report contains:

case
├── allegation
├── attachments
├── reporter identity
├── internal notes
├── interviews
├── investigation findings
└── resolution

Does everyone who can access the case need to see every field?

Usually not.

An investigator may need to read the allegation but not know the reporter's identity.

Someone reviewing evidence may need attachments but not internal interview notes.

A compliance lead may need to approve the final decision without seeing unnecessary personal information.

So instead of:

can_view_case

you start needing permissions closer to:

can_view_report
can_view_reporter_identity
can_view_evidence
can_view_internal_notes
can_add_evidence
can_interview
can_assign_case
can_close_case

This matters for privacy, but it also changes your domain model.

The reporter's identity should not just be another field conveniently returned by:

GET /cases/:id

If identity deserves stronger protection, model it that way.

Different storage.

Different access policy.

Different audit trail.

Possibly different encryption boundaries.

The data model should reflect the sensitivity model.

Anonymity is not a boolean

Developers are often tempted to model anonymity like this:

{
  "anonymous": true
}

But anonymity is not really a property of the report.

It is a property of the entire system around the report.

You can remove the name field and still collect:

  • IP addresses;
  • analytics identifiers;
  • session metadata;
  • authentication information;
  • reverse-proxy logs;
  • device fingerprints;
  • email notifications containing sensitive context.

The UI may tell the user:

Your report is anonymous.

Meanwhile the infrastructure may know exactly where it came from.

That doesn't necessarily mean those systems are malicious.

It often means nobody modeled anonymity as an architectural requirement.

For sensitive reporting, a better question is:

Which pieces of information could allow us to identify this person, and do we actually need them?

That's data minimization as an engineering decision, not just a privacy-policy sentence.

Anonymous follow-up creates another design problem

If you don't know who the reporter is, how do you ask them another question?

You still need conversations like:

Can you tell us approximately when this happened?

or:

Do you still have the original file?

Traditional messaging assumes identity.

Anonymous reporting can't.

One pattern is to issue an opaque credential when the report is created:

report_id
access_token

The reporter stores that credential and uses it to return later.

Something conceptually like:

POST /reports

201 Created

{
  "report_id": "RPT-8FH2K",
  "access_token": "<opaque-secret>"
}

The token is not an account.

It doesn't need an email address.

It simply proves that whoever holds it is allowed to access the reporter-facing side of that specific case.

That lets the system provide bidirectional communication without forcing identity.

But then more questions appear:

  • Can the token be recovered?
  • Can administrators see it?
  • Should it be stored hashed?
  • Can it be rotated?
  • What happens if it is leaked?
  • How long does it remain valid?

The apparently simple requirement "allow anonymous follow-up" becomes an authentication design problem.

Evidence needs history, not just storage

Attachments are another deceptively simple feature.

The product requirement may begin as:

Users can upload evidence.

So you create:

attachments

and store files somewhere.

But once those files may influence an investigation, the system needs to answer more questions.

Where did this file come from?

When was it uploaded?

Was it replaced?

Who downloaded it?

Did anyone modify its metadata?

Was it deleted?

If it was deleted, why?

A useful evidence record might look more like:

Evidence
--------
id
case_id
original_filename
storage_key
content_hash
submitted_at
submitted_by
source_type
status

And then every important operation becomes an event:

EVIDENCE_UPLOADED
EVIDENCE_VIEWED
EVIDENCE_DOWNLOADED
EVIDENCE_MARKED_IRRELEVANT
EVIDENCE_RESTRICTED

Notice what is missing:

EVIDENCE_SILENTLY_DISAPPEARED

For sensitive systems, destructive CRUD operations deserve suspicion.

Sometimes the better model is not:

DELETE FROM evidence
WHERE id = ?;

but something closer to:

status = discarded
discard_reason = duplicate
discarded_by = investigator_42
discarded_at = ...

The original remains protected according to retention rules, while the investigation history remains understandable.

Whether you need immutable storage, hashing, signed records or stronger chain-of-custody controls depends on the system.

But auditability should be designed before you need it.

Your audit log is security infrastructure

Most applications have logs.

That doesn't automatically mean they have an audit trail.

An application log might say:

GET /api/cases/381 200

An investigation audit trail should answer something more useful:

actor: user_827
action: viewed_reporter_identity
case: case_381
timestamp: ...
reason: assigned_investigator

Those are different things.

For highly sensitive operations, I want to know:

  • who performed the action;
  • which case it affected;
  • what kind of data was accessed;
  • when it happened;
  • whether the action was authorized;
  • when relevant, why it happened.

And the audit system itself needs protection.

If administrators can rewrite the audit trail, it isn't much of an audit trail.

Investigation state is richer than open/closed

Another place where domain complexity leaks into the software is case status.

The naive model:

open
closed

doesn't tell you much.

So maybe you add:

new
triage
investigating
resolved
closed

Better.

But eventually you discover that workflow state and investigation outcome are different concepts.

A case might be:

workflow_status = closed

while its outcome is:

outcome = inconclusive

That matters because an inconclusive report is not the same thing as a false report.

A more expressive model separates them:

workflow_status:
  new
  triage
  investigating
  awaiting_information
  decision_pending
  closed

outcome:
  substantiated
  partially_substantiated
  unsubstantiated
  inconclusive

Why care?

Because software shapes behavior.

If your UI forces investigators to choose only:

true
false

you are embedding an oversimplified policy into the product.

Your enum is making an organizational decision.

Conflicts of interest belong in the domain model

This is another thing I initially thought belonged entirely to company policy.

It doesn't.

Suppose Alice is normally an investigator.

A report arrives involving Alice.

The system should not rely on another administrator remembering:

Oh, we probably shouldn't assign that one to Alice.

The conflict should be representable.

For example:

CaseParticipant
---------------
case_id
user_id
relationship

relationships:
  reporter
  subject
  witness
  investigator
  reviewer
  conflicted

Now authorization can use domain information.

Conceptually:

def can_access_case(user, case):
    if not user.has_permission("investigate"):
        return False

    if case.has_conflict(user):
        return False

    return case.is_assigned_to(user)

Real systems will be more complex.

But the important point is this:

conflict of interest stops being a note in a policy PDF and becomes something the application can enforce.

That's a much stronger guarantee.

Overrides should be possible — and uncomfortable

Eventually someone will need emergency access.

Maybe every normal investigator is conflicted.

Maybe a legal hold requires access.

Maybe an incident needs escalation.

Hard-coding "never" into authorization rules can make a system unusable.

But the opposite is also dangerous:

super_admin = god_mode

A useful pattern is controlled break-glass access.

For example:

override requires:
- elevated permission
- explicit reason
- re-authentication
- audit event
- optional second approval

You are not making the action impossible.

You are making it deliberate and visible.

That difference matters.

Sensitive workflows make generic admin panels dangerous

A lot of SaaS products are built around the idea that the customer administrator owns everything.

For many products, that's reasonable.

For sensitive reporting systems, it can be exactly the wrong assumption.

The person who bought the software may not be entitled to inspect every report.

The company owner may be the subject of a report.

The account administrator may work in the department being investigated.

So tenant ownership and data access cannot automatically mean the same thing.

This is one of those cases where traditional B2B SaaS assumptions start breaking.

The customer owns the workspace.

That does not necessarily mean every customer administrator should be able to read every piece of information inside it.

The hardest requirements often appear after POST /reports

When we first think about a reporting system, it's natural to focus on intake.

The form.

Validation.

File uploads.

Anonymous submission.

Those are visible.

They are easy to put on a roadmap.

But most of the difficult engineering decisions happen afterward:

submit
  ↓
triage
  ↓
conflict detection
  ↓
assignment
  ↓
evidence collection
  ↓
restricted interviews
  ↓
decision
  ↓
follow-up
  ↓
retention

Every arrow hides authorization decisions.

Every box contains potentially sensitive data.

And every shortcut can affect whether users trust the system.

That's why I no longer think of anonymous reporting as a form with a back office.

It's a context-sensitive authorization system wrapped around an investigation workflow.

The form is just where the data enters.

A few questions I now ask much earlier

If I were designing another sensitive workflow from scratch, I'd ask these before choosing the database schema:

Can someone be authorized globally but forbidden from one specific case?

Is identity access separate from case access?

Can sensitive information disappear without leaving a trace?

Can users communicate without revealing their identity?

Can the system represent conflicts of interest?

What happens when normal authorization rules need an emergency override?

Do our statuses reflect the real domain, or just make the UI convenient?

If those questions arrive late, changing the architecture becomes much more painful.

If they arrive early, they shape a much better system.

AI assistance disclosure: AI was used during drafting and editing. The technical concepts and product decisions were reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Hiring a Legacy Modernisation Partner: 8 Questions to Ask Before You Sign
description:
Every modernisation proposal looks good on page one. There is a confident timeline, a diagram with arrows pointing towards "the cloud", and a team slide full of smiling people you may never meet again after the kickoff.

If you run technology at a mid-sized company in the UAE, you will probably sit through several of these pitches before you choose a partner to help modernise a legacy system. The proposals start to blur together. The differences only show up six months later, when the plan meets your actual database.

Here are the questions that tend to separate a partner who will finish the job from one who will finish the slide deck.

1. "What will you need from us in the first month?"

A good partner knows the project depends on your people as much as theirs. If the answer is "nothing, we'll handle everything", be careful. Nobody can modernise a system they cannot ask questions about.

What to do: ask for a named list. Which of your people, how many hours a week, which systems they need access to, and by when. If they cannot tell you this before you sign, they have not thought about your project yet. They have thought about a project.

2. "How will you learn what the current system actually does?"

The documentation is out of date. It always is. The real rules live in stored procedures, scheduled jobs, and the head of someone in Finance who has been there since 2011.

What to do: ask how they run discovery. Listen for words like tracing real transactions, reading the code, profiling the data, and sitting with the people who use it. Be wary of "we'll review your documentation" as the whole answer.

3. "What is the first thing that goes live, and when?"

A plan where nothing reaches production for nine months is a plan to discover problems late and expensively.

What to do: ask them to name the first small, real change they would ship, and roughly when. A faster report, one integration moved behind an API, one module running on the new stack. If the first release is "everything, in phase three", push back.

4. "Would you rewrite this, or replace it in pieces? Why?"

There is no single right answer, but there should be a reason. A partner who always recommends a full rewrite, whatever the system, is selling a method rather than solving your problem.

What to do: ask them to walk through the trade-offs for your system specifically. How long would you run old and new side by side? What happens to changes requested during the project? What would make them change their recommendation?

5. "Who exactly will be working on this?"

The senior architect in the pitch meeting is impressive. The question is whether you will see them again after week two.

What to do: ask for the names and roles of the actual delivery team, and how much of their time is committed to you. Ask to speak with the person who will lead it day to day, not only the person selling it. Agree in writing what happens if key people are swapped out.

6. "How do you handle data residency and our regulator?"

In the UAE, where your data lives and who can reach it matters, especially in banking, insurance, healthcare and government-linked work. These questions should come up in the first conversation, not the week before go-live.

What to do: ask which cloud regions they plan to use, how they handle production data in test environments, and whether they have worked with your sector's rules before. If they need to "check with the team" on all of it, note that.

7. "How will we know it is working, before the project ends?"

Status reports full of green ticks feel reassuring right up until they don't. Percent complete is not an outcome.

What to do: agree on a small set of measures you can both see, such as release frequency, how long key jobs take, incidents on migrated parts, and one business number the owner already tracks. Ask how often they will report against those, and what happens when one moves the wrong way.

8. "What happens when you leave?"

Every engagement ends. The worst outcome is a shiny new system that only the vendor understands, which is the same problem you started with, just more modern.

What to do: ask how knowledge transfers to your team during the project, not just at the end. Who owns the code and the cloud accounts? Will there be documentation that describes the system as built, and runbooks your team has actually used? Ask to see an example of a handover from a previous project.

A quick way to compare proposals

Put the answers side by side in a simple table. One row per question, one column per partner. You are not looking for the most polished answer. You are looking for the most specific one.

Specific answers name people, dates, systems and trade-offs. Vague answers name values. "We're agile and customer-focused" is a nice sentence. It is not a plan.

Also ask each partner for one reference from a project that went badly, and what they changed afterwards. Every team has one. The honest ones will tell you about it.

The point of asking

Choosing a modernisation partner is really choosing who you will be stuck in a room with when something goes wrong at month four. The questions above will not guarantee a smooth project. They will show you, before you sign, how a team thinks when the answer is not on their slide.

If you have hired for one of these projects, which question do you wish you had asked earlier?

Originally published on LinkedIn by Latent Digital Solutions FZCO. Learn more at latentdigitalsolutions.com.

title: Heroku is in sustaining engineering mode now, and that's a different kind of risk than a price increase
description:
On February 6, 2026, Heroku’s chief product officer Nitin T Bhat published a short post titled “An Update on Heroku,” announcing that the platform was moving to what Salesforce calls a sustaining engineering model. The post is specific about what that means in practice: Enterprise Account contracts will no longer be offered to new customers, and the engineering focus going forward is “stability, security, reliability, and support,” with an explicit statement that this comes “rather than introducing new features.” Existing customers, the post says, see no immediate change: pricing, billing and day-to-day service stay the same, and existing Enterprise contracts continue to be honored and can renew. Salesforce’s own framing for the shift is that it’s redirecting product and engineering investment toward “areas where we can deliver the greatest long-term customer value,” specifically enterprise AI products, which is the actual business reason behind the change, stated plainly rather than inferred.

This is a different kind of story than the pricing changes other platforms have made this year, and it deserves to be treated differently. A price going up or a bandwidth allowance getting cut is a cost question: run the numbers, decide if the new number still works. Software that stops moving forward is a different, slower-moving kind of risk, and it’s worth being precise about what it actually changes day to day, rather than reaching for either “nothing to worry about” or “Heroku is dead,” neither of which is accurate.

What does “sustaining engineering” actually mean for Heroku users?
The term itself isn’t exotic. It’s a recognized mode in long-lived commercial software: a product that’s past its growth phase gets a smaller, dedicated team whose job is keeping it running correctly, patched and secure, without the team that would normally be building what’s next. Heroku’s own post is careful to say this isn’t a shutdown notice. Apps already running stay running. Pipelines, teams, and the existing add-on ecosystem are explicitly called out as unaffected. Billing doesn’t change for customers paying by credit card through the dashboard. None of that is spin; it matches what sustaining engineering means everywhere else it’s used, and Heroku’s wording avoids overstating or understating it.

What the post does confirm, directly, is the part that matters for anyone planning around Heroku for the next few years: no new features. Not “fewer” features, not “a slower cadence,” the stated posture is that new capability development is not what the team is doing anymore. Combined with no new Enterprise contracts for new customers, the practical read is that Heroku the product, as of February 2026, is not something a team should expect to keep up with developments in the broader platform space on. Whatever the buildpack ecosystem looks like in two years, whatever regions get added to competing platforms, whatever managed-database feature becomes standard elsewhere, Heroku’s answer to all of it is very likely “that’s not something we’re building,” because the team whose job that would have been isn’t doing that job anymore.

What that costs in practice, for a team still on it today
For a team with a stable app, modest growth, and no plans to add new kinds of workloads, this genuinely might not matter for a long while. The post is honest that existing functionality keeps working, and “stability, security, reliability and support” is a real commitment, not an empty one, assuming Salesforce holds to it. Security patches for the existing buildpack stack, bug fixes for existing features, these are explicitly still in scope.

The exposure shows up in a few specific, foreseeable places. New framework or language runtime support is the first: a team that adopts a new version of a framework, or a language runtime Heroku hasn’t already built support for, has no reason to expect Heroku to add it, because that’s new feature work by definition. New regions are the second: infrastructure expansion is product development, and a company in sustaining mode has no stated reason to build new regions, which matters for any team whose latency requirements or compliance needs change over the life of the product. The third, and the one that compounds quietly, is responsiveness to bugs that aren’t security-critical: “stability and reliability” covers keeping existing behavior correct, but a non-critical bug that’s inconvenient rather than dangerous is exactly the kind of issue a smaller, maintenance-focused team reasonably deprioritizes, because that’s what a shrunk roadmap is for. None of these are catastrophic on their own. Together, over two or three years, they describe a platform that quietly falls further behind the part of the category that’s still actively built, while continuing to run correctly for exactly the workload it already supported on the day of the announcement.

Why this is a structural risk specific to renting the whole stack
The deeper point isn’t about Heroku specifically, it’s about what it means to depend entirely on one company’s product roadmap for your own infrastructure. On a fully managed platform, a customer has no path to keep the parts of the service they value moving forward if the vendor’s own priorities change. There’s no server to patch yourself, no infrastructure layer underneath the product that the customer still controls, the entire thing is the vendor’s roadmap, and when that roadmap gets reprioritized, every customer’s future capability gets reprioritized along with it, with no way to opt out short of leaving the platform entirely.

That’s the specific risk sustaining engineering represents, and it’s worth being fair about why Salesforce made the call: a 2026 enterprise software company redirecting investment toward enterprise AI is a rational business decision given the market, and Heroku, nearly two decades old, is a mature product with a well-known shape rather than a growth bet. Nothing about the decision is reckless or dishonest, the announcement itself is unusually direct about what’s changing and why. The risk isn’t that Salesforce did something wrong. It’s that any customer fully inside one company’s managed stack has no lever to pull when that company’s internal priorities shift, because the infrastructure was never theirs to begin with.

What a BYO-server model changes about this specific risk
A platform that runs on servers the customer owns can’t fully eliminate this risk, the control-plane software itself is still built by a company with its own roadmap and its own priorities that could shift. But it changes what’s actually at stake if that happens. The server itself, a plain Linux box at DigitalOcean, Hetzner or Vultr, running an ordinary Docker container behind a standard reverse proxy, doesn’t go stale because the control plane’s roadmap changes. If Railyard stopped shipping new features tomorrow, the apps already deployed keep running on infrastructure the customer already owns and controls directly over SSH, with no dependency on Railyard’s continued development to keep serving traffic. The worst case for a customer in that scenario is losing access to a dashboard and some automation convenience, not losing the infrastructure the app actually runs on, because that infrastructure was never the vendor’s to begin with.

That’s the structural answer to “what if the company behind my platform deprioritizes it,” and it’s a meaningfully different answer than anything available to a customer on a fully managed platform. It doesn’t require Railyard, or any BYO-server platform, to promise it will never happen here; it requires the architecture to make the consequence survivable if it does, which is a guarantee a rented stack can’t offer no matter how well-run the vendor is.

The honest takeaway
Heroku’s February 2026 announcement isn’t a crisis for anyone running on it today, and it isn’t dishonest or poorly communicated, if anything it’s a more direct statement than most companies give when deprioritizing a mature product. The actual lesson is about the category of risk itself: a team that depends entirely on a managed platform is also, by construction, depending entirely on that one company’s internal roadmap decisions staying aligned with the team’s own needs indefinitely, with no fallback if they stop being aligned. That’s a real structural property of renting the whole stack, independent of how good or bad any particular vendor’s intentions are, and it’s worth weighing on its own terms, separately from whatever the current pricing or feature set looks like on the day a team signs up.

FAQ
When did Heroku enter sustaining engineering mode? Heroku’s chief product officer, Nitin T Bhat, announced the shift on February 6, 2026, in a post titled “An Update on Heroku.”

Is Heroku shutting down? No. Existing apps, pipelines, teams and add-ons keep working, and credit-card customers see no change to pricing or billing. Sustaining engineering means no new features and no new Enterprise contracts for new customers, not a shutdown.

Will Heroku add new features or regions? The announcement is explicit that new feature development is not the team’s focus going forward, which also means new regions and new framework or runtime support shouldn’t be expected.

Is this a bigger risk than a price increase? It’s a different kind of risk. A price increase is a cost question you can calculate once. A platform that stops moving forward is a risk that compounds slowly over years, as the rest of the category keeps shipping and a frozen platform doesn’t.
